=== NOTES 5:84 | Biodiversity – Levels, Values, Measurement; India As A Megadiverse Country
## SUB 0 | Meaning, Definition and Levels of Biodiversity
[84:0:0] - Term **"biodiversity"** coined by **Walter G. Rosen (1985)**; **popularised by E.O. Wilson** – not Tansley (coined "ecosystem"), Darwin or Barrow.
[84:0:1] - **Biodiversity** = the range/variety of **different species** in an environment; includes **genetic diversity** within populations as well as the diversity of **species and ecosystems** (not atmosphere, lithosphere or "environment").
[84:0:2] - **CBD (1992) definition:** variability among living organisms from **all sources** (terrestrial, marine, other aquatic) and the **ecological complexes** of which they are part – **within species, between species and of ecosystems**.
[84:0:3] TABLE head: Level | Meaning / example
  [84:0:3.0] Genetic | Variation within a species – the basic source; all rice varieties are *Oryza sativa* but differ in size, aroma, nutrients; lets a population adapt and respond to natural selection
  [84:0:3.1] Species | Variety of species in an area – richness + abundance
  [84:0:3.2] Ecosystem (ecological) | Variety of habitats/ecosystems in a region; one ecosystem cannot replace another
[84:0:4] - **Narrow genetic base:** the cultivated **banana** (seedless, vegetatively propagated Cavendish clones) may be wiped out by disease – a classic case for genetic diversity.
[84:0:5] - **Crop diversity in space and time** = **polyculture** (mixed/inter-cropping and rotation), not monoculture.
[84:0:6] - Chinese, Americans, Indians and Black Africans = **one species, *Homo sapiens*** (tigers–lions–cats or pigeons–doves–partridges are different species).
[84:0:7] - **Biomes:** no two biomes are exactly alike because **climate and geographic location** give unique combinations of plants, animals and soils (A and R true, R explains A).
[84:0:8] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.53-54; NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.11, p.14; app notes 5:84 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Measuring Biodiversity – Alpha, Beta, Gamma
[84:1:0] TABLE head: Measure | Scale
  [84:1:0.0] Alpha (α) | Within one habitat/area at a local scale – mean species diversity / species richness there
  [84:1:0.1] Beta (β) | Comparison between ecosystems – change (turnover) in species composition along a gradient
  [84:1:0.2] Gamma (γ) | Overall diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region (total geographical area)
  [84:1:0.3] Endemism | Species restricted to a specific region
  [84:1:0.4] Species richness / evenness | Number of species / their relative abundance (low evenness = few species dominate)
[84:1:1] - Terms alpha, beta, gamma by **R.H. Whittaker**; indices: **Shannon-Wiener** and **Simpson**.
[84:1:2] - Forest A (2 tigers, 6 deer, 7 rabbits) vs B (1, 6, 8): **same richness, A more even**.
[84:1:3] TABLE head: Measure | Key characteristic (match, NTRUHS)
  [84:1:3.0] Phylogenetic diversity | Evolutionary relationships between species
  [84:1:3.1] Ecological diversity | Diversity of habitats/ecosystems in a region
  [84:1:3.2] Genetic diversity | Variety of genetic traits within species populations
  [84:1:3.3] Species diversity | Species richness and evenness in a community
[84:1:4] - **Functional diversity:** range of **ecological roles** performed by organisms.
[84:1:5] - Field sampling: **mist nets** capture **birds and bats**; dipnets, creel surveys and seines are aquatic methods.
[84:1:6] > Alpha index asked twice (RAS 2018); two match questions (NTRUHS Mains).
[84:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 2.1 p.2, p.10; Rocket Environment p.53-54; app notes 5:84 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Richness Patterns – Latitude, Altitude, Himalaya
[84:2:0] - **Latitudinal gradient:** biodiversity **increases towards the equator** and falls towards the poles – greatest in **lower latitudes** and, along mountains, in **lower altitudes** (UPSC 2011: both true).
[84:2:1] - Ants: ~**10 species near the North Pole vs ~2,000 at the equator**.
[84:2:2] - Richest: **tropical rainforests** (land), **coral reefs** (sea).
[84:2:3] - Tropics richest: **long undisturbed evolutionary time (no glaciation)**, stable climate, more solar energy → productivity.
[84:2:4] - **Butterflies:** maximum species in **tropical countries**; books and keys give "butterflies cannot tolerate low temperatures" as the reason (A and R true, R explains A).
[84:2:5] - **Himalaya** rich because it is a **confluence of different biogeographical zones** (Palearctic + Indo-Malayan) – not rainfall, absence of invasives or low human interference.
[84:2:6] - Estimates: about **1.5 million** living species described (+300,000 fossil); **Wilson (1992) 10–50 million**; **Robert May ~7 million**. **Over 70%** of recorded species are animals (**insects** richest); plants ~**22%**.
[84:2:7] - **Species-area relationship** (**Humboldt**, log S = log C + Z log A).
[84:2:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.12-14; NextGen Part 2.1 p.10, p.14; app notes 5:84 sub 2
## SUB 3 | Values of Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services
[84:3:0] TABLE head: Value | Meaning
  [84:3:0.0] Consumptive | Used locally, not sold: fuelwood, fodder, wild food
  [84:3:0.1] Productive | Sold commercially: timber, fibre, medicines, genetic material
  [84:3:0.2] Ecosystem services | Soil formation, prevention of soil erosion, recycling of waste, pollination, clean air and water, climate
  [84:3:0.3] Social / cultural | Sacred groves, indigenous knowledge
  [84:3:0.4] Aesthetic | Beauty, ecotourism
  [84:3:0.5] Option | Unknown future uses – new drugs, crop genes
[84:3:1] - **Most significant aspect:** **maintenance of the ecosystem**; role in sustainable development: **supports ecosystem services such as food, water and air quality**.
[84:3:2] - **Butterfly decline (UPSC 2017):** pollination of some plants affected ✓; fall in populations of **wasps, spiders and birds** that eat them ✓; fungal infections ✗ → **I and III**.
[84:3:3] - **Himalayan nettle** (*Girardinia diversifolia*): sustainable source of **textile fibre** (UPSC 2019).
[84:3:4] - **Rivet popper hypothesis** (**Paul Ehrlich**): losing a key rivet (**keystone species**) may collapse the ecosystem.
[84:3:5] - **TEEB:** **G8+5** initiative, **2007**; hosted by **UNEP** (not IMF/WEF); led by **Pavan Sukhdev**; draws attention to the **economic benefits of biodiversity** and helps decision-makers **recognise, demonstrate and capture** its value → **2 and 3 only**.
[84:3:6] - **Dasgupta Review (2021):** **Partha Dasgupta** for the **UK Treasury**; nature as an asset.
[84:3:7] - **International Day for Biological Diversity: 22 May** (22 March = World Water Day). CBD in force **29 Dec 1993**.
[84:3:8] - **National Biodiversity Congress, Thiruvananthapuram (Feb 2017):** focal theme **"Mainstreaming Biodiversity for Sustainable Development"**.
[84:3:9] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.54; NextGen Environment APPSC Part 1.2 p.12; app notes 5:84 sub 3
## SUB 4 | India as a Megadiverse Country
[84:4:0] - **17 megadiverse countries** (UNEP-WCMC; Conservation International 1998: **≥5,000 endemic plants** + border marine ecosystems): Australia, Brazil, China, Colombia, DR Congo, Ecuador, **India**, Indonesia, Madagascar, Malaysia, Mexico, Papua New Guinea, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, USA, Venezuela (**not Thailand**).
[84:4:1] - **LMMC** negotiating bloc: **Cancun Declaration 2002**; India a member.
[84:4:2] TABLE head: Item | India
  [84:4:2.0] Land / species / people | 2.4% / 7–8% / ~18%
  [84:4:2.1] Endemism | Over 30% of animals endemic
  [84:4:2.2] Ranks | 10th plant-rich; 11th endemic higher vertebrates; 6th centre of crop origin
  [84:4:2.3] Hotspots | 4 of 36
  [84:4:2.4] Biogeography | 2 realms, 5 biomes, 10 zones, 25 provinces
[84:4:3] - **2025 additions** (**BSI + ZSI**, 1 Jul 2026): **709 animal species = 483 new + 226 records**; 353 plant taxa; top: **Kerala** 98.
[84:4:4] # New species in news
[84:4:5] TABLE head: Species | Where
  [84:4:5.0] Night frog "Mewasingi" | Kozhikode, Kerala (2019)
  [84:4:5.1] Fish *Schizothorax sikusirumensis* | Arunachal Pradesh (Siku and Sirum rivers, 2023)
  [84:4:5.2] Himalayan Forest Thrush (keys: "tailless bird") | Arunachal Pradesh / China (2016)
  [84:4:5.3] "Tailless rabbit looking like a rat" (a pika, *Ochotona*) | Sikkim
[84:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 2.1 p.3, p.9; app notes 5:84 sub 4
## SUB 5 | Biogeographic Zones and Natural Range of Indian Fauna
[84:5:0] - **Rodgers and Panwar (WII, 1988):** **2 realms** (**Palearctic + Indo-Malayan**), **5 biomes**, **10 zones**, **25 provinces**.
[84:5:1] TABLE head: Zone | Note
  [84:5:1.0] Trans-Himalaya | Cold desert; ~5.7% of land
  [84:5:1.1] Himalaya | Most faunal species
  [84:5:1.2] Western Ghats | High endemism; Silent Valley – largest population of lion-tailed macaques
  [84:5:1.3] Deccan Peninsula | Largest zone (~42%); 5 provinces; Andhra Pradesh lies here
[84:5:2] - **Deccan provinces (APPSC FRO):** **Central Highlands, Chotanagpur, Eastern Highlands/Plateau, Central Plateau, Deccan South** → **five**.
[84:5:3] TABLE head: Animal | Natural range
  [84:5:3.0] Asiatic lion | Gir – only India
  [84:5:3.1] One-horned rhino | Kaziranga, Pobitora ("Mini Kaziranga"); also Nepal
  [84:5:3.2] Double-humped (Bactrian) camel | Nubra Valley, Ladakh; also Central Asia (not India-only)
  [84:5:3.3] Nilgiri tahr | Western Ghats only (Eravikulam, Kerala)
  [84:5:3.4] Hoolock gibbon | NE India – India's only ape
  [84:5:3.5] Saltwater crocodile | Bhitarkanika, Sundarbans
  [84:5:3.6] Red panda | Eastern Himalaya
  [84:5:3.7] Chinese pangolin | North-East India
  [84:5:3.8] Gharial | Chambal
[84:5:4] - **UPSC 2019:** only the **Asiatic lion** is naturally found in India only.
[84:5:5] - **Turtle diversity:** **Assam** is the most species-rich State (about 20 of India's ~29 freshwater species), not Odisha.
[84:5:6] - **Marsupials** (young carried in **pouches**) do **not occur naturally in India**; "they thrive only in montane grasslands with no predators" is false (UPSC 2023 ×2).
[84:5:7] - **Walrus:** natural habitat the **Arctic region** (not Antarctica).
[84:5:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 2.1 p.3-4, p.9, p.14; Assam Tribune 'Near-extinct turtles thriving in temple ponds' (web); app notes 5:84 sub 5-6
## SUB 6 | Classic Species Facts – Animal and Plant Diversity
[84:6:0] TABLE head: Group / species | Fact
  [84:6:0.0] Arthropoda | Largest animal phylum (insects, crustaceans, spiders); Mollusca second
  [84:6:0.1] Reptilia | Mostly terrestrial; dry cornified skin with scales/scutes; no external ear openings
  [84:6:0.2] Ants (tribe Attini) | Well-known cultivators of fungi
  [84:6:0.3] Poisonous species | Butterflies (Monarch – cardenolides from milkweed), fish (pufferfish), frogs (poison-dart) → all three
  [84:6:0.4] Portuguese man o' war | *Physalia physalis*, a floating colonial hydrozoan
  [84:6:0.5] Green mussel | *Perna viridis* – edible marine mussel of India (*Pila* = apple snail, *Sepia* = cuttlefish)
  [84:6:0.6] Common krait (*Bungarus caeruleus*) | Venom mainly neurotoxic
  [84:6:0.7] Cleistogamy (closed self-pollinating flowers) | *Viola*, Oxalis, Commelina
  [84:6:0.8] 'On the Origin of Species' (1859) | Charles Darwin
[84:6:1] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:84 sub 0; general knowledge
## SUB 7 | Agro-biodiversity and Biopiracy
[84:7:0] - **N.I. Vavilov:** **8 centres** of origin; **Hindustan (Indo-Burma):** rice, sugarcane, mango, pigeon pea, brinjal, cucumber, black pepper.
[84:7:1] - **Nokrek** (Garo Hills, Meghalaya) = **Citrus Gene Sanctuary**; **Borjuli** (Assam, BHS) = *Oryza rufipogon*, wild ancestor of **rice**.
[84:7:2] TABLE head: Case | Outcome
  [84:7:2.0] Turmeric (US patent, challenged by CSIR) | Revoked 1997
  [84:7:2.1] Neem (EPO; W.R. Grace) | Revoked 2000
  [84:7:2.2] Basmati (RiceTec) | Most claims withdrawn
  [84:7:2.3] Hoodia (San people, southern Africa) | Benefit-sharing deal
[84:7:3] - **Bioprospecting** = search for commercially valuable compounds and genes; **biopiracy** = patenting without consent.
[84:7:4] - **TKDL** (**2001**, **CSIR + AYUSH**) – makes traditional knowledge available as **prior art** to patent offices.
[84:7:5] - **ABS:** CBD 1992 → **Nagoya Protocol 2010**; **Biological Diversity Act 2002** (amended **2023**).
[84:7:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:84 sub 7
## SUB 8 | Andhra Pradesh Biodiversity
[84:8:0] - **Eastern Ghats:** **Mahanadi to the Nilgiris**; highest peak **Arma Konda (~1,680 m, ASR district)**; **Mahendra Girulu** in **Srikakulam** (not Anantapur); **not a global hotspot**.
[84:8:1] - **Seshachalam BR (2010):** **Red Sanders**, ***Cycas beddomei*** (a **cycad**), Golden Gecko; Seshachalam–Nallamala: tigers, elephants, **Chenchus**.
[84:8:2] - **Jerdon's courser** (Critically Endangered): **sparse scrub forest with bare ground** – **Sri Lankamalleswara WLS (Kadapa)**; **rediscovered 1986** (not mangroves).
[84:8:3] - **Grey slender loris:** **dry Eastern Ghats scrub**.
[84:8:4] - **APSBB:** ~**13,000 BMCs**; **5% of Red Sanders profits** to farmers.
[84:8:5] - **Mangrove cover (ISFR):** Andhra Pradesh **fourth** among States/UTs (after West Bengal, Gujarat, A&N).
[84:8:6] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:84 sub 8

[n94c96904591] sub0
  What does species diversity, the variety of species in an area, take into account?
  *Both species richness and abundance | Only the number of species, irrespective of abundance | Only variation in genes within a single species | Only the variety of climatic zones
  x: Species diversity is the variety of species in an area and includes both richness and abundance.
[na03bb9c1719] sub0
  Which of the following is NOT correct about ecosystem diversity?
  It refers to the variety of ecosystems in an area | Boreal conifers cannot do the job of tropical deciduous trees in every context | Rainforests, deciduous forests and boreal ecosystems are examples of different ecosystems | *One ecosystem can always replace the functions of another
  x: One ecosystem cannot simply replace another's functions.
[nenvironment-25-2] sub0
  Which of the following is NOT correct?
  Endemic species are restricted to a particular geographical area. | Invasive alien species harm native ecosystems or species. | Alien species are introduced outside their natural range. | *Genetic diversity refers to the variety of ecosystems.
  x: Genetic diversity is variation within a species; the variety of ecosystems is ecosystem diversity.
[n3b27b27daaf] sub0
  Who coined the word 'biodiversity'?
  *Walter G. Rosen | E.O. Wilson | R.H. Whittaker | Norman Myers
  x: Walter G. Rosen coined the word (1985) and E.O. Wilson popularised it; alpha, beta and gamma diversity terms come from Whittaker.
[n898c2b83f7f] sub0
  The CBD defines biodiversity as variability among living organisms from terrestrial, marine and other aquatic ecosystems and the ____ of which they are part.
  food chains | biomes | habitats | *ecological complexes
  x: The CBD definition covers organisms from all these sources together with the ecological complexes to which they belong.
[n01521990bda] sub1
  What do species richness and species evenness refer to, respectively?
  Relative abundance and total number of species | *Total number of species and their relative abundance | Change between ecosystems and total regional diversity | Genetic diversity and ecosystem diversity
  x: Species richness is the number of species, while species evenness indicates their relative abundance. Low evenness means that a few species dominate.
[n2abe6efa1b4] sub1
  What is the total diversity across the ecosystems of a whole region called?
  Alpha diversity | *Gamma diversity | Beta diversity | Functional diversity
  x: Gamma diversity is the regional total; beta diversity is species turnover between ecosystems and alpha is diversity within one area.
[n80f254fcb52] sub1
  Which pair of indices is used for measuring species diversity?
  *Shannon-Wiener index and Simpson index | Simpson index and Human Development Index | Shannon-Wiener index and Gini index | Palmer index and Whittaker index
  x: The Shannon-Wiener and Simpson indices are measures of species diversity.
[ndba6af73cde] sub1
  Forest A has 2 tigers, 6 deer and 7 rabbits; Forest B has 1 tiger, 6 deer and 8 rabbits. Compared with Forest B, what does Forest A have?
  Greater species richness | More individuals | *Same richness but greater evenness | Lower evenness
  x: Both have three species and 15 individuals, but individuals are more equally distributed in Forest A, so it is more even.
[necf8a4f0f0a] sub1

  the number of crop species cultivated by humans | *the range of ecological roles performed by organisms | only the number of fossil species in a region | the geographical extent of a biosphere reserve
  x: Functional diversity measures the range of ecological roles. Its components include functional richness, functional evenness and functional divergence.

  Alpha diversity | *Beta diversity | Gamma diversity | Functional diversity
  x: Beta diversity is diversity between ecosystems (species turnover); alpha is within a habitat and gamma is regional.

=== NOTES 5:85 | Biodiversity Hotspots in India, Endemism and Biological Diversity Act 2002
## SUB 0 | India's Four Hotspots – Which Region Is, Which Is Not
[85:0:0] TABLE head: Hotspot | Indian part | Shared with
  [85:0:0.0] Himalaya | Entire Indian Himalaya – Eastern Himalaya (Sikkim, Arunachal, N. West Bengal) and Western Himalaya | Pakistan, Nepal, Bhutan, Tibet, Myanmar
  [85:0:0.1] Indo-Burma | North-East (south of the Brahmaputra) + Andaman Islands | Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Vietnam, S. China (Yunnan)
  [85:0:0.2] Western Ghats and Sri Lanka | Entire Western Ghats (Sahyadri) | Sri Lanka (one single hotspot)
  [85:0:0.3] Sundaland | Only the Nicobar Islands | Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei
[85:0:1] - **Andamans = Indo-Burma; Nicobars = Sundaland** – "Andaman group is part of Sundaland" is the INCORRECT statement (APPSC NTRUHS). Indo-Burma does **not** cover western India.
[85:0:2] - The Eastern Himalaya was first counted in Indo-Burma; the **2004 reappraisal** split it into Indo-Burma and the newly defined **Himalaya** hotspot.
[85:0:3] - **Old framing (25 hotspots, 1999–2000):** India had **two** – the **North-East / Eastern Himalaya** and the **Western Ghats**. So "two hotspots in India" = **Eastern Himalayas and Western Ghats** (APPSC G1, RAS 2008, UPPCS 2012, RAS 2013); now **four**.
[85:0:4] TABLE head: Region | Global hotspot?
  [85:0:4.0] Western Ghats, Eastern Himalaya, North-East, Andaman (Indo-Burma), Nicobar (Sundaland) | Yes
  [85:0:4.1] Eastern Ghats | No (rich in endemics, not a hotspot)
  [85:0:4.2] Aravallis, Vindhyas, Satpuras, Shivaliks | No
  [85:0:4.3] Thar Desert, Deccan Plateau, Central India | No
  [85:0:4.4] Sundarbans, Manas, Cherrapunji, Gangetic Plains, Gujarat | No
  [85:0:4.5] Naro Hills (MP) | No – not a globally accepted hotspot (MPPSC 2023)
[85:0:5] - **"India has four hotspots i.e. Eastern Himalayas, Western Himalayas, Western Ghats and Andaman & Nicobar"** (IAS 2010) is **wrong**: the four are Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats–Sri Lanka, Sundaland. With "hotspots only in tropics" also false → **neither** (NextGen, PMF).
[85:0:6] - Threats by hotspot: **Western Ghats** – monocultures, invasive species, tourism and infrastructure, hydropower, fires; **Himalaya** – young fragile geology, **landslides**, infrastructure; **Indo-Burma** – **jhum** (shifting cultivation), logging, hunting; **Sundaland/Nicobar** – invasives, the **2004 tsunami**.
[85:0:7] > Most-asked angle (≈17 PYQs): pick the hotspot – almost always **Western Ghats** or **Eastern Himalaya**; the odd one out is a desert, the **Eastern Ghats**, the Vindhyas or a plain.
[85:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 03 p.9, p.11-13; PMF Environment Part 03 p.21; Rocket Environment p.53, p.59; Shankar Environment Part 13 p.18-19; app notes 5:85 sub 2
## SUB 1 | Endemic and Signature Species of India's Hotspots
[85:1:0] - **Endemism:** a species occurs naturally in **one region only** (opposite: cosmopolitan).
[85:1:1] TABLE head: Species | Where / key fact
  [85:1:1.0] Lion-tailed macaque (wanderoo, EN) | Western Ghats only – Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka (not AP); upper canopy of evergreen forests; diurnal
  [85:1:1.1] Malabar (large-spotted) civet (CR) | Southern Western Ghats; nocturnal; first reported from Travancore
  [85:1:1.2] Sambar (VU) | Widespread deer; mostly crepuscular / nocturnal; state animal of Odisha
  [85:1:1.3] Great Indian (Great Pied) Hornbill (VU) | Western Ghats, NE India, Himalayan foothills; largest hornbill in India; state bird of Arunachal Pradesh and Kerala
  [85:1:1.4] Hangul (Kashmir stag) (CR) | Endemic to Kashmir; only viable population in Dachigam NP; state animal of J&K
  [85:1:1.5] Nilgiri tahr | Western Ghats (not Himalaya); Eravikulam NP has the largest population
  [85:1:1.6] Nilgiri marten, Malabar spiny dormouse | Western Ghats (Agasthyamalai)
  [85:1:1.7] Podocarpus (Nageia) wallichianus | Only endemic gymnosperm tree of the Western Ghats
  [85:1:1.8] Nicobar pigeon / Hoolock gibbon | Sundaland / Indo-Burma
  [85:1:1.9] Asiatic lion | Gir, Gujarat
[85:1:2] - **Birds of the hotspots (UPSC 2020):** **Ceylon frogmouth, Coppersmith barbet, Grey-chinned minivet, White-throated redstart** are all **birds**.
[85:1:3] - **Not a bird (UPSC 2022):** **Golden Mahseer** (Tor putitora) is a **fish** of Himalayan streams; Indian Nightjar, Spoonbill, White Ibis are birds.
[85:1:4] - **UPSC 2023 (nocturnal):** Malabar civet nocturnal; lion-tailed macaque diurnal; sambar disputed (crepuscular) → official key **only one**.
[85:1:5] TABLE head: AP endemic plant / animal | Where
  [85:1:5.0] Boswellia ovalifoliolata | Andhra Pradesh (APPSC 2022)
  [85:1:5.1] Kalanchoe cherukondensis, Pimpinella tirupatiensis | AP – Eastern Ghats (Cherukonda hills; Tirumala)
  [85:1:5.2] Cycas beddomei, Golden Gecko (micro-endemic) | Seshachalam hills, AP
  [85:1:5.3] Lilium chitrangadae (Dzükou lily) | Dzükou valley, Manipur–Nagaland – NOT AP (APPSC FSO 2025)
[85:1:6] - **AP:** Eastern Ghats (Seshachalam, Nallamala) are rich in endemics (Red Sanders, Golden Gecko) but **not a global hotspot**; three new plant species reported there in **May 2026**.
[85:1:7] > Angles: state/region of an endemic (macaque, hangul, hornbill), "which is NOT endemic to AP", and "how many are nocturnal / which is not a bird".
[85:1:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Species Part 01 p.7, p.10, p.14-15, p.28, p.72; PMF Species Part 03 p.9; PMF Species Part 02 p.8-9; Rocket Environment p.33; flowersofindia.net (Dzukou lily); app notes 5:85 sub 4
## SUB 2 | Hotspot Concept, Criteria and Count
[85:2:0] - **Definition:** a biogeographic region with a significant reservoir of biodiversity that is **threatened with destruction** – i.e. **exceptional (endemic) plant diversity + serious habitat loss**, not just "maximum biodiversity".
[85:2:1] - Concept introduced by **Norman Myers (British ecologist), 1988**; adopted by **Conservation International (CI) in 1989**, which **reassessed** it from 1996. **Not** BirdLife International, IUCN or WWF.
[85:2:2] - Basis: **richness, endemism and threat**. **Habitat destruction** is the main cause of biodiversity loss.
[85:2:3] TABLE head: Criterion (both needed – "two strict criteria") | Threshold
  [85:2:3.0] Endemism | At least 1,500 endemic vascular plant species (over 0.5% of world total)
  [85:2:3.1] Threat | Lost at least 70% of original habitat (30% or less natural vegetation left) – not 90%
[85:2:4] - **UPSC 2011:** Western Ghats–Sri Lanka and Indo-Burma recognised for **species richness, endemism, threat perception** (1, 3 and 5) – not vegetation density, ethno-botany or adaptation.
[85:2:5] - **APPSC Group 2:** hotspots are characterised by **endemic flowering plants and threat perception**.
[85:2:6] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [85:2:6.0] 1988 | Myers proposes the concept
  [85:2:6.1] 1989 | CI adopts it
  [85:2:6.2] 1999 | CI identifies 25 hotspots (numerical thresholds; Myers et al., 2000)
  [85:2:6.3] 2011 | 35th: Forests of East Australia
  [85:2:6.4] 2016 | 36th: North American Coastal Plain
[85:2:7] - Count: 25 → 34 → 35 → **36** (present; "as of 2023" also 36).
[85:2:8] - Once **15.7%** of Earth's land; about **86%** of that habitat lost; now only about **2.3–2.5%** of land.
[85:2:9] - Hold about **50% of vascular plants** (1,50,000 species) and **42% of terrestrial vertebrates** as endemics.
[85:2:10] - Most lie in the **tropics**, but hotspots are **not only tropical**: **temperate** ones include the **Mediterranean Basin** (incl. the **Eastern Mediterranean**), California Floristic Province, North American Coastal Plain. **North-western Australia is not** a hotspot (the Australian ones are SW Australia and East Australian forests) → UPSC 2009: **Eastern Himalayas and Eastern Mediterranean only**.
[85:2:11] - **Hottest hotspots:** **8** with highest endemism under greatest threat; include **Western Ghats–Sri Lanka**, Indo-Burma, Sundaland, Madagascar, Philippines.
[85:2:12] - **Coldspots:** relatively low diversity but losing habitat fast; still matter for rare species, ecosystem functions and genetic diversity.
[85:2:13] TABLE head: Concept | Body | Basis
  [85:2:13.0] Biodiversity hotspot | Conservation International (Myers) | 1,500+ endemic plants and 70%+ habitat lost; large regions
  [85:2:13.1] Key Biodiversity Area | IUCN-led partnership (global standard, 2016) | Single sites important for global persistence of biodiversity
  [85:2:13.2] Global 200 | WWF | Priority ecoregions (terrestrial, freshwater, marine) chosen for representativeness
  [85:2:13.3] Important Bird and Biodiversity Areas (IBAs) | BirdLife International (a global partnership of conservation NGOs) | Bird sites – BirdLife did not originate the hotspot concept (UPSC 2015)
[85:2:14] - **India's share (TSPSC 2023):** **2.4%** of world land, about **7–8%** of recorded species; main threat = habitat loss and fragmentation (urbanisation, infrastructure, deforestation, pollution, climate change).
[85:2:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.7-8; NextGen Environment APPSC 03 p.9, p.12; PMF Environment Part 03 p.19-20; PMF Environment Part 03 p.77-78 (BirdLife); Shankar Environment Part 13 p.18; Rocket Environment p.43, p.53; examday.ai UPSC 2009 Q (Mediterranean); app notes 5:85 sub 0-1
## SUB 3 | Western Ghats – India's Richest Biodiversity Region
[85:3:0] - Also **Sahyadri**; about **1,600 km** through **6 States**: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu (not AP).
[85:3:1] - "**Water tower of peninsular India**": feeds Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery. One of the **8 hottest hotspots**; the **most biodiversity-rich / "biodiversity-saturated" area of India** in PYQs (UPPSC 2015, 2019).
[85:3:2] - **Silent Valley NP** (Nilgiri BR, Kerala) – the "richest biodiversity" answer among valleys (CGPSC 2011), against Kashmir valley, Valley of Flowers, Surma valley.
[85:3:3] - About **5,000** vascular plants, **1,700 (34%)** endemic, **58 endemic genera**; ~433 plant species shared only with Sri Lanka.
[85:3:4] - **UNESCO World Heritage Site 2012**: serial site of **39 component areas in 7 clusters**. IUCN 2025 World Heritage Outlook: "**significant concern**".
[85:3:5] - **New species:** **Feb 2017** – Delhi University (S.D. Biju) described **7 new night frogs (Nyctibatrachus)**, **4 of them miniature** (12–15 mm).
[85:3:6] TABLE head: Panel | Year | Recommendation
  [85:3:6.0] WGEEP – Madhav Gadgil (set up by MoEF 2010, report 2011) | 2010 | Whole Ghats as ESA, graded ESZ I–III; 142 talukas in 44 districts
  [85:3:6.1] HLWG – K. Kasturirangan | 2012 | Set up after State opposition; ESA limited to about 37% (~60,000 sq km)
[85:3:7] - MoEF&CC issued **draft** ESA notifications across six States (2018 onwards, still not final); legal force on notification under the **EP Act, 1986**.
[85:3:8] - Supreme Court ordered eviction of encroachers in **Agasthyamalai Biosphere Reserve** (Kerala–TN; UNESCO MAB 2016).
[85:3:9] > Gadgil and Kasturirangan reports = **protection of the Western Ghats** (UPSC 2016; APPSC 2019).
[85:3:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.10-12; NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.5-7; PMF Environment Part 03 p.51; PMF Species Part 03 p.12; Rocket Environment p.53; newswise.com (PeerJ, 21 Feb 2017); app notes 5:85 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Biological Diversity Act 2002 and 2023 Amendment
[85:4:0] - Gives effect to **CBD (1992)**; passed by Parliament in **December 2002** (Lok Sabha 2 Dec, Rajya Sabha 11 Dec); Presidential assent **5 February 2003** (Act 18 of 2003).
[85:4:1] TABLE head: Tier | Body | Role
  [85:4:1.0] National | NBA, Chennai (2003) | Foreign/commercial access and IPR; advises Centre; civil court powers
  [85:4:1.1] State | SBBs; UT Biodiversity Councils | Commercial use by Indian entities
  [85:4:1.2] Local | BMCs | Document biodiversity, prepare PBRs, levy collection fees
[85:4:2] - **Section 37:** Biodiversity Heritage Sites. **Section 38:** threatened species (1,500+ plants declared by States).
[85:4:3] - **Amendment Act 2023** (in force **1 April 2024**): offences **decriminalised** (penalties only); **AYUSH** practitioners and codified traditional knowledge exempt from prior intimation; cultivated medicinal plants exempt.
[85:4:4] - **Biological Diversity Rules, 2024** replace the 2004 Rules, with a statutory National Biodiversity Authority Fund.
[85:4:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 06 p.94-98; Rocket Environment p.40; Shankar Environment Part 22 p.1; wipo.int/wipolex (BD Act details); app notes 5:85 sub 5
## SUB 5 | BMCs, PBRs and Biodiversity Heritage Sites
[85:5:0] - **PBRs are prepared by BMCs** (APPSC 2019). About **2.62 lakh BMCs** (2024); ~**2.72 lakh PBRs** (Jun 2026).
[85:5:1] - BMCs are key to **Nagoya Protocol** objectives and can levy collection fees (UPSC 2023).
[85:5:2] - **BHS:** notified by the **State Government** in consultation with local bodies (Section 37(1)); no change to ownership or livelihood rights; traditional uses continue.
[85:5:3] - Count: **54** (NBA, March 2026); 45 (Feb 2024) → 48 (Apr 2025).
[85:5:4] TABLE head: BHS | State
  [85:5:4.0] Nallur Tamarind Grove (first, 2007) | Karnataka
  [85:5:4.1] Ameenpur Lake (first water-body BHS) | Telangana
  [85:5:4.2] Borjuli wetland (wild rice Oryza rufipogon, Jul 2026) | Assam
  [85:5:4.3] Kasampatty | Tamil Nadu
[85:5:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.12-13; NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.13; PMF Environment Part 06 p.95-96; app notes 5:85 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Access and Benefit Sharing
[85:6:0] - Commercial benefits from bioresources shared with providing communities; covers plant, animal, microbial resources and traditional knowledge; **excludes human genetic material**. CBD 1992 → **Nagoya Protocol 2010**.
[85:6:1] - **Kani model:** Kani tribe's knowledge of **Arogyapacha** (Trichopus zeylanicus) → **TBGRI** drug **Jeevani** (anti-fatigue).
[85:6:2] - ABS raised over **₹266 crore** since 2008: **Red Sanders 45%** (₹120 crore), seed sector 32.3%.
[85:6:3] - Repository rule: **25–40%** to repository, **60–75%** to local communities via SBBs/UTBCs.
[85:6:4] - **AP:** APSBB vision of **zero biodiversity loss by 2050**; Red Sanders makes AP vulnerable to biopiracy and the largest ABS earner.
[85:6:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 03 p.19 (biopiracy, Nagoya); PMF Environment Part 06 p.96; app notes 5:85 sub 7

=== NOTES 5:86 | Loss of Biodiversity – Causes, Invasive Alien Species, Iucn Red List Categories
## SUB 0 | Causes of Biodiversity Loss – Habitat Destruction First
[86:0:0] # The most-asked fact
[86:0:1] - **Greatest / most important / main cause:** **habitat destruction (loss of natural habitats and vegetation)** – NextGen: "the primary and major reason for biodiversity loss"; IPBES also ranks it first. Not climate change, invasives, over-hunting or pollution alone.
[86:0:2] - **Deforestation → biodiversity loss:** cutting and burning forests **destroys natural habitats, driving species to extinction and disrupting ecosystems**.
[86:0:3] - **Primary driver of deforestation and habitat loss:** **agricultural expansion and urban development** (also land clearance for agriculture, mines, dams, harbours, industries, settlements); in the world the major cause of deforestation is **expansion of agriculture** (not paper industry, firewood or fires).
[86:0:4] - Main cause overall = **human influence**: habitat alteration and loss, exotic species, over-exploitation, pollution, GMOs; **over-consumption of resources** destroys habitats, raises pollution and drives climate change.
[86:0:5] - In India: habitat loss (urbanisation, infrastructure, mining, farming) comes first, then climate change, invasives, pollution, over-exploitation.
[86:0:6] - Loss of biodiversity is a major problem resulting from **modern agriculture** (monoculture, agro-chemicals).
[86:0:7] # Evil Quartet vs HIPPO
[86:0:8] TABLE head: Evil Quartet (NCERT / NextGen) | HIPPO (popularised by E. O. Wilson)
  [86:0:8.0] Habitat loss and fragmentation | Habitat destruction
  [86:0:8.1] Over-exploitation (Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon) | Invasive species
  [86:0:8.2] Invasion of alien species (Nile perch → 200+ cichlids lost in Lake Victoria) | Pollution
  [86:0:8.3] Co-extinctions | human Population
  [86:0:8.4] — | Over-harvesting
[86:0:9] - **HIPPO** was popularised by **E. O. Wilson**. **Co-extinction** is only in the Evil Quartet; **pollution** and **population** only in HIPPO. Newer lists add **climate change** and **disease**.
[86:0:10] # Fragmentation and edge effect
[86:0:11] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [86:0:11.0] Fragmentation | Large habitats broken into small patches; hits migratory animals and wide-ranging mammals and birds hardest
  [86:0:11.1] Edge effect | Patch boundaries get more light, wind, heat, predators and weeds; as fragments shrink, interior species decline
[86:0:12] - Tropical rainforest cover fell from **14% to 6%** of the land surface; Amazon cleared for soybean and cattle.
[86:0:13] # Disturbs vs restores ecological balance
[86:0:14] TABLE head: Disturbs (a cause of loss) | Restores (NOT a cause)
  [86:0:14.0] Roads, urbanisation, extension of agriculture, clear-felling, jhum (shifting) cultivation, mining, quarrying, encroachment, exploitation of forest produce | Afforestation of degraded land, sacred groves, protected areas, biosphere reserves, wildlife corridors
  [86:0:14.1] Draining wetlands, mangroves to shrimp farms | Removal of invasives with native restocking
[86:0:15] > Exam angle: "greatest / main / most important cause" (habitat destruction ×8), "all of the above", primary driver (agriculture + urban development), and NOT-a-cause pickers (afforestation, sacred groves, biosphere reserves).
[86:0:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.3-4; NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.10; NextGen Rocket Environment p.53 ("Main biodiversity-loss factor: habitat destruction"), p.43, p.51; app notes 5:86 sub 0-1
## SUB 1 | Threats in Statement Questions and Species Declines
[86:1:0] # Accepted threats vs distractors
[86:1:1] TABLE head: Threat (correct) | NOT a threat (distractor)
  [86:1:1.0] Global warming, habitat fragmentation, invasion of alien species | Promotion of vegetarianism
  [86:1:1.1] Loss of habitat, loss of genetic variation | Loss of appetite
  [86:1:1.2] Habitat pollution, over-exploitation, illegal wildlife trade, forest fires | Creation of biosphere reserves, expansion of protected areas
[86:1:2] - UPSC 2012 / RAS 2016: threats = **1, 2 and 3** (global warming, fragmentation, alien species), not vegetarianism.
[86:1:3] - Direct threats (NextGen): habitat destruction, exotic species, diseases, pollution, **genetic assimilation**.
[86:1:4] - **Extinction-prone traits:** large body size, small population, low reproductive rate, **narrow (specialised) niche**, **lack of genetic variability**, endemism; a **broad niche** makes a species adaptable – NOT a cause.
[86:1:5] - When a species becomes extinct, **its obligately associated species also go extinct** (co-extinction) – so "associated species do not become extinct" is false.
[86:1:6] # Specific declines
[86:1:7] TABLE head: Group | Cause
  [86:1:7.0] Vultures (Gyps) | Diclofenac, a veterinary NSAID given to cattle – kidney failure in vultures eating carcasses; vet use banned 2006; meloxicam is the safe substitute
  [86:1:7.1] Birds in India | Habitat reduction and pesticides, chemical fertilisers, mosquito repellents (not bio-pesticides or organic manure)
  [86:1:7.2] House sparrow | Popularly linked to cell-tower radiation (besides loss of nesting sites, pesticides); IUCN: LC
  [86:1:7.3] Wildlife in general | Loss of habitat, illegal trade, forest fires; population growth acts mainly indirectly
[86:1:8] > Exam angle: statement-code questions (1, 2 and 3), NOT-a-cause, vulture–diclofenac (UPSC 2012), extinction-prone traits.
[86:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.10 (PYQ: 1, 2 and 3) and p.6 (diclofenac); NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.8; PMF Environment Part 3 p.99-100; PMF Species & PAN Part 1 p.80 (house sparrow LC); app notes 5:86 sub 0, 3
## SUB 2 | IUCN Red List Categories and Criteria
[86:2:0] - **Nine** categories, highest to lowest risk: **EX → EW → CR → EN → VU → NT → LC**, plus **DD** and **NE**.
[86:2:1] TABLE head: Code | Full form | Meaning
  [86:2:1.0] EX | Extinct | No reasonable doubt that the last individual has died, after exhaustive surveys – no fixed number of years
  [86:2:1.1] EW | Extinct in the Wild | Survives only in cultivation, captivity or as a naturalised population well outside its past range
  [86:2:1.2] CR | Critically Endangered | Extremely high risk of extinction in the wild (not "critically extinct")
  [86:2:1.3] EN | Endangered | Very high risk; "species in danger of extinction"; numbers reduced to a critical level
  [86:2:1.4] VU | Vulnerable | High risk; continuous decline from over-exploitation or habitat destruction
  [86:2:1.5] NT | Near Threatened (not "Not Threatened") | Close to qualifying for a threatened category
  [86:2:1.6] LC | Least Concern | Widespread and abundant
  [86:2:1.7] DD | Data Deficient | Inadequate information
  [86:2:1.8] NE | Not Evaluated | Not yet assessed
[86:2:2] - **Threatened = CR + EN + VU.** "Rare" (older Indian usage) = not endangered or vulnerable now but at risk.
[86:2:3] - **50-year rule:** older books say a species is extinct if **not seen in the wild for 50 years** (a 1980s suggestion); IUCN today uses "no reasonable doubt" instead.
[86:2:4] - **Extirpation** = local extinction: a species gone **from a specific area but surviving elsewhere** (e.g. tigers extirpated from Kawal and Sri Venkateswara NP).
[86:2:5] # Criteria A-E
[86:2:6] TABLE head: Criterion | Basis
  [86:2:6.0] A | Declining population (past, present, projected)
  [86:2:6.1] B | Geographic range (size, fragmentation, decline)
  [86:2:6.2] C | Small population size and decline
  [86:2:6.3] D | Very small or restricted population
  [86:2:6.4] E | Quantitative analysis of extinction risk (PVA)
[86:2:7] - Economic value in trade is NOT a criterion.
[86:2:8] > Exam angle: CR full form (APPSC Group 2), "species in danger of extinction" = endangered, extirpation, 50-year rule.
[86:2:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.8, p.11-12; NextGen Rocket Environment p.34 (nine categories); Shankar Environment Part 10 p.12-13; PMF Environment Part 3 p.86 (extirpated); https://theconversation.com/when-is-a-species-really-extinct-182555 (50 years); app notes 5:86 sub 6

## SUB 4 | Red Data Book, IUCN and Biodiversity Reports
[86:4:0] # Red Data Book / Red List
[86:4:1] - Published by **IUCN**; lists **threatened (endangered) plants and animals** in danger of extinction – **not** endemic species of hotspots, **not** protected sites.
[86:4:2] - IUCN's endangered-species list = **Red List**; Brown, White, Black, Green, Yellow lists are distractors. "Red" symbolises danger.
[86:4:3] - Red List started **1964**; first Red Data Book volumes issued **1966** by IUCN's Species Survival Commission; nickname "**Barometer of Life**"; measures **extinction risk**.
[86:4:4] TABLE head: Page colour | Meaning
  [86:4:4.0] Red / pink | Endangered / critically endangered
  [86:4:4.1] Green | Formerly threatened, now recovered
[86:4:5] - **IUCN Green Status (2021)** measures species **recovery**.
[86:4:6] - Red List **2026-1 (July 2026)**: **175,909** assessed; **49,505 (~28%)** threatened. India's **Red List Roadmap**: **70,000** species by **2027**, led by the **NBA**; 7,076 Indian animal species in Red List categories.
[86:4:7] # IUCN
[86:4:8] - **International Union for Conservation of Nature** (and Natural Resources); founded **1948**; HQ **Gland, Switzerland** (older books: Morges); a union of governments and NGOs – **NOT a UN agency**.
[86:4:9] - **Species Survival Commission** → **Invasive Species Specialist Group (ISSG)**, which manages the **Global Invasive Species Database** and the "100 of the World's Worst" list.
[86:4:10] - World Conservation Congress 2025: **Abu Dhabi**, "Our World, Our Future". **Phoenix Species Project** (Aug 2026): **$200 million**, Re:wild and Bezos Earth Fund, to recover **100** most threatened species.
[86:4:11] # Report → publisher
[86:4:12] TABLE head: Report / database | Publisher
  [86:4:12.0] Red List / Red Data Book | IUCN
  [86:4:12.1] Global Invasive Species Database | IUCN SSC ISSG
  [86:4:12.2] Living Planet Report (biennial, since 1998) / Living Planet Index (vertebrate populations since 1970) | WWF with Zoological Society of London
  [86:4:12.3] Global Assessment on Biodiversity (2019): ~25% of species threatened, up to 1 million face extinction | IPBES (not WWF)
[86:4:13] - **Living Planet Report 2022:** global biodiversity and planet health; average **69% decline** in monitored wildlife populations **since 1970** (LPR 2024: 73%).
[86:4:14] > Exam angle: "Red Data Book published by / contains" (×10), IUCN full form, ISSG parent body (UPSC 2023), LPR 2022 statements.
[86:4:15] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.8; NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.11-12; NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.10 (ISSG); NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.1-2 (IPBES, LPR 2022); NextGen Rocket Environment p.34, p.41; Shankar Environment Part 10 p.11; PMF Environment Part 3 p.29, p.69; app notes 5:86 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Invasive Alien Species
[86:5:0] - **Invasive alien species:** non-native organisms introduced outside their natural range that "**arrive, survive and thrive**", outcompete natives and cause economic, environmental and health harm; exotic plants that **crowd out native plants** = **invasive plants**.
[86:5:1] - Three tests: **non-native origin, uncontrolled spread, measurable harm** (NOT commercial usefulness). Defined in India under the **WPA 1972** (Amendment 2022, **Section 62A**: Centre regulates/prohibits IAS; new **Schedule IV** = CITES-appendix specimens, NOT invasives).
[86:5:2] - Invasives contributed to nearly **40%** of known animal extinctions since the **17th century**; threaten **1 in 10** Red List species; damage per species is higher in the **Global South**.
[86:5:3] - Invasive plants cut **medicinal plants, fruits and fodder grass** used by indigenous communities, and degrade the **herbivore forage on which tigers depend** – both harms are real.
[86:5:4] # Invasives in India
[86:5:5] TABLE head: Species | Origin | Note
  [86:5:5.0] Water hyacinth (*Eichhornia*, now *Pontederia crassipes*) | South America (Amazon) | World's worst / most problematic aquatic weed; "Terror of Bengal"; depletes oxygen
  [86:5:5.1] Water lettuce (*Pistia*), *Salvinia* | Tropical America | Free-floating invasive aquatic weeds
  [86:5:5.2] *Vallisneria* (tape grass) | Native submerged plant | NOT invasive – an aquarium/oxygenating plant
  [86:5:5.3] Parthenium (carrot / Congress grass) | Tropical America | Came with imported wheat in the 1950s
  [86:5:5.4] *Lantana camara* | Central/South America | Brought as an ornamental; Verbenaceae (not Asteraceae); allelopathic; IUCN 100 worst; ~25% of Amrabad TR forest floor
  [86:5:5.5] *Prosopis juliflora* (Seema Chintakaya, Ganda babool, Vilayati Kikar) | Mexico, South America, Caribbean | Reduces biodiversity where it grows; deep roots lower groundwater, raise soil salinity (Rayalaseema); degraded Banni grasslands
  [86:5:5.6] African catfish (*Clarias gariepinus*) | Africa | Predatory; banned; preys on waterfowl in Keoladeo
  [86:5:5.7] Senna spectabilis | South America (not North America) | Nilgiri-Bandipur-Wayanad
  [86:5:5.8] Red-eared slider | North America | Pet trade
  [86:5:5.9] Mosquitofish | United States | Mosquito control
  [86:5:5.10] Giant African snail | Africa | Takes over native habitats
[86:5:6] - Invasive fish of concern: **African catfish, Nile tilapia, red-bellied piranha, alligator gar**.
[86:5:7] - **Native or not (UPSC 2024):** **cashew** (Brazil, by the Portuguese, first to Goa) and **papaya** (tropical America) are introduced; only **red sanders** is native → "**only one**".
[86:5:8] # Laws, actions and targets
[86:5:9] TABLE head: Law / framework | Provision
  [86:5:9.0] Destructive Insects and Pests Act, 1914 | Stops entry of crop pests and diseases into India and their inter-state spread
  [86:5:9.1] Plant Quarantine Order, 2003 | Regulates plant imports; pest risk analysis, phytosanitary checks
  [86:5:9.2] DPPQS | Under the Agriculture Ministry (not MoEFCC); fumigates uncertified imports with methyl bromide
  [86:5:9.3] CBD Article 8(h) | Prevent, control or eradicate alien species
  [86:5:9.4] Kunming-Montreal GBF Target 6 | Cut introduction and establishment of IAS by at least 50% by 2030 (Target 3 = 30x30)
[86:5:10] - **Ujani reservoir, Maharashtra:** **BNHS** began India's **first community-driven** removal and native restocking (suckermouth catfish, tilapia, African catfish) (Aug 2026).
[86:5:11] - **Tamil Nadu** cleared **Prosopis** from **517 villages in 32 districts** (May 2026); recovery depends on the landscape's earlier condition; blanket eradication is debated.
[86:5:12] > Exam angle: worst aquatic weed (×4), Prosopis in news (UPSC 2018 ×2), NOT-invasive picker (Vallisneria), DIPA year, native-to-India count.

## SUB 6 | Extinction – Mass Extinctions and Co-extinction
[86:6:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [86:6:0.0] Extinction | Disappearance of all members of a species (death of the last individual), globally
  [86:6:0.1] Extirpation | Local extinction only
  [86:6:0.2] Co-extinction | Loss of one species drags down its obligate partners (plant–pollinator, host–parasite)
  [86:6:0.3] Background extinction | Slow natural loss at a low steady rate
  [86:6:0.4] Mass extinction | High percentage of species lost in a short geological period
  [86:6:0.5] Sixth extinction | Present, human-driven wave – over-exploitation of resources, habitat loss and fragmentation, ecosystem destruction, pollution, climate change
[86:6:1] - **Five** mass extinctions so far; the **fifth** (end-Cretaceous, ~**66 million years ago**) ended the dinosaurs – **asteroid-impact theory of Luis Alvarez** (1980, with Walter Alvarez).
[86:6:2] - Sixth extinction: rates **100-1,000 times** pre-human rates (NextGen); IPBES: tens to hundreds of times background. It is not about GM crops, monoculture or a feared meteorite.
[86:6:3] - **Dodo** (Mauritius): classic **co-extinction** case – the tree whose seeds it dispersed (*Calvaria*/tambalacoque) failed to reproduce.
[86:6:4] - IUCN Red List (2014): **784** extinctions in 500 years; 128 bird species lost in 500 years. Extinct: **passenger pigeon, Steller's sea cow** (over-exploitation), Bali, Javan and Caspian tigers.
[86:6:5] - **Extinct in the Wild:** Hawaiian crow, Père David's deer (only in captivity).
[86:6:6] - **India:** **cheetah** declared extinct **1952** – the only large mammal lost since Independence; ZSI lists **cheetah, pink-headed duck, mountain quail** as extinct from India (not the passenger pigeon).
[86:6:7] > Exam angle: definition (extinction, extirpation), sixth extinction (UPSC 2018 ×2), dodo (UPSC 1998 ×2), Alvarez (SSC 2019).
[86:6:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.10-11; NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.4-5; NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.8; PMF Species & PAN Part 1 p.76 (dodo EX); app notes 5:86 sub 3; Alvarez, dodo tree: general knowledge, not checked

  [86:7:0.1] Gooty (peacock) tarantula (*Poecilotheria metallica*) | CR | Nandyal/Gooty, Nallamala forests; a spider, not a crustacean; arboreal, insectivorous; habitat limited to some forest patches; WPA Sch II; CITES App. II
  [86:7:0.2] Jerdon's courser | CR | Nocturnal; Sri Lankamalleswara WLS (Kadapa); not flightless; rediscovered 1986
  [86:7:0.3] Golden gecko | Endemic | Seshachalam / Tirumala micro-habitats (not only Western Ghats)
  [86:7:0.4] Cycas beddomei | Endemic, endangered | Eastern Ghats cycad

## SUB 8 | Keystone, Flagship and Umbrella Species
[86:8:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning | Examples
  [86:8:0.0] Keystone | Effect disproportionately large for its numbers; determines whether many other species persist; its loss changes the occurrence of others | Top predators (tiger), vultures, fig trees
  [86:8:0.1] Flagship | Charismatic species to win public support | Tiger, Asiatic lion
  [86:8:0.2] Umbrella | Protecting it protects many others | Tiger; pygmy hog
  [86:8:0.3] Endemic | Found only in one region | Red sanders, golden gecko, Gooty tarantula
[86:8:1] - Tiger is flagship, keystone and umbrella species.
[86:8:2] > Exam angle: definition of keystone (UPSC 2000, APPSC FSO).
[86:8:3] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment Part 10 p.13; PMF Environment Part 3 p.17-18; app notes 5:86 sub 8
## SUB 9 | Climate Change and Consequences of Loss
[86:9:0] - Warming causes **coral bleaching**, ocean acidification, shifts in ecosystem boundaries and **disrupted migration**; rising temperatures **shift species ranges** and raise extinction risk in hotspots (Jun 2026); a warming Arctic is opening to **alien plants** (Feb 2026).
[86:9:1] - Loss disrupts species interactions, **pollination**, **nutrient cycling**, water and soil services → lower **food security** for resource-dependent communities; once lost, biodiversity cannot be recreated.
[86:9:2] - **Zoonotic spillover** rises with habitat disruption and wildlife trade → **One Health** approach (humans, animals, ecosystems).
[86:9:3] > Exam angle: own MCQs only (assertion-reason, consequences).
[86:9:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 04 p.10; app notes 5:86 sub 2

=== NOTES 5:87 | Conservation – In-situ (protected Areas, Biosphere Reserves) and Ex-situ (zoos, Gene Banks, Seed Banks)
## SUB 0 | Biosphere Reserves and the MAB Programme
[87:0:0] # Concept (most asked)
[87:0:1] - **Biosphere Reserve (BR):** large terrestrial/coastal/marine area recognised under **UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme** (launched **1971**; not IUCN); UNESCO calls BRs "learning places for sustainable development".
[87:0:2] - **Purpose:** conserve the **genetic diversity** of the whole landscape **together with the traditional life of local/tribal people** – so the "most important strategy for conservation of biodiversity together with traditional human life" is the **biosphere reserve**, not an NP, sanctuary or botanical garden.
[87:0:3] - Designation **does not change legal status or ownership**; a BR may contain one or more NPs/sanctuaries. **IN-MAB Committee (MoEFCC)** recommends sites; State prepares the management plan; funding **60:40** (**90:10** for NE and three Himalayan States). **Seville Strategy (1995)** added social, cultural and economic needs.
[87:0:4] - Not a protected-area category under the WPA 1972 (those are NP, sanctuary, conservation reserve, community reserve).
[87:0:5] TABLE head: Zone | What is allowed
  [87:0:5.0] Core | Strictly protected (usually NP/WLS); no human activity
  [87:0:5.1] Buffer | Limited activity: research, education, training, limited recreation
  [87:0:5.2] Transition | Settlements, farming, forestry, tourism
[87:0:6] # India's 18 BRs (13 in UNESCO's World Network, WNBR)
[87:0:7] TABLE head: BR | State | Notified | In WNBR
  [87:0:7.0] Nilgiri (first; only 3-State BR) | TN–Kerala–Karnataka | 1986 | 2000
  [87:0:7.1] Nanda Devi (Nanda Devi + Valley of Flowers NPs) | Uttarakhand | 1988 | 2004
  [87:0:7.2] Nokrek (Tura Range, Garo Hills; peak 1,412 m, highest in Garo Hills) | Meghalaya | 1988 | 2009 (May)
  [87:0:7.3] Gulf of Mannar (first marine BR; largest UNESCO-approved, ~10,500 km²) | Tamil Nadu | 1989 | 2001
  [87:0:7.4] Sundarbans (Ganga–Brahmaputra delta) | West Bengal | 1989 | 2001
  [87:0:7.5] Great Nicobar | A&N Islands | 1989 | 2013
  [87:0:7.6] Manas | Assam (not Meghalaya) | 1989 | No
  [87:0:7.7] Similipal | Odisha | 1994 | 2009
  [87:0:7.8] Dibru-Saikhowa | Assam | 1997 | No
  [87:0:7.9] Dihang-Dibang | Arunachal Pradesh | 1998 | No
  [87:0:7.10] Pachmarhi | Madhya Pradesh | 1999 | 2009
  [87:0:7.11] Khangchendzonga | Sikkim | 2000 | 2018
  [87:0:7.12] Agasthyamalai (Kani tribe) | Kerala–TN | 2001 | 2016
  [87:0:7.13] Achanakmar-Amarkantak | MP–Chhattisgarh | 2005 | 2012
  [87:0:7.14] Great Rann of Kutch (largest, ~12,454 km²) | Gujarat | 2008 | No
  [87:0:7.15] Cold Desert (16th BR; Pin Valley NP, Kibber, Chandratal) | Himachal Pradesh | 2009 | 2025 (13th WNBR site)
  [87:0:7.16] Seshachalam Hills (AP's only BR) | Andhra Pradesh | 2010 | No
  [87:0:7.17] Panna | Madhya Pradesh | 2011 | 2020
[87:0:8] - **Count (as of 2026):** **18 BRs**, **13 in WNBR**; outside WNBR now: **Manas, Dibru-Saikhowa, Dihang-Dibang, Great Rann of Kutch, Seshachalam**. Cold Desert joined in late **2025** (MAB-ICC, Hangzhou) – older keys list it as "not in MAB".
[87:0:9] - **Area order:** **Nanda Devi (5,860) > Pachmarhi (4,982) > Agasthyamalai (3,500) > Panna**.
[87:0:10] - **Nallamalai is not a BR** (it is a hill range holding NSTR). **Bundala** BR (MAB, 2005) is in **Sri Lanka**.
[87:0:11] > Exam angle: State of a BR (match), WNBR yes/no, year added (Agasthyamalai 2016, Nokrek 2009), count 18, Sundarbans = Ganga–Brahmaputra delta, BR = conservation with traditional life.
[87:0:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.14, 06 p.1-3; NextGen Rocket Environment p.42 (BR–State–year table); PMF Species & PAs Part 3 p.36-41 (18 BRs, 13 in MAB, Cold Desert 2025, Nokrek 1,412 m, areas); PMF Environment Part 3 p.42-44 (UPSC 2014 BR question); Shankar Environment Part 13 p.14-17; app notes 5:87 sub 4
[87:0:13] - **Citrus Gene Sanctuary (Nokrek):** in-situ site for **crop wild relatives** (wild citrus).
[87:0:14] - **Manas BR** is linked with the **Manas Wildlife Sanctuary/NP** (contiguous with Royal Manas NP, Bhutan).
[87:0:15] - **Sundarbans BR** has the most animal species of any Indian BR (**2,626**).
## SUB 1 | In-situ and Ex-situ Conservation
[87:1:0] TABLE head: Basis | In-situ (on-site) | Ex-situ (off-site)
  [87:1:0.0] Where | Within the natural habitat | Outside it, in a controlled setting
  [87:1:0.1] Examples | National park, wildlife sanctuary, biosphere reserve, reserved/protected forest, nature reserve, sacred groves | Botanical garden, zoo, safari park, seed/gene bank, cryobank (cryopreservation), tissue culture, captive breeding
  [87:1:0.2] Saves | Whole ecosystem and its genetic diversity | The species or its genes
[87:1:1] - "Not an in-situ site" = **Botanical Garden** (UPSC 2011, UPPCS 2018). Genetic diversity in **National Parks** is maintained by **in-situ conservation**.
[87:1:2] - **In-situ is generally most effective:** species keep interacting with their environment; ex-situ helps education, research and reintroduction but needs space and money and cannot save the ecosystem.
[87:1:3] - **Captive breeding** for species whose habitat is lost, e.g. Gangetic gharials bred and released; 10 captive-bred **Asian Giant Tortoises** released in **Ntangki NP (Nagaland)**.
[87:1:4] - **Meristem culture** = virus-free propagation. "Biological diversity" coined by **Raymond F. Dasmann**.
[87:1:5] > Exam angle: "which is NOT in-situ / which is ex-situ" – botanical garden, zoo, seed bank and cryopreservation are ex-situ.
[87:1:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.7-9 (in-situ, ex-situ, PYQ); NextGen Rocket Environment p.44 (in-situ/ex-situ lists, Dasmann); PMF Environment Part 3 p.41; app notes 5:87 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Protected-Area Categories, Eco-sensitive Zones and Global Coverage
[87:2:0] TABLE head: Category (WPA 1972) | Key feature
  [87:2:0.0] National Park | Declared by State (Centre also may); no rights, no grazing, no collection of biomass/forest produce; boundary altered only on NBWL recommendation
  [87:2:0.1] Wildlife Sanctuary | Some rights allowed; grazing and firewood collection regulated by the Chief Wildlife Warden
  [87:2:0.2] Conservation Reserve | 2002/2003 amendment; government land, usually adjoining/linking PAs
  [87:2:0.3] Community Reserve | 2002/2003 amendment; private or community land a community volunteers; declared by the State Government; managed by a Community Reserve Management Committee (not the Chief Wildlife Warden); sanctuary restrictions (no hunting) apply; residents' rights not affected
[87:2:1] - Local people may **not collect biomass in National Parks** (they may in BR transition zones, Ramsar wetlands and, regulated, in sanctuaries).
[87:2:2] - **Network (2026):** **1,134 PAs** (981 in 2020): 109 NPs, 573 WLS, 127 conservation, 75 community reserves; ~**5.32%** of India's area; 58 tiger reserves. First community reserve: **Keshopur-Chhamb (Punjab)**. Biosphere reserve is NOT a PA category.
[87:2:3] # Eco-sensitive Zones (ESZ)
[87:2:4] - **Purpose:** **"shock absorbers"** / transition zones around NPs and sanctuaries (MoEFCC guidelines), to minimise forest depletion and human–animal conflict.
[87:2:5] - Notified under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** – **not the WPA 1972**; they **do not ban all activity except agriculture** (only mining, polluting industry, major hydro etc. are prohibited; hotels, tree felling regulated; agriculture, organic farming permitted) → UPSC 2014: **neither statement correct**.
[87:2:6] - **Wildlife Action Plan 2002-16** / MoEF 2011 guidelines: up to **10 km**; **Supreme Court (June 2022):** minimum **1 km** ESZ, no mining inside PAs or within 1 km.
[87:2:7] # Global coverage
[87:2:8] - **2014:** protected areas covered **15.2% of land** and **8.4% of coastal-marine areas** (marine areas under national jurisdiction).
[87:2:9] - **30x30** = Target 3 of the **Kunming-Montreal GBF** (2022): 30% of land and oceans by 2030; **OECMs** (e.g. Aravalli Biodiversity Park, Gurugram, India's first, 2022) count towards it. **WDPA** is run by **UNEP-WCMC** with IUCN.
[87:2:10] > Exam angle: NP = no biomass collection; ESZ = shock absorber under EP Act; community reserve statements; 2014 coverage figure.
[87:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.10-14 (NP vs sanctuary rights), 06 p.4-6 (ESZ, conservation/community reserves, UPSC 2014 PYQ); PMF Environment Part 3 p.42-47 (ESZ activities; UPSC 2023 community reserve); Shankar Environment Part 13 p.9-12; NextGen Rocket Environment p.25; UN SDG Report 2016 Goal 14 (unstats.un.org: 8.4% marine 2014); app notes 5:87 sub 1-3
[87:2:12] - **Ocean protection (Apr 2026):** nearly **10%** of the ocean protected, but only ~**3%** fully/highly protected; 1.66% of the high seas.
[87:2:13] - **Clearance:** projects affecting wildlife in or around PAs need clearance from the **Standing Committee of the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL)**.
[87:2:14] - **Wildlife sanctuaries** are notified by the **State Government under the WPA 1972**, not by UNESCO.
[87:2:15] - **OECM:** recognised by conservation **outcomes**; recognition does **not change land ownership or legal authority** (sacred groves, greenbelts, wetlands).
[87:2:16] - **Community Reserve purpose:** protects **fauna, flora and traditional/cultural values and practices** of the community.
## SUB 3 | National Parks, Marine Protected Areas and ICMBAs
[87:3:0] TABLE head: Protected area | Where / note
  [87:3:0.0] Valley of Flowers NP | Uttarakhand (Chamoli); lies completely in the temperate alpine zone; with Nanda Devi NP the World Heritage Site and BR core
  [87:3:0.1] Silent Valley NP | Kerala (Palakkad); tropical evergreen forest; hydro project dropped (Silent Valley movement)
  [87:3:0.2] Desert National Park | Rajasthan (Jaisalmer–Barmer); Great Indian Bustard
  [87:3:0.3] Keibul Lamjao NP | Manipur; floating NP on Loktak phumdis
  [87:3:0.4] Suklaphanta (Shuklaphanta) | Nepal (wildlife reserve, an NP since 2017)
  [87:3:0.5] Ntangki NP | Nagaland – captive-bred Asian Giant Tortoises released
[87:3:1] # Marine conservation
[87:3:2] - **First marine sanctuary and first Marine National Park:** **Gulf of Kachchh** (Jamnagar, Gujarat; corals, molluscs, dolphins, turtles, sea birds) – "the Marine/Oceanic National Park" of India = **Kachchh**.
[87:3:3] - **Gulf of Mannar Marine NP** (Tamil Nadu) is a marine NP; Bhitarkanika, Gahirmatha and Sundarbans are mangrove/turtle areas, not marine NPs.
[87:3:4] - **National Centre for Marine Biodiversity (NCMB):** India's first, at **Jamnagar**, Gujarat.
[87:3:5] - India has identified **106 Important Coastal and Marine Biodiversity Areas (ICMBAs)**; **Naupada** ICMBA (swamp) is in **Srikakulam**, AP.
[87:3:6] - **ICMAM** (Integrated Coastal and Marine Area Management) Project Directorate: **Chennai** (MoES; launched 1998).
[87:3:7] - Palk Bay (448 km²) = first **Dugong Conservation Reserve**; A&N and Lakshadweep = India's first **Hope Spots** (2013, Mission Blue).
[87:3:8] > Exam angle: which NP is in which State/zone; first marine NP = Gulf of Kachchh; NCMB Jamnagar; 106 ICMBAs.
[87:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.2 (NCMB Jamnagar), p.19, p.56; NextGen Environment APPSC 03 p.8 (Silent Valley); PMF Species & PAs Part 3 p.1 (Marine NP Gulf of Kachchh, India's first), p.3 (Naupada swamp, Srikakulam), p.35 (Valley of Flowers); Shankar Environment Part 5 p.20 (ICMAM), Part 13 p.12 (MPAs); Rocket CA 2026 Part 02 p.144 (Desert NP, Rajasthan); app notes 5:87 sub 5-6
[87:3:10] - **Vaan Island** (Gulf of Mannar Marine NP): coral restoration (Jun 2026).
[87:3:11] - **IBAs** are designated by **BirdLife International**; Indian partner **BNHS**.
[87:3:12] - **Anamalai TR** (TN): India's first **Hornbill Conservation Centre** (2026).
[87:3:13] - **Great Indian Bustard (Godawan)** is the **State bird of Rajasthan**.
[87:3:14] - **TRAFFIC** (1976): wildlife-trade monitoring network of **WWF and IUCN**; IUCN keeps the **Red List**.
[87:3:15] - **IUCN** publishes the **Red List** of threatened species and defines PA categories.
[87:3:16] - **TRAFFIC**, the WWF–IUCN wildlife-trade network, was set up in **1976**.
## SUB 4 | Gene Banks, Seed Vaults and Cryopreservation
[87:4:0] - **Cryopreservation:** in **liquid nitrogen at −196 °C**; the gas used in cryo-banks is **nitrogen**; metabolism stops. Stores gametes, embryos, seeds, pollen, tissues, DNA – **semen straws / cattle sperm for artificial insemination** are kept in liquid nitrogen.
[87:4:1] - Seeds keep longest in **cool and dry** conditions (low moisture and temperature slow respiration and fungi).
[87:4:2] TABLE head: Facility | Location / fact
  [87:4:2.0] Svalbard Global Seed Vault | Spitsbergen, Norway; world's largest secure seed vault, in permafrost (~−18 °C)
  [87:4:2.1] Chang La seed vault | High-altitude pass in Ladakh; joint venture of NBPGR and DIHAR (DRDO)
  [87:4:2.2] National Gene Bank | ICAR-NBPGR, New Delhi
  [87:4:2.3] International Rice Genebank | IRRI, Los Baños, Philippines
  [87:4:2.4] Field gene bank | NBRI's Banthara (Lucknow) – preserves endangered plants, identifies useful wild plants, checks biopiracy
  [87:4:2.5] Millennium Seed Bank | Kew (Wakehurst), UK
[87:4:3] - APPSC G1: all three seed-vault statements (Svalbard, Chang La, NBPGR+DIHAR) are **correct** → "none incorrect".
[87:4:4] - ICAR bureaux: NBAGR **Karnal** (livestock), NBFGR **Lucknow** (fish), NBAIM **Mau** (microbes); 2nd National Gene Bank (Budget 2025-26): 10 lakh lines. **LaCONES** (CCMB Hyderabad) = India's frozen zoo.
[87:4:5] > Exam angle: −196 °C / liquid nitrogen (asked four times), Svalbard = Norway, rice gene bank = Philippines.
[87:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.7 (Svalbard, Norway), 06 p.6-7 (National Gene Bank NBPGR, cryopreservation −196 °C); NextGen Rocket Environment p.44 (cryobank ex-situ); Praveen CA-360 Aug 2026 p.45 (NBRI Banthara, Lucknow); app notes 5:87 sub 8
[87:4:7] - **LaCONES** with Nehru Zoological Park bred the **Indian mouse deer** for reintroduction.
[87:4:8] - **Field gene banks** are living collections for **vegetatively propagated crops and crops with recalcitrant seeds** (mango, coconut, banana).
[87:4:9] - **Svalbard** capacity: **4.5 million** seed samples (capacity, not holdings).

## SUB 6 | Community Conservation – Sacred Groves and the Bishnois
[87:6:0] - **Sacred groves:** forest patches preserved by communities on **religious belief** (trees and wildlife venerated) – a **traditional method of conserving tree cover**; an **in-situ** practice, comparable to today's **biosphere reserves** (community-protected nature).
[87:6:1] TABLE head: Local name | State
  [87:6:1.0] Devrai / Devrahati | Maharashtra
  [87:6:1.1] Kavu | Kerala
  [87:6:1.2] Orans | Rajasthan
  [87:6:1.3] Law Kyntang / Law Lyngdoh | Meghalaya
  [87:6:1.4] Devarakadu | Karnataka
  [87:6:1.5] Sarna | Jharkhand
[87:6:2] - **Bishnois, Khejarli (Jodhpur), 1730:** **Amrita Devi** and **363** Bishnois hugged khejri trees and were killed by the king's men.
[87:6:3] - **Amrita Devi Bishnoi Wildlife Protection Award** (GoI): individuals/communities from **rural areas** showing courage in protecting wildlife; **Rs 1 lakh** cash.
[87:6:4] > Exam angle: sacred groves = traditional/in-situ conservation; Bishnois tree-hugging; award description.
[87:6:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.5 (sacred groves); Shankar Environment Part 13 p.12-13 (sacred groves), Part 11 p.14 (Khejarli 1730), Part 14 p.9 (Amrita Devi Bishnoi award); PMF Environment Part 3 p.47, p.53; NextGen Rocket Environment p.44; app notes 5:87 sub 7

=== NOTES 5:89 | Species-specific Conservation Projects – Tiger, Elephant, Dolphin, Gib, Vulture, Cheetah
## SUB 0 | Project Tiger – Launch, First Reserves and Tiger Reserves
[89:0:0] # Launch
[89:0:1] - **Project Tiger:** launched **1973** (Centrally Sponsored Scheme) on the advice of a **task force set up by PM Indira Gandhi**; aim = **save the tiger from extinction** by keeping viable populations in their natural habitats (core-buffer strategy).
[89:0:2] - **First reserve:** **Jim Corbett NP (Uttarakhand)**, under Project Tiger from **1 April 1973**; Corbett = India's first NP (1936, Hailey NP); not Bandhavgarh, Gir or Sundarbans.
[89:0:3] - **First nine reserves (1973):** Corbett, Kanha, Manas, Palamau, Similipal, Melghat, Bandipur, **Ranthambhore** and Sundarbans – so Ranthambhore became a tiger reserve in **1973** (1955 and 1980 are distractors; Ranthambhore NP itself dates from 1980).
[89:0:4] - **Launch order of projects:** Project Tiger 1973 → Crocodile project 1975 → Project Elephant 1992 → Indian Rhino Vision 2020 (2005) → Project Snow Leopard 2009 → Project Lion and Project Dolphin 2020 → Project Cheetah 2022.
[89:0:5] - **Five new national projects (MoEFCC, 2026):** dolphin, Asian elephant, **gharial**, **GIB**, **Olive Ridley** (not snow leopard).
[89:0:6] - **Tiger = National Animal of India**; the special projects in India's wildlife programme are for **tigers and elephants** (Project Tiger 1973, Project Elephant 1992).
[89:0:7] # Tiger reserves – famous ones
[89:0:8] TABLE head: Reserve | Fact
  [89:0:8.0] Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam (AP) | Largest TR – core 2,596 sq km, total ~3,728 sq km (NTCA: core 2,595.72 + buffer 1,132.10); AP's only TR; so "India's largest tiger habitat" = Andhra Pradesh
  [89:0:8.1] Manas (Assam) | One of the first nine (1973); known for tigers (also an elephant reserve, UNESCO site)
  [89:0:8.2] Sariska, Ranthambhore (Rajasthan) | Tiger reserves (not lion, deer or bear)
  [89:0:8.3] Kanha (MP) | Mascot Bhoorsingh the Barasingha (first TR with a mascot)
  [89:0:8.4] Kamlang (Arunachal) | 50th tiger reserve (2017)
  [89:0:8.5] Pakke (Arunachal) | India Biodiversity Award 2016 for its Hornbill Nest Adoption Programme
  [89:0:8.6] Bandipur (Karnataka) | Among the first to use drones (UAVs) for wildlife management and fire watch
  [89:0:8.7] Madhav (MP) | 58th and newest TR (March 2025); 57th Ratapani (Dec 2024)
[89:0:9] - **Chilka** is a lagoon / Ramsar site, **NOT** a tiger reserve (Dudhwa, Kanha, Manas are).
[89:0:10] - **Now (Sep 2026): 58 tiger reserves**, started with 9 in 1973.
[89:0:11] - **Corbett renaming (Oct 2021):** MoS Ashwini Kumar Choubey said Corbett would be renamed **Ramganga National Park** (its 1950s name); no renaming was notified – the park keeps Corbett's name.
[89:0:12] - **Corridors:** projects in tiger corridors need **NBWL Standing Committee** clearance; a third railway line threatens the **Satpura-Melghat** corridor.
[89:0:13] > Exam angle: "first TR" = Corbett; "largest TR" = Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam; "not a TR" = Chilka.
