## SUB 1 | Tiger Estimation, NTCA and Global Tiger Efforts
[89:1:0] # Counting tigers
[89:1:1] - **Pugmark technique:** old method – footprints used to **estimate the population** of tigers and other wild animals; now only an index of occurrence.
[89:1:2] - **Now:** **camera trapping** (stripes; **ExtractCompare** software) + **DNA from scats**; census is based on **double sampling** (ground survey + camera traps).
[89:1:3] - **M-STrIPES** = **Monitoring System for Tigers – Intensive Protection and Ecological Status**: software-based patrolling and monitoring system launched in tiger reserves by **NTCA and WII in 2010** → context = **maintenance of tiger reserves**; double sampling + M-STrIPES are used for **counting tigers**.
[89:1:4] - **All India Tiger Estimation:** every **4 years** by **NTCA with WII**; 2022 (5th cycle) = **3,682** tigers (upper limit 3,925); India has ~**70-75%** of the world's wild tigers.
[89:1:5] TABLE head: State (2022) | Tigers
  [89:1:5.0] Madhya Pradesh | 785
  [89:1:5.1] Karnataka | 563
  [89:1:5.2] Uttarakhand | 560
  [89:1:5.3] Maharashtra | 444
[89:1:6] # NTCA
[89:1:7] - **NTCA:** statutory body under the **2006 WPA amendment** (Tiger Task Force advice); chaired by the **Union Environment Minister**; administers Project Tiger; **Sec 38V(3):** Tiger Conservation Plan for every reserve.
[89:1:8] - **MEE 2022:** 51 TRs assessed, **12 "Excellent"**.
[89:1:9] - **NTCA is also the implementing agency of Project Cheetah** (Kuno NP).
[89:1:10] # Global efforts
[89:1:11] - **Global Tiger Forum:** 1993-94, HQ **New Delhi**.
[89:1:12] - **Tiger Summit 2010:** **St Petersburg (Russia)**, 21-24 Nov 2010 – **TX2** = double wild tigers by **2022** (India achieved it in 2018); began **International Tiger Day, 29 July**.
[89:1:13] - **CA|TS** = **Conservation Assured | Tiger Standards** (2013): **14** Indian TRs accredited on Tiger Day 2021 (23 now).
[89:1:14] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 03 p.84-91; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.2-5; NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.1; app notes 5:89 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Vultures and Diclofenac
[89:2:0] # Why vultures vanished
[89:2:1] - **Cause:** **diclofenac**, a **painkiller (NSAID)** given to **cattle**; vultures eating the carcasses suffer **kidney failure (visceral gout)** – not viral/bacterial infection, food scarcity or nesting loss; confirmed by **Peregrine Fund** research (May 2003).
[89:2:2] - **Decline first noticed:** **Keoladeo NP, Bharatpur (1998)**.
[89:2:3] - **Ban:** veterinary diclofenac banned **May 2006**; **aceclofenac and ketoprofen** banned for animals (2023).
[89:2:4] - **Meloxicam** = safe alternative; it is a **non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID)** (prednisolone, betamethasone, hydrocortisone are steroids; atropine, alum, ranitidine are not anti-inflammatories).
[89:2:5] - **9** vulture species in India; **4 resident ones CR**: white-rumped (white-backed), slender-billed, long-billed (Indian), red-headed.
[89:2:6] # Conservation
[89:2:7] - **Vulture Recovery Plan / Action Plan 2006**; **Action Plan for Vulture Conservation 2020-25**: **State-level vulture committees**, more breeding centres, Vulture Safe Zones.
[89:2:8] - **Tamil Nadu** was the first to set up a **State-Level Committee for Vulture Conservation** (GO 19 Oct 2022).
[89:2:9] - **Jatayu Conservation Breeding Centre, Pinjore (Haryana)** – first (2001); **Asia's first Gyps Vulture Reintroduction Programme (2016): Pinjore** – two Himalayan griffons released.
[89:2:10] - **SAVE** = **Saving Asia's Vultures from Extinction** (consortium; 2011 Nepal-India programme).
[89:2:11] - **Coringa WLS (AP)** hosts the CR **white-backed and long-billed vultures**.
[89:2:12] - **Aug 2026:** world's first release of captive-bred **slender-billed vultures** (5 birds, BNHS centre, **Assam**).
[89:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.6; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.9-12; PMF Environment 03 p.99-101; https://kygcms.tn.gov.in/cms_migrated/document/press_release/pr191022_e_1826.pdf (TN committee, web search); app notes 5:89 sub 5
## SUB 3 | Ganges River Dolphin and Project Dolphin
[89:3:0] - **National Aquatic Animal:** **Ganges River Dolphin** (*Platanista gangetica*), declared **5 October 2009** (not crocodile, Olive Ridley, gharial, coral or jellyfish); **5 October = National Dolphin Day**.
[89:3:1] - **Dolphins are mammals** (cetaceans), not fish, amphibians or reptiles.
[89:3:2] - **Status:** IUCN **Endangered** (not Vulnerable); WPA **Schedule I**; CITES App. I; found in **India, Nepal, Bangladesh** (Ganga-Brahmaputra-Meghna, Karnaphuli-Sangu).
[89:3:3] - **Threats:** **dams and barrages**, pollution incl. **agricultural chemicals**, **fishing-net entanglement**, poaching for oil – **NOT** "more crocodiles".
[89:3:4] - **Places:** **Vikramshila Gangetic Dolphin Sanctuary – Bhagalpur, Bihar**; **National Dolphin Research Centre – Patna** (India's and Asia's first); **National Chambal Sanctuary** (MP-Rajasthan-UP) = Gangetic dolphin, **mugger** and **gharial**.
[89:3:5] - **Guwahati city animal:** the **Gangetic dolphin** ("Sihu"), declared mascot by Kamrup Metropolitan district (June 2016) – first Indian city animal.
[89:3:6] - **Project Dolphin (2020):** riverine **and marine** dolphins and other cetaceans; first national estimate **6,327** dolphins (2025).
[89:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.4; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.19-20; PMF Environment 03 p.98; https://www.downtoearth.org.in/news/wildlife-biodiversity/gangetic-dolphins-declared-as-official-mascot-of-guwahati-54304 (web search); app notes 5:89 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Project Elephant
[89:4:0] - **Launched February 1992** (the 1991-92 plan year) as a **Centrally Sponsored Scheme** – not 1990.
[89:4:1] - **Objectives:** protect elephants, habitats and **corridors**; address **man-animal conflict**; **welfare of captive (domesticated) elephants** – so "only wild elephants" is wrong.
[89:4:2] - **33 Elephant Reserves in 14 States**; merged with Project Tiger in 2023 ("Project Tiger and Elephant Division").
[89:4:3] - **MIKE** = **Monitoring the Illegal Killing of Elephants** (CITES; South Asia since 2003).
[89:4:4] - **Biology:** herds led by a **female** (matriarch); gestation up to **22 months**; calves till about 50s (not "40 only"); largest State population = **Karnataka** (not Kerala); tuskless males = **makhnas**.
[89:4:5] - **Facts:** **National Heritage Animal (2010)**; India has ~**60%** of Asian elephants; population **22,446** (Apr 2026); **Rayala ER** = AP's only elephant reserve.
[89:4:6] - **Human cost:** elephants and tigers together kill about **one person a day** in India (MoEF data).
[89:4:7] - **Chronology:** WPA 1972 → Project Tiger 1973 → Project Elephant 1992 → Biological Diversity Act 2002.
[89:4:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.1-2; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.6-8; PMF Environment 03 p.95-96; https://www.savetheelephants.org/news/one-human-killed-each-day-in-last-3-years-as-conflict-with-wildlife-escalates-india (web search); app notes 5:89 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Project Cheetah, IBCA and Project Lion
[89:5:0] # Cheetah
[89:5:1] - **Cheetah** = the large wild cat that became **extinct in India (declared 1952)** – only large mammal lost since Independence; Asiatic cheetah survives only in **Iran**; India brought **African** cheetahs.
[89:5:2] - **Project Cheetah:** **world's first intercontinental large-carnivore translocation**; restores **open forest and grassland**; site **Kuno NP (Sheopur, MP)**; implementing agency **NTCA** (not AWBI).
[89:5:3] - **8 Namibian cheetahs (17 Sep 2022) = 5 females + 3 males**; book "The End of a Trail – The Cheetah in India" = **Divyabhanusinh**.
[89:5:4] TABLE head: Batch | Source | Date
  [89:5:4.0] 8 | Namibia | 17 Sep 2022, Kuno
  [89:5:4.1] 12 | South Africa | 18 Feb 2023
  [89:5:4.2] 2 females | Botswana | May 2026
[89:5:5] - **Second site:** **Gandhi Sagar WLS (MP)** – two males moved from Kuno, April 2025.
[89:5:6] # International Big Cat Alliance
[89:5:7] - Launched **April 2023, Mysuru**, for **50 years of Project Tiger**; treaty-based (2025); **Secretariat New Delhi** (not Geneva).
[89:5:8] - **7 big cats:** tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar, puma.
[89:5:9] - Open to **96 range countries** plus non-range countries.
[89:5:10] - **Cabinet (Feb 2024): ₹150 crore one-time support for five years (2023-24 to 2027-28)** – not two years.
[89:5:11] # Project Lion
[89:5:12] - **2020**; Asiatic lions of **Gir**; **891** lions (2025).
[89:5:13] - **Palpur-Kuno (MP)** was selected as the second home for **Gir lions** (SC order 2013); Gujarat did not act → Kuno went to cheetahs.
[89:5:14] - **Barda WLS** (Gujarat) proposed instead – criticised as **too close to Gir**.
[89:5:15] - **2018 Gir lion deaths:** **Canine Distemper Virus**.
[89:5:16] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.5; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.5-6, p.16; PMF Environment 03 p.87-94; app notes 5:89 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Great Indian Bustard, CMS and Other Species
[89:6:0] # Great Indian Bustard
[89:6:1] - *Ardeotis nigriceps* (Godawan), Rajasthan's state bird; IUCN **Critically Endangered**; main range **Thar (Rajasthan)**; in AP at **Rollapadu**.
[89:6:2] - **Threat:** collision with **overhead power lines** in solar and wind zones.
[89:6:3] - **M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (March 2024):** modified (did not uphold unchanged) the 2021 blanket undergrounding order; recognised a **right against adverse effects of climate change** under **Arts 14 and 21**.
[89:6:4] - Breeding at **Sam and Ramdevra, Jaisalmer**.
[89:6:5] # CMS (Bonn Convention)
[89:6:6] - **COP13: Gandhinagar, Feb 2020**; mascot **Gibi = GIB** (not Amur falcon); **Asian elephant, GIB and Bengal florican** added to **Appendix I** (endangered migratory species) – not the Bengal tiger.
[89:6:7] - **COP14: Samarkand, Feb 2024**. Amur falcon stopover: **Doyang reservoir**; **Pangti** = "Falcon Capital of the World" (Nagaland).
[89:6:8] # Other species
[89:6:9] - **Snow leopard:** **Nepal** was the first country with a **climate-smart snow leopard landscape plan** (Aug 2017); Project Snow Leopard **2009**; snow leopard = national symbol of **Kyrgyzstan** (Dec 2023).
[89:6:10] - **Naturally found in India:** black-necked crane, flying squirrel, snow leopard – **not** the cheetah (extinct).
[89:6:11] - **Sloth bear** = the street-performing ("dancing") bear.
[89:6:12] - **Gharials:** best seen in the **Chambal River** (National Chambal Sanctuary, 1979; India's only **tri-state riverine PA**: MP, Rajasthan, UP).
[89:6:13] - **Kharai camel (Kutch):** **swims up to 3 km** in seawater and **grazes mangroves**; it is domesticated (statement 3 false); survives in **coastal and dry ecosystems**.
[89:6:14] - **Crocodile Breeding and Management Project: 1975** (FAO-UNDP); **Baula** (saltwater crocodile) at **Dangamal, Bhitarkanika**; mugger at Ramatirtha (1984).
[89:6:15] - **Endangered status:** Asian elephant = **Endangered**; Indian crocodiles: gharial **CR**, mugger **VU**, saltwater **LC**.
[89:6:16] - **Whale shark:** Gujarat protection programme since **2004** (not 2006).
[89:6:17] - **Indian Rhino Vision 2020:** **2005**, Assam.
[89:6:18] ~~ Sources: PMF Species & PAN 01 p.63, p.66; PMF Environment 03 p.72, p.91-92, p.99; NextGen Environment APPSC 07 p.3-5; Rocket Environment p.31, p.33-34; https://www.business-standard.com/amp/article/news-ians/in-a-first-nepal-launches-climate-smart-snow-leopard-plan-117082301491_1.html (web search); app notes 5:89 sub 4, 7, 9
## SUB 7 | Marine Turtles, Dugong and Coastal Conservation
[89:7:0] - **Olive Ridley:** main killer = **mechanised fishing boats/trawler nets** (hence **Turtle Excluder Devices**); **Operation Olivia** = annual **Indian Coast Guard** operation off **Odisha** – nesting season is roughly **November-May** (not August).
[89:7:1] - **Mass nesting (arribada):** **Rushikulya (Odisha)**; **Srikakulam and Vizianagaram beaches (AP)**; National Marine Turtle Action Plan **2021**.
[89:7:2] - **Dugong:** a **mammal** (vulnerable), **herbivorous** (seagrass), **Schedule I**; found only in Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Gulf of Kutch and Andaman & Nicobar – **not the entire coast**; first **Dugong Conservation Reserve: Palk Bay, TN (2022)**.
[89:7:3] - **Hope Spots** (Mission Blue + IUCN): **Lakshadweep** and **Andaman and Nicobar**.
[89:7:4] - **MISHTI (2023):** mangrove restoration.
[89:7:5] TABLE head: Area | State | Focus
  [89:7:5.0] Gulf of Mannar | Tamil Nadu | Coral reefs, dugong
  [89:7:5.1] Malvan Marine Sanctuary | Maharashtra | Corals
  [89:7:5.2] Coringa WLS | AP (Kakinada) | Mangroves, Godavari estuary – not corals or dugong
  [89:7:5.3] Bhitarkanika | Odisha | Saltwater crocodile, mangroves
[89:7:6] - **Coringa:** often called India's **second-largest mangrove stretch** (PMF ranks Bhitarkanika second).

## SUB 8 | Species Recovery Programme and Conservation Organisations
[89:8:0] # Recovery programme
[89:8:1] - **Species Recovery Programme** under CSS-**Integrated Development of Wildlife Habitats** for **22** critically endangered species (snow leopard, Asiatic lion, GIB, Gangetic dolphin, dugong, vultures, Hangul, marine turtles…); **gharial and sloth bear** only recommended for inclusion (Jun 2026).
[89:8:2] - **Recovery Programme for Critically Endangered Species** funded via the **National CAMPA Advisory Council** for an initial **5 years** (APPSC 2019).
[89:8:3] - **Project HANUMAN (AP, 3 March 2026):** to reduce human-wildlife conflict.
[89:8:4] # Organisations

  [89:8:5.0] IUCN (1948) | — | Gland, Switzerland
  [89:8:5.1] WWF (1961) | Giant panda | Gland

  [89:8:5.3] WTI (1998) | — | Noida
  [89:8:5.4] WII (1982) | — | Dehradun
[89:8:6] - **BNHS** is an **NGO** (not an autonomous body under MoEF); it does action-based research, education and public awareness and runs nature trails and camps.
[89:8:7] - **Great hornbill** has a **casque** on its bill.

=== NOTES 5:90 | Forest and Wildlife Legal Framework – Ifa 1927, Fca 1980, Wpa 1972, Bd Act 2002
## SUB 0 | Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 – Year, Scope and Key Sections
[90:0:0] # Year and scope
[90:0:1] - **Enacted by Parliament in 1972** (assent 9 Sept 1972) – not 1962, 1974, 1982, 1986 or 1990; first comprehensive wildlife law.
[90:0:2] - **Protects wild animals, birds and plants** and manages their habitats – **not animals only**; it is the Act that **regulates National Parks and Wildlife Sanctuaries** (not EPA 1986, FCA 1980 or BD Act 2002).
[90:0:3] - **Poaching** = illegal hunting of wild animals – barred by the Act.
[90:0:4] - **66 sections, 7 chapters**; amended 1982, 1986, 1991, 1993, 2002, 2006, 2013, **2022**.
[90:0:5] # Key sections
[90:0:6] TABLE head: Section | Provision
  [90:0:6.0] 2(1) | "Animal" = amphibians, birds, mammals, reptiles, their young, eggs of birds and reptiles
  [90:0:6.1] 2(37) | "Wildlife"
  [90:0:6.2] 9 | Hunting of scheduled animals prohibited, subject to exceptions
  [90:0:6.3] 11 | Animal dangerous to human life (or crops), diseased or disabled beyond recovery may be captured/killed with the Chief Wildlife Warden's permission
  [90:0:6.4] 12 | Permits for education, research, scientific management, translocation
  [90:0:6.5] 38J | Teasing, molesting, injuring or feeding animals in a zoo prohibited
  [90:0:6.6] 39(1) | Wild animals = State Government property; in a Centre-declared sanctuary/NP = Central Government
  [90:0:6.7] 38V(3) | Tiger Conservation Plan for every TR (2006)
  [90:0:6.8] 62 | Centre may notify a non-Schedule I animal as vermin
[90:0:7] - **Gharial, Indian wild ass, wild buffalo** cannot be hunted by anyone except as the law permits (UPSC 2017: all three).
[90:0:8] - **UPSC 2022 (official key "1 and 2"):** wild animals are government property; a protected animal gets equal protection inside or outside PAs; mere *apprehension* of danger is not enough to kill it.
[90:0:9] - **Protected animal may be killed** when it endangers human life **and** when it is diseased – both true, but disease does not explain the danger clause.
[90:0:10] - **Mining:** barred inside NPs and sanctuaries; SC bars mining within **1 km** of every NP/sanctuary unless a larger ESZ is notified.
[90:0:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.25; NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.14; PMF Environment 06 p.71-76; app notes 5:90 sub 4
## SUB 1 | WPA Schedules and the 2022 Amendment
[90:1:0] TABLE head: Before 2022 (6 schedules) | After 2022 (4 schedules)
  [90:1:0.0] I and II: absolute protection (tiger, rhino) | I: highest protection
  [90:1:0.1] III and IV: lesser (game species) | II: lower protection
  [90:1:0.2] V: vermin (common crow, fruit bats, rats, mice) | III: protected plants
  [90:1:0.3] VI: specified plants – cultivation only with a licence | IV: CITES-listed specimens
[90:1:1] - **Number of schedules:** **6** in the 1972 Act (the usual key); **4** since the 2022 amendment (in force 1 April 2023).
[90:1:2] - **Schedule I effect:** a tortoise in Schedule I gets **the same protection as the tiger** (not "extinct in the wild" or "endemic").
[90:1:3] - **Schedule VI (old):** a **licence is required to cultivate** the plant; a specified plant cannot be picked, uprooted or traded without permission.
[90:1:4] - **Flying fox** = a **fruit bat** (Pteropus), not a kite, stork or vulture; it does **not** feed on blood. It was **vermin (Schedule V)**; since 2022 it is in **Schedule II**.
[90:1:5] - **Schedule I examples:** Asiatic lion, tiger, elephant, snow leopard, rhino, Gangetic dolphin, dugong, GIB, **blackbuck**; mugger (Kurnool, Sep 2026) and rock eagle-owl (Dharmavaram, Aug 2026) in news.
[90:1:6] # 2022 amendment
[90:1:7] - **Schedules 6 → 4**; vermin schedule deleted (Sec 62 power stays with the **Central Government**); **CITES** provisions (Management and Scientific Authorities); Centre regulates **invasive alien species** (African catfish, Lantana).
[90:1:8] - Voluntary **surrender of captive animals without compensation**; Chief Wildlife Warden in every State; Centre may notify conservation reserves.
[90:1:9] - Fines: specially protected animals – minimum **₹25,000** (from ₹10,000); general violations – maximum **₹1 lakh** (from ₹25,000).
[90:1:10] # Earlier amendments
[90:1:11] - **2002:** **NBWL** replaced the Indian Board for Wildlife; **Conservation Reserves** (government land, e.g. **Tsarap Chu**) and **Community Reserves** (private/community land).
[90:1:12] - **2006:** **NTCA and WCCB**.
[90:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.76-78; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.12; app notes 5:90 sub 5
## SUB 2 | Protected Areas and Community Reserves under WPA
[90:2:0] - **Five kinds:** wildlife sanctuary, national park, conservation reserve, community reserve, tiger reserve.
[90:2:1] - **Community Reserve (Sec 36C):** private/community land, declared by the **State Government**; run by a **Community Reserve Management Committee (Sec 36D)** – not the Chief Wildlife Warden.
[90:2:2] - In a community reserve **hunting is not allowed** and people may **collect non-timber forest produce**, but **traditional agriculture (jhum) is not allowed** → UPSC 2023: "only two" statements correct.
[90:2:3] - **NP vs sanctuary:** NP – no grazing, no human activity except as the Chief Wildlife Warden permits; sanctuary – regulated grazing.
[90:2:4] - **India's PAs:** **1,75,169.42 sq km = 5.32%** of land (2026).
[90:2:5] - **Eco-sensitive zone:** the **National Chambal Sanctuary (MP)** was notified as an ESZ on **2 March 2020**.
[90:2:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.71-72; Rocket Environment p.25-26; https://www.gktoday.in/national-chambal-sanctuary-declared-as-eco-sensitive-zone (web search); app notes 5:90 sub 5, 9
## SUB 3 | Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 / Van Adhiniyam
[90:3:0] - **Enacted 1980** (27 Dec 1980, in force from **25 Oct 1980**) – not 1976, 1978, 1981 or 1988.
[90:3:1] - **Sec 2:** **prior approval of the Central Government (MoEF)** to de-reserve a forest or use forest land for **non-forest purposes** – not the Collector, State or FSI. FCA = the Act that **regulates forest-land diversion**.
[90:3:2] - **2023 amendment:** renamed **Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980** (w.e.f. 29 Dec 2023); covers land notified as forest under IFA 1927 or any law, and land **recorded as forest on or after 25 Oct 1980**; **excludes land converted before 12 Dec 1996**.
[90:3:3] - **Exemptions:** strategic linear projects within **100 km** of IB/LoC/LAC; zoos, safaris, eco-tourism; no Gram Sabha consent required (a key criticism).
[90:3:4] - **Compensatory afforestation:** equal non-forest land, else **twice** the degraded forest land + **NPV**.
[90:3:5] - **T.N. Godavarman (1995 writ; 1996 order):** "forest" = every area recorded as forest **irrespective of ownership**; the 2023 amendment narrows this.
[90:3:6] - **AP diversions:** **3,474.57 ha** (1 Jan 2015-5 Feb 2019); **149.5687 ha** (1 Apr-31 Dec 2025).
[90:3:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.80-83; Rocket Environment p.12, p.18; app notes 5:90 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Indian Forest Act 1927 and Colonial Forest Laws
[90:4:0] TABLE head: Year | Law | Point
  [90:4:0.0] 1865 | First Indian Forest Act | Drafted 1865
  [90:4:0.1] 1878 | Indian Forest Act | Created reserved, protected, village forests
  [90:4:0.2] 1927 | Indian Forest Act | Consolidating law, still in force
[90:4:1] - **Degree of protection:** **Reserved > Protected > Village** forest; a **village forest** is a **reserved forest** assigned to a village community.
[90:4:2] - **Reserved forest (Ch II):** everything banned unless permitted; **Sec 26** = acts prohibited in a reserved forest, incl. punishable **trespass**.
[90:4:3] - **Protected forest:** activities allowed unless prohibited – people could take **head-loads of wood**, collect produce for their own use and **graze cattle** (entry not barred).
[90:4:4] - **Unclassed forest:** outside the reserved and protected categories. **Sec 35:** State may regulate non-government forests.
[90:4:5] - **2017 amendment** (ordinance 2017, Act 2018): **bamboo grown outside forest areas** removed from the definition of "tree" (**Sec 2(7)**) – may be felled and moved without permit. Bamboo **inside** forests is not freed.
[90:4:6] - **Colonial plantations:** British policy encouraged **monocropping through plantations** (tea, coffee, teak), a cause of environmental degradation.
[90:4:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.80, p.84; NextGen Environment APPSC 05 p.11; Rocket Environment p.18; app notes 5:90 sub 0, 2
## SUB 5 | National Forest Policy 1952 and 1988
[90:5:0] TABLE head: Feature | NFP 1952 | NFP 1988
  [90:5:0.0] National target | One-third | One-third (33%) of geographical area
  [90:5:0.1] Hills | 60% | Two-thirds
  [90:5:0.2] Classes / thrust | National, Protected, Village forests + Tree-lands (National Park not a class) | Ecological stability, people's participation
[90:5:1] - **NFP 1988 includes:** afforestation and wasteland development; reforestation in existing forests; **wood substitutes and alternative fuels** – NOT wide use of **insecticides and pesticides**. "Two-thirds of the country under forest" is wrong (hills only).
[90:5:2] - **Ecological balance:** Forest Policy, EPA 1986, Industrial and Educational Policy all relate to it (UPPSC: "all the above").
[90:5:3] - **Draft NFP 2018**; **NAPCC launched 2008** (not 2018).
[90:5:4] - **Order:** IFA 1927 → NFP 1952 → WPA 1972 → FCA 1980 → EPA 1986 → NFP 1988 → BD Act 2002 → FRA 2006.
[90:5:5] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.4, p.18; app notes 5:90 sub 3

  [90:6:0.6] AWBI | PCA Act 1960 | Chennai till 2018 → Ballabhgarh, Haryana | 1962

  [90:6:2.0] Save Kurma | Turtles

  [90:6:2.2] Clean Art | Mongoose-hair brushes

## SUB 7 | Biological Diversity Act 2002 and Which Act Protects What
[90:7:0] TABLE head: Act | What it does
  [90:7:0.0] WPA 1972 | Wild animals, birds, plants and habitats
  [90:7:0.1] EPA 1986 | Umbrella law – protection and improvement of the environment
  [90:7:0.2] FCA 1980 | Forest-land diversion
  [90:7:0.3] PCA Act 1960 | Cruelty to animals; parent Act of AWBI
  [90:7:0.4] BD Act 2002 | CBD, access and benefit sharing
[90:7:1] - **"Nature (Protection) Act, 2000"**, "Forests Protection Act 1982", "EPA 1996" do **not exist**.
[90:7:2] - **NGT** cannot hear **WPA 1972** or FRA 2006 cases.
[90:7:3] - **BD Act 2002:** three tiers – **NBA (Chennai, 2003)**, State Biodiversity Boards, **Biodiversity Management Committees** (prepare **People's Biodiversity Registers**); **Biodiversity Heritage Sites** under **Sec 37** (State Government).
[90:7:4] - **2023 amendment (in force 1 April 2024):** offences **decriminalised** (civil penalties); exemption for AYUSH practitioners and **BMC-certified** cultivated medicinal plants; NBA approval **180 → 90 days**; foreign entities **still need** prior NBA approval.
[90:7:5] - **AP (May 2026):** more than **13,500 BMCs**, **12,000 PBRs**.
[90:7:6] - **Constitution:** 42nd Amendment (1976) moved forests (**Entry 17A**) and wild animals and birds (**Entry 17B**) to the Concurrent List; inserted **Art 48A** (DPSP) and **Art 51A(g)** (Fundamental Duty). A State Bill amending WPA (e.g. Maharashtra 2026, Sec 12; leopard **Schedule I → II**) needs the **President's assent** because it amends a **central law**.
[90:7:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.12, p.40, p.66; NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.14; app notes 5:90 sub 1, 7, 9

=== NOTES 5:91 | Forest Rights Act 2006, Campa, Compensatory Afforestation, Jfm, Agroforestry
## SUB 0 | Afforestation, Forestry Terms and Their Benefits
[91:0:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [91:0:0.0] Afforestation | New forest on denuded, degraded or unproductive land
  [91:0:0.1] Reforestation | Re-establishing forest cover in existing / depleted forest areas
  [91:0:0.2] Social forestry | Trees for community needs; term used by the National Commission on Agriculture (1976)
  [91:0:0.3] Extension forestry | Trees along roadsides, canals and railway strips
  [91:0:0.4] Agroforestry | Trees + crops + livestock on the same land
[91:0:1] - **Benefits:** **afforestation controls floods** and **checks soil erosion by running water** (roots bind soil, slow run-off) – deforestation, overgrazing, urbanisation, tilling or removing topsoil worsen them.
[91:0:2] - **Floods worsened by:** unscientific agriculture, disturbing natural drainage channels, colonising flood-plains and river-beds – **NOT reforestation**.
[91:0:3] - **Criticism of social forestry:** drifted into **commercial monocultures** (eucalyptus); fix = mixed native species.
[91:0:4] - **Miyawaki method:** dense, multi-layered **mini-forests of native species in urban areas**; Japanese botanist **Akira Miyawaki**, **1970s**.
[91:0:5] - **Seed bomb (seed ball):** a ball of **mud/clay, dung and seeds** thrown on land to grow trees.
[91:0:6] - **Craib's thinning:** heavy early (advance) thinning of plantations, done in a regular crop **in anticipation of suppression** (I.J. Craib, South Africa).
[91:0:7] - **Wild animals** help natural regeneration through **seed dispersal** (e.g. elephants, hornbills).
[91:0:8] - **Vanamahotsav:** **K.M. Munshi, 1950**; first week of July.
[91:0:9] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.18; PMF Environment 06 p.90; PMF Environment 03 p.95; app notes 5:91 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Afforestation Schemes – NAP, NAEB, GIM, Nagar Van
[91:1:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Fact
  [91:1:0.0] NAEB | National Afforestation and Eco-development Board, set up by MoEF in August 1992
  [91:1:0.1] National Afforestation Programme (2002) | NAEB's flagship; decentralised, two-tier: Forest Development Agency (division) + JFMC (village); SFDA added later; now merged with GIM
  [91:1:0.2] Green India Mission | One of the 8 NAPCC missions; via JFMCs; partly National CAMPA
  [91:1:0.3] Nagar Van Yojana (2020) | Run by NAEB, funded by National CAMPA; 600 Nagar Vans + 400 Nagar Vatikas (2020-21 to 2026-27)
  [91:1:0.4] Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam | From 5 June 2024 (World Environment Day)
[91:1:1] - **Green India Mission goals:** increase forest/tree cover on **5 million ha** and improve the quality of forest cover on **another 5 million ha**; improve ecosystem services; raise forest-based livelihood income of about **3 million households** – "**2 million ha of non-forest land**" is NOT a goal.
[91:1:2] - **GIM revised 2021-30:** Aravallis, Western Ghats, Himalayas, mangroves; **CAG:** only **0.11 million ha** improved vs **1.4 million ha** target.
[91:1:3] - **NVY in AP:** **13** projects approved (2020-21 to 2023-24); 61 Nagar Vans sanctioned by 2024-25.
[91:1:4] - **Nyay Vatika (July 2025):** green space at the President's Bodyguard ground, Delhi, planted by the CJI and SC judges under the **Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam** campaign.
[91:1:5] - **State schemes:** **Apna Van Apna Dhan – Himachal Pradesh**; Haritha Haram – **Telangana**; Mukhyamantri Vriksharopan Protsahan Yojana – **Chhattisgarh**; AP – Great Green Wall, Nagar Van.
[91:1:6] - **AP State Forest Development Agency:** federates **22 FDAs**.
[91:1:7] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment Part 11 p.12; PMF Environment 06 p.88-89; Rocket Environment p.4; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.79; https://eparlib.sansad.in/bitstream/123456789/2988196/1/AU936_50zNvG.pdf (Lok Sabha reply, AP 13 projects; seen via web search, page not opened); https://lawchakra.in/legal-updates/cji-b-r-gavai-supreme-court-judges-van (web search); app notes 5:91 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Joint Forest Management and People's Forest Movements
[91:2:0] - **JFM:** origin **Arabari, West Bengal (1971-72)**; introduced by **NFP 1988**; **MoEF guidelines 1 June 1990** – JFM started in **1990**.
[91:2:1] - **AP:** JFM committees = **Vana Samrakshana Samithis (VSS)** – a **government-initiated** community conservation strategy (sacred groves, Arvari Sansad and Chipko are people's initiatives); Tribal Affairs Ministry ordered withdrawal of community titles given to **1,669 VSS**.
[91:2:2] - **Bishnois – Khejarli (Jodhpur), Rajasthan, 1730:** **Amrita Devi** and 363 Bishnois hugged **khejri** trees to stop felling for the Maharaja's palace.
[91:2:3] - **Amrita Devi Bishnoi Smriti / Wildlife Protection Award:** for **protection of forests and wildlife**.
[91:2:4] - **Chipko (1973, Garhwal, Uttarakhand):** **forest conservation** by hugging trees – Gaura Devi, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna.
[91:2:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.89; PMF Environment 03 p.53; Rocket Environment p.56; Shankar Environment Part 14 p.9; app notes 5:91 sub 4
## SUB 3 | Agroforestry
[91:3:0] - **National Agroforestry Policy, Feb 2014** – India the **first country** with one.
[91:3:1] - **GROW report (NITI Aayog, Feb 2024):** agroforestry covers **~8.65%** of India's geographical area (~28.42 million ha).
[91:3:2] - **ICAR-CAFRI:** **Jhansi**; **Sub-Mission on Agroforestry (SMAF)** under **PM-RKVY**; **TOFI** = MoEFCC-**USAID** programme.
[91:3:3] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.50; https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2005411 (web search: GROW 8.65%); app notes 5:91 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Compensatory Afforestation and CAMPA
[91:4:0] - **CA:** forest land diverted → **equal non-forest land**, or **twice the degraded forest land** (Central PSUs / no non-forest land); the agency pays **CA cost + NPV** before the project.
[91:4:1] - **CAMPA:** ad hoc by SC order (2004/2006); statutory via **Compensatory Afforestation Fund Act, 2016**: National and State Funds in the Public Accounts – **non-lapsable, interest-bearing**; split **90% States : 10% National**.
[91:4:2] - **National CAMPA** headed by the **Union Environment Minister**; exists at **national and State** levels; **people's participation is not mandatory** under the Act (UPSC 2019).
[91:4:3] - **Uses:** regeneration, wildlife, catchment treatment, village relocation, human-wildlife conflict, fires; **not** private urban housing. **₹66,000+ crore** held (2024), only **30-35%** used.
[91:4:4] - **FC Rules 2022:** **Accredited CA** = plantations raised **in advance** (land banks); dropped forest-dwellers' **consent** before diversion – disputed by **NCST**.
[91:4:5] - **Van (S.E.S.) Rules 2023:** afforestation under the **Green Credit Programme** can be swapped for CA.
[91:4:6] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.90-91; Shankar Environment Part 11 p.12; app notes 5:91 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Forest Rights Act 2006
[91:5:0] - **Nodal ministry:** **Tribal Affairs** (not Environment); cut-off **13 December 2005**.
[91:5:1] - **Eligible:** forest-dwelling **STs**; **OTFDs** with **3 generations (75 years)** of residence.
[91:5:2] - **Rights:** individual title on cultivated land up to **4 ha**; **community forest resource** management; **ownership of minor forest produce** – FRA defines MFP to include **bamboo**, tendu, honey, canes.
[91:5:3] - **Gram Sabha** starts the claim process; District Level Committee decides.
[91:5:4] - **Critical wildlife habitat:** NP/sanctuary areas kept inviolate, defined in the FRA.
[91:5:5] - **AP (2022):** **2,12,650** titles (2,10,828 individual, **1,822** community), mostly in **ITDA** areas; **Koya and Kondh** oppose **Polavaram** over land rights and rehabilitation.
[91:5:6] > UPSC 2019: IFA amendment frees bamboo only on non-forest land (statement 1 wrong); FRA bamboo = MFP and MFP ownership (2 and 3 right).
[91:5:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment 06 p.83-85; app notes 5:91 sub 5

=== NOTES 5:92 | Climate Change – Greenhouse Effect, Greenhouse Gases, Radiative Forcing, Evidence and Impacts
## SUB 0 | Greenhouse Gases – Which Are and Which Are NOT
[92:0:0] # The greenhouse gases
[92:0:1] TABLE head: Gas | Formula | Key fact
  [92:0:1.0] Water vapour | H2O | Most abundant GHG and the biggest overall (natural) contributor to the greenhouse effect (about half of it)
  [92:0:1.1] Carbon dioxide | CO2 | Main anthropogenic GHG; product of fossil-fuel combustion; about 66% of radiative forcing by long-lived GHGs (WMO); ~0.04% of air
  [92:0:1.2] Methane (marsh gas) | CH4 | Paddy fields, wetlands, cud-chewing animals, coal mines, landfills; main component of natural gas and biogas
  [92:0:1.3] Nitrous oxide (laughing gas) | N2O | Nitrogen fertilisers, burning fuels and crop residue; also a weak anaesthetic (used in anaesthesia)
  [92:0:1.4] Ozone | O3 | Stratospheric ozone = UV shield; tropospheric ozone = smog pollutant and GHG
  [92:0:1.5] CFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF6 | — | Synthetic (entirely man-made) fluorinated gases; CFCs are both GHG and ozone-depleting
[92:0:2] - **Natural GHGs:** water vapour, CO2, CH4, N2O, O3. **Synthetic:** CFCs, HFCs, PFCs, SF6 (do not occur naturally).
[92:0:3] - **Most important set:** **CO2, methane, nitrous oxide, water vapour**. **Most responsible pair for warming:** **CO2 and methane**. Four principal human-driven GHGs: CO2, CH4, N2O (+ fluorinated gases) – **never oxygen**.
[92:0:4] - **Statement sets:** "CO2, CFCs, CH4 and N2O are the main GHGs" – true; "marshes, paddy fields, cattle sheds and biogas plants add methane" – true; "CO2 and methane are commonly known GHGs" – true.
[92:0:5] - **Soot (black carbon), sulphur hexafluoride and water vapour** all warm the atmosphere (UPSC 2010: all three).
[92:0:6] - **Tropospheric ozone, methane, nitrous oxide** = a correct GHG group; aerosols, ammonia, lead and methanol are not GHGs.
[92:0:7] - **CFCs:** used as refrigerants, inactive (stable) in the lower atmosphere, destroy stratospheric ozone **and** are GHGs – "CFCs are not responsible for the greenhouse effect" is the **false** statement.
[92:0:8] - **Methane uses:** decomposition of methane gives **carbon black**, used in **printing ink**; Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down **HFCs** – 85% cut avoids about 70-72 billion t CO2e **by 2050**.
[92:0:9] # What is NOT a greenhouse gas
[92:0:10] TABLE head: Not a GHG | Why
  [92:0:10.0] Nitrogen (N2, di-nitrogen) – 78% of air | Does not absorb infrared
  [92:0:10.1] Oxygen (O2) – 21% of air | Does not absorb infrared
  [92:0:10.2] Argon (Ar) – 0.93% | Inert gas
  [92:0:10.3] Hydrogen | Not a GHG
  [92:0:10.4] Sulphur dioxide (SO2) | Causes acid rain (cools as sulphate aerosol)
  [92:0:10.5] Propane, sodium hydroxide, calcium carbonate | Fuel / chemical / solid mineral – not GHGs
[92:0:11] - **Carbon monoxide:** only an **indirect** GHG (TSPSC: "methane only" is a GHG, not CO); also the key to "which does **not** cause tropospheric ozone depletion" (UPPCS 2008).
[92:0:12] - **Oxides of sulphur and nitrogen** (SOx, NOx) do **not** warm directly; **nitrogen oxide (NO)** = "not a GHG found naturally" (UPPCS 2020). Strictly, the GHG is **nitrous oxide (N2O)**, not "nitrogen oxides".
[92:0:13] > Most-asked (×35): "which is NOT a GHG" – N2, O2, Ar, H2, SO2. Water vapour, CO2, CH4, N2O, O3 and CFCs are GHGs.
[92:0:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.13, p.57-58; NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.7-8; Shankar Environment 15 (OCR) p.8-10; NCERT Physical Geography (OnlyIAS) Part 8 p.9; PMF Environment Part 3 p.120 (laughing gas, anaesthetic); NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.2 p.6 (Kigali)
## SUB 1 | The Greenhouse Effect and Heating of the Atmosphere
[92:1:0] # Definition and mechanism
[92:1:1] - **Greenhouse effect** = natural warming of the **lower atmosphere** (surface and troposphere) by **absorption and re-radiation of heat** by GHGs – exam words: "**increase in atmospheric temperature due to concentration of GHGs**"; a **naturally occurring** phenomenon (not caused by biodegradable waste in water).
[92:1:2] - Concept first proposed by **Joseph Fourier** in the **1820s**.
[92:1:3] - Without it, Earth's average temperature would be about **−18°C** (Shankar: −19°C) instead of **+15°C**.
[92:1:4] - **Step 1:** atmosphere is **transparent to incoming short-wave** solar radiation.
[92:1:5] - **Step 2:** the surface re-emits **long-wave infrared** (8,000-25,000 nm) – **not ultraviolet**.
[92:1:6] - **Step 3:** CO2 and water vapour **strongly absorb infrared** (14,000-25,000 nm) – the atmosphere is **opaque to outgoing long-wave**.
[92:1:7] - **Step 4:** GHGs re-radiate heat in all directions, partly back to the surface: GHGs warm the air by **trapping heat** (not generating it).
[92:1:8] - **Glass analogy:** the glass of a greenhouse or of a **solar cooker** lets light in and stops long-wave heat going out – the same principle.
[92:1:9] - **Global warming** = gradual long-term rise in the average temperature of the atmosphere and oceans; mainly human (fossil fuels); GHGs **intensify** the natural effect (TSPSC: all four statements true).
[92:1:10] # Heating of the atmosphere – heat budget
[92:1:11] TABLE head: Insolation (100 units) | Share
  [92:1:11.0] Reflected (albedo): 27 from cloud tops, 2 from snow/ice, rest scattered | 35
  [92:1:11.1] Absorbed by the atmosphere | 14
  [92:1:11.2] Absorbed by the surface | 51
[92:1:12] - The atmosphere is heated **mainly by long-wave terrestrial radiation**, indirectly from the earth, not by incoming solar radiation (UPSC 2024: Statement I wrong, II right).
[92:1:13] - **Clouds and gases reflect about one-fourth** of insolation (27 units from cloud tops); the surface does **not** re-emit heat as UV (CGPSC 2023: only statement 2).
[92:1:14] - **Cloudy nights are warmer**: clouds stop heat radiating away from the ground and send it back.
[92:1:15] - **Fresh snow** has the highest albedo – reflects about **80-85%** of sunlight (more than sand desert, paddy or prairie).
[92:1:16] - UPSC 2025: heat trapped by the atmosphere maintains the average temperature, and CO2 is a good absorber (II, III true); "below freezing **everywhere** without an atmosphere" is too sweeping – the day side would be very hot, like the Moon.
[92:1:17] > The atmosphere is warmed from below: short-wave in, long-wave out. "Heated more by incoming solar radiation" is always the wrong statement.
[92:1:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.7-8; NextGen Rocket Environment p.13, p.58; Shankar Environment 15 (OCR) p.7-8; NCERT Physical Geography (OnlyIAS) Part 6 p.22, Part 8 p.9
## SUB 2 | Sources – Fossil Fuels, Deforestation, Paddy and Livestock
[92:2:0] - **Largest source of GHGs:** **burning fossil fuels** (coal, oil, gas) for electricity, transport and industry, plus **deforestation** – the human activities that contribute most to warming.
[92:2:1] - **Primary cause of present global warming** = **increase in GHG concentrations**, not ozone depletion, over-population or solar flares.
[92:2:2] - **Deforestation increases CO2** (stored carbon released, fewer sinks) and causes **loss of biodiversity**; "deforestation is decreasing CO2" is the **incorrect** statement. **Forest regeneration** mitigates the greenhouse effect.
[92:2:3] - **Primary causes of climate change (UPSC/UPPSC 2017):** excessive burning of fossil fuels, exploding numbers of oil-driven automobiles, heavy deforestation – **not increasing solar flares** (I, II and IV).
[92:2:4] - **AP Group-IV 2023:** coal and petroleum burning, deforestation, methane from animal waste – **all three** contribute.
[92:2:5] - Reducing warming: public transport, less refrigerant use, **afforestation** – all help.
[92:2:6] # Methane and nitrous oxide from farms
[92:2:7] TABLE head: Source | Gas | Why
  [92:2:7.0] Low-land (flooded) rice / paddy fields | Methane | Organic matter decays without oxygen (anaerobic); 50-100 million t/yr
  [92:2:7.1] Nitrogen fertilisers on rice and other crops | N2O | Soil microbes release N2O
  [92:2:7.2] Cud-chewing animals (enteric fermentation) | Methane | Rumen fermentation
  [92:2:7.3] Rice fields, coal mining, domestic animals | Methane (human) | —
  [92:2:7.4] Wetlands (largest natural), sea hydrates | Methane (natural) | —
[92:2:8] - **Rice** = the most important anthropogenic source of **both methane and nitrous oxide** (UPSC 2022); UPSC 2010: both statements on anaerobic methane and fertiliser N2O are correct.
[92:2:9] - UPSC 2008: **rice fields, coal mining, domestic animals and wetlands – all four** are methane sources.
[92:2:10] - Methane is **not** a fuel-exhaust gas of automobiles or industrial chimneys; among such options **wetland** is the source.
[92:2:11] - **Source matching (UPPSC 2017):** CO2 – thermal power stations; N2O – waterlogged paddy; SO2 – brick kilns; **CFC – automobile is the wrong pair** (CFCs come from refrigerants, foams, aerosols).
[92:2:12] > Paddy → methane (anaerobic); fertiliser → N2O; the TSPSC/UPSC rice questions ask for both.
[92:2:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.8, p.12; NextGen Rocket Environment p.13, p.57; Shankar Environment 15 (OCR) p.8-10; NCERT Physical Geography (OnlyIAS) Part 8 p.9
## SUB 3 | Contribution Order and Global Warming Potential
[92:3:0] # Two different measures
[92:3:1] TABLE head: Measure | Order and shares
  [92:3:1.0] Whole (natural) greenhouse effect | Water vapour biggest (about half; most abundant)
  [92:3:1.1] Share of enhanced (human) warming – textbook (NCERT Biology XII; NextGen) | CO2 60% > CH4 20% > CFCs 14-15% > N2O 5-6%
  [92:3:1.2] Radiative forcing by long-lived GHGs (WMO) | CO2 ~66% > CH4 ~16% > N2O ~6% > CFCs
[92:3:2] - **Increasing order of contribution (TSPSC 2023):** **N2O < CH4 < CO2**.
[92:3:3] - **Highest contribution to total global warming / main component / largest concentration among CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs** = **CO2**. **Second most abundant anthropogenic GHG** after CO2 = **methane**.
[92:3:4] - **Water vapour**: humans raise it only **indirectly**, by warming the air (warmer air holds more water vapour) – APPSC Degree Lecturers 2023.
[92:3:5] # Global Warming Potential (GWP)
[92:3:6] - **GWP** = heat a gas absorbs over a period (usually **100 years**) relative to the **same mass of CO2** (GWP 1, the reference).
[92:3:7] TABLE head: Gas | GWP (100 yr) | Lifetime | Main anthropogenic source
  [92:3:7.0] CO2 | 1 | 50-200 years (and longer) | Fossil fuels, deforestation, cement
  [92:3:7.1] Methane | 21 (older IPCC) / 28-36 (newer) | ~12 years | Paddies, livestock, landfills, wetlands
  [92:3:7.2] N2O | 310 (older) / 265-298 | ~114-120 years | Fertilisers and biomass burning
  [92:3:7.3] HFCs | 140-11,700 | 1-270 years | Refrigerants (CFC substitutes)
  [92:3:7.4] PFCs (perfluoromethane) | 6,500-9,200 | 800-50,000 years | Aluminium production
  [92:3:7.5] SF6 | 23,900 (highest) | 3,200 years | Dielectric fluid in switchgear
[92:3:8] - **Ascending GWP:** **CO2 < CH4 < N2O < HFC** (Degree Lecturers 2017).
[92:3:9] - CFCs contain **carbon, fluorine and chlorine**; entirely man-made.
[92:3:10] > "Largest contributor to the greenhouse effect" with water vapour offered → water vapour; without it → CO2.
[92:3:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.7, p.9-10; NextGen Rocket Environment p.13, p.58; Shankar Environment 15 (OCR) p.8-10; byjus.com / vedantu.com NCERT Bio XII 60-20-14-6 (search results)
## SUB 4 | Observed Impacts and Evidence
[92:4:0] TABLE head: Area | Observed change
  [92:4:0.0] Glaciers | Retreat worldwide; Gangotri melting = global warming
  [92:4:0.1] Sea level | Rising (melting ice + thermal expansion) – changes coastlines
  [92:4:0.2] Weather | Extreme events, altered rainfall, early flowering (mango), crop-pattern change
  [92:4:0.3] Health | Spread of diseases, heat stress
  [92:4:0.4] Ocean heat | Oceans took over 90% of the extra energy (1971-2010)
  [92:4:0.5] Ice sheets | Greenland and Antarctic both losing mass
  [92:4:0.6] Arctic sea ice | Down 3.5-4.1% per decade (1979-2012)
  [92:4:0.7] Antarctic sea ice | Sharp decline since 2015 (not expanding)
[92:4:1] - Impacts of global warming: **melting glaciers, sea-level rise, weather changes, rise in temperature** – all four (UPSC 2009); "better global communication" is not an impact.
[92:4:2] - **Matching (APPSC):** global warming – rising sea levels; air pollution – respiratory illness; sub-regional temperature – **patches of cooling**; habitat loss – biodiversity extinction.
[92:4:3] - **Floods** = disasters caused by **indirect** human action (printed key); wars and pollution are direct.
[92:4:4] - **Anthropocene** = proposed name for the epoch of human impact (Holocene is the current official epoch).
[92:4:5] - **Indicators of past climate change:** floral (plant fossils), cryogenic (glaciation), tectonic (continental drift) – MPPSC 2015 key: "long-term change" is not an indicator.
[92:4:6] # Evidence
[92:4:7] - **Keeling curve:** CO2 record at **Mauna Loa, Hawaii**, since **1958** (Charles David Keeling). **Ice cores**: air bubbles give past CO2 and temperature.
[92:4:8] - **WMO** publishes the **Greenhouse Gas Bulletin**. Bulletin 2025 (data for 2024): CO2 **423.9 ppm**, highest in about **2 million years**; rise of **3.5 ppm** in 2024, largest since 1957; CO2 **152%**, CH4 **266%**, N2O 125% of pre-industrial (CO2 ~278-280 ppm then).
[92:4:9] - **2024** = first calendar year above **1.5°C**; each of the last three decades warmer than any since **1850**; long-term warming about **1.3°C** (UNSG brief, Jun 2026).
[92:4:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.10, p.12; Shankar Environment 15 (OCR) p.6-7; app's notes 5:92 sub 7-8 (WMO bulletin, UNSG brief)
## SUB 5 | Radiative Forcing, Feedbacks, Tipping Points and Warming Limits
[92:5:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [92:5:0.0] Radiative forcing | Change in Earth's energy balance (W/m²) caused by a factor such as a GHG
  [92:5:0.1] Climate sensitivity | Warming after a doubling of CO2 over pre-industrial
  [92:5:0.2] Albedo feedback | Ice melts → lower albedo → more heat absorbed → more melting (positive feedback)
  [92:5:0.3] Water vapour feedback | Warmer air holds more water vapour → traps more heat
  [92:5:0.4] Methane hydrates | Methane locked in ice lattices in permafrost and seabed
  [92:5:0.5] Tipping points | Thresholds where small changes trigger self-perpetuating shifts, irreversible on human timescales
[92:5:1] - **WMO Bulletin (Oct 2025):** methane ≈ **16%** of forcing by long-lived GHGs; **CO2** drove about 81% of the **54% rise** in warming effect, 1990-2024.
[92:5:2] - Beyond about **2°C**, parts of the **Amazon** could turn to **savanna**.
[92:5:3] - **UPSC 2014 (beyond 3°C):** terrestrial biosphere tends to a **net carbon source** and **widespread coral mortality** – 1 and 2 only; "all wetlands disappear" and "no cereals anywhere" are extreme.
[92:5:4] - **Safe warming?** Paris uses **1.5°C and 2°C** as limits, but **no level is proven "safe"** (AP Asst. Director key: "No one knows").
[92:5:5] - Remaining **1.5°C carbon budget**: about **130 Gt CO2** from start of 2025. **UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025**: updated NDCs → **2.3-2.5°C**; **Limiting Overshoot (Sep 2026)**: **2.6°C** on current policies.
[92:5:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.10; NextGen Rocket Environment p.14 (Paris limits); app's notes 5:92 sub 5, 9 (WMO, UNEP)
## SUB 6 | Carbon Footprint, Carbon Pricing and Removal
[92:6:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [92:6:0.0] Carbon footprint | Total GHGs (CO2) emitted by the activities of a person, organisation or product, in t CO2 per year
  [92:6:0.1] Carbon credit | Tradable permit to emit one metric tonne of CO2 or equivalent
  [92:6:0.2] Social cost of carbon | Money value of the long-term damage from one tonne of CO2 emitted in a given year
  [92:6:0.3] Carbon sequestration | Storing carbon in sinks: soil, biochar, agroforestry, forests
  [92:6:0.4] CCUS | Captures CO2 from point sources (factory flue gases)
  [92:6:0.5] Direct Air Capture (DAC) | Removes CO2 from ambient air – sequestration; CO2 for plastics, food processing, and synthetic low-carbon aviation fuel (UPSC 2025: all three)
  [92:6:0.6] Carbon bomb | Fossil project able to emit over 1 Gt CO2; LINGO lists 425 (India: Gevra, Rajmahal)
[92:6:1] - **Singapore**: carbon tax **from 2019** (announced Feb 2018, under Paris commitments).
[92:6:2] - India: CCUS road map covers **industry**; agriculture removal = soil carbon, biochar, agroforestry; country-level social cost of carbon **$86/t CO2**.
[92:6:3] - **EU CBAM** fully enforced from **1 Jan 2026**.
[92:6:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.12 (carbon footprint, carbon bombs); app's notes 5:92 sub 9 (SCC, DAC, CCUS, CBAM)
## SUB 7 | Short-lived Climate Pollutants and Black Carbon
[92:7:0] - **SLCPs:** **black carbon, methane, HFCs, tropospheric ozone** – short life, strong warming; not water vapour, N2O or SF6.
[92:7:1] - **Black carbon** = **short-lived pollutant from incomplete combustion** (biomass and diesel); darkens snow and ice → lower albedo → faster melt; it is not methane, not from CFCs and does not deplete ozone.
[92:7:2] - **Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC)**, 2012: tackles **methane, black carbon and HFCs**; launched by a few countries with UNEP – **not a G20 initiative** (UPSC 2017: statement 2 only).
[92:7:3] - **Tropospheric ozone**: a **secondary pollutant** (NOx + VOCs in sunlight); **cuts crop yields**, worst in summer.
[92:7:4] - Aerosols: **black and brown carbon warm; sulphate droplets cool**.
[92:7:5] - **Global Methane Pledge**: COP26 Glasgow (2021); cut methane **30% from 2020 levels by 2030**; **India has not signed**. UNSG **Call to Action on Methane**: **London Climate Action Week**, 24 Jun 2026.
[92:7:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC Part 8.1 p.10; Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 01 p.21, p.23 (Global Methane Status Report, CCAC/UNEP, 30% by 2030); app's notes 5:92 sub 6 (CCAC, Methane Pledge); general knowledge, not checked (CCAC founders)
## SUB 8 | Emissions – Sectors and Top Emitters
[92:8:0] TABLE head: Sector (global GHG, 2016) | Share
  [92:8:0.0] Energy (electricity, heat, transport, industry energy) | ~73%
  [92:8:0.1] Agriculture, forestry and land use | ~18%
  [92:8:0.2] Direct industrial processes (incl. cement) | ~5%
[92:8:1] # Top emitters
[92:8:2] TABLE head: Country (Global Carbon Budget 2025, CO2 in 2024) | Billion t
  [92:8:2.0] China | 12
  [92:8:2.1] USA | 4.9
  [92:8:2.2] India (3rd) | 3.2
[92:8:3] - India's **per capita** CO2: about **2.2 t** (2024).
[92:8:4] - **GHG Emission Intensity Target (Amendment) Rules 2025** – under the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**.
[92:8:5] ~~ Sources: app's notes 5:92 sub 4 (Global Carbon Budget 2025, EPA rules)

=== NOTES 5:94 | Impacts of Climate Change on India – Monsoon, Agriculture, Himalayan Glaciers, Sea-level Rise, Extreme Events
## SUB 0 | Observed Impacts – Ice Sheets, Sea Level, Tipping Points and Species
[94:0:0] # Already observed (cryosphere)
[94:0:1] - **Observed consequence (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2023):** a **significant reduction in ice-sheet mass** – Greenland and Antarctica have lost mass for about two decades (Greenland ~278 bn t/yr and Antarctica ~155 bn t/yr in 2006-15; loss has **quadrupled since the 1990s**). Falling global temperature, more forest cover and fewer heatwaves are the opposite of what is observed.
[94:0:2] - **Effects of climate change (NextGen):** rising sea levels, **shrinking mountain glaciers**, accelerating loss of the cryosphere, ocean acidification.
[94:0:3] - **Most fragile, first affected (UKPSC 2010):** the **Arctic and Greenland ice sheet** – the Arctic warms **about four times** faster than the global average (polar amplification).
[94:0:4] - **WMO (2025 report):** oceans hold **over 90% of excess heat**; Arctic sea ice near record low; glacier loss threatens water for **about 2 billion people** (not 200 million).
[94:0:5] - **Ice core = cryogenic indicator** of past climate (UPPCS 2015): drilled from Antarctic/Greenland ice sheets or mountain glaciers; the **lower layers are older**; trapped air bubbles record past CO₂. Pollen, tree rings and evaporites are not cryogenic.
[94:0:6] TABLE head: Place | Feature
  [94:0:6.0] Okjökull, Iceland | First glacier declared "dead" (2014; memorial plaque 2019)
  [94:0:6.1] Quelccaya, Peru | Largest tropical ice cap; retreating ~200 ft/yr
  [94:0:6.2] Tebua Tarawa and Abanuea (Kiribati) | Uninhabited islets submerged in 1999
  [94:0:6.3] Kiribati, Tuvalu | Inhabited islands at risk of submergence
  [94:0:6.4] Maldives | World's first underwater Cabinet meeting (2009) to highlight sea-level rise
  [94:0:6.5] IndARC | India's first underwater observatory in the Arctic (Kongsfjorden, Svalbard, 2014; UPSC 2015) – not a radar, satellite or Antarctic base
[94:0:7] # Sea-level rise
[94:0:8] - **Long-term (eustatic) change:** caused by **melting of ice sheets** and thermal expansion of seawater (CDS 2016). Atmospheric pressure, water density and floating **icebergs** cause only short-term or no change.
[94:0:9] - **Principal causes:** **thermal expansion + melting glaciers and ice sheets**; global sea level up **~20 cm (1901-2018)**, ~11 cm since 1993; the rate has doubled to ~4.5 mm/yr. **Melting polar ice and sea-level rise** = most important effect of warming.
[94:0:10] - "Sea-level rise of one metre by 2070" is **not** a correct statement (IPCC: ~0.43-0.84 m by 2100).
[94:0:11] # Tipping points
[94:0:12] - **Tipping point:** a threshold where **small changes trigger large, self-perpetuating, potentially irreversible** shifts.
[94:0:13] - **Loss of Arctic (sea) ice = potential tipping point (APPSC G2 2025):** bright ice (high albedo) melts → darker ocean absorbs more heat → more melting. Cutting CO₂ or less solar radiation are not tipping points.
[94:0:14] TABLE head: Tipping elements (listed) | NOT tipping elements
  [94:0:14.0] Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, AMOC, permafrost, warm-water coral reefs, Amazon, Arctic sea ice (near record lows) | Sahara dunes, Deccan basalts, European temperate deciduous forests
[94:0:15] - **UNSG Brief #12 (Jun 2026):** warming ~1.3°C; **coral 1.2°C threshold already crossed** (most fragile; recovery from mass bleaching takes **more than 15 years**); the **Amazon** beyond ~2°C may flip to savanna and turn from a **carbon store into a carbon source**; beyond 3°C the land biosphere may become a source.
[94:0:16] - **Amazon:** ~17-18% already lost; makes ~50% of its own rain.
[94:0:17] TABLE head: Impact (IPCC SR1.5, 2018) | 1.5°C | 2°C
  [94:0:17.0] Coral reefs lost | 70-90% | >99%
  [94:0:17.1] Ice-free Arctic summer | Once a century | Once a decade
[94:0:18] # Global effects by region and species
[94:0:19] - **TSPSC 2023 match:** **bush fires – Australia/USA**; **locust swarming – Africa/Middle East**; **heat wave – Antarctica** (record 2022 heat); **permafrost melt – Arctic** → A-IV, B-III, C-I, D-II.
[94:0:20] - **Rutgers University study (2019):** warming wipes out about **twice as many ocean species** as land species (APPSC G1).
[94:0:21] - **IPBES 2019:** ~8 million species; **up to 1 million threatened**; **~40% of amphibians**.
[94:0:22] - Species shift **poleward and upslope** (cooler toward higher latitudes and elevations).
[94:0:23] > Angles: "which is already observed" (ice-sheet loss), "which is a tipping point" (Arctic ice), the odd non-tipping element (Sahara dunes), place-feature pairs (Maldives, Okjökull, IndARC).
[94:0:24] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.10, p.12; PMF Environment Part 05 p.48, p.71-72, p.79, p.81-83, p.92; Rocket Environment p.13; PMF Lens Aug 2026 (01) p.34 (IndARC); app notes 5:94 sub 5, 7, 8
## SUB 1 | India's Temperature Record and Warmest Years
[94:1:0] - **Assessment of Climate Change over the Indian Region (2020):** by the **Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES)** – India's **first national climate assessment**; India warmed **about 0.7°C over 1901-2018** (not "more than 2°C").
[94:1:1] TABLE head: Year | IMD Statement on Climate of India
  [94:1:1.0] 2019 | 7th warmest year since 1901; Bihar suffered most from extreme weather (heat wave + lightning deaths)
  [94:1:1.1] 2020 | Average yearly temperature 25.78°C
  [94:1:1.2] 2024 | Warmest year since 1901 (+0.65°C)
  [94:1:1.3] 2025 | 8th warmest (+0.28°C over 1991-2020)
[94:1:2] - **IMD:** est. **1875**, HQ **New Delhi** (Mausam Bhawan), under MoES.
[94:1:3] # World's warmest years
[94:1:4] - **2016** was the world's warmest year on record when asked (APPSC Degree Lecturers) – now **2024** is the warmest (**~1.60°C** above pre-industrial, first calendar year above 1.5°C; **Copernicus Climate Change Service**, an **EU** programme).
[94:1:5] - **WMO (Dec 2009):** **2009** likely the **fifth warmest** year on record (APPSC G2 2011); now the past 11 years (2015-2025) are the 11 warmest; 2023-25 average first crossed 1.5°C.
[94:1:6] TABLE head: Report | Publisher | Headline
  [94:1:6.0] State of the Global Climate (2025 edition, 2026) | WMO | Indicators "flashing red", accelerating change
  [94:1:6.1] Global Annual to Decadal Climate Update | WMO (lead centre: UK Met Office) | 1.3-1.9°C for 2026-30
  [94:1:6.2] Emissions Gap Report 2025 "Off Target" | UNEP | 2.3-2.5°C even with NDCs
  [94:1:6.3] Lancet Countdown 2025 | The Lancet | Heat deaths up 23% since 1990s; dengue potential +85% in India
[94:1:7] - **WMO:** set up **1950**, UN specialised agency **1951**, HQ Geneva. **IPCC:** set up **1988** by **WMO + UNEP**.
[94:1:8] > Angle: dated rankings – check the year: 2019 = 7th warmest in India; 2016 → 2024 warmest globally.
[94:1:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 05 p.72; Praveen CA-360 May 2026 p.65 (IMD); PMF Environment Part 06 p.32; app notes 5:94 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Heat Waves, IMD Alerts and Wet-bulb Temperature
[94:2:0] - **Heat wave (IMD):** max at least **40°C in plains** and at least **30°C in hilly regions** (37°C at coastal stations), with a departure of 4.5-6.4°C from normal; or actual max **≥45°C regardless of normal** (severe ≥47°C). "30°C plains / 40°C hills" → **neither** statement correct.
[94:2:1] - **Causes:** meandering **Rossby waves → heat domes**; **loo** over the Gangetic plains; global warming – **not** cold Arabian Sea currents.
[94:2:2] TABLE head: Colour | Meaning | Action
  [94:2:2.0] Green | Normal | No action
  [94:2:2.1] Yellow | Watch / alert | Be updated
  [94:2:2.2] Orange | Severe | Be prepared
  [94:2:2.3] Red | Extreme | Take action
[94:2:3] # Wet-bulb temperature
[94:2:4] - Lowest temperature air reaches by evaporative cooling; combines **heat + humidity**; equals **dry-bulb at 100% humidity**.
[94:2:5] - **~35°C wet-bulb = survivability limit**: **sweat can no longer cool the body**. **World Bank:** India among the first places to cross it routinely → implication = survival of humans and animals hit because shedding body heat by perspiration fails (**II only**, UPSC 2025); floods, cyclones and droughts in peninsular India are not what the wet-bulb warning implies.
[94:2:6] - Indians faced **19.8 heatwave days** in 2024 (Lancet Countdown).
[94:2:7] # Heat action and health
[94:2:8] - **Ahmedabad (2013): South Asia's first Heat Action Plan**.
[94:2:9] - **AP:** heat rising in **Palnadu, Kurnool, Anantapur**; hottest place **Rentachintala (Palnadu)**; **APSDMA Heatwave Action Plan 2026** – heatwaves kill more in AP than any other natural disaster; the **AP Heat Wave Action Plan** is cited as an **early-warning and preparedness** measure; **Rayalaseema – heat stress and chronic drought**.
[94:2:10] - **Health:** warmer and wetter → **dengue and malaria** spread; floods → cholera; waterlogging → leptospirosis.
[94:2:11] > Angles: plains/hills thresholds (40/30), colour codes (Red = Take Action, Orange = Be Prepared), wet-bulb implication.
[94:2:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 p.2; PMF Environment Part 05 p.73-74; PMF Internal Security and DM Part 02 p.56 (IMD colours); app notes 5:94 sub 1
## SUB 3 | Climate Risk Index and Vulnerability
[94:3:0] - **Global Climate Risk Index (CRI):** published by **Germanwatch** (German think-tank, **Bonn**) – not UNEP, WMO or the World Bank; ranks countries by observed losses from extreme weather; released at COPs.
[94:3:1] TABLE head: CRI edition | India's rank
  [94:3:1.0] CRI 2019 (data 2017) | 14th
  [94:3:1.1] CRI 2020 (data 2018) | 5th
  [94:3:1.2] CRI 2021 (16th edition, data 2019) | 7th (score 16.67)
  [94:3:1.3] CRI 2026 (Nov 2025, 1995-2024) | 9th long-term; 15th for 2024; ~430 events, ~$170 bn losses, ~80,000 deaths
[94:3:2] - **Children's Climate Risk Index:** by **UNICEF (2021)**, not WHO in 2005 – ranks countries by children's **exposure** to climate shocks and their **vulnerability** (access to essential services); Children's Climate Risk Report 2026 (UNICEF).
[94:3:3] - **CCPI** (Germanwatch, NewClimate Institute, CAN): India **23rd** in CCPI 2026 (from 10th).
[94:3:4] # Vulnerability in India
[94:3:5] - **NICRA:** 651 districts assessed → **310** highly / very highly vulnerable.
[94:3:6] - **DST (2021)** most vulnerable states: **Jharkhand**, Mizoram, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Bihar, Arunachal Pradesh, West Bengal.
[94:3:7] - **AP SAPCC:** north and central AP very high; southern coast moderate; **south-west relatively low**. Energy-sector adaptation needed because **heat and erratic rain threaten thermal and hydropower generation**.
[94:3:8] - **World Bank:** **45 million** Indians could be pushed into extreme poverty within 15 years.
[94:3:9] > Angle: who publishes CRI (Germanwatch) and India's rank in a named edition.
[94:3:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 05 p.64-65, p.91-92; NextGen Environment APPSC 14 p.1 (Germanwatch); Praveen CA-360 Apr 2026 p.79; Praveen CA-360 Jun 2026 p.83 (UNICEF); app notes 5:94 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Agriculture, Monsoon and Adaptation
[94:4:0] # Agriculture
[94:4:1] - **Climate-Smart Village** approach = part of **CCAFS** (Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security) research programme of **CGIAR** (headquartered in **France**, Montpellier); **ICRISAT (Patancheru, Hyderabad)** is a CGIAR centre → all three statements correct (UPSC 2021).
[94:4:2] - Climate change is already **reducing wheat** output; **wheat/maize lose 4-10% yield per 1°C**; extreme heat cuts **milk yield 15-25%** (FAO-WMO, Apr 2026).
[94:4:3] TABLE head: Programme | Detail
  [94:4:3.0] NICRA | ICAR project, 2011, led by CRIDA, Hyderabad
  [94:4:3.1] ACASA-India | GIS atlas of crop vulnerability to climate change
  [94:4:3.2] Varieties | 2,996 climate-resilient varieties released 2014-2025; heat-tolerant wheat HD 3385
[94:4:4] # Monsoon, water and drought
[94:4:5] - **Over 80% of rain in under 100 days**; SW monsoon ≈ **75%** of annual rain; **NE monsoon (Oct-Dec) ≈ 11%**.
[94:4:6] - **Each 1°C warming → ~7% more moisture** → heavier rain; extreme **pre-monsoon** rain events **doubled** (1981-2020). **El Niño weakens** the SW monsoon.
[94:4:7] - **68%** of India drought-prone; droughts = **meteorological, agricultural, hydrological**. **National Water Mission:** **20%** better water-use efficiency.
[94:4:8] - **Urban floods:** floodplain encroachment, wetland loss, poor drainage and more intense rain.
[94:4:9] # Social impact and adaptation
[94:4:10] - **UPPSC 2017 A-R:** climate change is increasing **social tension** (A); more frequent and intense extreme water events threaten **food security** (R) → both true, **R explains A**.
[94:4:11] - **AP and PMFBY (APPSC G2 A-R):** extreme weather (floods, droughts, cyclones) caused big crop losses in AP (**R true**), but AP's PMFBY coverage did **not** rise steadily – AP left PMFBY for its own free crop-insurance scheme from 2019-20 (**A false**).
[94:4:12] TABLE head: Measure | Detail
  [94:4:12.0] Crop insurance | PMFBY (2016); weather-based insurance
  [94:4:12.1] Bio-shields | Mangroves and Casuarina shelterbelts on the AP coast
  [94:4:12.2] Early warning | CWC flood forecasts at ~350 stations (not 3,500)
[94:4:13] > Angles: CCAFS/CGIAR statements, A-R on social tension and food security.
[94:4:14] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment Part 03 p.1 (UPSC 2021 question); PMF Environment Part 06 p.55 (GACSA, FAO); Rocket Disaster Mgmt p.22-23 (68% drought-prone); CivicCentre daily CA 5 Nov 2026 p.4-5 (PMFBY in AP); app notes 5:94 sub 2, 3, 9
## SUB 5 | Coasts and Cyclones – India and Andhra Pradesh
[94:5:0] - **Cyclone-prone area:** about **8% of India's land area** (NDMA); ~5,700 km of coastline cyclone-prone.
[94:5:1] - Cyclones are **more frequent in the Bay of Bengal**, but Arabian Sea cyclones rose **52%** (2001-2019) and very severe ones 150%.
[94:5:2] - **Marine heatwaves** doubled since 1982; raise cyclone **winds up to 20%** and **rain up to 12%** → rapid intensification; in 2025 **more than 90%** of oceans had marine heatwaves.
[94:5:3] - **INCOIS (Hyderabad):** Coastal Vulnerability Index from **7 parameters**. **NCCR, Chennai:** **33.6%** of India's coastline eroding (1990-2018).
[94:5:4] # AP coast
[94:5:5] - **AP coastline 1,053 km** (3rd; revised 2025), Srikakulam to Nellore; Godavari delta = **Konaseema**; erosion hotspot **Uppada (Kakinada)**.
[94:5:6] - AP cyclones (**Hudhud, Titli, Michaung**) peak **October-December**.
[94:5:7] > Angle: % of land prone to cyclones (8%).
[94:5:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Internal Security and DM Part 02 p.45; PMF Environment Part 05 p.77, p.84, p.89; RUNBOOK settled facts (coastline, PIB 4 Dec 2025); app notes 5:94 sub 5
## SUB 6 | Himalayan Glaciers and GLOFs
[94:6:0] - **Himansh:** high-altitude glacier research station of **NCPOR (Goa)** in **Lahaul-Spiti** (Himachal), above 4,000 m, set up **2016** to study Himalayan glacier response to climate.
[94:6:1] - **GSI:** glacier mass balance, GLOF mapping and the Himalayan glacier inventory.
[94:6:2] - **Gangotri** has retreated about **1,727 m since 1935** (≈1,700 m); melting due to global warming.
[94:6:3] TABLE head: Event | Place | Date
  [94:6:3.0] Chamoli disaster | Uttarakhand | Feb 2021
  [94:6:3.1] South Lhonak lake GLOF | Sikkim | Oct 2023
  [94:6:3.2] Nepal flash floods | Nepal | Aug 2026
[94:6:4] - **Gangabal and Nundkol lakes** (Harmukh, Ganderbal, **Jammu and Kashmir**): highly GLOF-prone.
[94:6:5] - **Hanging glaciers** cling to steep slopes (not valley floors); **permafrost thaw** releases **methane and CO₂**.
[94:6:6] - **ICIMOD (Kathmandu)** – HKH Snow Update. **NMSHE:** **12 thematic areas**. Melt threatens **lean-season river flows and hydropower**.
[94:6:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 05 p.79-80; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.10; app notes 5:94 sub 4

## SUB 1 | Kyoto Protocol, CDM and Carbon Credits
[95:1:0] - **Kyoto Protocol:** adopted **11 Dec 1997** at **Kyoto, Japan (COP3)**; in force **16 Feb 2005**; **first legally binding** treaty with GHG targets; called on **industrialised (Annex I) nations** to cut emissions (~5% below **1990** in 2008-12) – deals with **greenhouse gases / climate change**, not ozone (Montreal), poverty or arms.
[95:1:1] - **Binding on Annex I only**; **USA never ratified**; **Canada withdrew** (announced 12 Dec 2011, effective Dec 2012) – first to leave.
[95:1:2] - **Six gases:** CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆; **NF₃** added only for the 2nd period. **Methane** is a more potent GHG than CO₂.
[95:1:3] - **Doha Amendment (2012):** 2nd period **2013-2020**, **18%** below 1990; in force 31 Dec 2020.
[95:1:4] - **India acceded to Kyoto in August 2002** (UNFCCC 1992 → Kyoto 2002; First Five Year Plan 1951 came first).
[95:1:5] TABLE head: Mechanism | Between | Unit
  [95:1:5.0] International Emissions Trading | Annex I ↔ Annex I | Allowances
  [95:1:5.1] CDM (Article 12) | Annex I (Annex B) party runs a project in a developing country | CERs
  [95:1:5.2] Joint Implementation | Annex I project in another Annex I country | ERUs
[95:1:6] - **CDM:** the market-based device under the UNFCCC/Kyoto that lets developing countries get funds and technology from developed countries; it **encourages** (does not prohibit) developed-country investment in developing countries; CDM projects are **not** confined to Annex I countries.
[95:1:7] - **Annex I** is a UNFCCC/Kyoto grouping (not Cartagena); **CERs** come from the CDM (issued by the **CDM Executive Board**), not Nagoya → only "CDM – Kyoto" is correctly matched (UPSC 2016).
[95:1:8] # Carbon credits and markets
[95:1:9] - **Carbon credit concept:** originated from the **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** – not the Rio Earth Summit, Montreal Protocol or G-8; **1 credit = 1 tonne CO₂e**; **carbon trading** belongs to Kyoto, **not Montreal**.
[95:1:10] - **Paris Article 6:** **6.2** bilateral deals (India-Japan **JCM**, Aug 2025); **6.4** UN-run Paris Agreement Crediting Mechanism (credits = **A6.4ERs**), successor to the CDM; rules completed and **fully operational at COP29**; first 6.4 credits: clean-cooking project in **Myanmar**.
[95:1:11] - **GHG Protocol** (WRI + WBCSD): an **international accounting tool** for governments and businesses to quantify and manage GHG emissions – not a UN incentive scheme or REDD+ initiative.
[95:1:12] > Angles: pairs (Annex I / CER / CDM), "carbon credit originated from", CDM "not true" statements, Canada's withdrawal.
[95:1:13] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 06 p.14-21, p.33-34, p.57; Rocket Environment p.8, p.14, p.29, p.64; Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.167 (JCM); app notes 5:95 sub 1, 2

## SUB 3 | UNFCCC and the Family of Environmental Conventions
[95:3:0] TABLE head: Treaty | Adopted | In force | Remember
  [95:3:0.0] UNFCCC | 9 May 1992, New York; opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit (June 1992) | 21 March 1994 (after 50 ratifications) | 198 Parties; Secretariat Bonn
  [95:3:0.1] Kyoto Protocol | 11 Dec 1997 | 16 Feb 2005 | First binding targets
  [95:3:0.2] Paris Agreement | 12 Dec 2015 (signed from 22 April 2016) | 4 Nov 2016 | India ratified 2 Oct 2016; meeting of Parties = CMA
[95:3:1] - **First major international agreement on climate change** = the **UNFCCC** (the 1987 Montreal Protocol is on ozone).
[95:3:2] - **Objective:** stabilise **greenhouse-gas** concentrations at a level that prevents **dangerous anthropogenic interference** (GHG mitigation – not just CO₂ or fossil fuels). Two instruments: **Kyoto Protocol** and **Paris Agreement**. **IPCC AR1 (1990)** fed into it.
[95:3:3] TABLE head: Group | Members | Obligation
  [95:3:3.0] Annex I | Industrialised + economies in transition | Lead emission cuts
  [95:3:3.1] Annex II | OECD members of Annex I | Provide finance and technology to developing countries
  [95:3:3.2] Non-Annex I | Developing countries incl. India | No binding cuts
[95:3:4] - **CBDR-RC:** developed countries, with most **historical emissions**, should lead – **Rio Declaration Principle 7**, UNFCCC Art. 3.1, Paris Art. 2.2.
[95:3:5] # Conventions – which address GHGs?
[95:3:6] TABLE head: Convention | Signed | Subject
  [95:3:6.0] Ramsar | 2 Feb 1971 | Wetlands
  [95:3:6.1] CITES (Washington) | 1973 | Trade in endangered species
  [95:3:6.2] Montreal Protocol | 16 Sep 1987 | Ozone-depleting substances; Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs (a GHG)
  [95:3:6.3] Kyoto Protocol | 11 Dec 1997 | GHG emission cuts
  [95:3:6.4] Paris Agreement | 22 Apr 2016 (signing) | Temperature goal
  [95:3:6.5] Basel Convention | 1989 | Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes – does not focus on GHGs
  [95:3:6.6] CBD | 1992 | Biodiversity; Cartagena (2000) = biosafety/GMOs; Nagoya (2010) = access and benefit sharing
  [95:3:6.7] Rotterdam / Stockholm / Minamata | 1998 / 2001 / 2013 | Prior informed consent / POPs / mercury
[95:3:7] - **Not correctly matched (MPPSC 2017):** "**Carbon trading – Montreal Protocol**" (it is Kyoto); First World Climate Conference **1979**, First Earth Summit → **Agenda 21**, Earth Summit +5 → **1997** are correct.
[95:3:8] - **Earth Summit (Rio, 1992):** Agenda 21, UNFCCC, CBD; its Local Agenda 21 spread the slogan **"Think globally, act locally"**.
[95:3:9] - **UNEP** (1972, Nairobi) addresses global environmental challenges; the **IPCC** assesses climate science; the **EPA** is the US regulator – India's pollution regulator is the **CPCB** → only 1 and 3 correct.
[95:3:10] > Angles: dates (1992 / 21 March 1994), "first agreement on climate", which treaty is not about GHGs (Basel), date-matching.
[95:3:11] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.6-8, p.29-30, p.48, p.64-65, p.71; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.11; NextGen Environment APPSC 09 p.9 (Basel); PMF Environment Part 06 p.14; app notes 5:95 sub 0, 8
## SUB 4 | Paris Agreement and NDCs
[95:4:0] - **Goal:** hold warming **well below 2°C** and pursue **1.5°C** above pre-industrial levels (APPSC FBO: **1.5°C**).
[95:4:1] - **Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs):** each country sets its own (not centrally, UN- or capacity-determined); **INDCs** = **Intended NDCs**, the **plans of action to combat climate change** submitted before Paris; NDCs every **5 years**; each must go beyond the last (**ratchet**).
[95:4:2] - **Legal nature (APPSC G2 Mains 2025):** a **legally binding treaty**, but only the **procedure** binds (prepare, communicate, report NDCs); **NDC targets bind no party** – not the **USA, China, India or EU** → "**None of these**".
[95:4:3] TABLE head: Article | Subject
  [95:4:3.0] 6.2 / 6.4 | Carbon markets
  [95:4:3.1] 9.1 | Finance from developed countries
  [95:4:3.2] 13 | Enhanced Transparency Framework; Biennial Transparency Reports (first due end-2024)
  [95:4:3.3] 14 | Global Stocktake every 5 years (first at COP28)
  [95:4:3.4] 28 | Withdrawal: notice after 3 years from entry into force; effect 1 year after notice
[95:4:4] # India's NDC
[95:4:5] TABLE head: NDC | Emissions-intensity cut (2005 base)
  [95:4:5.0] INDC 2015 | 33-35% by 2030 (+40% non-fossil power, 2.5-3 bn t carbon sink)
  [95:4:5.1] Updated 2022 | 45% by 2030
  [95:4:5.2] 2031-35 NDC | 47% by 2035
[95:4:6] - **NDC 3.0:** economy-wide, all gases, 1.5°C-aligned.
[95:4:7] - **USA and Paris:** withdrawal announced 2017, effective **4 Nov 2020**; **rejoined 19 Feb 2021**; **left a second time on 27 January 2026**.
[95:4:8] > Angles: 1.5°C / well below 2°C, "NDC" wording, binding or not, India's 33-35%.
[95:4:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 06 p.25, p.27-29, p.35; Rocket Environment p.14; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.12 (33-35%); app notes 5:95 sub 3

## SUB 6 | IPCC – Body and Reports
[95:6:0] - Set up **1988** by **WMO and UNEP**; Secretariat **Geneva**; does **no original research**; each report has a **Summary for Policymakers**; **Nobel Peace Prize 2007** with **Al Gore**. **WMO** (1950; UN agency 1951; HQ **Geneva**) grew out of the **International Meteorological Organization (1873)**.
[95:6:1] - Working Groups: **WG I** physical science; **WG II** impacts, adaptation, vulnerability; **WG III** mitigation.
[95:6:2] - **ARs:** AR1 1990, AR2 1995, AR3 2001, AR4 2007, **AR5 2014**, AR6 2021-23 (Synthesis **20 Mar 2023**); **AR7** began **July 2023** (Special Report on **Climate Change and Cities**, 2027).
[95:6:3] TABLE head: Report | Finding
  [95:6:3.0] SR1.5 (Oct 2018) | Warming likely reaches 1.5°C between 2030 and 2052; net CO₂ must fall ~45% from 2010 by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050; deep, rapid cuts (not gradual)
  [95:6:3.1] SRCCL (Aug 2019) | Land, desertification, food security
  [95:6:3.2] SROCC (Sep 2019) | Marine heatwaves more frequent (doubled since 1982)
  [95:6:3.3] AR6 SYR (2023) | 1.1°C (2011-2020); 1.5°C likely in the early 2030s; 70-85% renewable electricity by 2050; carbon budget ~500 GtCO₂ from 2020
[95:6:4] - **AR6 on India:** warming **faster than the global average**; Gangotri retreated ~1,700 m; **black carbon lowers snow albedo**.
[95:6:5] - **SSPs** (AR6) replaced the **RCPs** (AR5); **SSP3 = Regional Rivalry**.
[95:6:6] > Angles: SR1.5 numbers (2030-2052; net zero by 2050), what each WG does.
[95:6:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 05 p.67-71; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.10; Rocket Environment p.8, p.41; app notes 5:95 sub 9
## SUB 7 | India in Climate Negotiations
[95:7:0] - **Per capita:** India's per-capita emissions are far **below** industrialised nations (about 2.9 t CO₂e vs USA 18 t, China 11 t) – in 2012 India was the **lowest per-capita** emitter among the USA, UK, China and India.
[95:7:1] - **BASIC** (4 members: Brazil, South Africa, India, China): India **attended** the 19th BASIC meeting at **Sun City** (so "did not attend" is the untrue statement, JPSC 2016).
[95:7:2] - **Blocs:** **G77 and China** (largest developing-country group); LMDC; **AOSIS** (small islands, push 1.5°C). At **Bonn SB64 (June 2026)** India with G77+China, LMDC, BASIC sought agenda space on **Article 9.1** finance.
[95:7:3] - **COP26:** **Panchamrit**; India pushed **"phase down"** of unabated coal. **Not signed:** Global Methane Pledge, **Glasgow Leaders' Declaration on Forests and Land Use**, COP28 renewables pledge, COP28 health declaration. **COP33 bid** made at **COP28**, withdrawn April 2026.
[95:7:4] - **Net zero 2070** (later than 2050) – development needs and **coal dependence**; wants **clean, affordable technology and finance**; coal measures incl. **wet scrubbers**, ESPs, gasification.
[95:7:5] - **EU CBAM** (iron/steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, electricity; definitive 1 Jan 2026): India – **violates CBDR-RC, green protectionism**; 12th BRICS Environment Ministers (New Delhi, Aug 2026): "unilateral, punitive, discriminatory, protectionist".
[95:7:6] - **Platforms:** G20 New Delhi 2023 – **Green Development Pact**, **Global Biofuels Alliance**; **Voice of Global South** Summits since **Jan 2023**; **Mission LiFE** – individual behaviour change; **ISA** – COP21 (2015), India + France, HQ **Gurugram**, first intergovernmental body headquartered in India.
[95:7:7] - **Carbon space** = room for developing countries to grow; sea-level-rise refugees fall outside the **1951 Refugee Convention**.
[95:7:8] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 06 p.17, p.34-35, p.39, p.51-52; app notes 5:95 sub 10

[96:1:0] # Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI)
[96:1:1] - Published by **Germanwatch, NewClimate Institute and Climate Action Network (CAN) International**; annually **since 2005**, released at the COP; 59 countries + EU (≈92% of emissions); weights: GHG 40%, renewables 20%, energy use 20%, climate policy 20%.
[96:1:2] - Top three ranks are left **empty** (no country does enough).
