  [96:1:3.0] 2017 (Nov 2016, COP22 Marrakech; 58 countries) | 20th
  [96:1:3.1] 2018 (Nov 2017) | 14th
  [96:1:3.2] 2019 (Dec 2018, COP24 Katowice) | 11th
  [96:1:3.3] 2020 (10 Dec 2019, COP25 Madrid) | 9th – first time in the top 10
  [96:1:3.4] 2021 | 10th
  [96:1:3.5] 2024 | 7th
[96:1:4] - "India's rank **in 2019**" (JL 2020) = the index **released in 2019** = **CCPI 2020 → 9th**; the CCPI **2019** edition (released Dec 2018) had India **11th**.

## SUB 2 | Panchamrit and Net Zero 2070
[96:2:0] - Announced by the PM at **COP26, Glasgow, 1 Nov 2021**. Hook: **500-50-1-45-2070**.
[96:2:1] TABLE head: # | Pledge | By
  [96:2:1.0] 1 | 500 GW non-fossil energy capacity (not 250 GW) | 2030
  [96:2:1.1] 2 | 50% of energy requirements from renewables (not 60%) | 2030
  [96:2:1.2] 3 | Cut projected (cumulative) carbon emissions by 1 billion tonnes | 2030
  [96:2:1.3] 4 | Cut carbon (emissions) intensity of the economy by 45% (from 2005) | 2030
  [96:2:1.4] 5 | Net zero (not 2045 or 2050) | 2070
[96:2:2] - TSPSC JL 2023: true = **II, III and IV** (I says 250 GW; V says 2045). COP26 "NOT true": "60% of energy from renewables" (it is 50%).
[96:2:3] - **Net zero** = residual emissions **balanced by removals** (forests, carbon capture) – **not** zero gross emissions, and **not** a fixed 2050 date for every country (UPPCS 2021: only statement 2 correct). India's year **2070** is later than developed countries' 2050, defended by **CBDR-RC** and development needs.
[96:2:4] - **LT-LEDS** presented at **COP27 (Nov 2022)**; 7 transitions: low-carbon electricity, transport, urban adaptation and efficient buildings, decoupling industry, **CO2 removal**, forest cover, low-carbon finance. **Not**: expansion of fossil-fuel power.
[96:2:5] - **India's Net Zero Portal** and **NAPCC Dashboard** (MoEFCC, **16 Sep 2026**): **voluntary** registration and disclosure of net-zero targets (Scope 1, 2; Scope 3 voluntary).
[96:2:6] - **IEA "Net-Zero by 2050"** roadmap: **May 2021**.
[96:2:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket Environment p.15, p.17; PMF Environment Part 06 p.35; Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.138, p.161; app notes 5:96 sub 1
## SUB 3 | India's NDCs – INDC 2015 to NDC 3.0 (base year 2005)
[96:3:0] - **INDC** = each country's own pledged post-2020 **climate-change action plan**, submitted before COP21 Paris (IAS 2016) – not refugees, AIIB or SDGs.
[96:3:1] TABLE head: Commitment | INDC 2015 (2030) | Updated NDC, Aug 2022 (2030) | NDC 3.0 (2035) | Progress
  [96:3:1.0] Emissions-intensity cut of GDP | 33-35% | 45% | 47% | 36% by 2020
  [96:3:1.1] Non-fossil share of installed capacity | ~40% | 50% | 60% | Crossed 50% June 2025; 54.18% on 30 June 2026
  [96:3:1.2] Extra carbon sink | 2.5-3 bn t CO2e | Unchanged | 3.5-4.0 bn t | 2.29 bn t added
[96:3:2] - **Base year 2005**; Aug 2022 target **45%** (APPSC G-IV 2022). NDCs prepared by **MoEFCC**, approved by the **Union Cabinet**.
[96:3:3] TABLE head: Version | Date | Feature
  [96:3:3.0] INDC | Oct 2015, before COP21 | Eight goals, three quantitative; 4 of 8 NAPCC missions on adaptation
  [96:3:3.1] Updated NDC | Aug 2022 | Took in two Panchamrit pledges (45% intensity, 50% non-fossil); added Mission LiFE
  [96:3:3.2] NDC 3.0 (2031-35) | Cabinet Mar 2026; submitted 24 Apr 2026 | LiFE embedded; adaptation (coasts, farms, Himalaya); low-cost finance
[96:3:4] - Updated NDC did **not remove adaptation**. By 31 Dec 2025, India and **Argentina** were the only G20 members without a 2035 NDC.
[96:3:5] > Traps: 33-35% (not 30-35%); the target is **installed capacity**, not generation.
[96:3:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket CA 2026 Part 02 p.182; Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.161; PMF Lens 2026-04 (04) p.1; Praveen CA-360 Mar 2026 p.88; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.11; app notes 5:96 sub 0
## SUB 4 | Energy Transition and Carbon Sink
[96:4:0] - An effective **positive measure** against climate change = **expansion of carbon sinks through afforestation** (AP Panchayat Secretary) – not subsidising electricity or removing all fuel subsidies.
[96:4:1] - Non-fossil **51.5%** of capacity (Nov 2025); **generation share only ~25%** (storage shortage).
[96:4:2] - **3rd** in renewable capacity, after China and the USA (IRENA 2026, 250.50 GW end-2025).
[96:4:3] - **Green Hydrogen Mission**: **₹19,744 crore**; **5 MMT/yr by 2030**. **Nuclear Energy Mission**: **5 indigenous SMRs by 2033**.
[96:4:4] - **Pumped storage**: **258 GW** identified; **7 GW** operational; >17 GW more by 2030. First standalone BESS: 180 MW (**Gujarat**). AP: **Pinnapuram 1,680 MW** integrated RE + pumped storage.
[96:4:5] - Carbon-sink programmes: **Green India Mission** (**5 Mha new + 5 Mha improved**); **MISHTI** (~540 sq km of **mangroves**). Forest and tree cover **~24.6%** (2021).
[96:4:6] - India has **not signed** the Global Methane Pledge.
[96:4:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.161; Rocket Environment p.14; app notes 5:96 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Mission LiFE
[96:5:0] - **LiFE = Lifestyle for Environment** – an **India-led global mass movement** to nudge **individual and community action** to protect the environment (TSPSC 2023).
[96:5:1] - Idea first put forward at **COP26 (2021)**; LiFE Global Movement **5 June 2022**; Mission launched **20 Oct 2022** at **Kevadia (Ekta Nagar), Gujarat**, by the **PM** with the **UN Secretary-General** – not 5 June 2021, not Maharashtra, not the President.
[96:5:2] - **P3** = **Pro-Planet People**; **75 LiFE actions under 7 themes** (save energy, save water, say no to single-use plastic, sustainable food, reduce waste, e-waste, healthy lifestyles). Aligned schemes: **UJALA** (LED bulbs), **PAT** (industrial efficiency).
[96:5:3] ~~ Sources: daily CA 22 Oct 2026 (octlatest-daily-em-ca-2026-10-22) p.5; Rocket CA 2026 Part 02 p.182; app notes 5:96 sub 3
## SUB 6 | Carbon Markets – CCTS and Green Credit Programme
[96:6:0] TABLE head:  | CCTS | Green Credit Programme
  [96:6:0.0] Launch | Notified June 2023 | Oct 2023
  [96:6:0.1] Law | Sec 14AA, Energy Conservation Act 2001 (amended 2022) | EPA 1986
  [96:6:0.2] Run by | BEE (Ministry of Power) | ICFRE, Dehradun
  [96:6:0.3] Nature | India's first mandatory compliance carbon market | Incentive for voluntary environmental actions
[96:6:1] - CCTS = **compliance** mechanism (energy-intensive sectors get GHG Emission Intensity targets; beating them earns tradeable **Carbon Credit Certificates**) + **offset** mechanism (voluntary). **Intensity-based, not cap-based**; supports the **45%** intensity target.
[96:6:2] - **282 obligated entities** (Oct 2025: aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper). **UK CBAM** recognises CCTS as a carbon price from **1 Jan 2027**.
[96:6:3] - GCP afforestation can be exchanged against **compensatory afforestation** obligations.
[96:6:4] - **Surat ETS**: particulate matter cut **20-30%**. **Khasi Hills REDD+** (Meghalaya): India's first **Plan Vivo**-certified REDD+ project.
[96:6:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:96 sub 4

=== NOTES 5:99 | Air Pollution – Sources, Pollutants, Naaqs, Aqi, Ncap, Stubble Burning and Acid Rain
## SUB 0 | Carbon Monoxide and Other Pollutants – Health Effects
[99:0:0] # Carbon Monoxide (CO) – the most-asked pollutant
[99:0:1] - **Source:** **incomplete combustion** of carbon fuels – **vehicle exhaust** (main pollutant gas in exhaust), **cigarette smoke**, coal/wood burning. CO2 comes from **complete** combustion.
[99:0:2] - **Nature:** **colourless, odourless**, poisonous; "odourless poisonous gas in coal smoke" = CO.
[99:0:3] - **Effect:** binds **haemoglobin** → **carboxyhaemoglobin**; affinity **200–250 times** that of oxygen → cuts the blood's **oxygen-carrying capacity**; can affect the **bloodstream leading to death** → usually called the "**most dangerous**" air pollutant.
[99:0:4] - **Not** converted to CO2 in the body, does **not** destroy haemoglobin's structure, not mainly a digestive/liver/kidney poison (UPSC 2010, MPPSC 2012).
[99:0:5] - "Forms an **irreversible** complex with haemoglobin" (UPPCS 1996) – books answer **CO**; strictly the bond is reversible but very stable (CO is released slowly).
[99:0:6] - Flashcard: CO breathing is harmful because **it competes with oxygen in the blood**.
[99:0:7] TABLE head: Pollutant | Main source | Part / effect
  [99:0:7.0] Carbon monoxide | Incomplete combustion, vehicles, cigarettes | Blood stream – carboxyhaemoglobin, hypoxia, death
  [99:0:7.1] Asbestos dust | Asbestos mining, cement sheets | Lung – asbestosis
  [99:0:7.2] Lead | Leaded petrol (old), smelters, batteries, paints | Brain / nervous system; blood pressure, kidney
  [99:0:7.3] Mercury | Coal burning, industry | Stomach (UPPSC 2012 match key) / nervous system
  [99:0:7.4] SO2 | Coal/oil burning, power plants, smelting | Eye, throat and lung irritation, asthma; acid rain
  [99:0:7.5] NOx | High-temperature combustion – vehicles, power plants, lightning | Eye/airway irritation; smog, acid rain
  [99:0:7.6] H2S | Decaying vegetation and animal matter (chief), sewage, refineries | Rotten-egg smell; toxic
  [99:0:7.7] Fly ash | Burning coal in thermal power plants | Lung disease; captured by ESP
  [99:0:7.8] PM2.5 / PM10 | Combustion, road and construction dust, biomass | Heart/lung disease; PM2.5 enters blood, crosses placenta
  [99:0:7.9] Ground-level O3 | Secondary (photochemical) | Asthma, chest pain, crop damage
[99:0:8] - **UPPSC 2012 match:** Asbestos – Lung, Lead – Brain, Mercury – Stomach, CO – Blood stream → **3 1 2 4**.
[99:0:9] - **Lead** from **petrol** combustion (anti-knock **tetraethyl lead, TEL**) – the metal polluting city air with many vehicles; leaded petrol is **phased out in India (2000)**.
[99:0:10] - **Most injurious exhaust components:** **CO and lead** (old leaded-petrol era).
[99:0:11] - **Cigarette smoke:** **CO and benzene** (also nicotine, HCN, arsenic, formaldehyde).
[99:0:12] - **Inorganic gaseous pollutants:** HCN, H2S, CO, CO2, SO2, NOx (methane and phosgene are carbon compounds usually grouped as organic).
[99:0:13] - **Asthma** is caused / aggravated by **air pollution**; **rickets** is **not** caused by smog directly (smog cuts UV → less vitamin D; rickets is a deficiency disease).
[99:0:14] - **Bio-gas / gobar gas** = mainly **methane** (50–65%) + CO2 (35–50%), traces of H2, N2, H2S.
[99:0:15] - Gases: **ozone = O3**; **CFCs** deplete the stratospheric ozone layer.
[99:0:16] - Other links: **ammonia** (fertilisers + livestock, 77–80%) drives secondary particles; **ammonium sulphate** (from SO2 + NH3) ≈ one-third of India's PM2.5; **magnetite** particles (combustion, brake wear) found in brain tissue – possible Alzheimer's link; **cadmium** from metal smelting, PAHs from incomplete burning; PM2.5 crosses the placenta (AIIMS, 3 June 2026).
[99:0:17] - Burden: WHO ~**7 million** deaths a year; fossil-fuel air pollution ~**1.72 million** premature deaths in India (2022); NCR winter PM2.5 ~35 times the WHO limit; IIT Delhi: curbing power-plant SO2 could prevent ~1.24 lakh deaths a year.
[99:0:18] > Exam angle: ≈20 PYQs ask the same fact – CO + haemoglobin. Pick CO whenever the stem says "blood", "oxygen-carrying", "colourless gas from exhaust and cigarettes", "incomplete combustion" or "most dangerous".
[99:0:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.1-5, p.8; Rocket Environment p.21, p.63; Rocket Chemistry p.35, p.43-44; PMF Environment Part 04 p.3-5; Shankar Environment Part 06 p.6, p.10; PMF Environment Part 07 p.97
## SUB 1 | Sources of Air Pollution – Natural, Vehicles, Industry
[99:1:0] TABLE head: Basis | Examples
  [99:1:0.0] Natural | Forest fires, volcanic eruptions (SOx, ash), dust storms, natural decay (methane, H2S), lightning (NOx), pollen, spores
  [99:1:0.1] Anthropogenic | Combustion of coal, petrol, diesel (basic source of air pollution), vehicles, industries, thermal plants, fireworks
  [99:1:0.2] Point / line / area / diffuse | Chimneys of industries / automobile exhaust along roads / industrial estates, mining / sprayed fertilisers and pesticides
[99:1:1] - **Main source in Indian cities: automobile (vehicular) emissions** (APPSC G2 Mains 2025). Main pollutants of metros (MPPSC 2018 key): **CO and SO2**.
[99:1:2] - **Composition of air:** N2 78%, O2 21%, CO2 0.04% – **N2, O2, helium are not pollutants**; CO, NO2, SO2, ground-level O3, lead dust, smoke are.
[99:1:3] - **CO2** is the usual "**not an air pollutant**" answer (greenhouse gas, quantitative pollutant; not in NAQI).
[99:1:4] - **Vehicles:** CO, NOx, unburnt hydrocarbons, PM, (old) lead. **Diesel engine:** much **CO at low temperature** (incomplete burning), much **NOx at high temperature**.
[99:1:5] - **Steel industry:** oxides of **sulphur, nitrogen, CO and CO2 – all four** (UPSC 2014).
[99:1:6] - **Largest SO2 source (US EPA, UPSC 2024): power plants using fossil fuels** (~73%), then other industry; not ships, locomotives or ore extraction.
[99:1:7] - **SO2 + fossil fuel:** SO2 is the air-pollutant gas released by burning fossil fuel (H2, N2, O2 are not).
[99:1:8] - **Delhi PM (IIT Kanpur study, 2016):** **road dust** (incl. construction dust) is the largest PM2.5/PM10 source annually (~38% PM2.5); in **winter** secondary particles, vehicles and biomass burning lead.
[99:1:9] - **Delhi winter peak:** A true, but "vehicle combustion increases in winter" is false – winter peaks come from **temperature inversion, calm winds, stubble smoke**.
[99:1:10] - **Stubble burning in Punjab** (and Haryana) contributes more to Delhi's air than Rajasthan or firewood use.
[99:1:11] - **Transport and technology:** more travel → more pollution; transport releases lead, NOx, CO (ozone forms from them – secondary); burning fuel harms health.
[99:1:12] - Blackened vessel bottom while cooking = **fuel not burning completely**.
[99:1:13] - **Sita Ashok** tree = prevention of dust pollution (UPPCS 2007).
[99:1:14] - **Eutrophication** = water pollution, not air (smog, acid rain, asbestosis are air-related).
[99:1:15] - **PM2.5 main source in India** (printed key): **vehicular emissions**.
[99:1:16] - **Silver oxide** is not a major primary air pollutant (SOx, CO, NOx are).
[99:1:17] - NCR: **transport** is the largest primary source, ~**23%** of the winter load (CAQM synthesis report, Jan 2026).
[99:1:18] - Fuels: **coal** most polluting; diesel gives more PM than petrol; CNG/LPG still release **CO2**; **LPG** burns without smoke; biogas mainly CO2 + traces of H2S; **hydrogen** gives only water (no CO, SO2, PM); wood and cow-dung give smoke, CO, PM.
[99:1:19] > Exam angle: "natural source" = forest fires/volcanoes; "urban source" = vehicles; "steel / crop residue releases which" = all of them.
[99:1:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 09 p.14; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.1-3; Rocket Environment p.21, p.35; PMF Environment Part 04 p.3, p.9-10; Shankar Environment Part 06 p.5-6; IIT Kanpur study summary (governancenow.com)
## SUB 2 | Acid Rain – Causes, Chemistry, pH and Effects
[99:2:0] - **Definition:** precipitation (rain, snow, fog, mist) with **pH below 5.6**; normal rain ≈ 5.6 (carbonic acid from CO2). Term coined **1872** by **Robert Angus Smith** (Manchester coal burning).
[99:2:1] - **pH scale** = **acidity / basicity**; 0–14; **7 neutral**, below 7 acidic; each unit = **tenfold** change. **Human blood ≈ 7.4** (slightly basic).
[99:2:2] - **Causing gases: SO2 and NOx** (oxides of **sulphur and nitrogen**) – **not** CO, CO2, O3, CH4, CFCs, H2S, HCl or "oxides of hydrogen". Main single factor: **SO2**.
[99:2:3] - **Ozone** only speeds up the oxidation (photo-oxidant) – it is not a cause (UPSC 2022: **2 and 4 only**).
[99:2:4] - **Chemistry:** SO2 / NOx + water + O2 + photo-oxidants → **H2SO4 (~two-thirds)** + **HNO3 (~one-third)** → both **sulphuric and nitric acid** are components; acid falls from atmosphere to the ground.
[99:2:5] - Acid rain occurs due to the **reaction between clouds (water) and sulphur dioxide** (UPPCS 2001).
[99:2:6] TABLE head: Gas | Anthropogenic | Natural
  [99:2:6.0] SOx | Coal power plants, smelting of sulphide ores, H2SO4 plants, refineries, industries | Volcanoes, oceans, decay
  [99:2:6.1] NOx | Vehicles, power plants, biomass burning | Lightning, forest fires
[99:2:7] - **Deposition:** wet (rain, snow, fog) and **dry** – about **half** of atmospheric acidity returns dry.
[99:2:8] - **Effects:** acidifies lakes (fish die, aluminium released), damages forests and soils (leaches Ca, Mg), corrodes limestone/marble (**Taj Mahal "marble cancer"** – SO2, Mathura refinery), harms health (**respiratory ailments**).
[99:2:9] - **Taj Trapezium Zone** ~10,400 sq km (Agra, Fatehpur Sikri, Agra Fort; not Sanchi); **M.C. Mehta v. UoI (1996)** barred coal/coke.
[99:2:10] - **Transboundary:** Scandinavia receives acid rain from UK/central Europe; **India = largest SO2 emitter (2022)**.
[99:2:11] - **Control:** low-sulphur fuel, **FGD scrubbers** (trap SO2), low-NOx burners, catalytic converters; **liming** = remedial (not preventive).
[99:2:12] TABLE head: Instrument | Year | Focus
  [99:2:12.0] LRTAP (UNECE) | 1979 | First binding treaty on transboundary air pollution
  [99:2:12.1] Helsinki Protocol | 1985 | 30% sulphur cut
  [99:2:12.2] Sofia Protocol | 1988 | Freeze NOx
  [99:2:12.3] Gothenburg Protocol | 1999 | SO2, NOx, NH3, VOCs
[99:2:13] > Exam angle: ~17 PYQs; the answer is almost always "SO2 and NOx" / "pH below 5.6" / "sulphuric and nitric acid".
[99:2:14] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 p.4-5; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.7; Rocket Environment p.21, p.63; Rocket Chemistry p.21; PMF Environment Part 04 p.11, p.13-14, p.48-49; app notes 5:99 sub 9-10
[99:2:15] - **Acid-rain countries (books):** **Norway** (most among China/Japan/Norway/USA) and **Canada** – classic transboundary receivers (UPPCS 2000, 2011); strictly East Asia/China now has heavy acid rain, Germany's Black Forest was also hit.
[99:2:16] - **Maximum acid in acid rain:** **sulphuric acid (H2SO4)**, then nitric acid; HCl and carbonic acid are minor.
[99:2:17] - **A-R (IAS 2003):** coal thermal plants cause acid rain through **SO2** (sulphur in coal); oxides of carbon are emitted too but do not explain it → **A and R true, R not the explanation**.
## SUB 3 | AQI, NAAQS, WHO Guidelines and Monitoring Networks
[99:3:0] # National Air Quality Index (NAQI)
[99:3:1] - Launched **April 2015** under **Swachh Bharat Abhiyan** (MoEFCC/CPCB; developed with IIT Kanpur); first for **10 cities**; motto "**One Number – One Colour – One Description**".
[99:3:2] - **8 pollutants** (up to 24-hour averaging): **PM10, PM2.5, NO2, SO2, CO, O3, NH3, Pb**. **Not included: CO2, methane, benzene**. UPSC 2016: of CO2, CO, NO2, SO2, methane → **CO, NO2, SO2 (2, 3 and 4 only)**.
[99:3:3] TABLE head: AQI | Category | Colour
  [99:3:3.0] 0–50 | Good | Dark green
  [99:3:3.1] 51–100 | Satisfactory | Light green
  [99:3:3.2] 101–200 | Moderately polluted | Yellow
  [99:3:3.3] 201–300 | Poor | Orange
  [99:3:3.4] 301–400 | Very poor | Red
  [99:3:3.5] 401–500 | Severe | Maroon
[99:3:4] # NAAQS (CPCB, 2009)
[99:3:5] - **12 pollutants**: the 8 above + **benzene, benzo(a)pyrene, arsenic, nickel**; **ozone** added for the first time in 2009.
[99:3:6] TABLE head: Pollutant | NAAQS annual | NAAQS 24-hour | WHO AQG 2021
  [99:3:6.0] PM2.5 | 40 µg/m³ | 60 µg/m³ | 5 annual; 15 (24-hr)
  [99:3:6.1] PM10 | 60 µg/m³ | 100 µg/m³ | 15 annual; 45 (24-hr)
  [99:3:6.2] SO2 | 50 (20 in eco-sensitive areas) | 80 µg/m³ | 40 (24-hr)
  [99:3:6.3] NO2 | 40 µg/m³ | 80 µg/m³ | 10 annual
[99:3:7] - **WHO AQG 2021 (UPSC 2022 → 1 and 4 only):** ozone peaks in **sunny** weather, not inclement weather; **PM2.5** (not PM10) crosses the lung barrier into blood; **excess ozone triggers asthma**.
[99:3:8] - **RSPM:** CPCB treats RSPM as **PM10 (< 10 µm)**; old books/UPPCS 2017 key: "**less than 5 µm**".
[99:3:9] # Monitoring networks
[99:3:10] TABLE head: Network | Feature
  [99:3:10.0] NAMP (CPCB, 1984) | Regular monitoring at all locations of SO2, NO2, RSPM/PM10 and PM2.5 – not CO2
  [99:3:10.1] CAAQMS | Real-time stations; data via SAMEER app (CPCB)
  [99:3:10.2] SAFAR | MoES/IITM Pune; new SAFAR system for Delhi unveiled 2018 by Dr Harsh Vardhan; app SAFAR-Air (city air quality, first 4 cities)
  [99:3:10.3] AUM photonic system | Indigenous (GVP-SIRC, Visakhapatnam; DST) real-time remote monitoring of air quality
  [99:3:10.4] WMO Global Atmosphere Watch | Global stations in Algeria (Assekrem), Kenya (Mt Kenya), Brazil …; India has no GAW global station (printed key)
  [99:3:10.5] Precipitation chemistry | IMD, under WMO GAW / BAPMoN
[99:3:11] - NAMP size: **1,646 stations in 603 cities** (March 2026).
[99:3:12] > Exam angle: "how many pollutants" = 8 (NAQI) / 12 (NAAQS); CO2 and methane are never in the index.
[99:3:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.2-4; Rocket Environment p.35; PMF Environment Part 04 p.49-53; WMO GAW Global stations page (search result community.wmo.int); DST AUM release (dst.gov.in/node/4791, search result); app notes 5:99 sub 4-5
## SUB 4 | Smog, Primary and Secondary Pollutants
[99:4:0] TABLE head: Type | Formed from | Conditions
  [99:4:0.0] Classical / London smog (sulphurous, 1952) | Smoke + fog + SO2 | Cold, humid; grey/black
  [99:4:0.1] Photochemical / Los Angeles / summer smog | NO2/NOx + hydrocarbons (VOCs) + sunlight → ozone, PAN (oxidising agents) | Warm, sunny, traffic; brownish – "brown air"
[99:4:1] - **Smog** = smoke + fog; essentially caused by **oxides of nitrogen and sulphur**; photochemical smog **always contains ozone**; ozone is **produced** during its formation (hydrocarbons, NOx are inputs, not products).
[99:4:2] - TSPSC 2023 pairs: classical smog = smoke, fog, SO2 ✔; photochemical smog = high concentration of **oxidising agents** ✔ → **both**.
[99:4:3] - **Primary** pollutants (emitted directly): CO, CO2, SO2, NOx, fly ash, lead. **Secondary** (formed in air): **O3, PAN, smog**, ammonium sulphate → "**not a primary pollutant**" = **ozone**; "secondary pollutant" = **smog**.
[99:4:4] - **Tropospheric ozone precursors:** NOx, CO, methane/VOCs – **water vapour is not** one.
[99:4:5] - Stratospheric ozone is **not** an air pollutant (shields UV); ground-level ozone is.
[99:4:6] - Smog effects: breathing problems, bronchitis; heavy smog cuts UV → less vitamin D (rickets rise) – but **rickets is not a smog disease** (SSC 2018).
[99:4:7] - **Asian Brown Cloud (UNEP, 2002):** layer of soot, black carbon, sulphate aerosols over **South Asia** (Indo-Gangetic plain) and the Indian Ocean, **January–March** (dry season), from biomass and fossil-fuel burning.
[99:4:8] > Exam angle: "brown air", "always contains", "produced during", "secondary" – answer ozone / photochemical smog.
[99:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 09 p.12-13; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.3-4; Rocket Environment p.22, p.63; PMF Environment Part 04 p.8-11; Shankar Environment Part 06 p.5-7
## SUB 5 | National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), PRANA and Swachh Vayu Survekshan
[99:5:0] - **Launched 10 January 2019** by **MoEFCC** – PAN-India **time-bound national strategy** for prevention, control and abatement of air pollution at **regional and urban scales**, plus augmenting the monitoring network; also the answer to "GoI initiative to control industrial emissions" (APPSC G2 Mains 2025).
[99:5:1] - **Original target: 20–30% cut in PM10/PM2.5 by 2024**, base **2017** (so "by 2025" is wrong).
[99:5:2] - **Revised (September 2022): up to 40% PM10 reduction (or meeting NAAQS) by 2025-26** (the year asked = **2026**).
[99:5:3] - Coverage: **130 cities in 24 States/UTs** (non-attainment = failed NAAQS for five years; earlier 131/102); coordinated by **CPCB with SPCBs**; legal base **Air Act 1981**; City Action Plans; performance-linked grant ₹16,425 crore.
[99:5:4] - **PRANA** = Portal for Regulation of Air-pollution in Non-Attainment cities – **monitors NCAP implementation**; launched **7 September 2021**.
[99:5:5] - **Highest % PM10 cut, 2017-18 → 2023-24: Varanasi (230 → 73 µg/m³, 68%)**, then Bareilly (61%), Firozabad (59%) (MoEFCC/PIB).
[99:5:6] - **Swachh Vayu Survekshan**: annual city ranking under NCAP since 2022-23; awards on **Swachh Vayu Diwas, 7 September** (5th SVS awards, 7 Sep 2026). Indore first among million-plus cities in SVS 2023 and 2025; Surat in SVS 2024.
[99:5:7] - Results: 2024-25 vs 2017-18 – 103 cities cut PM10; only 22 of 130 met PM10 NAAQS. NGT (May 2026): 86% of spend went to road dust.
[99:5:8] - Programme match: MoEFCC – NCAP; MoES – SAFAR; Jal Shakti – Namami Gange (NRCP, NLCP are water programmes).
[99:5:9] > Exam angle: year = **2019**; revised target = **40% by 2026**; PRANA = monitoring NCAP.
[99:5:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.7; Rocket Environment p.36; Rocket CA 2026 Part 02 p.23-24; Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.29; PMF Environment Part 04 p.53-54; PIB document doc20241128458601 (Varanasi 68%); app notes 5:99 sub 6
## SUB 6 | Control Devices and Cleaner Fuels
[99:6:0] TABLE head: Device | Removes
  [99:6:0.0] Electrostatic precipitator (ESP) | Particulate matter (fly ash) from industrial smoke
  [99:6:0.1] Bag filter (baghouse) | Dust by fabric filtration
  [99:6:0.2] Cyclone separator / collector | Coarse particles by centrifugal force ("cyclone divider" is not a device)
  [99:6:0.3] Wet / venturi scrubber | Gases (SO2) and particles
  [99:6:0.4] FGD | Up to 95% SO2 from flue gas
[99:6:1] - **Catalytic converter:** **platinum, palladium, rhodium** catalysts turn CO → CO2, HC → CO2 + H2O, NOx → N2; needs **unleaded petrol**.
[99:6:2] - **Fuel efficiency (IAS 2000 key):** radial tyres, multipoint fuel injection, catalytic converter → **1, 3 and 4**; strictly a catalytic converter cuts emissions, and a streamlined body cuts drag.
[99:6:3] - Fuel injection promotes **complete combustion**.
[99:6:4] - **CNG = mainly methane (CH4)**; cleaner because it gives very little SOx/NOx, less pollution and fewer GHGs – all three true.
[99:6:5] - Fuels by pollution: coal > diesel > petrol > CNG/LPG; **hydrogen** cleanest (only water).
[99:6:6] - Other measures: BS-VI nationwide 1 April 2020 (BS-V skipped), PUC, RFID pollution charge on Delhi-bound trucks, FAME-II, SATAT (compressed biogas), E20 ethanol blending, Methanol Economy (NITI Aayog), vehicle scrappage policy (2021), OCEMS for red-category industries in Delhi-NCR, ban on pet coke and furnace oil.
[99:6:7] - BS-III from 1 April 2005 in NCR + 10 cities. **FGD** mandated 2015 for coal plants; only **39 of 537** had it when the mandate was relaxed (2025).
[99:6:8] - **WAYU** (Wind Augmentation PurifYing Unit) – CSIR-NEERI with IIT Bombay; roadside purifier installed in **Delhi** (ITO, Mukarba Chowk) in September 2018.
[99:6:9] > Exam angle: ESP = particulates; converter = Pt/Pd/Rh; CNG = methane.

## SUB 7 | Bioindicators and Indoor Air Pollution
[99:7:0] - **Lichens** (symbiotic **algae + fungi**) are the best **bioindicators of air pollution**, especially **SO2** – they **do not grow in polluted areas** (so "lichens grow well in polluted areas" is false). **Mosses** indicate heavy-metal deposition.
[99:7:1] - **Indoor pollution:** solid fuels (wood, cow-dung, coal), tobacco smoke, VOCs, radon, CO, mosquito coils; **maximum indoor chemical pollution: burning coal** (Jharkhand 2021); worst hit **women and children**; the four most serious pollutants in biofuel smoke: particulates, CO, polycyclic organic matter, formaldehyde.
[99:7:2] - Biological indoor pollutants: pollen, mites, pet hair, fungi → allergies, asthma.
[99:7:3] - Intercity buses: cabin air 2–3 times WHO limits (IntrCity study, 15 Mar 2026).
[99:7:4] > Exam angle: "bioindicator / indicator of SO2 / do not grow in polluted area" = lichen.

## SUB 9 | Stubble Burning, CAQM, GRAP and Cloud Seeding
[99:9:0] - **Crop / biomass residue burning** (October–November, Punjab, Haryana, UP) releases **CO, methane, ozone (secondary), SO2** – all four (UPSC 2019), plus NOx, CO2, black carbon, VOCs.

=== NOTES 5:101 | Water Pollution – Sources, Eutrophication, Namami Gange, Sewage Treatment, Groundwater Contamination
## SUB 0 | Water-borne Pollutant Diseases
[101:0:0] TABLE head: Disease | Contaminant | Key fact
  [101:0:0.0] Minamata | Methyl mercury | Japan, 1956; bacteria turn mercury into methyl mercury, biomagnified through fish; neurological damage
  [101:0:0.1] Itai-itai ("ouch-ouch") | Cadmium | Japan (Toyama, mass case 1950); mining wastewater used to irrigate rice; painful bones and joints
  [101:0:0.2] Blue baby syndrome | Nitrate in drinking water | Methaemoglobinaemia – nitrate → nitrite → methaemoglobin in the blood, which cannot carry oxygen; infants
  [101:0:0.3] Fluorosis | Fluoride | Dental mottling (children under 8), skeletal fluorosis, stiff painful joints
  [101:0:0.4] Knock-knee (genu valgum) | Fluoride | Skeletal fluorosis – outward bending of legs from the knees
  [101:0:0.5] Arsenicosis / blackfoot disease | Arsenic | Skin lesions, skin and lung cancer
  [101:0:0.6] Contact dermatitis | Nickel | Allergic skin rash (SSC CGL 2017)
[101:0:1] - **Mercury → Minamata; nitrate → blue baby** (IAS 2017). Fluoride is **not** matched with "indigestion" (UPPSC 2017 key), though NextGen/Shankar list gastro-intestinal problems among fluorosis effects.
[101:0:2] - "In the blood" = **methaemoglobin**; "in drinking water" = **nitrate**.
[101:0:3] - **Metal-toxicity diseases:** Minamata and Itai-itai; **dermatitis** is the usual "NOT metal toxicity" answer (SSC 2018), though nickel allergy causes it.
[101:0:4] - **DDT** at high concentration disturbs **calcium metabolism in birds** (thin eggshells); **nitrates + phosphates → eutrophication**.
[101:0:5] TABLE head: Pollutant | Main source (APPSC NTRUHS)
  [101:0:5.0] Arsenic | Inorganic compounds in agriculture, mining, manufacturing; fly ash
  [101:0:5.1] Mercury | Coal-fired power plants, incinerators, industry, historic gold mining
  [101:0:5.2] Fluoride | Minerals – apatite, micas, hornblende – released from rocks
  [101:0:5.3] Chromium | Tannery / leather wastewater
[101:0:6] - Fluorosis chemistry: fluoride replaces hydroxyl in **hydroxyapatite → fluorapatite**.
[101:0:7] > Most-asked angle (~22 PYQs): match the disease to the metal – Itai-itai = cadmium (×7), blue baby = nitrate (×5), knock-knee = fluoride (×3).
[101:0:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.12-13; PMF Environment Part 04 p.67-68, p.73; Shankar Environment Part 06 p.18; app notes 5:101 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Measuring Water Pollution – DO, BOD, Coliform, Solids
[101:1:0] TABLE head: Parameter | Measures | Unpolluted water
  [101:1:0.0] DO | Oxygen dissolved in water | > 8–9 mg/L
  [101:1:0.1] BOD | Oxygen bacteria need to decompose organic matter | < 4 mg/L
  [101:1:0.2] COD | Oxygen to oxidise all organic matter (biodegradable + non-biodegradable) | < 5 mg/L
[101:1:1] - River pollution is measured by its **dissolved oxygen**: more pollution → **less DO**.
[101:1:2] - **BOD = standard criterion for pollution assay in aquatic ecosystems** (UPSC 2017), i.e. organic pollution in **water** – not soil or air. **High BOD = heavy organic/microbial pollution, e.g. sewage**; low BOD = good water.
[101:1:3] - **Coliform count** (MPN/100 ml) = **faecal contamination by human wastes** – the predominant human-body pollutant of the **Ganga**; higher total coliform = mixing of human faeces.
[101:1:4] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [101:1:4.0] Suspended solids | Retained on a filter – silt, clay (APPSC 2023)
  [101:1:4.1] Dissolved solids / TDS | Salts passing the filter (sodium salts, nitrate)
  [101:1:4.2] Turbidity | Cloudiness from suspended solids, measured in NTU
[101:1:5] - Water-changing agents: **effluents** alter physico-chemical characteristics (UPSC 1996). **Sulphur dioxide** is an **air** pollutant, not a water pollutant (zinc, copper, nickel are).
[101:1:6] - **Aquatic organisms respire faster** because **water holds far less dissolved oxygen than air**.
[101:1:7] > Asked ~15 times: what BOD/DO/coliform indicates; "dissolved oxygen" is the river-pollution answer.
[101:1:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.10, p.13-14; PMF Environment Part 04 p.64-65, p.71; app notes 5:101 sub 1
## SUB 2 | Ganga Governance and Namami Gange
[101:2:0] TABLE head: Year | Body / plan | Key fact
  [101:2:0.0] 1985 | Central Ganga Authority | PM chair; renamed National River Conservation Authority, Sept 1995
  [101:2:0.1] 1985 | Ganga Action Plan-I | First river action plan (MoEF); Rajiv Gandhi, Varanasi; 25 main-stem towns
  [101:2:0.2] 1993 | GAP-II | Tributaries – Yamuna, Gomti, Damodar, Mahananda; merged into NRCP 1995
  [101:2:0.3] 2009 (Feb) | National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) | Under Sec 3 of the EP Act 1986; PM chair; river basin = unit of planning; declared Ganga the National River
  [101:2:0.4] 2011 | NMCG | Registered society; implementing arm
  [101:2:0.5] 2016 | National Ganga Council | Replaced NGRBA; PM chair, Jal Shakti Minister vice-chair
[101:2:1] - **GAP launch date:** most books and keys give **1985** (approved, Central Ganga Authority set up); the formal launch by Rajiv Gandhi was in **June 1986** (14 June 1986, Varanasi).
[101:2:2] - Five tiers: **National Ganga Council (PM) → Empowered Task Force (Jal Shakti Minister) → NMCG → State Ganga Committees → District Ganga Committees**; legal base: **River Ganga Authorities Order, 2016**.
[101:2:3] - **Namami Gange:** integrated conservation mission, flagship approved **2014** (announced 2014-15), outlay **₹20,000 crore** (2015–2020); **Namami Gange-II ₹22,500 crore** (2021–26). Twin goals **Nirmal Dhara + Aviral Dhara**; pillars of the mission's vision: **Nirmal Ganga, Aviral Ganga**, Jan Ganga, Gyan Ganga (+ Arth Ganga).
[101:2:4] - **Eight main pillars:** Sewerage Treatment Infrastructure, River-Front Development, River-Surface Cleaning, Bio-Diversity, Afforestation, Public Awareness, **Industrial Effluent Monitoring**, **Ganga Gram**. **Not pillars:** River Aquifer Management, Boat and Ship Effluent Monitoring, uranium mining.
[101:2:5] - Namami Gange is a key Indian initiative for **SDG 6 (clean water and sanitation)**; UN listed it among the top 10 **World Restoration Flagships**.
[101:2:6] - Most sewerage infrastructure projects (31 Dec 2021, APPSC key): **Bihar**.
[101:2:7] - **Feb 2020 MoU** (NMCG + SPMG-Uttarakhand + Indorama Charitable Trust): **ghat at Badrinath, ghats and crematoria at Gangotri**.
[101:2:8] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [101:2:8.0] Arth Ganga | River-linked economy: natural farming, river tourism, treated-water reuse, artisans (first NGC meeting 2019)
  [101:2:8.1] JALAJ | Livelihood centres (NMCG + WII)
  [101:2:8.2] Ganga Praharis | Trained local volunteers for river biodiversity
  [101:2:8.3] Ganga Utsav | Annual river festival
[101:2:9] - Results: first **dolphin estimate 6,327** (March 2025). **Global River Cities Alliance:** launched at **COP28, Dubai (Dec 2023)**, **led by NMCG**; members – river cities worldwide plus partner countries and agencies.
[101:2:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 04 p.85-88; Rocket Environment p.3; governancenow.com 'Namami Gange: of promises and achievements' (GAP launched June 1986); app notes 5:101 sub 7-8
## SUB 3 | Eutrophication and Algal Blooms
[101:3:0] - **Eutrophication = nutrient (N, P) enrichment of a water body** – the **natural ageing of a lake by nutrient (biological) enrichment** of its water; human-accelerated = **cultural eutrophication**.
[101:3:1] - Triggers: fertiliser runoff (**nitrates, phosphates**), sewage, detergents, aquaculture effluent – not idol immersion as such and not a fall in nitrogen inputs.
[101:3:2] - Chain: **enrichment → algal bloom → algae decay → decomposition uses up DO → hypoxia, fish kills**. So eutrophication **increases** algae and **decreases** DO (both statements true, UPPSC 2019/2020).
[101:3:3] - **Algal bloom:** excessive growth of planktonic (free-floating) algae – deteriorates water quality and causes **fish mortality**.
[101:3:4] - **Hypoxia:** reduction of oxygen in water (or air) threatening aerobic organisms → **dead zones**.
[101:3:5] - Stages: **oligotrophic → mesotrophic → eutrophic → hypereutrophic**.
[101:3:6] - **Harmful algal blooms in Indian seas** (UPSC 2011): nutrient discharge from **estuaries**, monsoon **land run-off** and **upwelling** – all three.
[101:3:7] - Blooms of pigmented **dinoflagellates** in estuaries = **red tides**.
[101:3:8] > Asked ~14 times: definition ("over-supply of nutrients", "natural ageing of a lake"), its effect on DO and algae.
[101:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.12-13; PMF Environment Part 04 p.73-74, p.77; Rocket Environment p.22; app notes 5:101 sub 3
## SUB 4 | Sources of Water Pollution and Sewage Treatment
[101:4:0] - **Point sources:** municipal and industrial discharge pipes; **non-point:** agricultural and urban runoff.
[101:4:1] - **Largest contributor to water pollution in India: untreated sewage**; only about **28%** of urban sewage is treated (2026).
[101:4:2] - Agricultural water polluters: **chemical fertilisers and excessive pesticides**.
[101:4:3] - **Sand mining** in river beds: raises **turbidity**, **pollutes groundwater** and **lowers the water table** (UPSC 2018) – it does not reduce salinity.
[101:4:4] - **AP's main water polluters:** Pharma City (Vizag), tanneries, paper mills, aquaculture.
[101:4:5] - **Dairy effluent** and ritual offerings can have BOD far above sewage.
[101:4:6] TABLE head: Technology | Function
  [101:4:6.0] Activated sludge | Conventional STP process; settled sludge is digested to biogas
  [101:4:6.1] SBR (sequencing batch reactor) | Treats in batches in one tank
  [101:4:6.2] MBR (membrane bioreactor) | Activated sludge + membrane filtration – wastewater treatment (UPSC 2024)
  [101:4:6.3] Ozonation | Ozone kills micro-organisms; leaves no residue (ozone is not radioactive, but that is not why it disinfects)
[101:4:7] - **Treat domestic sewage before release** – the healthy practice (burning plastics/leaves is not).
[101:4:8] - **Rain water** collected after 30–40 minutes of rain is clean but **deficient in minerals**.
[101:4:9] - **CETP** = shared plant for clusters of **small-scale industries**; **India's first CETP: Jeedimetla (near Hyderabad, then Andhra Pradesh), 1989**. AP runs **9 CETPs**; **Zero Liquid Discharge** example: **Tiruppur** (Tamil Nadu).
[101:4:10] - **HAM** for Namami Gange approved **2016**; first HAM STP **Haridwar**. **AMRUT 2.0: 20% reuse** of treated wastewater; thermal plants within **50 km** of an STP must use treated wastewater. BOD discharge limit relaxed **10 → 30 mg/L** (criticised: more organic pollution allowed).
[101:4:11] - **IISER Pune** (Jan 2023) reported a new material that removes pollutants from water.
[101:4:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.10-11; PMF Environment Part 04 p.64, p.81-84; app notes 5:101 sub 0, 6
## SUB 5 | Groundwater Contamination
[101:5:0] TABLE head: Contaminant | Where
  [101:5:0.0] Arsenic | Ganga-Brahmaputra plains – West Bengal (maximum, Bengal basin, Kolkata), Bihar, Jharkhand, UP, Assam; extends into Bangladesh
  [101:5:0.1] Fluoride | Rajasthan highest (CGWB 2024), Haryana, Karnataka; Nalgonda (Telangana) is the classic fluorosis district; AP also hit
  [101:5:0.2] Nitrate | About 56% of districts exceed 45 mg/L; mainly fertiliser
  [101:5:0.3] Uranium | Malwa (Punjab), Rajasthan; > 30 ppb also in AP, Telangana
[101:5:1] - **Arsenic** is the **non-biotic** (chemical) pollutant of groundwater; bacteria, algae, viruses are biotic.
[101:5:2] - Drinking-water pollutants in parts of India (IAS 2013): **arsenic, fluoride, uranium** – not sorbitol or formaldehyde.
[101:5:3] - **Nalgonda technique** (fluoride removal): **alum + lime + bleaching powder**.
[101:5:4] - **UP Ground Water (Management and Regulation) Act, 2019 (UP cabinet, 2020):** registration of submersible pumps mandatory; rainwater harvesting mandatory in private schools/colleges; it **does penalise** polluting groundwater through boring pipes.
[101:5:5] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 04 p.67-69; NextGen Environment APPSC 10 p.13; Rocket Environment p.22; app notes 5:101 sub 5

## SUB 8 | Polluted Stretches, Reports and AP Water Bodies

  [101:8:0.1] 2022 | 311 (279 rivers) | 46
  [101:8:0.2] 2025 report (2023 data) | 296 | 37

=== NOTES 5:103 | Solid Waste, Plastic Waste, E-waste, Biomedical and Construction Waste – Rules and Management
## SUB 0 | Plastic Waste – Rules, Ban and Microplastics
[103:0:0] # Rules timeline and thickness
[103:0:1] TABLE head: Year | Instrument | Provision
  [103:0:1.0] 2011 | Plastic Waste (M&H) Rules | Carry bags 40 microns
  [103:0:1.1] 2016 | PWM Rules 2016 | 50 microns; extended to villages; PWM fee; EPR; plastic roads, waste-to-oil, waste-to-energy
  [103:0:1.2] 12 Aug 2021 | PWM Amendment Rules 2021 | 75 microns from 30 Sep 2021; 120 microns from 31 Dec 2022; phase out identified SUP by 2022
  [103:0:1.3] 16 Feb 2022 | EPR Guidelines on plastic packaging (Schedule II) | In force on notification; widely taught as "from 1 July 2022" with the SUP ban
  [103:0:1.4] 1 Jul 2022 | SUP ban | 19 identified items banned
  [103:0:1.5] 2024 | PWM Amendment Rules 2024 | Defined biodegradable plastics; makers need CPCB certification
  [103:0:1.6] 2025-2026 | PWM Amendment Rules 2025 / 2026 | QR/barcode EPR tracking; rigid recycled content 30% → 60% by 2028-29; shortfalls carried forward up to 3 years
[103:0:2] - Compostable plastics must meet **IS/ISO 17088**.
[103:0:3] # Single-use plastic (SUP) ban – 1 July 2022
[103:0:4] - India's measure against plastic pollution: **banning identified single-use plastics** (not all plastic, not all food containers).
[103:0:5] - **19 items**: ear buds with plastic sticks, balloon sticks, plastic flags, candy and ice-cream sticks, **thermocol for decoration**, plates, cups, cutlery, straws, cigarette-packet films, PVC banners < 100 microns. NOT banned: **HDPE milk bottles**. The ban covers only **~11%** of plastic waste (CSE).
[103:0:6] - Enforcement: **SPCBs/PCCs and local bodies**, with a National Level Task Force and State Special Task Forces.
[103:0:7] - **NGT (2019)** fined **25 States/UTs ₹1 crore** each for missing the deadline for plastic waste management action plans.
[103:0:8] # EPR for plastic packaging
[103:0:9] - **EPR:** the producer's duty for environmentally sound management of its product **till end of life** – collection and recycling after use.
[103:0:10] - **PIBOs** = Producers, Importers and Brand Owners; recyclers generate tradable EPR certificates on the **CPCB portal**.
[103:0:11] TABLE head: Category | Example | Recycled content 2025-26 → 2028-29
  [103:0:11.0] I – Rigid | PET, HDPE bottles | 30% → 60%
  [103:0:11.1] II – Flexible | Carry bags, chips packets | 10% → 20%
  [103:0:11.2] III – Multi-layered | Multi-layer packs | 5% → 10%
[103:0:12] # Plastic types, additives, microplastics
[103:0:13] TABLE head: Code | Plastic
  [103:0:13.0] 1 | PET (bottles)
  [103:0:13.1] 2 | HDPE
  [103:0:13.2] 3 | PVC
  [103:0:13.3] 4 | LDPE
  [103:0:13.4] 5 | PP
  [103:0:13.5] 6 | PS
  [103:0:13.6] 7 | Others incl. polycarbonate
[103:0:14] - **Bisphenol A (BPA):** key building block of **polycarbonate** (and epoxy resins); leaches from bottles and food containers; endocrine disruptor.
[103:0:15] - **Contain plastic – all three:** **cigarette butts** (cellulose acetate filter), **eyeglass lenses**, **car tyres** (synthetic rubber) (UPSC 2025).
[103:0:16] - A bottle that keeps its shape with hot water is taken to be **thermosetting** plastic (CDS 2019 key); polyethylene is the polymer made from ethylene gas.
[103:0:17] - Plastic waste: **toxic fumes** when burnt, lasts long, **cannot be composted**.
[103:0:18] - **Microplastics: < 5 mm**; nurdles = primary pellets 1–5 mm. **Microbeads** (cosmetics) are a concern because they **harm marine ecosystems** (UPSC 2019); banned in cosmetics. **Synthetic-rubber tyre wear** is a big source of ocean microplastics – tyres of **natural rubber** cut it. FSSAI found microplastics in all tested sugar and salt.
[103:0:19] - **Plastic pollution** = accumulation of non-biodegradable waste in the oceans that threatens marine life.
[103:0:20] - **Plastic-eating fungus** *Aspergillus tubingensis*: found at a waste dump in **Islamabad, Pakistan** (2017).
[103:0:21] - **IIT Kharagpur** made eco-friendly food packaging from **cucumber peels**. **India's largest charkha** made of used plastic waste was inaugurated in **Noida** (Gandhi 150).
[103:0:22] # Global action
[103:0:23] TABLE head: Country / body | First
  [103:0:23.0] Bangladesh | First to ban thin plastic bags (2002)
  [103:0:23.1] France | First to ban disposable plastic cups, plates and cutlery (law 2016)
  [103:0:23.2] Portugal (Hi Fly airline) | World's first single-use-plastic-free passenger flight (Dec 2018)
  [103:0:23.3] New Zealand | First to ban thin plastic produce bags in supermarkets (July 2023)
  [103:0:23.4] Puducherry | Decided (2017) to ban manufacture and use of plastics below 51 microns
  [103:0:23.5] Odisha (Puri district) | Swachhata Darpan Award (DDWS, 2019) for innovative plastic-waste management
[103:0:24] - China's **National Sword Policy (2018)** and Thailand's 2025 measure limit plastic-waste imports.
[103:0:25] - **Global Plastics Treaty:** UNEA-5.2 (Nairobi, March 2022) "**End Plastic Pollution**" → INC; **INC-5.2 Geneva (Aug 2025) – no agreement** (production caps, chemicals of concern, finance); **INC-5.3 (Geneva, Feb 2026)** elected chair **Julio Cordano**.
[103:0:26] > Exam angle: thickness sequence 40 → 50 → 75 → 120 microns; SUP phase-out year 2022; BPA = polycarbonate; microbeads = marine harm; "first country" items.
[103:0:27] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 4 p.96-105 (microplastics, microbeads UPSC 2019, BPA from polycarbonate, PWM Rules 2016-2025, banned items, recycled-content table, treaty); tnpcb.gov.in "4th Amendment (EPR guidelines) Feb 2022" (immediate effect, via web search); odishatv.in "Puri bags national award for innovation in plastic waste management" (via web search); NextGen Environment APPSC 08 p.10-11 (plastics); app notes 5:103 sub 5
## SUB 1 | Swachh Bharat Mission and Swachh Survekshan
[103:1:0] TABLE head: Programme | Year | Focus
  [103:1:0.0] ILCS | 1980-81 | Dry latrines → pour-flush; free manual scavengers
  [103:1:0.1] Central Rural Sanitation Programme | 1986 | Rural latrines
  [103:1:0.2] Total Sanitation Campaign (TSC) | 1999 | Community-led
  [103:1:0.3] Nirmal Gram Puraskar | 2003 | Award for ODF panchayats
  [103:1:0.4] Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan | 2012 | Renamed TSC; brand ambassador Vidya Balan; became SBM in 2014
  [103:1:0.5] Swachh Bharat Mission (Abhiyan) | 2 Oct 2014 | Toilets, ODF by 2 Oct 2019; inspired by Mahatma Gandhi's dream of a clean India
[103:1:1] - SBM is the flagship campaign to improve **sanitation** (not PM-JAY, TB elimination or Mission Indradhanush). Top priority now = **household latrines**. The prior subsidy for building family toilets was dropped – an **incentive is paid after construction**.
[103:1:2] - "India achieved 100% rural sanitation (ODF, 2019) under Swachh Bharat – Swasth Bharat" is true but does not explain why governments frame sustainable development strategies (A–R: both true, R not the explanation).
[103:1:3] # SBM-Grameen
[103:1:4] - Run by the **Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation, Ministry of Jal Shakti** (from 2019). Phase I: **over 10 crore toilets**; coverage 39% → 100% (2014-2019). **Rural Sanitation Strategy 2019–2029** (Jal Shakti, Sept 2019).
[103:1:5] - **ODF Plus** levels: **Aspiring → Rising → Model**. **IHHL incentive ₹12,000**; greywater **₹280/capita** (up to 5,000 people) and ₹660/capita (above 5,000).
[103:1:6] - **SLWM assistance by village size:** up to 150 households ₹7 lakh; up to 300 ₹**12 lakh**; up to 500 ₹15 lakh; above 500 ₹20 lakh.
[103:1:7] - **GOBARdhan (2018):** cattle dung, farm and solid waste → **biogas and bio-slurry**. **Swachhata Hi Seva:** fortnight shramdaan since **2017**. **Swachh Bharat Diwas:** 2 October.
[103:1:8] # SBM-Urban
[103:1:9] - SBM-U launched **2 Oct 2014**, run by the **Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA)**. **SBM-U 2.0:** launched **1 Oct 2021**, 2021-26, **₹1.41 lakh crore**; aim **"Garbage Free" cities**; permanent **RRR Centre** in every city; **SATAT–GOBARdhan: 500 new CBG plants**.
[103:1:10] TABLE head: Certification | Meaning
  [103:1:10.0] ODF+ | Functional, clean, maintained toilets
  [103:1:10.1] ODF++ | + safe faecal-sludge management
  [103:1:10.2] Water+ | + used water treated before discharge
  [103:1:10.3] Garbage Free City | 1, 3, 5, 7 stars
[103:1:11] - **NAMASTE** (2023): safety and dignity of sanitation workers; extended in 2024 to waste pickers (formalising informal workers).
[103:1:12] # Swachh Survekshan (SS)
[103:1:13] - Annual urban survey from **2016**, by **MoHUA**, conducted by the **Quality Council of India**; SS Grameen from 2018.
[103:1:14] TABLE head: Edition | Result
  [103:1:14.0] Swachh Bharat Survey 2015 | Cleanest Mysore (476 cities)
  [103:1:14.1] SS 2017 (4 May 2017) | Cleanest Indore; dirtiest Gonda (UP)
  [103:1:14.2] SS 2019 | Indore 1st
  [103:1:14.3] SS League 2020 (Q1-Q2 result, 31 Dec 2019) | Indore cleanest among 10 lakh+ cities
  [103:1:14.4] SS 2020 | Three AP cities in the top 10 (Vijayawada, Tirupati, Visakhapatnam)
  [103:1:14.5] SS 2023 (8th edition) | Theme "Waste to Wealth"; Indore and Surat jointly cleanest
  [103:1:14.6] SS 2024-25 (9th; 17 Jul 2025) | Super Swachh League: Indore (1st, 8th time), Surat, Navi Mumbai; new-category cleanest big city Ahmedabad, then Bhopal, Lucknow
  [103:1:14.7] SS 2025-26 (10th; awards Nov 2026) | Theme "Swachhata Ki Nayi Pehel"; Vijayawada among top 3 of the Super Swachh League (with Navi Mumbai, Surat); six AP ULBs awarded
[103:1:15] - **Indore** = model **zero-waste**, landfill-free city (door-to-door segregation and processing).

## SUB 2 | Disposal and Treatment Methods
[103:2:0] TABLE head: Method | Process | Suited to
  [103:2:0.0] Open dumping | Untreated, uncovered, unsegregated waste on land | Not viable – flies, rats, leachate
  [103:2:0.1] Landfill | Most common and economic method in India; most urban household waste ends here | Residual waste; last resort
  [103:2:0.2] Sanitary landfill | Waste compacted in cells and covered with earth every day; liners (clay/plastic) + leachate collection protect groundwater; adopted as a substitute for open-burning dumps | Only residual inert waste; costly
  [103:2:0.3] Composting (aerobic) – Indore method | Microbes (bacteria, fungi) oxidise organics; material turned at intervals; 2–4 weeks | Wet/organic waste
  [103:2:0.4] Bangalore method (anaerobic) | Pits with alternate layers of MSW and night soil; 4–6 months | Organic waste
  [103:2:0.5] Vermicomposting | Earthworms break waste down (vermiculture) | Household organic waste
  [103:2:0.6] Incineration | Controlled burning at high heat in oxygen; cuts volume ~90%; steam for power; emits pollutants, toxic ash | Hazardous, infectious/biomedical
  [103:2:0.7] Pyrolysis | Thermo-chemical decomposition (heating) without oxygen → gas, oil, char (carbon-based fuels) | Mixed waste; costly
  [103:2:0.8] Plasma gasification | Extreme thermal process (electricity + very high temperature), no combustion → syngas (H2 + CO); inorganics → slag | All organic wastes
  [103:2:0.9] RDF | Shredded, dehydrated high-calorific dry MSW | Fuel in cement kilns and thermal plants
[103:2:1] - **Pyrolysis and plasma gasification = waste-to-energy technologies** (UPSC 2019); compost and vermicompost give manure, not energy.
[103:2:2] - **Compost:** biodegradable waste decomposed in pits; rich in organic matter and nutrients; earthworms and microbes **speed up** (not slow down) decomposition. In composting both aerobes and anaerobes degrade organic matter. **Vermiculture** = the science of **raising earthworms**.
[103:2:3] - **Biomining** uses bacteria, **fungi** or plants to extract metals from ores and solid wastes; composting also uses fungi.
[103:2:4] - Urban India uses **composting, incineration and landfilling – "all the above"**.
[103:2:5] - **Other pollution solutions:** **Oilzapper** = bacterial mix for oil spills and oily sludge; **bioremediation** uses organisms to remove pollutants; **UV purification** kills microbes in drinking water; **hydrogen fuel cells** emit only **water vapour**.
[103:2:6] - **Better method to reduce the solid-waste problem: recycling** (not burning, sea dumping or compressing). **Composting household waste** cuts methane and helps reduce global warming; **burning household waste** does not reduce GHG emissions.
[103:2:7] TABLE head: Waste | Disposal method
  [103:2:7.0] Organic | Composting
  [103:2:7.1] E-waste | Recycling
  [103:2:7.2] Hazardous / biomedical | Incineration (biomedical at a common treatment facility)
  [103:2:7.3] Broken glass pieces | Landfilling
  [103:2:7.4] Non-recyclable high-calorific dry waste | RDF / co-processing in cement kilns
[103:2:8] - **Trade-offs of the four main methods (APPSC G2 2025 match):**
[103:2:9] TABLE head: Method | Pro / con
  [103:2:9.0] Landfilling | Low cost, but long-term environmental impact
  [103:2:9.1] Incineration | Reduces volume, but emits pollutants
  [103:2:9.2] Composting | Useful by-products (manure, biogas), but needs land
  [103:2:9.3] Recycling | Conserves resources, but needs infrastructure
[103:2:10] > Exam angle: match method → function (incineration = burning; pyrolysis = waste to fuel; plasma = extreme heat; composting = biological decay); "most common method in India" = landfilling.
[103:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 08 p.14, 09 p.1-8 (dumping, landfill most common, sanitary landfill, Indore/Bangalore, incineration 90%, pyrolysis); NextGen Rocket Environment p.45, 64 (compost, earthworms speed decomposition, pyrolysis/plasma = WtE); PMF Environment Part 4 p.107-109 (sanitary landfill substitute for open-burning dumps, plasma gasification, biomining with fungi, RDF); Shankar Environment Part 7 p.7-8; app notes 5:103 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Biodegradable vs Non-biodegradable; Kinds of Waste
[103:3:0] # Definitions
[103:3:1] - **Solid waste:** discarded or abandoned material in **solid, liquid, semi-solid or containerised gaseous** form; includes urban, agricultural, biomedical and radioactive wastes.
[103:3:2] - **Liquid waste (sewage):** fluids from washing, flushing or manufacturing. **Sullage** = waste water from **kitchens** and bathrooms (grey water), not from toilets (black water/sewage), factories or hospitals.
[103:3:3] - **E-waste (ITU):** discarded electrical and electronic equipment and parts **not meant for reuse**. **Biomedical waste:** waste from **diagnosis, treatment or immunisation of humans or animals** (blood, sharps, cultures, discarded medicines).
[103:3:4] - **Garbage** = putrescible kitchen/market waste; **rubbish** = household/commercial waste other than garbage and ashes.
[103:3:5] # Biodegradable vs non-biodegradable
[103:3:6] - **Biodegradable:** decomposed by micro-organisms (mainly **bacteria**) into simpler harmless substances. **Aerobic** decomposition → **compost**; **anaerobic** → **methane (biogas)**.
[103:3:7] - **Non-biodegradable:** mainly inorganic; cannot be broken down by microbes, so it accumulates; **recycling** is the ideal option for it.
[103:3:8] TABLE head: Biodegradable | Non-biodegradable
  [103:3:8.0] Sewage, faecal matter, urine, domestic garbage, food/kitchen waste, vegetable and fruit peels, cow dung, paddy husk | Plastic, polythene bags, plastic cups, DDT, insecticides/pesticides, asbestos
  [103:3:8.1] Paper, wood, grass, leaves, plant waste, cellulose, starch, proteins | Tin, aluminium foil, metal scrap, mercury, lead
  [103:3:8.2] Wool (natural keratin fibre), cotton, leather | Glass bottles, China clay cups, polystyrene cups
  [103:3:8.3] Natural rubber | Synthetic rubber/tyres, nylon, Teflon, PVC
  [103:3:8.4] Polymers: polylactic acid (PLA), PHBV, polyglycolic acid, Nylon-2-Nylon-6 | Polyethylene, polystyrene, polycarbonate
[103:3:9] - **Polythene** is a **polymer of ethylene (C2H4)** – carbon and hydrogen only; polythene bags cannot be destroyed by bacteria because they are synthetic **polymers**.
[103:3:10] - Biodegradable polymers are eco-friendly because microbes degrade them; non-biodegradable plastics persist and break into **microplastics**.
[103:3:11] - **Biodegradable plastics** (e.g. PLA) are a better alternative, but some need much energy and resources to make and can still pollute on disposal – both statements true (TSPSC 2023).
[103:3:12] - **Industrial wastes:** **thermal power plants** give fly ash (non-biodegradable) – they produce the most non-biodegradable waste; **gypsum** comes from **fertiliser** plants, not food processing. Food processing, paper, cotton, textile and sugar mills give mostly non-hazardous, biodegradable waste.
[103:3:13] TABLE head: Litter | Time to degrade
  [103:3:13.0] Paper | 10–30 days
  [103:3:13.1] Woollen items | about 1 year
  [103:3:13.2] Tin, aluminium and other metal items | 100–500 years
  [103:3:13.3] Plastic bags | up to 1 million years
[103:3:14] # Categories
[103:3:15] TABLE head: Category | What it holds
  [103:3:15.0] Municipal (MSW) | Household + commercial: organics, plastics, paper, metals, street and market waste
  [103:3:15.1] Agricultural | Crop residues, paddy husk, cattle dung (biodegradable; dung → biogas under GOBARdhan)
  [103:3:15.2] Construction & demolition | Mostly inert – concrete, bricks, dirt, rocks, debris
  [103:3:15.3] Hazardous | Paints, batteries, pesticides, chemicals, fluorescent lamps, aerosol cans
  [103:3:15.4] Biomedical / E-waste / Radioactive | Separate rules (see later sub-sections)
[103:3:16] - **Hazardous waste – four classic criteria:** **ignitability, corrosivity, reactivity, toxicity** (NOT biodegradability). **Household hazardous waste:** **paints and batteries**, bulbs, aerosol cans, tyres.
[103:3:17] - **Healthcare waste (WHO):** **~85% general non-hazardous, ~15% hazardous** (infectious, chemical, radioactive).
[103:3:18] - **Land pollution:** its significant cause is the **disposal of solid waste** (not rainfall or planting trees).
[103:3:19] > Exam angle: "which is NOT biodegradable" – tin, plastic, PVC, insecticides, glass; "which IS" – wool, peels, leather, natural rubber, PLA, sewage.
[103:3:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 08 p.3-13 (definitions, biodegradable/non-biodegradable, wool PYQ, garbage, rubbish, industrial wastes); NextGen Rocket Environment p.45, 63-64 (sewage biodegradable; plastic/DDT/asbestos not); PMF Environment Part 4 p.100, 106 (polyethene = ethylene polymer; gypsum from fertiliser plants); app notes 5:103 sub 0
## SUB 4 | 3R, Circular Economy and Industrial By-products
[103:4:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [103:4:0.0] 3R | Reduce, Reuse, Recycle ("Regain" is NOT one of the 3Rs)
  [103:4:0.1] Top priority | Reduction at source – practising reduce, reuse, recycle cuts waste at source (not disposables, open dumping or street burning)
  [103:4:0.2] Reuse | Using the item again in the same form
  [103:4:0.3] Recycling | Converting waste materials into other usable materials
  [103:4:0.4] 5R | Adds Refuse and Repurpose (or Recover)
  [103:4:0.5] Least preferred | Landfilling
  [103:4:0.6] RRR Centre | Permanent in every city under SBM-U 2.0
[103:4:1] - **Circular economy:** minimises waste by **reusing and recycling materials** (not using products till they break, landfilling or banning manufacture). **Unplanned waste generation** is NOT sustainable development.
[103:4:2] - **Zero waste management:** **segregation at source, separate collection of each kind, community involvement** – all of the above. **Indore** is the model zero-waste city.
[103:4:3] - **Legacy waste:** old MSW in dumpsites; **biomining** sorts it into recyclables, RDF, bio-soil and inert fill.
[103:4:4] TABLE head: Waste | Source industry | Reuse
  [103:4:4.0] Fly ash | Coal thermal plants | Bricks, roads, replaces part of Portland cement (up to ~35%); contains toxic elements (arsenic, lead, mercury) – not only SiO2 and CaO; use mandatory within 300 km
  [103:4:4.1] Steel slag | Steel plants | Road base, agricultural soil, cement (all three – UPSC 2020); Surat steel-slag road
  [103:4:4.2] Red mud | Alumina refining | Bricks, tiles
  [103:4:4.3] Phosphogypsum | Phosphoric acid / phosphatic fertiliser plants | Gypsum substitute, soil conditioner
  [103:4:4.4] Chromium sludge | Tanneries | – (hazardous)
[103:4:5] - **Green rural roads (UPSC 2020):** **copper slag, cold-mix asphalt, geotextiles** are preferred; hot-mix asphalt and Portland cement are not.
[103:4:6] > Exam angle: 3Rs (and the odd one out "Regain"); recycling definition; fly ash statements (UPSC 2015).
[103:4:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.45 (recycling = processing waste into usable material); PMF Environment Part 3 p.115-116 (fly ash uses, UPSC 2015, toxic elements); PMF Environment Part 4 p.106 (steel slag UPSC 2020, red mud, gypsum); NextGen Environment APPSC 11 p.12-13 (fly ash notification); app notes 5:103 sub 2
## SUB 5 | Solid Waste Management Rules and Indian Data
[103:5:0] TABLE head: Rules | Key points
  [103:5:0.0] MSW (Management and Handling) Rules 2000 | ULBs collect, segregate, store, transport, process, dispose; primary goal promoting segregation
  [103:5:0.1] SWM Rules 2016 (8 Apr 2016) | Replaced the MSW Rules 2000; apply beyond municipal areas (urban agglomerations, census towns, industrial townships, railways, airports, defence, pilgrimage places); 3 streams – wet (biodegradable), dry, domestic hazardous; brand owners with non-biodegradable packaging must set up a collect-back system (producer responsibility for packaging life cycle); user fees and spot fines; exact criteria for siting landfills and waste-processing facilities (landfill 100 m from river, 200 m from pond, 500 m from highways/habitations, 20 km from airports); industries within 100 km of an RDF plant replace 5% fuel with RDF
  [103:5:0.2] SWM Rules 2026 (under EPA 1986; in force 1 Apr 2026; replaced 2016) | 4 streams: wet, dry, sanitary, special care (green, blue, red, black bins); landfills only for non-recyclable inert residue; higher landfill fee for unsegregated waste; legacy dumps mapped with time-bound biomining; Environmental Compensation = polluter pays
[103:5:1] - SWM 2016 did NOT require five categories, did NOT bar moving waste between districts, and was NOT limited to ULBs and industrial townships.
[103:5:2] - 2016: used diapers/napkins wrapped and put in the **dry** bin; 2026: separate **sanitary** stream. **Special care** = domestic hazardous (batteries, bulbs, medicines, paint cans). Paper, plastics, metals, glass → **dry**.
[103:5:3] - **Bulk Waste Generators** (2026): process wet waste on site or hold an **EBWGR** certificate.
[103:5:4] - In 2016 MoEFCC notified **six sets of waste rules** (solid, plastic, e-waste, biomedical, hazardous, C&D); **CPCB** (with SPCBs) is the nodal body for standards and monitoring of waste treatment.
[103:5:5] - **Supreme Court:** clean environment part of **Art. 21** (Feb 2026); **18 Aug 2026** – **generators**, not only sanitary workers, answerable for waste at the doorstep. Draft "SWM Rules 2024" (proposed 1 Oct 2025) were not the notified rules.
[103:5:6] - **Collection chain:** door-to-door → segregated transport → **transfer station → Material Recovery Facility (MRF) → processing/recycling** → residual landfill.
[103:5:7] # Indian data
[103:5:8] TABLE head: Item | Figure
  [103:5:8.0] Waste generated (MoEF, 2016) | 62 million tonnes a year (plastic 5.6 MT, biomedical 0.17 MT ≈ 1.7 lakh t, hazardous 7.9 MT); 165 MT by 2030
  [103:5:8.1] Composition | ~55–60% biodegradable, 15–20% recyclable, rest inert/hazardous
  [103:5:8.2] Urban share; processing | ~60% urban; SBM-U processing 16% (2014) → 82% (2026)
  [103:5:8.3] Highest solid-waste State | Maharashtra
  [103:5:8.4] Mega city with most solid waste per person | Delhi
  [103:5:8.5] Rural trend | Shift from biodegradable towards plastic, sanitary and other non-biodegradable waste
  [103:5:8.6] India's first major nurdle landing | Kerala, MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck (2025)
[103:5:9] > Exam angle: SWM 2016 replaced MSW 2000; "which statement on SWM 2016 is correct" = landfill/processing site criteria; 3 streams (2016) vs 4 streams (2026).
[103:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 4 p.109-111 (SWM Rules 2016: replace 2000 rules, 3 streams, collect-back, site criteria, UPSC 2019); PMF Lens Feb 2026 p.5 and Praveen CA-360 Feb 2026 magazine p.139 (SWM Rules 2026: 4 streams, 1 Apr 2026, EBWGR, polluter pays); Shankar Environment Part 7 p.8 (62 MT; 0.17 MT biomedical); NextGen Rocket Environment p.64 (SWM key provision = site criteria); downtoearth.org.in/news/solid-waste-management-rules-2016-53443 (sixth set of waste rules, via web search); app notes 5:103 sub 1, 4
## SUB 6 | E-waste
[103:6:0] # Rules
[103:6:1] - **EPR in Indian law was first introduced by the e-Waste (Management and Handling) Rules 2011** (UPSC 2019; not the BMW Rules 1998, Recycled Plastic Rules 1999 or Hazardous Wastes Rules 2016). Rocket Environment p.45 credits the Plastic Waste (M&H) Rules 2011 – a source slip; UPSC's answer is the e-waste rules.
[103:6:2] - **E-Waste (Management) Rules 2016:** 21 products; PROs, deposit-refund scheme, e-waste exchange.
[103:6:3] - **E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022:** notified by **MoEFCC in November 2022**; in force **1 April 2023** (not Nov 2022); **106 EEE items incl. solar PV** waste; do NOT apply to packaging plastics or radioactive waste (separate rules).
[103:6:4] - Collection of e-waste is the **producer's** responsibility (EPR); only **registered** producers, manufacturers, refurbishers and recyclers may deal; producers register on the **CPCB portal** and buy **digital EPR certificates** from registered recyclers; annual targets on past sales.
[103:6:5] - **Battery Waste Management Rules 2022** replaced the 2001 rules.
[103:6:6] # Magnitude
[103:6:7] - India = **3rd-largest** e-waste generator (after **China, USA**); about **2.2 million tonnes (2025)**. **Mumbai** = largest e-waste-producing city (ASSOCHAM); Maharashtra the top State.
[103:6:8] - **3.54 lakh tonnes** collected and processed in **FY 2020-21** (of 13.46 lakh t generated); 11.59 lakh t recycled in FY 2024-25.
[103:6:9] - **Global E-waste Monitor** (**ITU and UNITAR**) 2024: **62 Mt** in 2022, only **22.3%** formally recycled; 82 Mt by 2030.
[103:6:10] # Recycling chain and hazards
[103:6:11] - Chain: consumer → collection centre / producer take-back → **authorised dismantler → authorised recycler** → recovered materials. Citizens should **sell or give old electronics to authorised recyclers** (not burn, bin or dump them).
[103:6:12] - **78%** processed informally; informal hubs **Seelampur (Delhi), Moradabad (UP)**. "Invisible e-waste": vapes, USB cables, LED accessories.
[103:6:13] - **R2 (Responsible Recycling) Code of Practices:** environmentally responsible practices in the **electronics recycling industry** (UPSC 2021).
[103:6:14] - Old computers release **beryllium, cadmium, chromium, mercury, lead**, PCBs, PBBs – NOT **heptachlor** (an insecticide) or **plutonium** (radioactive) (UPSC 2013).
[103:6:15] TABLE head: Constituent | Harm
  [103:6:15.0] Mercury | Brain, kidney; bioaccumulates in fish
  [103:6:15.1] Cadmium | Kidney and bone
  [103:6:15.2] Lead | Nervous system and kidney
  [103:6:15.3] PBBs / BFRs | Persistent; endocrine effects
[103:6:16] > Exam angle: first EPR = e-waste rules 2011; 2022 rules dates; 3.54 lakh t (FY 2021); heptachlor/plutonium are not e-waste; R2 = electronics recycling.
[103:6:17] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 5 p.6-11 (UPSC 2013 e-waste metals, CPCB table 3.54 lakh t, UNITAR monitor, 2011 rules first EPR – UPSC 2019, 2016/2022 rules, 21→106 items, April 2023); NextGen Rocket Environment p.45-46, 64 (R2 code; EPR credited to PWM&H Rules 2011); Shankar Environment Part 2 p.1, 23 (UPSC questions); app notes 5:103 sub 6
## SUB 7 | Biomedical, Hazardous and C&D Waste; Conventions
[103:7:0] # Biomedical waste (BMW)
[103:7:1] - **BMW Management Rules 2016** replaced the **1998 Rules (10 categories)**; amended 2018, 2019; **4 colour categories**; **barcoding** and GPS tracking; no on-site facility if a common facility is within 75 km.
[103:7:2] TABLE head: Colour | Waste | Treatment
  [103:7:2.0] Yellow | Anatomical, soiled, expired medicines, chemical | Incineration / plasma pyrolysis / deep burial
  [103:7:2.1] Red | Contaminated recyclable plastics (tubes, IV sets, catheters, syringes without needles) | Autoclave/microwave + shredding
  [103:7:2.2] White (translucent) | Sharps – needles, blades | Autoclave, shredding, encapsulation
  [103:7:2.3] Blue | Glassware, metallic implants | Disinfection, recycling
[103:7:3] - BMW must be treated before disposal **to prevent the spread of infection and protect human health**. **COVID-19:** CPCB guidelines (2020) + **COVID19BWM** app.
[103:7:4] - **BMW generated (MoEF 2016): 0.17 million tonnes a year** (about 484 t/day).
[103:7:5] # Hazardous waste
[103:7:6] TABLE head: Law | Provision
  [103:7:6.0] EPA 1986 | Passed after Bhopal (1984); umbrella for hazardous-waste rules
  [103:7:6.1] MSIHC Rules 1989 | Manufacture, storage, import of hazardous chemicals
  [103:7:6.2] CAEPPR Rules 1996 | Chemical-accident crisis groups (central, state, district, local)
  [103:7:6.3] Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 | No-fault insurance, immediate relief
  [103:7:6.4] HOWM Rules 2016 | Hierarchy: prevention > minimisation > reuse > recycling > recovery > co-processing > safe disposal
[103:7:7] - Disposal in **secure landfills** – landfill is the last resort. **TSDF at Dundigal (Hyderabad Waste Management Project)**: set up under an **India–Australia** bilateral aided project (AusAID, 1995-99).
[103:7:8] TABLE head: Disaster | Chemical
  [103:7:8.0] Bhopal, 2-3 Dec 1984, Union Carbide | Methyl isocyanate
  [103:7:8.1] LG Polymers, Visakhapatnam, May 2020 | Styrene vapour
[103:7:9] # Construction and demolition (C&D) waste
[103:7:10] - ~**12 million tonnes** a year; first recycling plant **Burari (Delhi)**. **Environment (C&D Waste Management) Rules 2025**: effective **1 April 2026**; **EPR** for producers with projects of **20,000 sq m+**; recycling targets **25% (2025-26) → 100% (2028-29)**.
[103:7:11] # Conventions
[103:7:12] TABLE head: Convention | Subject
  [103:7:12.0] Basel (1989; in force 1992) | Transboundary movement of hazardous wastes and their disposal; uses PIC; India ratified June 1992
  [103:7:12.1] Rotterdam (1998; in force 2004) | Prior Informed Consent for hazardous chemicals and pesticides in trade
  [103:7:12.2] Stockholm (2001) | POPs; now incl. PFAS, chlorpyrifos
  [103:7:12.3] Minamata (2013) | Mercury; dental amalgam phase-out by 2034; ends mercury lamps
  [103:7:12.4] ITPGRFA / UNCCD | Plant genetic resources / desertification
[103:7:13] - **Transboundary movement of waste** = physical transfer of hazardous waste across borders for reprocessing or storage, often to developing countries (a global issue).
