=== NOTES 5:104 | Carbon Emissions, Carbon Footprint, Carbon Sequestration, Carbon Credits and Carbon Trading
## SUB 0 | Carbon Sinks, Blue Carbon, REDD+ and Carbon Monitoring
[104:0:0] # Sinks
[104:0:1] - **Carbon sink:** a reservoir that accumulates and stores carbon. **Natural sinks: forests, soil, oceans** (chlor-alkali plants are NOT sinks). Forests act as sinks when they grow in density or area.
[104:0:2] - **Blue carbon:** carbon captured by **oceans and coastal ecosystems** – **mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes** (all three are blue-carbon ecosystems). Forest/soil carbon is not "blue"; fossil carbon is in petroleum and gas.
[104:0:3] - **Best sink per unit area = blue carbon ecosystems:** they store several times more carbon per area than tropical rainforests (seagrass ~3 times). Glaciers are not sinks.
[104:0:4] - **Tropical peatlands:** most carbon **per hectare** of any terrestrial ecosystem.
[104:0:5] - **Carbon fertilisation:** **increased plant growth** because more atmospheric CO2 raises photosynthesis (~**70%** of Earth's recent greening). Not warming, not ocean acidity.
[104:0:6] - **Bhutan** = carbon-negative country. Net zero = emissions balanced by removals.
[104:0:7] # Forest carbon stock (ISFR)
[104:0:8] TABLE head: Report | Figure
  [104:0:8.0] ISFR 2019 – India | 7,124.6 million tonnes
  [104:0:8.1] ISFR 2019 – Andhra Pradesh (incl. TOF patches > 1 ha) | ~220 Mt (805 Mt CO2e) = 3.08% of India's forest carbon
  [104:0:8.2] ISFR 2023 (Dec 2024) – India | 7,285.5 million tonnes, up 81.5 Mt over 2021; total sink ~30.43 bn t CO2e
[104:0:9] # IPCC carbon pools (5)
[104:0:10] - Above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter, soil organic carbon. **Atmospheric oxygen is NOT a pool.**
[104:0:11] # REDD+ and forest-carbon finance
[104:0:12] - **REDD+** = Reducing Emissions from **Deforestation and Forest Degradation** (+ conservation, sustainable management, enhancement of stocks).
[104:0:13] - **UN-REDD** (2008; **UNDP, FAO, UNEP**): proper design contributes to **biodiversity protection, forest resilience and poverty reduction – all three** (UPSC 2016).
[104:0:14] - **Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (World Bank):** global partnership of governments, businesses, civil society and indigenous peoples; **helps countries with REDD+** finance and technical aid. It does **not** fund universities/scientists for forestry research (UPSC 2015: I and III).
[104:0:15] - **Khasi Hills Community REDD+ Project** (East Khasi Hills, **Meghalaya**): **India's first community REDD+ project, Plan Vivo certified**; run by Khasi **himas**; ~27,000 ha (UPSC 2026).
[104:0:16] # Carbon monitoring
[104:0:17] - **National Carbon Project** – under the **ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme**: assesses **carbon pools, fluxes and net carbon balance** of India's terrestrial biomes and builds **remote-sensing spatial databases** (statements I and III). NOT "space technology for sequestration".
[104:0:18] TABLE head: CO2-observing satellite | Agency
  [104:0:18.0] OCO-2 | NASA
  [104:0:18.1] GOSAT | Japan
[104:0:19] > Exam angle: definition of blue carbon (×2), REDD+ statements (×2), FCPF, best sink per area, carbon fertilisation, NCP goals (×2), AP share of forest carbon, first Plan Vivo REDD+ project.
[104:0:20] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 p.3-4 (sinks, blue carbon); NextGen Rocket Environment p.68 (Sheet #39: blue carbon, carbon fertilisation, Bhutan); NextGen Environment APPSC 08 p.1 (FCPF PYQ); PMF Environment Part 2 p.42 (seagrass ~3x rainforest per area); PMF Environment Part 5 p.90; Shankar Environment Part 2 p.13, Part 19 p.20 (UN-REDD); thehansindia.com (AP 3.08%, ISFR 2019); planvivo.org (Khasi Hills); sambuz.com NCP presentation; app notes 5:104 sub 2, 4
## SUB 1 | Carbon Sequestration, CCS and Carbon Removal
[104:1:0] - **Carbon sequestration:** capturing and long-term storing of atmospheric CO2 – in plants (afforestation), soil, oceans or geological formations. **Afforestation = capturing and storing CO2.**
[104:1:1] - **CCS (Carbon Capture and Storage), "also known as carbon sequestration":** capture at a stationary point source (power plant, cement plant) → transport → storage (**3 steps**); store only. APPSC key for "technology that captures and stores CO2 from industrial processes" = **carbon sequestration**.
[104:1:2] - **CCUS:** capture, then **use or store**; supports coal gasification and the hydrogen economy.
[104:1:3] TABLE head: Method | Meaning
  [104:1:3.0] Geological storage | Abandoned/uneconomic coal seams, depleted oil and gas reservoirs, deep saline formations – all three (UPSC 2017)
  [104:1:3.1] Enhanced rock weathering | Finely ground basalt spread on farmland binds CO2 as carbonate
  [104:1:3.2] Ocean alkalinity enhancement | Adding lime/alkaline minerals to seawater
  [104:1:3.3] Mine storage | Industrial CO2 pumped into abandoned mines as carbonated water
  [104:1:3.4] Direct Air Capture (DAC) | CO2 straight from ambient air anywhere; a sequestration method; CO2 used in plastics, food/beverage processing; with hydrogen gives synthetic aviation fuel (UPSC 2025: all three)
  [104:1:3.5] BECCS | Bioenergy + CCS → net-negative emissions
[104:1:4] - UPSC 2023: basalt on farms, lime in oceans, CO2 into abandoned mines – **all three** are discussed for carbon capture and sequestration.
[104:1:5] - **Blue carbon (mangroves) is a sink, not geological storage.**
[104:1:6] - **NET Power** (La Porte, Texas): **Allam-Fetvedt cycle** – burns gas in oxygen with **supercritical CO2** as working fluid; claims power as cheap as a gas combined-cycle plant while **capturing nearly all CO2**.
[104:1:7] - **DST:** five **CCU testbeds** in the **cement** sector – a first-of-its-kind research cluster.
[104:1:8] > Exam angle: definition of sequestration/CCS (×3), storage sites (×2), "how many methods" (×2), DAC statements, Net Power.
[104:1:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 14 p.3 (CCS, CCUS, sequestration); NextGen Rocket Environment p.68 (geological storage sites); Shankar Environment Part 16 p.16-17 (CCS also known as carbon sequestration); PMF Environment Part 5 p.103 (enhanced rock weathering), p.107-108 (UPSC 2023, 2025 PYQs); technologyreview.com (Net Power); app notes 5:104 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Carbon Credits, Markets and Carbon Taxes
[104:2:0] # Credits
[104:2:1] - **1 carbon credit = 1 tonne (1,000 kg) of CO2 / CO2e** avoided or removed – not of carbon.
[104:2:2] - **Kyoto Protocol (1997):** caps on GHG emissions; credit system ratified with Kyoto; credits go to countries/groups that cut emissions below quota; goal = limit emissions. **CDM** issues **CERs** (Certified Emission Reductions); JI issues ERUs.
[104:2:3] - **Prices set by supply and demand** on exchanges – **NOT fixed by UNEP** or any body (UPSC 2011 "not correct" option).
[104:2:4] - **ERPA (May 2011):** World Bank (for IBRD/BioCarbon) and **Himachal Pradesh** government – CERs from the Mid-Himalayan watershed (forestry) project.
[104:2:5] TABLE head: Voluntary standard | Run by
  [104:2:5.0] Verified Carbon Standard (VCS) | Verra
  [104:2:5.1] Gold Standard | Founded by WWF
[104:2:6] # India's compliance market
[104:2:7] - **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS):** notified **June 2023** under **Sec. 14AA, Energy Conservation Act 2001** (NOT EP Act); run by **BEE** (Ministry of Power); trades **Indian Carbon Credits**; India's **first mandatory compliance** market; 7 sectors, ~477 Mt CO2e.
[104:2:8] - **Oct 2025:** emission-intensity targets under CCTS for **aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp & paper** (282 entities). Carbon pricing covers **29%** of global GHGs.
[104:2:9] - **Net Zero Portal** (**MoEFCC**, 16 Sep 2026): voluntary registration/disclosure of net-zero commitments; launched with the NAPCC Dashboard.
[104:2:10] - **Budget 2026-27 carbon credit programme:** follows the DST roadmap – industrial, not farmer-only. India–Japan **Joint Crediting Mechanism** (Paris Art. 6.2).
[104:2:11] # Carbon taxes and border levies
[104:2:12] - **New Zealand:** first to **propose** a tax on agricultural (livestock) emissions ("burp tax", 2022, later scrapped) (APPSC G1); also credited (UPSC 2006) as first to propose a carbon tax for its people.
[104:2:13] - **Denmark:** first to **levy** a livestock carbon tax, **from 2030**.
[104:2:14] - **EU CBAM:** levy on imports to stop **carbon leakage**; transitional 2023, **definitive 1 Jan 2026**; covers iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, electricity (not textiles). **Article 9**: carbon price already paid (e.g. CCTS) is deductible.
[104:2:15] - **UK CBAM:** from **1 Jan 2027**; Sep 2026 UK recognised CCTS as a qualifying carbon price.
[104:2:16] > Exam angle: "not correct" about credits (×2), 1 credit = 1,000 kg CO2, ERPA statements, first to propose a carbon / livestock tax (×2).
[104:2:17] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 6 p.19-20 (CER = 1 t CO2; UPSC 2011 PYQ, prices not fixed), p.35 (NZ burp tax 2022); Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.138 (Net Zero Portal, MoEFCC, 16 Sep 2026), p.167 (JCM Art. 6.2); app notes 5:104 sub 5-6
## SUB 3 | Footprints and Measurement Tools
[104:3:0] TABLE head: Footprint | Measures
  [104:3:0.0] Carbon footprint | Total GHGs produced, directly and indirectly, to support human activities (t CO2/yr; individual, organisation, product)
  [104:3:0.1] Ecological footprint | Land and water needed to produce what we consume and absorb our waste; unit global hectare (gha)
  [104:3:0.2] Water footprint | Freshwater used – blue, green, grey water
  [104:3:0.3] Scope | Emissions
  [104:3:0.4] Scope 1 | Direct, from owned sources (e.g. diesel generator)
  [104:3:0.5] Scope 2 | Purchased electricity or heat
  [104:3:0.6] Scope 3 | Rest of value chain (manufacture, transport of inputs)
[104:3:1] - **Common Carbon Metric** (supported by **UNEP**): measures energy use and GHG emissions of **building operations** (UPSC 2021).
[104:3:2] - Carrying capacity = population an area can support; not a footprint.
[104:3:3] > Exam angle: definition match (carbon vs ecological footprint), unit = global hectare, Common Carbon Metric (×2).
[104:3:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.12 (carbon footprint); NextGen Rocket Environment p.43 (ecological footprint, global hectare), p.68 (Common Carbon Metric); Shankar Environment Part 23 p.12-13, Part 3 p.2; app notes 5:104 sub 1
## SUB 4 | Carbon-neutral and Green Firsts
[104:4:0] TABLE head: First | Fact
  [104:4:0.0] First country to commit to zero deforestation | Norway (June 2016; public procurement)
  [104:4:0.1] First carbon-positive settlement | Phayeng (Chakpa village, Imphal West, Manipur)
  [104:4:0.2] First on-site net zero building | Indira Paryavaran Bhawan, New Delhi (MoEFCC; inaugurated Feb 2014; passive design + on-site solar)
  [104:4:0.3] World's first fully solar-powered airport | Cochin (2015)
  [104:4:0.4] First carbon-neutral airport in Asia-Pacific | Delhi (2016); India's first Level 5 net-zero airport (2024)
  [104:4:0.5] First carbon-neutral panchayat | Palli (Samba, J&K), 2022
  [104:4:0.6] Maharashtra's first net-zero village | Bela Gram (Bhandara), 2026
  [104:4:0.7] Modal-shift project with Verra VCS | Maruti Suzuki Gujarat rail siding (world's first)
[104:4:1] - **Ladakh** carbon-neutral effort: solar water lifting, passive solar buildings, geothermal heating, EVs.
[104:4:2] > Exam angle: "first" recall – Phayeng district, Cochin airport, Paryavaran Bhawan, Norway.

## SUB 5 | Carbon Emissions – Emitters, Sources and Targets
[104:5:0] - **Biggest CO2 emitter: China** (~30-32%) > USA (~13%) > **India (3rd, ~8%)**; India has only ~3% of historical emissions (Global Carbon Budget 2025).
[104:5:1] - India per capita: about **2 tonnes** CO2 vs world ~4.7 t – **lowest in the G20**.
[104:5:2] - Sources: **fossil-fuel burning** – petrol and diesel in automobiles; **coal** in thermal power (CO2, NOx, SO2).
[104:5:3] TABLE head: India sector | Share of GHG emissions
  [104:5:3.0] Cement | ~6%
  [104:5:3.1] Aluminium | ~2.8%
  [104:5:3.2] Waste | 2.56% (2020, BUR-4)
[104:5:4] - **Coal thermal power – steps:** **supercritical technology** (higher efficiency, less coal/CO2 per unit); **Dec 2015 MoEFCC emission norms** (new limits for PM, **SO2, NOx, mercury**; water use). No freeze on coal capacity or gas conversion was ordered.
[104:5:5] - **Biomass co-firing:** 5% (FY 2024-25) → **7% (FY 2025-26)**, watched by the **SAMARTH** mission.
[104:5:6] - **NITI Aayog** decarbonisation roadmaps (cement, aluminium, MSMEs): round-the-clock RE, nuclear, CCUS.
[104:5:7] - **Carbon bombs:** fossil projects able to emit **over 1 Gt CO2** in their lifetime (LINGO list, 425 worldwide); India: **Gevra (Chhattisgarh)**, **Rajmahal (Jharkhand)** coal mines.
[104:5:8] - **2035 NDC:** **47%** emission-intensity cut vs 2005; **60%** non-fossil power capacity; net zero 2070.
[104:5:9] > Exam angle: biggest emitter, "recent step" for coal power plants.
[104:5:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 6 p.16 (China biggest, India third); NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.12 (carbon bombs, LINGO); NextGen Rocket Environment p.68 (sources); Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.161 (NDC ~60% non-fossil by 2035); downtoearth.org.in (Dec 2015 TPP norms, supercritical); app notes 5:104 sub 0
## SUB 6 | WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature)
[104:6:0] - Founded **1961**; HQ **Gland (Vaud canton), Switzerland**; symbol giant panda; works for **wildlife and biodiversity conservation** (protects species and forests).
[104:6:1] - Renamed World Wide Fund for Nature in 1986 (silver jubilee); **WWF-India** set up 1969, renamed **World Wide Fund for Nature-India in 1987**.
[104:6:2] - Helped launch Project Tiger (1973); TRAFFIC is a WWF–IUCN alliance; founded the Gold Standard.
[104:6:3] > Exam angle: HQ, mandate, WWF-India rename year.
[104:6:4] ~~ Sources: Daily CA 22 Oct 2026 p.5 (WWF 1961, Gland); NextGen Rocket Environment p.41 (WWF mandate, TRAFFIC); NextGen Environment APPSC 06 p.5 (renamed 1986, panda, Project Tiger); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWF-India (1969)

## SUB 1 | Eco-labels, Blue Flag and Green Credits
[105:1:0] TABLE head: Label | By / year | Scope
  [105:1:0.0] Ecomark | 1991, Government of India (environment ministry, with BIS standards) | Voluntary label for environment-friendly consumer products
  [105:1:0.1] Ecomark Rules | 26 Sep 2024; replaced the 1991 scheme | Correct labelling; stop misleading green claims
  [105:1:0.2] Blue Flag | FEE (Foundation for Environmental Education), Denmark | Beach eco-label (33 criteria)
  [105:1:0.3] PRAMAAN | – | Voluntary third-party certification for sustainable forestry and agroforestry
[105:1:1] - **Ecomark categories:** soaps and detergents, paper, plastics, **cosmetics, aerosols** – **NOT drugs and antibiotics**.
[105:1:2] - **Blue Flag in India:** July 2019 – MoEFCC shortlisted **12 beaches** to apply (incl. Rushikonda, AP); **8** recommended in 2020 and certified; BEAMS programme; Blue Flag is by FEE, not UNEP, MoEFCC or IUCN.

=== NOTES 5:106 | Environmental Hazards and Disaster Management – Dm Act 2005, Ndma and Ndrf, Sendai Framework, Disaster Types and Mitigation
## SUB 0 | Global Frameworks – Yokohama, Hyogo, Sendai, UNDRR and DRR Days
[106:0:0] # From IDNDR to Sendai
[106:0:1] TABLE head: Framework / event | Year / period | Key fact
  [106:0:1.0] IDNDR (International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction) | 1990–1999 | Proclaimed by the UNGA in 1989; first concerted UN effort; prompted India's DM Cell
  [106:0:1.1] Rio Earth Summit | 1992 | Earlier than all the DRR frameworks
  [106:0:1.2] Yokohama Strategy (1st WCDRR – World Conference on Natural Disaster Reduction) | 23–27 May 1994, Yokohama | First global guidelines on prevention, preparedness, mitigation
  [106:0:1.3] UNISDR | 1999 | Secretariat for the International Strategy for Disaster Reduction
  [106:0:1.4] Hyogo Framework for Action (2nd WCDRR, Kobe) | 2005–2015 | 5 priorities; aim: reduce disaster losses in lives and social, economic, environmental assets
  [106:0:1.5] Sendai Framework (3rd WCDRR, Sendai, Japan) | 2015–2030 | Adopted 18 March 2015; 4 priorities, 7 targets; voluntary, non-binding
  [106:0:1.6] Global Platform for DRR | May 2017 | Held at Cancun, Mexico
  [106:0:1.7] UNISDR → UNDRR | 1 May 2019 | Geneva; custodian of Sendai; convenes the Global Platform
[106:0:2] - **Chronology:** Rio (1992) → Yokohama (1994) → Hyogo (2005) → Sendai (2015). **All three WCDRRs were hosted by Japan.**
[106:0:3] - **UNISDR** = **United Nations International Strategy for Disaster Reduction**; **DRR** = **Disaster Risk Reduction**.
[106:0:4] - Statement trap (APPSC FRO 2022): states met at Yokohama in May 1994 – true; "the decade 1994–2004 was declared IDNDR at Yokohama" – **false** (IDNDR = 1990s, proclaimed 1989).
[106:0:5] - **Post-2015 frameworks** with a bearing on India's DRR: **Sendai, SDGs (2015–2030), Paris Agreement** – all three; **Hyogo is NOT** one of them.
[106:0:6] # Sendai – four priorities and seven targets
[106:0:7] - Priorities: **1** Understanding disaster risk; **2** Strengthening disaster risk governance; **3** Investing in DRR for resilience; **4** Enhancing preparedness for effective response and **"Build Back Better"**.
[106:0:8] TABLE head: Target | Aim (by 2030 unless stated)
  [106:0:8.0] A | Reduce global disaster mortality
  [106:0:8.1] B | Reduce number of affected people
  [106:0:8.2] C | Reduce direct economic loss in relation to global GDP
  [106:0:8.3] D | Reduce damage to critical infrastructure and disruption of basic services
  [106:0:8.4] E | Increase countries with national and local DRR strategies – by 2020
  [106:0:8.5] F | Enhance international cooperation to developing countries
  [106:0:8.6] G | Access to multi-hazard early warning systems and risk information
[106:0:9] - Principles: States have the primary role; all-of-society; multi-hazard (natural + man-made); people-centred.
[106:0:10] # Days and conferences
[106:0:11] TABLE head: Day / event | Date
  [106:0:11.0] International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction | 13 October (began 1989)
  [106:0:11.1] National Day for Disaster Reduction (India) | 29 October
  [106:0:11.2] World Tsunami Awareness Day | 5 November (UN, since 2015; Japan's "Inamura-no-hi")
  [106:0:11.3] World Humanitarian Day | 19 August – 2017 theme #NotATarget
  [106:0:11.4] World Meteorological Day | 23 March
  [106:0:11.5] Earth Day / World Environment Day / World Habitat Day | 22 April / 5 June / 5 October
  [106:0:11.6] NDRF Raising Day | 19 January
[106:0:12] - **7th AMCDRR** (Asian Ministerial Conference on DRR): **New Delhi, 3–5 November 2016** – **PM's 10-Point Agenda** announced (India's roadmap aligned with Sendai).
[106:0:13] - **10-Point Agenda** includes: all development sectors to imbibe DRM principles, risk coverage for all, women's leadership, risk mapping, technology, **network of universities**, social media, local capacity, learning from every disaster, **greater cohesion in international response** – it does **NOT** list "youth leadership".
[106:0:14] - **PREVIEW** = UNEP's **Global Risk Data Platform** (spatial data on global risk from natural hazards).
[106:0:15] - **CDRI** (2019): India-led Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure; secretariat New Delhi.
[106:0:16] > Most asked: Sendai year/period/priorities, Yokohama 1994, IDDRR 13 Oct, Tsunami Day 5 Nov. IDNDR strictly 1990–1999 (some books "1991–2000" / "1990–2000").
[106:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.12-13, p.50, p.56, p.59-62, p.74; PMF Internal Security & DM Part 2 p.44; app notes (old-notes.txt)
## SUB 1 | DM Act 2005, NDMA, NDRF and the National Set-up
[106:1:0] # The Act and the plans
[106:1:1] - **DM Act 2005**: Presidential assent **23 December 2005**; Act No. 53; **11 chapters, 79 sections**; triggered by the **2004 tsunami** (and Bhuj 2001). Sec 3 NDMA, Sec 8 NEC, Sec 14 SDMA, Sec 25 DDMA, **Sec 42 NIDM**, **Sec 44 NDRF**, Sec 46 NDRF (fund), Sec 47 NDMF, Sec 48 SDRF.
[106:1:2] - **NDMA**: first set up by executive order in **2005**; formally **notified 27 September 2006** under the Act – most keys answer "**2005**" for "when was NDMA formed/constituted".
[106:1:3] - **NDMA functions (Sec 6)**: lays down **policies**, **approves the National Plan**, **approves plans of Union Ministries/Departments**, lays down guidelines for **State Authorities** (so "does not interfere with State Plans" is wrong).
[106:1:4] - **National Plan**: prepared by the **NEC**, **approved by NDMA**. **First NDMP 2016** – document dated **May 2016**, **released by the PM on 1 June 2016**; revised 2019. Its response part lists **18** broad activities.
[106:1:5] - **National Policy on DM (NPDM)**: approved **22 October 2009**; approach **holistic, pro-active**, multi-disaster, technology-driven – **from relief-centric to prevention, mitigation, preparedness**.
[106:1:6] - DM Act gives **PRIs and ULBs** a legal role; the **2025 amendment** adds Urban DM Authorities and statutory status to NCMC and HLC.
[106:1:7] # Who chairs what
[106:1:8] TABLE head: Body | Chair
  [106:1:8.0] NDMA | Prime Minister (ex-officio); up to 9 members
  [106:1:8.1] NEC | Union Home Secretary
  [106:1:8.2] NCMC (National Crisis Management Committee) | Cabinet Secretary
  [106:1:8.3] NPDRR; High Level Committee (fund approvals) | Union Home Minister
  [106:1:8.4] CCS | PM – nuclear, biological, chemical emergencies
  [106:1:8.5] SDMA / State Crisis Management Committee | Chief Minister / Chief Secretary
  [106:1:8.6] DDMA | District Collector / DM
[106:1:9] - **Primary responsibility for disaster management lies with the State Government**; the Centre (MHA) supports with resources, NDRF and funds.
[106:1:10] - **Nodal ministry: Ministry of Home Affairs** (shifted from Agriculture in **2002**, after Bhuj); MHA's DG Fire Services, Civil Defence & Home Guards gives **technical advice on fire protection, prevention and legislation** (fire = State subject).
[106:1:11] # Ministry by disaster
[106:1:12] TABLE head: Disaster | Nodal ministry
  [106:1:12.0] Chemical / industrial, forest fire | Environment, Forest & Climate Change
  [106:1:12.1] Biological / epidemics | Health & Family Welfare
  [106:1:12.2] Drought, hailstorm, frost, pest attack | Agriculture & Farmers Welfare
  [106:1:12.3] Cyclone, earthquake, tsunami (forecast) | Earth Sciences (IMD coordinates cyclone warnings)
  [106:1:12.4] Flood | Jal Shakti (CWC)
  [106:1:12.5] Nuclear / radiological | Dept of Atomic Energy
  [106:1:12.6] Rail / air / road accidents | Railways / Civil Aviation / Road Transport
[106:1:13] # NDRF and other institutions
[106:1:14] - **NDRF**: raised **2006** (Sec 44) with **8 battalions**; **12 by 2017**; **16 now** (as of 2026), drawn from CAPFs; ~1,149 per battalion; motto "Aapada Seva Sadaiv Sarvatra"; Academy **Nagpur**; regional HQ for AP–Telangana–Karnataka **Vijayawada**.
[106:1:15] - **National Civil Defence College**: founded **29 April 1957** at **Nagpur** (as Central Emergency Relief Training Institute); National Fire Service College also at Nagpur.
[106:1:16] - **Mock exercises** are conducted regularly by **NDMA** (with NIDM, NDRF and States). **Aapda Mitra** trains community volunteers as first responders.
[106:1:17] - **First Indian Disaster Management Congress**: **29 November 2006**. **SACHET**: NDMA alert system on the Common Alerting Protocol (C-DOT).
[106:1:18] - **Funds:** SDRF = primary State fund (Centre 75:25 general, 90:10 special category); NDRF fund for severe calamities; NDMF/SDMF for mitigation (after 15th FC). 11th FC → National Calamity Contingency Fund; 13th FC → NDRF/SDRF.
[106:1:19] - **Notified disasters** (SDRF/NDRF aid): **12** – cyclone, drought, earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, hailstorm, landslide, avalanche, cloudburst, pest attack, frost & cold wave – **14 since Aug 2026** with **heatwave and lightning** (Finance Commission advice, MHA notification); no man-made disaster is notified.
[106:1:20] > NDRF battalions is a moving number: 8 (2006) → 12 (2017) → 16 (now). NCMC = Cabinet Secretary, not Home Minister.
[106:1:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.2-3, p.7-8, p.32-33, p.37-38, p.41-42, p.49-50, p.53-56, p.63; PMF Internal Security & DM Part 2 p.46-49; PMF Lens Aug 2026 (2) p.28 (notified disasters 12→14); web: Business Standard, Aug 2017 (NDRF 12 battalions, search result); app notes
## SUB 2 | Concepts – Hazard, Vulnerability, Risk and Classification
[106:2:0] # Key terms
[106:2:1] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [106:2:1.0] Hazard | A circumstance/event that poses potential harm or danger
  [106:2:1.1] Disaster | When a hazard meets vulnerability and causes serious harm beyond coping capacity
  [106:2:1.2] Vulnerability | Susceptibility to harm – physical, social, economic, environmental
  [106:2:1.3] Risk | Risk = Hazard × Vulnerability / Capacity – infinite capacity → zero risk
  [106:2:1.4] Vulnerability profile | Assessment of the susceptibility of a community or system to hazards
  [106:2:1.5] Hazard mapping | Mapping areas at risk of various hazards
[106:2:2] - "**All disasters are hazards but all hazards are not disasters**" – taught as **true** (a hazard becomes a disaster only when it strikes a vulnerable community).
[106:2:3] - Disaster = hazard + **exposure** + **vulnerability** (+ location); **social status** alone is not a factor forming a disaster (APPSC key). **Gales** = a **hazard characteristic** (APPSC key).
[106:2:4] - **Disaster Crunch (Pressure-and-Release) Model**: vulnerability is **rooted in socio-economic processes**.
[106:2:5] - **DRR works best when it addresses the underlying causes of vulnerability**; objective of DM = **reduce loss of life and property**.
[106:2:6] - **Environmental vulnerability** = natural-resource depletion and degradation; **environmental degradation** magnifies drought and can trigger natural disasters (it is not itself a natural geological disaster).
[106:2:7] - Rising vulnerability comes from population growth, climate change, pollution – **not "stagnation in S&T"**. Development and disaster deaths are **inversely** related.
[106:2:8] - Most vulnerable: people in an **old city with narrow roads**; women and children.
[106:2:9] - **GIS**: manages large spatial data for **vulnerability and hazard assessment**.
[106:2:10] # Classification
[106:2:11] TABLE head: Class | Examples
  [106:2:11.0] Geophysical / geological | Earthquake, tsunami, landslide, volcano, avalanche
  [106:2:11.1] Hydrological | Flood, flash flood
  [106:2:11.2] Meteorological | Cyclone, tornado, thunderstorm, hailstorm
  [106:2:11.3] Climatological | Drought, heat wave, cold wave
  [106:2:11.4] Biological | Epidemics, pest attack, food poisoning (not hailstorm)
  [106:2:11.5] Man-made | Industrial, chemical, nuclear explosion, fire, transport, war
[106:2:12] - **Natural** disasters arise from environmental/geological phenomena; **man-made** from technological failure or human activity. **Urban flooding** = **mostly man-made**.
[106:2:13] - Floods: melting snow, lack of vegetation, broken dams – a **biological disaster does not cause flooding**.
[106:2:14] - Tsunami causes: undersea earthquake, underwater landslide, underwater volcano (and big explosions) – **underwater mining explosions** are the "not a cause" option.
[106:2:15] - Socio-natural hazards: floods worsened by deforestation; emerging hazards: cyber attacks, space weather.
[106:2:16] > Definition and "NOT a" items dominate; the classification table answers tsunami/landslide (geophysical) and hailstorm (not biological).
[106:2:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.10, p.40, p.47-48, p.57, p.68; PMF Internal Security & DM Part 2 p.42-43; app notes
[106:2:18] - **Mitigation (pre-disaster):** embankments, mangroves, land-use zoning; response = rescue and relief; recovery = rehabilitation and reconstruction.
[106:2:19] - **Resilience:** ability of a community to resist, absorb and recover quickly from a hazard; **capacity** = strengths and resources that reduce risk.
[106:2:20] - **Man-made subtypes:** technological, transport, and **social or complex** (terrorism, riots, war).
[106:2:21] - **Risk assessment dimensions:** hazard, vulnerability, exposure and **capacity** (Sendai Priority 1).
[106:2:22] - **Vulnerable groups:** age-based (children, elderly), gender-based, disability, socio-economic, location-based.
## SUB 3 | Mitigation, Safety and First Aid
[106:3:0] # Mitigation by hazard
[106:3:1] TABLE head: Hazard | Mitigation
  [106:3:1.0] Earthquake | Earthquake-resistant construction; reframing building codes and enforcing them (IS 1893, NBC)
  [106:3:1.1] Cyclone | Planting trees (shelter belts, mangroves) along the coast; cyclone shelters; IMD warnings
  [106:3:1.2] Flood | Desilting/dredging, afforestation, check dams, diversion levees, decongesting channels, depopulating flood plains – not "deindustrialisation"; basements worsen flood damage
  [106:3:1.3] Landslide | Regulate settlements; retaining walls; hazard zonation
  [106:3:1.4] Drought | Water conservation, check dams
[106:3:2] - **Strict enforcement of building codes** = a mitigation strategy; **tsunamis** are especially hard to mitigate.
[106:3:3] - **CWC flood bulletins**: **Orange** = severe – above danger level but **below HFL** (incl. within 0.5 m of it); **Red** = extreme – HFL reached or crossed.
[106:3:4] # Earthquake-safe buildings
[106:3:5] - Plan: **simple rectangular** (symmetric) – not star, oval or circular; RCC with **small windows and openings away from pillars**; door/window openings **small and centrally located**.
[106:3:6] - Roofs: a **pyramidal (hipped)** roof reduces wind force; heavy roofs are bad.
[106:3:7] - **Quake Safe guidelines** (APPSC key): buildings with **fire-fighting equipment in working order**.
[106:3:8] - After a quake use a **battery torch** (gas leaks – no candles or flames); outdoors stay **in an open field away from buildings**, trees, bridges.
[106:3:9] - **Seismic Vulnerability Assessment of Building Types in India** (NDMA, 2013): building-type catalogue and vulnerability functions – coordinated by **IIT Bombay**.
[106:3:10] - **CFLOWS-Chennai** (Coastal Flood Warning System app, 2019): developed by **IIT Bombay** with NCCR (MoES).
[106:3:11] - **Occupational hazard identification and risk analysis** standards: **Bureau of Indian Standards** (IS 15656).
[106:3:12] - **Stampede-free fair**: proper crowd control with police at various places.
[106:3:13] # First aid
[106:3:14] - Action plan **DRABC** = Danger, Response, **Airway**, Breathing, Circulation; **ABC** of life support: **A = Airway**.
[106:3:15] - Golden rule: **Be calm – don't panic**.
[106:3:16] > Mitigation PYQs are matching "hazard → measure"; earthquake-design items come from APPSC AEE/technical papers.
[106:3:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.4, p.26, p.30-31, p.43; NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.28 (CWC); web: cwc.gov.in flood-forecasting page (search result); app notes
[106:3:18] - **Seismic zoning** is an earthquake measure, not a cyclone measure; hazard zonation mapping = landslides; Flood Plain Zoning = non-structural.
[106:3:19] - **USA:** volcanoes cause the **fewest** annual deaths among natural hazards (tornadoes, heat, winter weather kill more).
[106:3:20] - **Landslide-prone regions:** Himalayas (most), Western Ghats, North-East – not the Deccan or Chambal valley.
## SUB 4 | Man-made Disasters – Bhopal, Chernobyl and Industrial Accidents
[106:4:0] TABLE head: Event | Year | Key fact
  [106:4:0.0] Bhopal gas tragedy | 2–3 December 1984 | Methyl isocyanate (MIC) from Union Carbide pesticide plant – a chemical (man-made) disaster
  [106:4:0.1] Great Smog of London | 1952 | Air pollution
  [106:4:0.2] Seveso (Italy) | 1976 | Dioxin release
  [106:4:0.3] Three Mile Island | 1979 | USA, partial meltdown
  [106:4:0.4] Chernobyl | 26 April 1986 | Nuclear reactor accident, Ukraine (then USSR); INES level 7
  [106:4:0.5] Kumbakonam school fire | 16 July 2004 | Tamil Nadu – 94 children died
  [106:4:0.6] LG Polymers, Visakhapatnam | May 2020 | Styrene vapour
[106:4:1] - MIC was used at Bhopal to make **pesticides** (carbaryl/Sevin); "NIC, OIC, CFC, chlorine, ammonia, phosgene" are the distractors.
[106:4:2] - Chemical accidents: MSIHC Rules 1989 + CAEPPR Rules 1996; nodal ministry **MoEFCC**.
[106:4:3] - **Rail-accident prevention**: replace over-aged tracks and bridges, fire sensing in coaches, road over/under bridges – **watershed structures are not** a rail measure.
[106:4:4] - **Nuclear explosion is not a natural disaster** (CBRN; CCS handles NBC emergencies).
[106:4:5] > Bhopal = MIC, 1984 – asked about 20 times in many forms.
[106:4:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.19-21, p.63; app notes

## SUB 8 | Heat Waves, Cold Waves and Community DRR
[106:8:0] - **Heat wave**: March–June; IMD forecasts; NDMA heat-wave action-plan guidelines (updated 2019); Heat Action Plans by States/cities; cool roofs; adjusted working hours = administrative measure.
[106:8:1] - **Cold wave**: November–March; NDMA Guidelines on Cold Wave and Frost **2021**; cold day = max departure −4.5°C to −6.4°C.
[106:8:2] - **Community DRR**: community = first responder; NDMA Disability-inclusive DRR guidelines **2019**; School Safety; gender mainstreaming (10-Point Agenda); 20 Model GPs in PRIs; social media complements, not replaces, official systems.
[106:8:3] - 2004 tsunami: up to **four times as many women as men** died in some areas.
[106:8:4] - Tsunami: Tsunami Ready villages – 24 in Odisha (UNESCO-IOC); ITEWC at INCOIS Hyderabad. ISRO's DMS programme and NDEM support all hazards.
[106:8:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Disaster Management p.68-73; app notes
[106:8:6] - **Social media** complements official warning systems – it does not replace them.

  *Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity | Risk = Hazard x Capacity / Vulnerability | Risk = Vulnerability + Capacity - Hazard | Risk = Capacity x Resilience / Hazard
  x: Risk rises with hazard and vulnerability and falls as coping capacity rises, so Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity. Putting capacity in the numerator (B) or adding/subtracting terms (C) reverses or breaks this logic, and D drops vulnerability entirely.

=== NOTES 5:108 | Biotechnology – Nature, Scope, Tools; Applications in Agriculture, Medicine and Industry
## SUB 0 | Genetics and DNA – Basics and Discoverers
[108:0:0] # DNA, genes and heredity (asked ~20 times)
[108:0:1] - **Genetics** = study of genes, **heredity and variation** (not only Mendel's laws or DNA structure).
[108:0:2] - **Gene** = the **unit of heredity** (a DNA segment coding for a trait); **DNA** controls hereditary characters; **chromosome** and nucleus only carry it.
[108:0:3] - **Nucleic acids (DNA, RNA)**: **storage and expression of genetic information** – not oxygen transport, energy or body temperature.
[108:0:4] - **DNA bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine**; **RNA has uracil in place of thymine** (A and G occur in both).
[108:0:5] - **RNA** is usually **single-stranded** (a "single helix"); DNA is a **double helix**.
[108:0:6] - DNA occurs in the **nucleus** and also in **mitochondria and chloroplasts** (they have their own DNA).
[108:0:7] - **Histones** = basic proteins in the **nucleus**; DNA wraps around them (nucleosomes, chromatin).
[108:0:8] - DNA can store and pass on information because its two strands are **complementary** (A–T, G–C): each strand is a template (UPSC 2001).
[108:0:9] - **Mutation** = change in the **base sequence** of a gene (transversion is only one kind of substitution).
[108:0:10] - **Phenotype** = observable traits; **genotype** = genetic make-up.
[108:0:11] - **Genetic code**: triplet codons for **20 amino acids**; non-overlapping, non-ambiguous, commaless; has **start and stop codons**; "universal" – nearly so (a few mitochondrial exceptions).
[108:0:12] - **Gene mapping** (position of genes on a chromosome) helps trace **livestock pedigree** and breed **disease-resistant animals**; it cannot explain "all human diseases" (UPSC 2011 → I and III).
[108:0:13] # Discoverers
[108:0:14] TABLE head: Scientist | Contribution
  [108:0:14.0] Gregor Mendel | Pea hybridisation; laws of inheritance; father of genetics (and of modern genetics)
  [108:0:14.1] Friedrich Miescher | First isolated DNA ("nuclein"), 1869
  [108:0:14.2] James Watson and Francis Crick (+ Wilkins) | Double-helix structure of DNA, 1953; Nobel 1962 (Rosalind Franklin's X-ray data; Pauling, Mendel are distractors)
  [108:0:14.3] Arthur Kornberg | DNA polymerase I (1956); synthesised DNA in vitro; Nobel 1959
  [108:0:14.4] Barbara McClintock | Jumping genes (transposons) in maize; Nobel 1983
  [108:0:14.5] Har Gobind Khorana (with Nirenberg, Holley) | Interpreted the genetic code – how the nucleotide sequence controls protein synthesis (Nobel 1968); made the first artificial gene (1970–72) – not the helix model
  [108:0:14.6] Hugo de Vries | Mutation theory
  [108:0:14.7] Arber, Nathans, Smith | Restriction enzymes
  [108:0:14.8] Lederberg and Tatum | Bacterial conjugation
  [108:0:14.9] Zinder and Lederberg | Bacterial transduction
  [108:0:14.10] Ambros and Ruvkun | microRNA – silences target genes by post-transcriptional regulation
[108:0:15] - **SRC** = first oncogene (1970); **IgM** = first antibody in a new infection.
[108:0:16] > Trap: "helix model" = Watson–Crick, never Khorana; "father of genetics" = Mendel, never Morgan, Darwin or Lamarck.
[108:0:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.2, p.4, p.14, p.16-17, p.19, p.21-23, p.64-65, p.73; PMF General Science 04 p.8-9, p.18, p.31-37; Britannica "Har Gobind Khorana" (web search, Nobel citation and first synthetic gene); app notes 5:108 sub 1-2
[108:0:18] - **Carbohydrates** contain only **C, H and O** (no nitrogen).
## SUB 1 | Microbes in Industry – Fermentation, Vinegar and Curd
[108:1:0] # Microbe → product (asked ~20 times)
[108:1:1] TABLE head: Microbe | Product
  [108:1:1.0] Lactobacillus (bacterium) | Curd – turns lactose into lactic acid (sour milk, curd, sour taste); souring/spoiling of milk
  [108:1:1.1] Yeast – Saccharomyces cerevisiae (fungus) | Ethanol – wine, beer (malt sugar → alcohol by fermentation), bread, toddy
  [108:1:1.2] Acetobacter | Vinegar = dilute aqueous acetic acid (CH3COOH, ethanoic acid)
  [108:1:1.3] Aspergillus niger | Citric acid
  [108:1:1.4] Methanogens | Biogas (methane)
  [108:1:1.5] Diatoms | Diatomaceous earth
[108:1:2] - **Anaerobic respiration of yeast** gives **alcohol** (ethanol) + CO2 – not water, methane or acetic acid.
[108:1:3] - **Milk → curd** is done by **bacteria** (Lactobacillus), not a vitamin or an enzyme alone; sourness = **lactic acid** (not acetic, citric or tartaric).
[108:1:4] - **India's national microbe (2012): Lactobacillus** (*L. delbrueckii* subsp. *bulgaricus*), chosen by children on the Science Express.
[108:1:5] - **Vinegar:** made by Acetobacter from fermented sugarcane juice/molasses/ethanol; acid = **acetic acid** – **not benzoic**, tartaric, lactic, citric or formic; used as a **preservative** (RAS 2016 → A, B, D). "Sour taste of vinegar" with no acetic option → **None of these**.
[108:1:6] - Other food acids (contrast): tartaric – tamarind, grapes; citric – lemon, orange; oxalic – tomato, spinach; malic – apple; **formic (methanoic) – nettle and ant sting**; "acetic acid – potato" is a wrong pair.
[108:1:7] - Industry uses **bacteria, microalgae and fungi** – all three (IAS 1998). **Yeast and mushrooms = fungi** (no chlorophyll).
[108:1:8] - **Mushrooms:** some are **medicinal**, some **psychoactive** (psilocybin), some **insecticidal**, some **bioluminescent** – **all four** true (UPSC 2023).
[108:1:9] - **Diatoms** in lungs/bone marrow help diagnose **death by drowning** (forensic).
[108:1:10] - Microbes clean **oil spills**: **Pseudomonas putida** – A.M. Chakrabarty's genetically engineered oil-eating "superbug" (Diamond v. Chakrabarty, 1980: first patent on a living organism).
[108:1:11] - First eukaryote genome fully sequenced: **yeast S. cerevisiae, 1996** (IAS 1997).
[108:1:12] # Enzymes and products
[108:1:13] - **Protease** is made commercially from **both plants and microbes** – **papain** (papaya), bromelain (pineapple), *Bacillus* proteases in detergents; trypsin is animal (pancreas).
[108:1:14] - Recombinant enzymes: **chymosin – cheese**; amylase – bread; **pectinase – fruit juice**.
[108:1:15] - **Xylitol** (sugar substitute for diabetics) from **sugarcane bagasse** by ultrasound-assisted fermentation – **IIT Guwahati** (announced Aug 2022).
[108:1:16] - **2G ethanol** from crop residue: **IOCL Panipat**; E20 blending. **Bioplastics** = PLA, PHA. **India's first biodiesel plant: Kakinada, AP**.
[108:1:17] - **Gobar-Dhan** biogas; municipal waste → CNG in Hyderabad, Pune. **DBT biofuel targets**: fuel from agri residue and municipal waste, algal fuels, SAF, integrated biorefineries.
[108:1:18] - First microbe-made semiconductor diode (cadmium sulphide) – yeast **Schizosaccharomyces pombe**.
[108:1:19] - **DRDO** herbal products: **Lukoskin** (with DIBER) – leucoderma; **Eczit** – eczema; **Amtooth** – toothache.
[108:1:20] > Trap: curd = bacterium (Lactobacillus); bread, beer, wine, toddy = yeast (Saccharomyces); vinegar = Acetobacter.
[108:1:21] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.2, p.108-109, p.114, p.122-128; NextGen Rocket Chemistry p.19, p.27, p.45-47, p.51; NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 5 p.32 (bioethanol by fermentation); scroll.in (national microbe, web search); app notes 5:108 sub 7
[108:1:22] - **Amylase** hydrolyses **starch → maltose/glucose** (invertase: sucrose).
[108:1:23] - **Fermentation** = **incomplete oxidation of sugar without oxygen** (anaerobic) → alcohol or lactic acid.
[108:1:24] - **Biogas** forms by **anaerobic fermentation (digestion)** of biomass by methanogens – not oxidation or aerobic respiration.
## SUB 2 | Medical Biotechnology – Stem Cells, Antibodies, Gene Therapy
[108:2:0] # Antibodies and hybridoma (asked 5 times)
[108:2:1] - **Hybridoma technique: Georges Köhler and César Milstein, 1975** – fusion of an antibody-making **B cell with a myeloma cell**; used for commercial production of **monoclonal antibodies** (not interferon or antibiotics).
[108:2:2] - **Monoclonal antibodies**: **man-made (lab) proteins** that bind one specific antigen and so modulate immune function; used against viral infections such as **Nipah** (m102.4) – UPSC 2025: **I, II and III**.
[108:2:3] - **Plasma cells** (from B cells) **form antibodies**.
[108:2:4] # Stem cells and transplants
[108:2:5] - **Stem cells** divide, self-renew and can become **any/many cell types**; focus of research on serious diseases (endodermal, ectodermal, muscle cells are already specialised).
[108:2:6] - **Bone-marrow stem cells** = the bioethically non-controversial alternative to embryonic stem cells. **Mesenchymal stem cells** were first found in **bone marrow** (a place, not a person).
[108:2:7] - National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research: **2017**.
[108:2:8] - **First human heart transplant: Christian Barnard, South Africa, 1967** (William Harvey = blood circulation).
[108:2:9] - **Test-tube baby (IVF):** ovum **fertilised in a test tube**, embryo **develops in the uterus**.
[108:2:10] # Genetic disease and gene therapy
[108:2:11] - **Haemophilia**: **hereditary**, **X-linked (sex-linked) recessive** clotting defect – **carried by women, appears in men** ("royal haemophilia", Queen Victoria); not caused by bacteria, virus or pollutants. Tay-Sachs and cystic fibrosis are autosomal.
[108:2:12] TABLE head: Therapy / product | Fact
  [108:2:12.0] Gene therapy, haemophilia A | India's first-in-human trial – Centre for Stem Cell Research, CMC Vellore (DBT/BRIC-inStem); lentiviral FVIII gene in the patient's own stem cells; results Dec 2024
  [108:2:12.1] CRISPR gene therapy | India's first indigenous CRISPR-based gene therapy – for sickle-cell disease (2026)
  [108:2:12.2] CAR-T (NexCAR19) | IIT Bombay + Tata Memorial, via ImmunoACT
  [108:2:12.3] RNAi (RNA interference) | Gene silencing: gene-silencing therapies, cancer therapy, virus-resistant crops – not hormone replacement (UPSC 2019 → I, II, IV)
  [108:2:12.4] Humulin | First recombinant-DNA drug (insulin)
[108:2:13] - **CSA6**: gene in the fungus **Candida albicans** found by **JNCASR** with Institut Pasteur (Aug 2022) – essential for its cell cycle; a possible antifungal target.
[108:2:14] # Vaccines
[108:2:15] - **India's first genetically engineered vaccine: Hepatitis B (Shanvac-B)** – not malaria, FMD or BCG.
[108:2:16] - India = largest vaccine maker; **~60%** of global demand. Platforms: mRNA, viral vector, protein subunit, DNA; **mRNA vaccine** makes cells produce the target **antigen**.
[108:2:17] TABLE head: Vaccine | Developer | Target
  [108:2:17.0] Covishield | Oxford–AstraZeneca; made by Serum Institute | COVID-19
  [108:2:17.1] Covaxin | Bharat Biotech with ICMR | COVID-19
  [108:2:17.2] ZyCoV-D | Zydus Cadila – first DNA vaccine | COVID-19
  [108:2:17.3] Cervavac (qHPV) | Serum Institute | HPV / cervical cancer (free HPV drive for 14-year-old girls from 28 Feb 2026)
  [108:2:17.4] R21/Matrix-M | Jenner Institute (Oxford) + Serum Institute; Novavax adjuvant | Malaria
  [108:2:17.5] Sputnik V | Gamaleya Institute, Russia | COVID-19
  [108:2:17.6] Moderna | Moderna, NIAID, BARDA | COVID-19
  [108:2:17.7] Rotavac | Bharat Biotech | Rotavirus
[108:2:18] - Polio: **Jonas Salk** – first successful vaccine; **Albert Sabin** – oral. **Edward Jenner** – smallpox vaccine, father of immunology.
[108:2:19] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.2-3, p.5, p.18-20, p.34, p.53, p.65, p.67, p.70, p.73-74, p.136-137; NextGen Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.6 (CRISPR sickle-cell); Part 02 p.110 (HPV drive); PMF S&T 02 p.105 (RNAi, UPSC 2019), p.115-120 (hybridoma, mAbs, UPSC 2025); PMF General Science 04 p.20 (haemophilia); PIB 25 Aug 2022 / web search (CSA6); BioSpectrum (web search, CMC Vellore haemophilia A); app notes 5:108 sub 6
[108:2:20] - Stem cells occur in **plants and all multicellular animals** (not mammals only); used for **drug screening** and **therapies** (UPSC 2012 → 2 and 3).
[108:2:21] - Stem cells also come from **adult tissues** (not only blastocysts); they **self-renew in vitro**; Indian centres have made cell lines (UPSC 2002 → 3 and 4).
## SUB 3 | DNA Fingerprinting
[108:3:0] # Basis and uses (asked 15 times)
[108:3:1] - **Developed by Alec Jeffreys (1984)**; in India pioneered by **Lalji Singh** (CCMB) – father of Indian DNA fingerprinting.
[108:3:2] - **Basis: DNA polymorphism** – highly variable repetitive regions (**VNTRs**); most DNA is the same in all people. Not the double helix, replication or "errors in base sequence".
[108:3:3] - Tissues of the same person show the **same pattern**; polymorphisms are **inherited** (child gets half from each parent) → **paternity**.
[108:3:4] - **Technique: Southern blotting** of DNA fragments (ELISA, RIA = antigen–antibody tests; Northern blot = RNA).
[108:3:5] - **Uses:** identity, **paternity** (not protein analysis, chromosome counting, gene therapy, cloning or rDNA), **forensic** cases, **rape and assault** (trace hair, saliva, dried semen are enough – A and R true, R explains A), **conservation** – "all of the above"; WWF-India's anti-poaching tool for **rhinos** (RhODIS – rhino DNA index).
[108:3:6] - **Samples:** blood, bone, hair **with root**, saliva, skin, semen – all usable; **burnt bones** lose usable DNA. **Biochips** = a technique, not a sample.
[108:3:7] - **First crime solved:** **England** – the murders of **1983** and 1986 (solved 1987–88).
[108:3:8] - **CDFD** (Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics): **Hyderabad**, under DBT.
[108:3:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.3-4, p.14-15, p.18, p.22, p.62-64; app notes 5:108 sub 3
[108:3:10] - **CCMB** (CSIR Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology): **Hyderabad**.
## SUB 4 | Animal Cloning
[108:4:0] # Dolly and other clones (asked 13 times)
[108:4:1] - **SCNT** (somatic cell nuclear transfer): nucleus of a body cell put into an **enucleated egg** = **nuclear transfer** – the technique of Dolly; application = **reproductive cloning** of animals (UPSC 2017) – not IVF.
[108:4:2] TABLE head: Clone | Animal | Fact
  [108:4:2.0] Dolly | Sheep | First mammal cloned from an adult somatic cell; Ian Wilmut, Keith Campbell; Roslin Institute, Edinburgh, Scotland; born 5 July 1996, died 14 Feb 2003 (lung disease); "first living cloned genetically engineered organism"
  [108:4:2.1] Samrupa | Buffalo | World's first cloned buffalo calf, 6 Feb 2009, NDRI Karnal (hand-guided cloning)
  [108:4:2.2] Garima | Buffalo | NDRI's second clone, 6 June 2009 (43 kg); Garima II (2010) also a cloned buffalo
  [108:4:2.3] Noori | Pashmina goat | SKUAST-Kashmir, 2012
  [108:4:2.4] Ganga | Cow, Gir breed | India's first cloned cow, NDRI Karnal (2023)
  [108:4:2.5] Injaz | Camel (female) | World's first cloned camel, Camel Reproduction Centre, Dubai
  [108:4:2.6] Glowing pigs | Transgenic | Taiwan, National Taiwan University, 2006
[108:4:3] - "First successful cloned animal" in exams = **sheep (Dolly)**.
[108:4:4] - **"Eve"** – claimed by Clonaid (Dec 2002) as the **first cloned human baby**; the claim was **never verified**.
[108:4:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.3-4, p.18, p.22-23; PMF S&T 02 p.121-125 (SCNT, Dolly, UPSC 2017); app notes 5:108 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Tools, Omics and Identification Techniques
[108:5:0] TABLE head: Tool | Use
  [108:5:0.0] PCR | Amplifies DNA; key enzyme DNA polymerase; denaturation → annealing → extension
  [108:5:0.1] Gel electrophoresis | Separates DNA by size
  [108:5:0.2] Restriction enzymes | Cut DNA ("molecular scissors") – EcoRI, BamHI, HindIII
  [108:5:0.3] Ligase | Only joins DNA
  [108:5:0.4] Plasmids | Vectors (pBR322)
  [108:5:0.5] Bioreactors | Large-scale culture
  [108:5:0.6] CRISPR–Cas9 | Genome editing
[108:5:1] - **Genome**: complete genetic information; zygote genome = DNA of **two gametes**; **human genome ≈ 3 billion bases**, over 99% shared.
[108:5:2] - **DNA sequencing** finds the base order (A, G, C, T); genetic information depends on the order of bases (A and R true, R explains A).
[108:5:3] - **Transcriptome**: the **full range of mRNA** molecules expressed by an organism; **varies with conditions**, unlike the genome (UPSC 2016).
[108:5:4] - **Microsatellite DNA** (short tandem repeats): **evolutionary relationships** among species, genetic diversity (UPSC 2023).
[108:5:5] - **DNA barcoding**: **species identification** from a short standard gene region (animals: mitochondrial **COI**) – distinguishes **look-alike species** and detects **undesirable material in processed food**; it **cannot tell age** (UPSC 2022 → B and C).
[108:5:6] - **Serological tests** (antigen–antibody reactions): **identification** – blood groups, pathogens and serotypes (**Widal, ELISA**); also used in serotaxonomy.
[108:5:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.64-69; PMF General Science 04 p.32-33 (DNA barcoding, UPSC 2022); PMF S&T 04 p.3 (transcriptome, UPSC 2016); serotaxonomy pages (web search); app notes 5:108 sub 1
[108:5:8] - **Human Genome Project** (1990–2003): **identification and mapping of all human genes** and sequencing of the human genome.
## SUB 6 | Nature and Scope of Biotechnology
[108:6:0] - **Biotechnology** = **industrial use of living organisms**, substances from them or their processes (e.g. yeast for liquor) (IAS 1993); CBD (1992): use of **biological systems** to **make or modify products**.
[108:6:1] - Traditional biotech: **curd**, bread, wine, vinegar; modern: rDNA, PCR, cloning, CRISPR. **Earliest biotechnologists: farmers**.
[108:6:2] - Applications: agriculture (GM crops), medicine (drugs, vaccines, diagnostics, gene therapy), industry (microbial products).
[108:6:3] TABLE head: Colour | Field
  [108:6:3.0] Red | Medical
  [108:6:3.1] Green | Agricultural
  [108:6:3.2] White | Industrial – enzymes, biofuels, bioplastics (NOT marine)
  [108:6:3.3] Blue | Marine
[108:6:4] - **Enzymes** = biological catalysts of reactions in living systems (not bacteria or DNA).
[108:6:5] - **Artificial enzymes (synzymes)** are made by **genetic/protein engineering** and by **synthesis of host molecules such as crown ethers** and cyclodextrins; **denaturing** proteins destroys enzyme activity (AEE 2019 → a and b).
[108:6:6] - **Bionics** = using properties of biological systems in the mechanical world; **bionomics** = organism and environment; **bionomy** = laws of life; **biometry** = statistics of biology.
[108:6:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.6, p.61; synzyme lecture notes (gyansanchay.csjmu.ac.in, web search); app notes 5:108 sub 0

## SUB 8 | Policy, Institutions and Bioeconomy
[108:8:0] TABLE head: Policy / body | Fact
  [108:8:0.0] BioE3 Policy | Biotechnology for Economy, Environment and Employment; Cabinet August 2024; DBT-BIRAC priority Precision Biotherapeutics

## SUB 9 | Bioremediation – Meaning and Methods
[108:9:0] - **Bioremediation**: removal or degradation of pollutants by **organisms or their enzymes**; covers soil, water, air – oil spills, heavy metals, pesticides, solvents; engineered microbes may be used. **Slower but cheaper** than conventional (thermal, chemical) clean-up, no secondary pollution; results vary with pollutant and site.
[108:9:1] - Not bioremediation: burning/incineration (thermal), **biomagnification** (DDT, mercury rising up food chains), **eutrophication** (nutrient-driven algal blooms), biofortification.
[108:9:2] TABLE head: Basis | In-situ | Ex-situ
  [108:9:2.0] Site | At the site, no excavation; passive, cheapest, slow | Excavated, treated elsewhere
  [108:9:2.1] Techniques | Bioventing, biosparging, bioaugmentation | Landfarming, composting, biopiles, bioreactors (bioreactors fastest)
[108:9:3] # Techniques
[108:9:4] TABLE head: Technique | How / target
  [108:9:4.0] Bioaugmentation | Adds chosen degrading microbes – oil spills
  [108:9:4.1] Biostimulation | Adds N, P, oxygen to native microbes – polluted lakes
  [108:9:4.2] Bioventing | Air/nutrients via wells into soil
  [108:9:4.3] Biosparging | Air injected below the water table – groundwater
  [108:9:4.4] Mycoremediation | Fungi – organic pollutants
  [108:9:4.5] Rhizofiltration | Roots absorb/precipitate contaminants from water
  [108:9:4.6] Rhizoremediation | Roots stimulate rhizosphere microbes
[108:9:5] # Phytoremediation and hyperaccumulators
[108:9:6] TABLE head: Sub-type / plant | Fact
  [108:9:6.0] Phytoextraction | Stored in shoots, harvested – water hyacinth (heavy metals)
  [108:9:6.1] Phytostabilisation | Roots immobilise contaminants
  [108:9:6.2] Phytodegradation | Plant enzymes break organics
  [108:9:6.3] Phytovolatilisation | Released to air in volatile form (mercury, selenium)
  [108:9:6.4] Pteris vittata (fern) | Arsenic
  [108:9:6.5] Indian mustard | Lead, cadmium, selenium
  [108:9:6.6] Thlaspi caerulescens | Zinc, cadmium
  [108:9:6.7] Alyssum | Nickel
  [108:9:6.8] Sunflower | Uranium, radionuclides
  [108:9:6.9] Eucalyptus (sewage ponds) | Transpires surplus wastewater
  [108:9:6.10] Bacillus flexus / Acinetobacter junii | Arsenate / arsenite
  [108:9:6.11] Ideonella sakaiensis (PETase) | PET plastic degradation
[108:9:7] - **Constructed wetlands**: plants and microbes break down and absorb sewage pollutants.
[108:9:8] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:108 sub 9-10 (no PYQ in this job)
[108:9:9] - **Bregoli** – a paper-industry by-product resembling **sawdust** – absorbs **oil spills** (with oil zapper and microbes).
[108:9:10] - Bioremediation **enhances natural biodegradation**; GE microbes can be designed for it; heavy metals (Cd, Pb) are **not readily and completely** treated (UPSC 2017 → I and III).

=== NOTES 5:109 | Eco-friendly Technologies in Agriculture – Ipm, Biofertilisers, Biopesticides, Organic and Natural Farming
## SUB 0 | Fertilisers, Plant Nutrients, Manures and Soil Health
[109:0:0] # Plant nutrients
[109:0:1] TABLE head: Group | Elements
  [109:0:1.0] Macronutrients (9) | C, H, O, N, P, K (primary), Ca, Mg, S (secondary)
  [109:0:1.1] Micronutrients (8) | Fe, Mn, Zn, Cu, B, Mo, Cl, Ni – trace amounts (< 1% of dry weight)
[109:0:2] - **Magnesium is a macronutrient** (secondary), not a micronutrient; **manganese and zinc are micronutrients** supplied by the soil.
[109:0:3] - Inorganic fertilisers supply the macronutrients **nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium (NPK)**; desirable soil NPK use ratio in India **4:2:1**.
[109:0:4] - **Zinc deficiency in maize = "white bud" / white tip of young leaves**; **Khaira** in rice is also zinc deficiency.
[109:0:5] - **Excess nitrogen delays maturity** (lush vegetative growth, lodging); phosphorus **hastens** maturity.
[109:0:6] # Fertiliser facts
[109:0:7] TABLE head: Fertiliser | Fact
  [109:0:7.0] Urea CO(NH2)2 | ~46% N – highest of common solid N fertilisers; nitrogen in amide form; 100/46 ≈ 2.2 kg urea gives 1 kg N; most popular for foliar spray (high solubility)
  [109:0:7.1] Ammonium nitrate / CAN / ammonium sulphate | 34% / 26% / 20.6% N
  [109:0:7.2] DAP (NH4)2HPO4 | 18% N, 46% P2O5 – balanced N + P supply
  [109:0:7.3] Superphosphate | Calcium dihydrogen phosphate (+ gypsum); acidic, so continued use lowers soil pH (< 7)
  [109:0:7.4] Potassic (MOP, SOP) | Disease and drought resistance, quality
  [109:0:7.5] Phosphatic | Root development, flowering, fruiting
  [109:0:7.6] Neem-coated urea | Slows dissolution of urea and nitrification → slow N release, higher N-use efficiency
[109:0:8] - Urea → ammoniacal (NH4+) → nitrate in soil; **ammoniacal N is preferred for paddy and potato** (held by soil, less lost in flooded fields).
[109:0:9] - Nitrogen is the main fertiliser for **wheat** (vegetative growth).
[109:0:10] - **Nitrogen-use efficiency** is raised by **split application, nitrification inhibitors and slow-release N fertilisers** (all of these).
[109:0:11] - **Balanced fertilisation** raises production, improves fertiliser-use efficiency and maintains soil productivity (all of these); legumes need little N, so their NPK is P- and K-heavy (exam key **1:2:2**).
[109:0:12] - Excess N: **soil acidification, nitrate leaching, eutrophication**; continuous chemical use: **lower soil organic matter**, fewer microbes, lower nutrient density in food.
[109:0:13] - Broadcasting granular fertiliser loses **50-70%** of the nitrogen; **PM-PRANAM**: States keep **50%** of the subsidy saved, as grants.
[109:0:14] # Nano fertilisers and Soil Health Card
[109:0:15] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [109:0:15.0] Nano urea (liquid) | IFFCO; launched June 2021; notified under the Fertiliser Control Order, 1985
  [109:0:15.1] Nano DAP | IFFCO; notified in the FCO March 2023
  [109:0:15.2] Soil Health Card | Launched 19 Feb 2015 at Suratgarh (Rajasthan); motto "Swasth Dharaa, Khet Haraa"; soil-test-based advice to check over-use of fertilisers; merged into RKVY in 2022-23
[109:0:16] # Organic manures and amendments
[109:0:17] TABLE head: Input | Meaning
  [109:0:17.0] Animal manure (FYM) | Dung, urine and litter of farm animals
  [109:0:17.1] Compost | Decomposed plant and animal waste – raises organic matter and microbial activity
  [109:0:17.2] Crop residue | Remains of harvested crops worked back into the soil
  [109:0:17.3] Green manure | Fresh crops (mostly legumes) ploughed in green – sunhemp (most suitable), dhaincha, sesbania, cowpea
  [109:0:17.4] Vermicompost | Organic waste converted into rich manure by earthworms (Eisenia fetida)
  [109:0:17.5] Biochar | Charcoal from pyrolysis of biomass (low oxygen)
[109:0:18] - **Biochar (UPSC 2020 – all three):** used in the **growing medium of vertical farming**, **promotes nitrogen-fixing and mycorrhizal microbes**, and **retains water** longer; also cuts leaching and acidity and stores carbon for millennia.
[109:0:19] - **Earthworms** improve soil fertility – **"farmers' friends"**; an earthworm has **more than two pairs** of "hearts" (aortic arches – 4 pairs in Pheretima).
[109:0:20] - **Humus** = dark **organic colloid** from decayed plant and animal matter.
[109:0:21] - AP plans **1,500 MT/day** of manure from **107 waste-processing centres** (Feb 2026); Kharif 2026 green-manure subsidy Rs 62.20 crore, **sunn hemp 50,311 quintals**.
[109:0:22] > Exam angle: urea 46% N / amide / 2.2 kg, DAP 18-46, micronutrient pickers (Mn, Zn; Mg is not), biochar statements (UPSC 2020, ×3), sunhemp, organic-amendment match, superphosphate lowers pH, SHC 19 Feb 2015.
[109:0:23] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.2-3, p.9-14, p.17-18; NextGen Rocket Chemistry p.55-57; NextGen Rocket Biology p.100; NextGen Rocket Environment p.45; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.51; app notes 5:109 sub 2, 10
## SUB 1 | Biofertilisers
[109:1:0] - **Biofertilisers** = living microbial inoculants (bacteria, algae, fungi) that **fix nitrogen, solubilise phosphorus** or decompose organic matter; they are **applied to seed/soil** (not only leaves), **do not alter soil chemistry** like chemicals, and **can be used with organic manures**.
[109:1:1] TABLE head: Biofertiliser | Type | Crop / role
  [109:1:1.0] Rhizobium | Symbiotic bacterium | Legumes (pea, pulses) – root nodules fix N2
  [109:1:1.1] Azotobacter | Free-living aerobic bacterium | Cereals – non-symbiotic N fixation
  [109:1:1.2] Azospirillum | Associative bacterium | Cereal roots (rice rhizosphere), no nodules
  [109:1:1.3] Blue-green algae (Anabaena, Nostoc) | Cyanobacteria | Paddy – fix atmospheric N into a form crops absorb (heterocysts)
  [109:1:1.4] Azolla | Aquatic fern with the BGA Anabaena | Water-logged rice fields; 2-3% N; often used with BGA
  [109:1:1.5] PSB | Bacteria | Solubilise phosphate
  [109:1:1.6] VAM / Mycorrhiza | Fungus–root association | Phosphatic biofertiliser (P uptake)
[109:1:2] - **Mycorrhiza (UPSC 2013 – all three):** increases **absorptive area / drought resistance**, helps plants **tolerate extreme pH**, and **resists disease** – hence used to rehabilitate degraded sites.
[109:1:3] - **Legumes** (pea) enrich soil with nitrogen; wheat, coffee, rubber, potato, sorghum do not.
[109:1:4] - Rhizobium, BGA and Azolla are **all** biofertilisers; **alfalfa** is a legume fodder, not a biofertiliser.
[109:1:5] - Not biofertilisers: Salvinia, Marsilea, Pteridium (ferns), Wolffia, Trapa, Lemna (other aquatic plants).
[109:1:6] > Exam angle: BGA → paddy (×5), Azolla = fern + Anabaena (×4), VAM = phosphatic, mycorrhiza statements, biofertiliser statements (CDS 2010: I and IV).
[109:1:7] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.15-17; NextGen Rocket Biology p.100-103, p.128; app notes 5:109 sub 3
## SUB 2 | Sustainable Agriculture and Environmental Impact of Modern Farming
[109:2:0] - **Sustainable agriculture:** produce food while **protecting the environment and conserving resources for future generations**; maintains soil fertility; may use synthetic inputs **judiciously** (unlike organic farming).
[109:2:1] TABLE head: Sustainable (exam answers) | Not sustainable
  [109:2:1.0] Crop rotation, organic farming | Excessive chemical fertilisers, overuse of pesticides
  [109:2:1.1] Multi-, inter-, mixed and contour cropping, green manure | Intense mono-cropping / monoculture
  [109:2:1.2] IPM, drip irrigation, reduced tillage | Over-irrigation
[109:2:2] - **Eco-friendly technology in agriculture = organic farming** (NextGen PYQ); GM crops, pesticide spraying and chemical fertilisers are not.
[109:2:3] - **Environmental impact (APPSC 2022, 2023, G2 Mains 2025 – I and II):** synthetic fertilisers/pesticides **pollute soil and water**; sustainable farming **prioritises soil health and biodiversity**. Modern agriculture **does** deplete freshwater, and monoculture **harms** ecosystem stability.
[109:2:4] - Most conspicuous effects of modern agriculture: **soil degradation, pollution and ecological imbalance – all of these**; indiscriminate agro-chemicals cause **secondary pest outbreaks, pesticide resistance** and ecosystem contamination.
[109:2:5] - **Rachel Carson, *Silent Spring* (1962):** pesticides (DDT) harming wildlife and the environment → a founding text of **environmental protection**.
[109:2:6] - **GACSA** (Global Alliance for Climate-Smart Agriculture): launched at the UN Climate Summit, New York, **2014**; facilitated by **FAO**; voluntary – **membership creates no binding obligations** (UPSC 2018: 2 only).
[109:2:7] - Agricultural science covers crop and soil cultivation and animal products; **rainwater harvesting** is a water-conservation technique (APPSC ACF key: NOT part of agricultural science technology).
[109:2:8] - **Carbosulfan** – Centre proposed a ban (29 Aug 2026) under the **Insecticides Act, 1968**: breaks down to highly toxic **carbofuran**, harms birds and aquatic life.
[109:2:9] - **Evergreen revolution** (M.S. Swaminathan): ZBNF, organic farming, water conservation, IPM.
[109:2:10] > Exam angle: statement pairs on agri impact (×3, same question), sustainable-practice pickers (×5), eco-friendly technology = organic farming, GACSA, Silent Spring.
[109:2:11] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.13; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.1; PMF Environment Part 7 p.4-8; PMF Environment Part 6 p.51, p.54; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 20 p.11; app notes 5:109 sub 0, 1
## SUB 3 | Pesticides, Fumigants and Mosquito Repellents
[109:3:0] TABLE head: Class | Examples
  [109:3:0.0] Insecticides | DDT, BHC, Sevin, allethrin, prallethrin, Bt
  [109:3:0.1] Fumigant | Aluminium phosphide (Celphos) – releases phosphine; used mainly to protect stored grain from insects (and rodents)
  [109:3:0.2] Fungicides | Bordeaux mixture (CuSO4 + lime); copper sulphate (blue vitriol, neela thotha) – kills fungi/algae in water tanks
  [109:3:0.3] Herbicides | 2,4-D (broadleaf weeds), sodium chlorate
  [109:3:0.4] Rodenticide | Zinc phosphide – rat poison
  [109:3:0.5] Broad-spectrum | Chloropicrin – also a tear gas
[109:3:1] # Mosquito repellents
[109:3:2] TABLE head: Substance | Note
  [109:3:2.0] Neem (margosa) | Chief natural mosquito repellent (exam answer)
  [109:3:2.1] Lemongrass / citronella | Natural repellent – citronella oil (UPSC 2021: lemongrass)
  [109:3:2.2] Pyrethrum | Botanical insecticide/repellent from chrysanthemum flowers; acts on insect nerves
  [109:3:2.3] Allethrin | Synthetic pyrethroid – the active chemical in mosquito coils and mats
  [109:3:2.4] Prallethrin | Pyrethroid in liquid vaporisers – a mosquito repellent, not a drug or dye
[109:3:3] - Calcium dihydrogen phosphate is **superphosphate**, a fertiliser – not a mosquito-repellent ingredient.
[109:3:4] > Exam angle: mosquito-repellent pickers (×8), zinc phosphide = rat poison, CuSO4 in water tanks, aluminium phosphide use.
[109:3:5] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Chemistry p.65, p.67; PMF Lens (pmf-lens-2026-02-12) p.3 (Celphos = grain fumigant); PMF Environment Part 7 p.3, p.9 (pyrethrum, neem); app notes 5:109 sub 6
## SUB 4 | Organic Farming – Sikkim, Schemes and Certification
[109:4:0] - **Organic farming** avoids synthetic fertilisers, pesticides, growth regulators and feed additives; relies on crop rotation, residues, manures, legumes, green manure, biofertilisers and biological pest control.
[109:4:1] - Main advantage: **reduced chemical input and improved soil health** – not guaranteed higher yields (yield dip of 2-3 years in transition).
[109:4:2] # Sikkim
[109:4:3] - **Sikkim = India's first fully organic State (January 2016)** and the **world's first 100% organic State**; **FAO Future Policy (Gold) Award 2018**; Lakshadweep = first organic UT.
[109:4:4] - NE States pursuing organic status: **Sikkim, Meghalaya, Nagaland**; **Assam is not one of them**.
[109:4:5] # Schemes and certification
[109:4:6] TABLE head: Scheme / body | Fact
  [109:4:6.0] PKVY (Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana) | 2015; organic farming by cluster approach (50 farmers / 50 acres) + PGS certification; AP's organic initiative among PMFBY/NFSM/RKVY options; portal jaivikkheti.in
  [109:4:6.1] MOVCD-NER | Organic value chains in the North-East (NPOP certification, exports)
  [109:4:6.2] NPOP | Since 2001, under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (not Rural Development); APEDA is the secretariat/implementing agency; third-party certification for exports
  [109:4:6.3] PGS-India | Participatory Guarantee System – locally relevant, producers and consumers participate, outside third-party certification; for the domestic market
  [109:4:6.4] NCOF | National Centre of Organic Farming, Ghaziabad (UP) – PGS secretariat
  [109:4:6.5] Large Area Certification | Under PKVY; Car Nicobar–Nancowry islands certified
[109:4:7] - **Padma Shri 2019** for organic farming: **Venkateswara Rao Yadlapalli** (Andhra Pradesh).
[109:4:8] - Rocket CA 2026: India's first **Basmati organic demo farm** – Tanda Bijaisi village, Pilibhit (UP).
[109:4:9] > Exam angle: Sikkim first organic State (×4), NPOP statements (UPSC 2018: 2 and 3, ×2), PGS definition, PKVY, Assam not organic, NCOF Ghaziabad.
[109:4:10] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.14, p.18-22; PMF Lens pmf-lens-2026-04-10 p.7-8 (NCOF Ghaziabad, PGS secretariat); NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.1; NextGen Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.7; app notes 5:109 sub 7, 11
## SUB 5 | Natural Farming – ZBNF, APCNF and NMNF
[109:5:0] # Zero Budget Natural Farming
[109:5:1] - **ZBNF** was developed by **Subhash Palekar** (Maharashtra; Padma Shri 2016) in the mid-1990s as an alternative to Green Revolution inputs; spread first through **Karnataka** (farmers' movement; general knowledge); in Union Budget 2019-20.
[109:5:2] - **Chemical fertilisers are not used** – on-farm **cow dung, urine, jaggery** preparations replace them; Palekar **opposes vermicompost**.
[109:5:3] TABLE head: Input / practice | Meaning
  [109:5:3.0] Jeevamrutha | Fermented microbial culture from cow dung and urine
  [109:5:3.1] Beejamrutha | Seed treatment
  [109:5:3.2] Achhadana | Mulching
  [109:5:3.3] Whapasa | Soil aeration and moisture
  [109:5:3.4] Agniastra, Brahmastra, Neemastra | Pest-management preparations
[109:5:4] - ZBNF promoted through **farmer collectives / organic clusters** (village clusters, SHGs).
[109:5:5] - **Natural vs organic:** natural farming uses on-farm inputs, avoids ploughing and bulk manures, is near zero-cost and uncertified; organic farming uses approved (often bought) inputs and is certified (PGS/NPOP).
[109:5:6] - **Permaculture:** Bill Mollison and David Holmgren; **Fukuoka**: *One-Straw Revolution* (1975).
[109:5:7] # Andhra Pradesh – APCNF
[109:5:8] - **APCNF = Andhra Pradesh Community-managed Natural Farming** (formerly ZBNF); launched **2016** by **Rythu Sadhikara Samstha (RySS)** under the AP Agriculture Department.
[109:5:9] - **2018 declared AP's Year of Natural Farming.**
[109:5:10] - Reach (Dec 2024): **9.53 lakh farmers on 3.58 lakh ha**; 14% of farmers, 28% of villages; target **41 lakh farmers, 19 lakh ha by 2028-29**; all gram panchayats by 2026-27; technical support to 12 States.
[109:5:11] - Awards: **Gulbenkian Prize for Humanity 2024** (11 July 2024, Lisbon); **Food Planet Prize 2026** (USD 1.5 million, Curt Bergfors Foundation, Sweden).
[109:5:12] - Kurnool study: APCNF farmers about **35% less likely to use pesticides**; Kenyan delegation praised the Guntur model (July 2026); **NTR district** QR-based traceability.
[109:5:13] # National Mission on Natural Farming (NMNF)
[109:5:14] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [109:5:14.0] Approved | 25 Nov 2024; standalone CSS
  [109:5:14.1] Outlay | Rs 2,481 crore (Centre 1,584 + States 897)
  [109:5:14.2] Targets | 7.5 lakh ha, 15,000 clusters, 10,000 Bio-Input Resource Centres, 1 crore farmers
  [109:5:14.3] Field workers | Krishi Sakhis (70,021)
[109:5:15] - **BPKP** (Bharatiya Prakritik Krishi Paddhati, 2020-21): sub-scheme of PKVY for natural farming; natural farming cuts cultivation cost by **20-40%**.
[109:5:16] > Exam angle: Palekar = ZBNF (×5), APCNF full form, AP Year of Natural Farming 2018, Gulbenkian Prize, ZBNF statements (UPSC 2018: only II).
[109:5:17] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 21 p.2; NextGen Indian Economy Part 1 APPSC 02 p.12; PMF Environment Part 7 p.22-25; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.51-53; Praveen CA-360 June 2026 p.9; app notes 5:109 sub 8, 9
## SUB 6 | Integrated Pest Management, Pests and Plant Diseases
[109:6:0] - **IPM (FAO):** use **all suitable techniques** to keep pest populations **below the economic injury level**; aim is to **optimise, not maximise**, control.
[109:6:1] - IPM = **combination of biological, cultural and mechanical methods**, chemicals only when needed (last resort); key element: **cultural control**.
[109:6:2] TABLE head: Component | Examples
  [109:6:2.0] Cultural | Crop rotation, resistant varieties, changed irrigation, trap crops
  [109:6:2.1] Mechanical / physical | Traps, hand collection, mulches
  [109:6:2.2] Biological | Predators, parasites, pathogens (green lacewing → aphids, ladybugs), NPV, pheromone traps
  [109:6:2.3] Chemical | Selective pesticides only when needed
[109:6:3] - **ICAR (2017): pests waste about 30-35% of India's annual crop yield.**
[109:6:4] # Plant diseases and vectors
[109:6:5] - Plant pathogens are spread by **birds, dust, rain and wind** (all four).
[109:6:6] TABLE head: Crop | Disease
  [109:6:6.0] Bajra | Green ear (downy mildew), ergot – "green hair/ear" is not a rice disease
  [109:6:6.1] Pea | Powdery mildew
  [109:6:6.2] Gram | Wilt
  [109:6:6.3] Okra | Yellow vein mosaic – virus spread by whitefly
[109:6:7] > Exam angle: IPM aim (below economic injury level), IPM combination, cultural control, ICAR pest loss 30-35%, crop–disease mismatch.
[109:6:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.13-14; PMF Environment Part 7 p.9; gktoday.in 27 Feb 2017 (ICAR, pests eat 30-35% of crop yield); app notes 5:109 sub 5
## SUB 7 | Biopesticides – Neem, Bt and Microbial Agents
[109:7:0] - **Biopesticides** are biodegradable, low in toxicity and short-lived; a key part of IPM.
[109:7:1] TABLE head: Biopesticide | Source | Target
  [109:7:1.0] Bt | Bacterium *Bacillus thuringiensis* – microbial/biological insecticide | Caterpillars, bollworms
  [109:7:1.1] Neem | Azadirachtin (antifeedant) | Wide range of insects and mites
  [109:7:1.2] NPV | Baculovirus | Helicoverpa, Spodoptera
  [109:7:1.3] Trichoderma | Fungus | Soil-borne wilt, root rot
  [109:7:1.4] Beauveria bassiana | Entomopathogenic fungus | Borers, whitefly
[109:7:2] - **Neem tree (UPSC 1999):** industrial source of **biopesticide and anti-fertility compound**.
[109:7:3] - **Neem statements (UPSC 2014): 1 and 3 only** – neem oil is a pesticide against insects and mites and has pharmaceutical uses; "neem seeds used to make biofuels and hospital detergents" is **not correct** (UPSC official key).
[109:7:4] - Other Bacillus species (B. subtilis, B. polymyxa, B. brevis) are not insecticides.
[109:7:5] > Exam angle: Bt = biological insecticide (×2), neem statements (×2), neem uses.
[109:7:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.14; NextGen Environment APPSC 13 p.1; PMF Environment Part 7 p.9; edukemy.com UPSC Prelims 2014 Q64; app notes 5:109 sub 4
