=== NOTES 5:110 | Precision Agriculture, Drip Irrigation and Other Resource-efficient Technologies
## SUB 0 | Soilless and Protected Cultivation – Hydroponics, Aeroponics, Phytotron
[110:0:0] TABLE head: Technique | Meaning
  [110:0:0.0] Hydroponics | Growing plants without soil, roots in mineral nutrient solution (sand, gravel or water may support them); still needs water, light, nutrients; ~90% less water
  [110:0:0.1] Aeroponics | Roots suspended in air and misted – no soil medium
  [110:0:0.2] Aquaponics | Fish culture + hydroponics; fish waste feeds plants
  [110:0:0.3] Vertical farming | Stacked indoor layers, year-round output where land is scarce
  [110:0:0.4] Greenhouse / polyhouse | Controlled microclimate; protection from weather, pests and diseases
  [110:0:0.5] Phytotron | Enclosed research greenhouse to grow plants under controlled conditions
[110:0:1] - **Aeroponics limits disease transmission** (less plant-to-plant contact, oxygen-rich roots) – so "disease transmission is its major disadvantage" is **incorrect**; aeroponic plants have **high dry-weight biomass** and need less nutrient input than hydroponics.
[110:0:2] - "Hydrophonics" in old papers = hydroponics, i.e. growth **without soil**, not without water.
[110:0:3] > Exam angle: hydroponics definition (×5), aeroponics INCORRECT statement, phytotron.
[110:0:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.28-30; Shankar Environment Part 20 (ocr) p.1 (aeroponics, hydroponics); app notes 5:110 sub 4
## SUB 1 | Micro-irrigation and Fertigation
[110:1:0] - **Localised (micro) irrigation:** water piped under low pressure and given in small discharges at each plant – **drip, micro-sprinkler, bubbler**; **conserves water** and **reduces water consumption** (vs flood, canal or open-field watering).
[110:1:1] TABLE head: Method | Efficiency | How water is applied
  [110:1:1.0] Drip | ~90% (highest) | To the root zone through emitters
  [110:1:1.1] Sprinkler | 70-80% | Through nozzles like rain; loses more to wind and evaporation
  [110:1:1.2] Flood / furrow | 30-50% | Surface methods
[110:1:2] - **Drip irrigation** = the technology that reduces farming's environmental impact in **water-scarce regions** (APPSC G2); drip limit = **higher initial cost**; Evergreen Revolution ("more output at lower ecological cost") – **M.S. Swaminathan**.
[110:1:3] # Fertigation
[110:1:4] - **Fertigation = applying fertiliser through irrigation water** (through the drip line); not chemigation (pesticides) or "microgation".
[110:1:5] - Advantages (**UPSC 2020: I, III and IV**): **controls alkalinity** of irrigation water, **more nutrients available**, **less leaching**. Efficient application of **rock phosphate** is **not** possible (it is insoluble).
[110:1:6] > Exam angle: micro-irrigation conserves water (×2), fertigation definition and advantages.
[110:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 20 p.11 (localised irrigation); PMF Environment Part 7 p.25-26 (fertigation in precision farming); Shankar Environment Part 2 (ocr) p.1 (UPSC 2020 fertigation PYQ); app notes 5:110 sub 0
## SUB 2 | Resource-conserving Technologies and Crop Practices
[110:2:0] TABLE head: Technology | Benefit
  [110:2:0.0] Zero tillage | New crop sown into previous residue; soil carbon sequestration, more earthworms, less runoff
  [110:2:0.1] Zero/reduced tillage + crop residue on field | Conserves water (UPSC 2017: 1 and 3); gypsum before irrigation does not
  [110:2:0.2] Contour bunding | Soil conservation on slopes
  [110:2:0.3] Relay cropping | Next crop sown before the standing crop is harvested
  [110:2:0.4] Laser land levelling | Uniform field; saves 20-25% irrigation water
  [110:2:0.5] SRI (alternate wetting and drying) | Less seed, water and methane
  [110:2:0.6] Direct-seeded rice | No nursery or transplanting; promoted with zero-till wheat (NICRA)
  [110:2:0.7] Sustainable Sugarcane Initiative | Single-bud chips / bud-chip settlings – very low seed cost, drip works well, more scope for intercropping; chemical fertilisers are still used (UPSC 2014: 1, 2 and 4)
[110:2:1] - **Carbon sequestration (UPSC 2012):** of contour bunding, relay cropping and zero tillage, **only zero tillage** (most keys).
[110:2:2] - **Sugarcane (UPSC 2020: 1 and 4):** **bud-chip settlings** raised in a nursery save seed material; **tissue-culture settlings** can be used. Single-budded setts germinate worse and survive worse than multi-bud setts in bad weather.
[110:2:3] - **Onion** is grown by **transplanting** nursery seedlings (maize, sorghum, soyabean are sown directly).
[110:2:4] - **Bio-drainage:** fast-transpiring trees such as **Eucalyptus** pump out excess water from waterlogged land.
[110:2:5] > Exam angle: UPSC statement questions on zero tillage, water conservation, sugarcane; onion transplanting; bio-drainage plant.
[110:2:6] ~~ Sources: Shankar Environment Part 20 (ocr) p.1 (zero tillage, relay cropping); Shankar Environment Part 2 (ocr) p.1 (UPSC 2012, 2017, 2020 PYQs); PMF Environment Part 7 p.6 (laser levelling); app notes 5:110 sub 3
## SUB 3 | Irrigation Schemes – PMKSY, Per Drop More Crop and APMIP
[110:3:0] - **PMKSY** (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana): launched **1 July 2015 (2015-16)**; motto **"Har Khet Ko Pani"** + **"Per Drop More Crop"**; aims to **enhance physical access of water on farm**, **expand assured irrigation**, **reduce wastage and raise water-use efficiency**, and achieve **convergence of investment in irrigation at field level**; creates protected irrigation by **harnessing rainwater at micro level** (watershed component).
[110:3:1] TABLE head: Component | Fact
  [110:3:1.0] AIBP, Har Khet Ko Pani | Ministry of Jal Shakti (DoWR)
  [110:3:1.1] Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) | Agriculture Ministry; drip and sprinkler; under PMKSY 2015-16 to 2021-22, under RKVY from 2022-23
  [110:3:1.2] Watershed Development (WDC-PMKSY 2.0) | Department of Land Resources (Rural Development)
  [110:3:1.3] Micro Irrigation Fund | Rs 10,000 crore corpus with NABARD; operational 2019-20
[110:3:2] - PDMC: **102 lakh ha** under micro-irrigation (2015-16 to 2025-26); priority to rainfed, water-stressed and critical groundwater blocks; NMSA subsidy up to 55%, capped at 5 ha.
[110:3:3] - Gross irrigated area **41.7% (2001-02) → 55.8%** of GCA (2022-23); Soil Health Cards issued: **25.55 crore** (Nov 2025).
[110:3:4] # Andhra Pradesh Micro Irrigation Project (APMIP)
[110:3:5] - AP Micro Irrigation programme introduced **2003**; APMIP now implemented State-wide under **PMKSY**; **AP ranked 1st** in micro-irrigation (2024-25), led by **Ananthapuramu**.
[110:3:6] TABLE head: Farmer category (drip) | Subsidy
  [110:3:6.0] SC/ST small and marginal | 100%
  [110:3:6.1] Other small and marginal | 90%
  [110:3:6.2] 5-10 acres | 70%
  [110:3:6.3] Above 10 acres | 50%
[110:3:7] - **7 Jan 2026**: automation-based micro-irrigation at **Governorpet, Vijayawada** – Minister **K. Atchannaidu**; APSES 2024-25 focus: precision farming, drones, IoT.
[110:3:8] > Exam angle: PMKSY launch and aims (×3).
[110:3:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.46; Praveen CA-360 July 2026 magazine p.37; NextGen AP Economy Static-1 Part 1 p.15; app notes 5:110 sub 1, 2
## SUB 4 | Precision Agriculture, Remote Sensing and Crop Monitoring
[110:4:0] - **Precision farming:** data-driven use of **GIS, GPS, remote sensing**, sensors and drones to apply water, fertiliser and pesticide where and when needed; tools include fertigation, greenhouse, mulching, micropropagation, high-density planting, drip.
[110:4:1] TABLE head: Tool | Use
  [110:4:1.0] Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (2012, Agriculture Ministry) | Institutionalises ISRO's crop forecasting (FASAL) and drought/disaster methodology
  [110:4:1.1] KISAN project (Oct 2015) | Space tech for crop-cutting experiments under PMFBY
  [110:4:1.2] GIS | Soil and Land Use Survey of India maps soils
  [110:4:1.3] Variable-rate technology | Inputs at varying rates within a field by sensor/GIS maps
  [110:4:1.4] GPS, drones, AI, sensors | Second Green Revolution / sustainable intensification
[110:4:2] - **Crop logging** = **plant (tissue) analysis** to assess the crop's nutrient requirement during growth (developed for sugarcane), not soil testing.
[110:4:3] > Exam angle: MNCFC (ISRO methodology), crop logging definition.
[110:4:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.25-27; app notes 5:110 sub 5
## SUB 5 | Drones, Digital Agriculture Mission, Solar Pumps and AI
[110:5:0] - **Kisan drones**: crop assessment, soil-health analysis, spraying; regulated by **DGCA** under the **Drone Rules, 2021**; spraying SOPs released by **Narendra Singh Tomar** (21 Dec 2021).
[110:5:1] - **Drone Shakti**: manufacturing and **Remote Pilot Certificate** training.
[110:5:2] - **Namo Drone Didi**: drones to **women SHGs**, target **15,000**, outlay **Rs 1,261 crore**, **80%** central assistance (max Rs 8 lakh).
[110:5:3] - **Drone Corporation of AP**: State-owned, **drone-as-a-service**; spraying in all 26 districts (Jan 2026).
[110:5:4] TABLE head: Digital Agriculture Mission | Fact
  [110:5:4.0] Approved | September 2024
  [110:5:4.1] Outlay | Rs 2,817 crore
  [110:5:4.2] DPI | AgriStack (Aadhaar-like, federated Centre-State), Krishi DSS (satellite, weather, soil, crop data), Soil Fertility Profile
[110:5:5] - **Digital crop survey**: plot-level, real-time crop acreage; AP **e-Crop (e-Panta)** through **Rythu Bharosa Kendras**; Karnataka **FRUITS** (2020).
[110:5:6] - **PM-KUSUM** (MNRE, 2019): A = solar plants on barren/fallow land; **B = standalone solar pumps**; **C = solarising grid-connected pumps**.

=== NOTES 5:112 | Regulation and Ethics of Biotechnology – Geac, Biosafety, Bioethics, Biopiracy, Ipr
## SUB 0 | GM Crops in India – Approvals, Bt Brinjal and GM Mustard
[112:0:0] TABLE head: GM crop | Trait | Gene / developer | Status
  [112:0:0.0] Bt cotton | Insect (bollworm) resistance | Cry1Ac (+Cry2Ab) from *B. thuringiensis*; Monsanto-Mahyco | Approved 2002 – the only GM crop commercially cultivated
  [112:0:0.1] Bt brinjal | Insect (pest) resistance – fruit and shoot borer | Cry1Ac; Mahyco + UAS Dharwad + TNAU | GEAC recommended 2009; moratorium 2010 (Jairam Ramesh)
  [112:0:0.2] GM mustard DMH-11 | Hybrid seed, higher yield; herbicide (glufosinate) tolerance via bar gene | Barnase-barstar from *Bacillus amyloliquefaciens*; Delhi University CGMCP, Deepak Pental | GEAC: 2017 recommendation, environmental release Oct 2022; SC split verdict July 2024
[112:0:1] - **Bt brinjal is a genetically modified brinjal** – developed for **insect/pest resistance**, not taste, drought, shelf-life, bacterial or fungal resistance.
[112:0:2] - **DMH-11 = Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11**, a GM hybrid of **mustard** (cross of Varuna × Early Heera-2), the transgenic crop **approved by GEAC and developed by Delhi University**.
[112:0:3] - **GM mustard statements (UPSC 2018):** pest-resistance gene ✗ (that is Bt); **genes allowing cross-pollination and hybridisation ✓**; developed by IARI + PAU ✗ (Delhi University) → **"2 (B) only"**.
[112:0:4] - **Monsanto's insect-resistant cotton (field trials 2001)** carries the toxin gene of ***Bacillus thuringiensis***.
[112:0:5] # Timeline
[112:0:6] TABLE head: Year | Event
  [112:0:6.0] 2002 | Bt cotton approved (March)
  [112:0:6.1] 2006 | PIL against GM crops in the Supreme Court
  [112:0:6.2] 2010 | Bt brinjal moratorium; State NOC mandatory for field trials
  [112:0:6.3] 2013 | SC-appointed Technical Expert Committee: 10-year moratorium on field trials
  [112:0:6.4] 2014 | GEAC clears trials of many crops
  [112:0:6.5] 2022 | DMH-11 environmental release
  [112:0:6.6] July 2024 | SC split verdict on DMH-11; Centre directed to frame a national GM crop policy
[112:0:7] - **Defiance:** farmers in **Maharashtra and Haryana** openly grew **unapproved Bt (HT) cotton and Bt brinjal** to protest regulatory delays.
[112:0:8] - Approval in India takes **7-10 years** vs **3-5 years** globally; overlapping DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI, NBA.
[112:0:9] > Exam angle: Bt cotton only GM crop (2002), Bt brinjal = pest resistance (×4), DMH-11 mustard (×3), Maharashtra-Haryana defiance.
[112:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.11-12 (Bt cotton only GM crop, Bt brinjal 2007/2010, DMH-11 Delhi University, timeline); NextGen Rocket Biology p.18 (Mahyco Bt brinjal; DMH-11 Deepak Pental); PMF S&T Part 3 p.14-18 (DMH-11 genes, 2022 approval, UPSC 2018, Bt brinjal Cry1Ac, UPSC 2011); PMF Environment Part 7 p.32, p.34 (Maharashtra farmers' protest planting); app notes 5:112 sub 2-3
## SUB 1 | GEAC and the Rules, 1989
[112:1:0] # GEAC – Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee
[112:1:1] TABLE head: Particular | Fact
  [112:1:1.0] Status | Apex statutory body that regulates GMOs and clears field trials, environmental release and commercial cultivation of GM crops
  [112:1:1.1] Law | Rules, 1989 (Hazardous Micro-organisms / Genetically Engineered Organisms) framed under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
  [112:1:1.2] Ministry | MoEFCC (Environment and Forests) – not Agriculture, Commerce or Rural Development
  [112:1:1.3] Chair | Special / Additional Secretary, MoEFCC; co-chair from the Department of Biotechnology
  [112:1:1.4] Name | Genetic Engineering "Approval" Committee renamed "Appraisal" Committee in July 2010
[112:1:2] - **GEAC (not NGT, DBT, ICAR, FSSAI or CPCB) gives clearance for testing, trials and cultivation of GM crops**; its permission is needed for any GM crop such as Bt cotton.
[112:1:3] - Functions also include approving **large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants**; fixing seed MRP is not its job.
[112:1:4] - **FSSAI** approves GM **food**; **ICAR** only does research and field trials – neither regulates GM cultivation.
[112:1:5] - Penalty for an unapproved GM variant: up to **5 years' jail and Rs 1 lakh fine** under the EPA.
[112:1:6] # Competent authorities under the Rules, 1989
[112:1:7] TABLE head: Committee | Level | Role
  [112:1:7.0] RDAC | DBT | Recombinant DNA Advisory Committee – policy
  [112:1:7.1] IBSC | Each institution (first tier) | Lab-level biosafety
  [112:1:7.2] RCGM | DBT | Monitors ongoing GM research, small trials; advises GEAC (does not approve release)
  [112:1:7.3] GEAC | MoEFCC | Large-scale trials, environmental release, commercial use
  [112:1:7.4] SBCC | State (Chief Secretary) | Inspect, investigate, punitive action
  [112:1:7.5] DLC | District (Collector) | Field-level monitoring
[112:1:8] - Approval chain: **IBSC → RCGM → GEAC → SBCC/DLC**; FSSAI is **not** one of the six competent authorities.
[112:1:9] - Field trials = **Biosafety Research Level (BRL-I, BRL-II)** trials; since **2010** a **State NOC** is mandatory for field trials.
[112:1:10] TABLE head: Related body | Law
  [112:1:10.0] NGT | NGT Act, 2010
  [112:1:10.1] CGWA | Section 3(3) of the EPA, 1986
  [112:1:10.2] CPCB | Water Act, 1974
[112:1:11] - **Eco-Sensitive Zones:** activities **regulated, not necessarily prohibited**.

## SUB 2 | IPR, Biopiracy and Farmers' Rights
[112:2:0] TABLE head: IPR | Protects
  [112:2:0.0] Patent | Inventions – a form of intellectual property
  [112:2:0.1] Copyright | Literary, artistic, musical works and cinematograph films (Berne Convention, 1886)
  [112:2:0.2] Trademark / GI | Brands / origin-linked goods
[112:2:1] - **Intellectual property** = creations of the human mind with commercial value.
[112:2:2] TABLE head: Provision / case | Point
  [112:2:2.0] Patents Act Sec 3(j) | Plants, animals, seeds, essentially biological processes not patentable; microbial processes are
  [112:2:2.1] Sec 3(d) | New form of a known substance needs enhanced efficacy – blocks evergreening; Novartis (2013): Glivec (imatinib) rejection upheld under 3(d)
  [112:2:2.2] PPV&FR Act, 2001 | Farmers may save, use, sow, exchange, share and sell seed – not branded seed of protected varieties; bars GURT varieties
  [112:2:2.3] PepsiCo FL-2027 (FC5) potato | Sued Gujarat farmers (2019), withdrew
[112:2:3] # Biopiracy
[112:2:4] - **Biopiracy:** commercial exploitation of native biological resources/traditional knowledge without fair compensation.
[112:2:5] TABLE head: Case | Outcome
  [112:2:5.0] Turmeric (wound healing, US patent) | Revoked after CSIR challenge
  [112:2:5.1] Neem (anti-fungal) | India won at the European Patent Office
  [112:2:5.2] Basmati (RiceTec, 1997) | CSIR challenge; key claims disallowed
  [112:2:5.3] Hoodia (appetite suppressant) | Benefit-sharing with the San (2003)
[112:2:6] - **TKDL (2001):** by **CSIR and the Ministry of AYUSH**; gives patent offices **prior-art** evidence.
[112:2:7] - Objection to GURT seeds: **loss of seed-saving**, dependence on companies.
[112:2:8] > Exam angle: Berne = copyright; films = copyright; patent = IP (flashcards ×4).
[112:2:9] ~~ Sources: PMF Environment Part 7 p.34 (biopiracy definition); OnlyIAS NCERT S&T Part 12 p.22 (patents on Basmati, biopiracy); app notes 5:112 sub 8-9; Berne Convention and copyright – general knowledge, not checked
## SUB 3 | The GM Debate – Biodiversity, Health and GM Food Law
[112:3:0] - **Reasons for resistance to Bt brinjal (UPSC 2012):** "gene from a soil **fungus**" ✗ (it is a **bacterium**); "terminator seeds" ✗ (Bt brinjal is not GURT); **health apprehension ✓; biodiversity concern ✓** → **3 and 4 only**.
[112:3:1] - **Genetic modification** is the technology flagged for **biodiversity** concerns – not solar panels, wind turbines or rainwater harvesting.
[112:3:2] TABLE head: Risk type | Examples
  [112:3:2.0] Environment | Gene flow, insect resistance, harm to non-target organisms, weediness, genetic homogenisation
  [112:3:2.1] Health | Toxicity, allergenicity, antibiotic resistance
  [112:3:2.2] Not a GM risk | Ozone depletion
  [112:3:2.3] Socio-economic | Seed monopoly, biopiracy, corporate control
[112:3:3] # GM food – import and labelling
[112:3:4] - **No GM food may be manufactured, imported or sold without approval of the competent authority (FSSAI)** – Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006; FSS (GM Foods) Regulations 2022.
[112:3:5] - From **1 March 2021**, imported major food crops need a **"non-GM cum GM-free" certificate**; draft labelling for foods with **1% or more** GM ingredient.
[112:3:6] - **India does import US apples** – after the **June 2023** WTO settlement India removed the extra duties on US apples, walnuts and almonds (UPSC 2024: Statement I wrong, II right).
[112:3:7] # Proposed regulators
[112:3:8] - **BRAI Bill, 2013:** a single biotech regulator; **lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha**.
[112:3:9] - **BioE3 Policy, 2024:** single-window clearance, regulatory sandboxes.
[112:3:10] > Exam angle: Bt brinjal resistance statements, genetic modification and biodiversity, GM food import law.
[112:3:11] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 3 p.17-18 (UPSC 2012 Bt brinjal reasons), p.9 (FSSAI GM food approval and imports); PMF Environment Part 7 p.33-34 (issues, biopiracy, FSSAI 1% labelling); NextGen Environment APPSC 12 p.9-10 (health and environment risks); app notes 5:112 sub 4, 6-7
## SUB 4 | Biosafety, Cartagena Protocol and Bioethics
[112:4:0] - **Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety** (to the **CBD**): transboundary movement of **living modified organisms (LMOs)**; adopted **January 2000 in Montreal**, in force **2003**; named after **Cartagena, Colombia**; India a party.
[112:4:1] - Global GM area: **USA** first, then Brazil, Argentina, Canada, **India 5th**.
[112:4:2] TABLE head: Biosafety level | Agents
  [112:4:2.0] BSL-3 | Serious airborne agents (e.g. TB)
  [112:4:2.1] BSL-4 | Lethal, no cure (e.g. Ebola)
[112:4:3] - **BWC** opened 1972, in force **1975**; India's **WMD Act, 2005** criminalises biological weapons; gap = **no unified national biosecurity framework**.
[112:4:4] # Bioethics
[112:4:5] - **Nuremberg Code (1947):** ethical principles for human experimentation from the **International Military Tribunal** trials of Nazi war criminals – not Hamburg, Leipzig or Stuttgart codes; basis of **informed consent**.
[112:4:6] - **National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** – **ICMR and DBT**.
[112:4:7] - **He Jiankui** (China, **2018**) – "CRISPR babies"; **"designer babies"** = selecting or modifying desired traits in offspring.
[112:4:8] > Exam angle: Cartagena in Colombia; Nuremberg Code.
[112:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Environment p.7-8, p.29 (Cartagena Protocol 2000, biosafety/LMOs, under CBD); OnlyIAS NCERT Post-independence World History Part 24 p.1-2 (International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg); app notes 5:111 sub 8, 5:112 sub 10
## SUB 5 | Regulating Genome-edited Crops
[112:5:0] - **SDN-1 and SDN-2** (no foreign DNA) were **exempted from the GMO rules in 2022**; they need only **IBSC (IBC) approval**, without the GEAC route; **SDN-3** (transgenic) stays under full GM control.
[112:5:1] - **Pusa Rice DST1:** drought + salinity tolerance; **DST gene knockout by SDN-1**; regulated **like a conventional crop**.
[112:5:2] - Contrast: Bt cotton (Bollgard II, 2006) – no major new GM cotton trait approved since ("Bt technology fatigue").
[112:5:3] > Own-MCQ area (no PYQ yet).
[112:5:4] ~~ Sources: PMF Lens Sep 2026 Part 2 p.65 (Bt fatigue), p.72-73 (Pusa Rice DST1 SDN-1, DST gene); app notes 5:112 sub 5

=== NOTES 5:113 | Nanotechnology – Nature, Scope, Applications, Nano Mission, Health and Environmental Concerns
## SUB 0 | Graphene, Fullerene and Carbon Nanotubes
[113:0:0] # Carbon nanomaterials (all sp², all pure carbon)
[113:0:1] TABLE head: Material | Structure | Remember
  [113:0:1.0] Graphene | Single atom-thick layer of graphite; 2D hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice | Made of carbon only – NOT silicon; thinnest and strongest material (~200 times steel; stronger than steel, brass, German silver); excellent electrical and heat conductor; ~97% transparent; flexible
  [113:0:1.1] Fullerene C60 | Hollow cage ("buckyball", soccer ball): 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons, 60 C atoms | Carbon allotrope – NOT a fluorine compound (Teflon is the fluorine polymer); semiconductor; drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts
  [113:0:1.2] Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) | Rolled graphene cylinders (1D tubes) | Stronger than steel by weight, light; metallic or semiconducting; drug delivery, biosensors, batteries
[113:0:2] - **Graphene uses:** **conducting electrodes for touch screens, LCDs and OLEDs**, fast transistors, flexible circuits, sensors, batteries and supercapacitors.
[113:0:3] - **Discoverers:** graphene isolated **2004** by **Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov** (Manchester) – **Nobel Physics 2010**; fullerene C60 found **1985** by **Kroto (Britain), Curl and Smalley (USA)** – **Nobel Chemistry 1996** (no "Faimen" on the team); named after architect **R. Buckminster Fuller**; **CNTs** – **Sumio Iijima (1991)**.
[113:0:4] - **Pairs angle (UPPCS):** Dry ice – solid CO2; Teflon – fluorine polymer; Sevin – insecticide; Keratin – protein; Mustard gas – chemical weapon; **Fullerene – carbon allotrope** (the wrongly matched pair).
[113:0:5] # UPSC 2012 – graphene statements
[113:0:6] - 1 (2D, good conductor) ✔, 2 (thinnest but strongest) ✔, 3 (**entirely silicon**) ✘, 4 (conducting electrodes for touch screens, LCDs, OLEDs) ✔ → **1, 2 and 4**.
[113:0:7] # UPSC 2020 – carbon nanotubes statements
[113:0:8] - 1 drug and antigen carriers ✔; 3 biochemical sensors ✔ (CNT biosensors); 2 artificial blood capillaries and 4 biodegradable are the contested ones.
[113:0:9] - **UPSC official key: (c) 1, 3 and 4** – CNTs can be degraded by some bacteria, fungi and enzymes; capillaries rejected (CNTs trigger platelet activation and clotting).
[113:0:10] - ⚠ Books differ: PMF answers (a) 1 and 2 (CNTs "not biodegradable"); many coaching keys gave (d) all four. Learn the official (c).
[113:0:11] > Exam angle: graphene = carbon, not silicon; fullerene = carbon, not fluorine; Iijima = nanotubes, Geim-Novoselov = graphene.
[113:0:12] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.700-702 (CNTs, graphene, UPSC 2012 and 2020); Rocket Chemistry p.23-25 (allotropes, structure, uses); upscsociology.in Prelims 2020 solution (official key c); vajiramandravi.com CNT solution; app notes 5:113 sub 1-2
## SUB 1 | Diamond, Graphite and Other Forms of Carbon
[113:1:0] TABLE head: Allotrope | Bonding | Key property → use
  [113:1:0.0] Diamond | sp³; 3D tetrahedral network, each C bonded to four | Hardest natural substance (Mohs 10); least compressible; electrical insulator (no free electrons) but excellent heat conductor; transparent, high refractive index → cutting tools, jewellery
  [113:1:0.1] Graphite | sp² layers held by weak van der Waals forces | Soft, slippery, opaque, black; good electrical conductor → pencil "lead" (graphite + clay), dry lubricant for heavy machines, electrodes, reactor moderator
  [113:1:0.2] Amorphous carbon | Non-crystalline | Coal, charcoal, coke, lampblack; charcoal = the amorphous form among diamond/graphite/fullerene; activated charcoal – high surface area
[113:1:1] - **Diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerene, CNTs are all pure carbon** – so diamond is an allotrope of **carbon**; **methane (CH4) is a compound, NOT an allotrope**.
[113:1:2] - **Sand** (silica, SiO2) has **no carbon**; graphite, diamond and coal do.
[113:1:3] - **Lubricant:** **graphite** – not wood, steel, tungsten, bauxite, phosphorus, cuprite, haematite or cryolite.
[113:1:4] - **Hardest:** diamond (not glass, quartz, platinum). **Wurtzite boron nitride** is believed (by simulation) to be ~18% harder, but it is rare and untested – keys keep **diamond** as the hardest naturally occurring substance.
[113:1:5] - **Electrical conductor:** **graphite** (free electrons in layers) – diamond, peat and charcoal are poor conductors.
[113:1:6] ~~ Sources: Rocket Chemistry p.23-25 (allotrope → type, structure, property, use); app notes 5:113 sub 2
## SUB 2 | Nanoscale – Size, Units and Properties
[113:2:0] - **1 nm = 10^-9 m** (one billionth of a metre); **1 Å = 10^-10 m**, so **1 nm = 10 Å**.
[113:2:1] - **Nanoparticle size: 1-100 nm** (APPSC 2018, APPSC G2 2019, UKPSC 2012) – not 0.1-1 nm (atomic scale) or 100-1000 nm; a particle with at least one dimension **below 10^-7 m (100 nm)** is a **nanoparticle**.
[113:2:2] - **Scale:** human hair ~80,000-100,000 nm; red blood cell ~7,000 nm; virus ~50-100 nm; DNA width ~2 nm.
[113:2:3] - **Why different:** very high **surface-area-to-volume ratio** (more reactive, catalytic) + **quantum size effect** (discrete energy levels); also superparamagnetism, lower melting point, self-assembly.
[113:2:4] - **Most important property of nanomaterials (RAS 2013 key): friction** – the huge surface-to-volume ratio makes friction and wear dominant at the nanoscale.
[113:2:5] - **Device miniaturisation** = **nanotechnology**, the 21st-century technology (UPPCS 2004).
[113:2:6] - **Nanogold:** gold nanoparticles show **surface plasmon resonance** – look **red, purple (or blue)** instead of yellow, yet stay gold (biocompatible; used in conductive inks and lateral-flow test kits). APPSC key: "**blue gold with properties similar to gold**".
[113:2:7] # Quantum structures
[113:2:8] TABLE head: Structure | Nano-confined dimensions | Example
  [113:2:8.0] Quantum well | One dimension nano, two large (2D) | thin films
  [113:2:8.1] Quantum wire | Two dimensions nano (1D) | nanowires, nanotubes
  [113:2:8.2] Quantum dot | All three nano (0D) | semiconductor nanostructure, about 2-10 nm (TSLPRB: ~10 nm)
[113:2:9] - **Quantum dots:** size-tuned colour – **smaller dots → blue**, larger → red; QLED displays, bio-imaging, solar cells; **Nobel Chemistry 2023 – Bawendi, Brus, Ekimov**.
[113:2:10] - **Other nanomaterials:** **nanoporous materials – separation and catalysis**; nanofibres – filtration, smart clothing, scaffolds; nanocrystals – LEDs, imaging.
[113:2:11] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.687-692, p.703 (scale, properties, SPR, dimensions, quantum dots, gold nanoparticles); app notes 5:113 sub 0, 2; testbook / byjus (RAS 2013 friction key)
## SUB 3 | Piezoelectric Nanogenerators and Nano Devices
[113:3:0] - **Piezoelectric effect:** electric charge from **mechanical stress (pressure)** in crystals, ceramics, polymers; reversible (field → deformation).
[113:3:1] - **NCL Pune nanogenerator:** electricity when **pressure** is applied → **piezoelectric effect** (APPSC G1 2018, 2019) – NOT photoelectric, photovoltaic, thermoelectric, magnetoelectric or induction.
[113:3:2] - **Quartz crystal in watches** and **gas-stove (electronic) lighters** = **piezoelectric effect** (IAS 1993; APPSC).
[113:3:3] - **Light nanogenerator (contrast):** **IASST Guwahati** (DST) – graphene oxide + polyaniline device that harvests **light** energy to power wearables.
[113:3:4] - **Nanoear (2012, LMU Munich):** an **optically trapped gold nanoparticle** – detects sound down to **–60 dB** (not –120 dB; not silica or silver).
[113:3:5] - **Internet of Nano Things (IoNT):** network of nanodevices connected to the internet.
[113:3:6] - **Other devices:** gold-nanoparticle lateral-flow kits (malaria, dengue, typhoid in ~15 min); **graphene bendable wearable sensors (IISc + C-DAC)**.
[113:3:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen S&T Group 2 Part 1 p.30 (IASST nanogenerator), p.38 (IoNT); PMF S&T Part 7 p.754-755 (piezoelectric materials); app notes 5:113 sub 5; general knowledge (nanoear, gas lighter)

  [113:4:0.1] 1974 | Norio Taniguchi (Tokyo University) | Coined the term "nanotechnology"
  [113:4:0.2] 1981 | Binnig and Rohrer | STM; Nobel Physics 1986

  [113:4:0.4] 1986 | Eric Drexler | "Engines of Creation" – popularised molecular nanotechnology
  [113:4:0.5] 1991 | Sumio Iijima | Carbon nanotubes
  [113:4:0.6] 2004 / 2010 | Geim and Novoselov | Graphene; Nobel Physics 2010
  [113:4:0.7] 2023 | Bawendi, Brus, Ekimov | Quantum dots; Nobel Chemistry 2023
[113:4:1] - **Father of Indian nanotechnology: C.N.R. Rao** – solid-state and nanomaterials chemist, chaired the Nano Mission Council; Bharat Ratna 2014.
[113:4:2] - **M.C. Roco** gave the four-generation classification of nanoproducts.

## SUB 5 | Indian Nano Applications and Facilities
[113:5:0] TABLE head: Institute | Development
  [113:5:0.0] IIT Delhi | Nasofilters – nanofibre nasal filters against dust and air pollutants
  [113:5:0.1] IIT Mandi | Smart, biodegradable, natural-polymer (chitosan) nanoparticles from renewable resources for colorectal cancer (Aug 2022; APPSC G1 2024)
  [113:5:0.2] ICAR-CIRCOT, Mumbai | India's first nano-cellulose plant – uses cotton linters and cotton waste
  [113:5:0.3] IIT Roorkee | Uttarakhand's first nano-fabrication facility – complements Semiconductor, Nano and Quantum missions – NOT Samudrayaan (deep-ocean mission)
  [113:5:0.4] Indian scientists (2002) | Electronic diode from CdS nanoparticles made by yeast (*Schizosaccharomyces pombe*)
  [113:5:0.5] CSIR-CGCRI | Silver-nanoparticle wound dressings (cut infections ~60%)
  [113:5:0.6] INST Mohali | Nano-formulations for Parkinson's; nano-cups for heat-based cancer therapy
  [113:5:0.7] IIT Bombay | Perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell, 27.3% efficiency
[113:5:1] - **Medicine:** targeted drug delivery (CNTs, **liposomes**, dendrimers), gene therapy, imaging (MRI contrast – iron oxide), antimicrobial **silver** nanoparticles.
[113:5:2] - **Environment and materials:** **nano-zero-valent iron** removes water contaminants; **nano-cellulose** – light, strong, biodegradable packaging and filters; **silicon nano-fabrication** – chips (ITO – displays, selenium – sensors).
[113:5:3] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.695-699 (applications); outlookindia.com 30 Aug 2022 (IIT Mandi); Rocket Chemistry p.26, p.69 (nano-fabrication Si, ITO, selenium); app notes 5:113 sub 6-7; general knowledge (Nasofilters, yeast diode)
## SUB 6 | Generations of Nanoproducts and Synthesis Tools
[113:6:0] TABLE head: Generation (M.C. Roco) | Nature | Examples
  [113:6:0.0] I | Passive nanostructures | Aerosols, colloids, polymers, ceramics, coatings
  [113:6:0.1] II | Active nanostructures | Targeted drugs, sensors, 3-D transistors, amplifiers
  [113:6:0.2] III | Systems of nanosystems | Robotics, 3-D networking, nanoelectronics
  [113:6:0.3] IV | Molecular nanosystems | Molecular manufacturing (molecular devices)
[113:6:1] - **Order (RAS 2016):** Aerosol → Targeted drugs → 3D networking → Molecular manufacturing (**A, D, B, C**). Third generation example = **robotics** (APPSC G2 2011).
[113:6:2] TABLE head: Tool / route | Fact
  [113:6:2.0] STM (1981) | Images atoms on conducting surfaces only
  [113:6:2.1] AFM (1986) | Works on non-conductors too
  [113:6:2.2] Top-down | Cut bulk down – lithography, milling, etching
  [113:6:2.3] Bottom-up | Build atom by atom – self-assembly, CVD, sol-gel
[113:6:3] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.695 (top-down, bottom-up); app notes 5:113 sub 3-4
## SUB 7 | Nanoparticles in Nature, Health and Environmental Concerns
[113:7:0] TABLE head: Origin | Examples
  [113:7:0.0] Natural | Volcanic ash, sea spray, clay, natural colloids (proteins, viruses)
  [113:7:0.1] Incidental | Soot, diesel exhaust, welding fumes
  [113:7:0.2] Engineered | Quantum dots, CNTs, nano-silver, TiO2
[113:7:1] - **Cosmetics:** **TiO2 and ZnO** nanoparticles in **sunscreens** (UV protection).
[113:7:2] - **UPSC 2022:** "nanoparticles do not exist in nature" ✘; metallic-oxide nanoparticles in cosmetics ✔; nanoparticles from commercial products entering the environment unsafe ✔ → **B and C**.
[113:7:3] - **Nanotoxicity:** enter by inhalation, ingestion, skin; cross the blood-brain barrier; **free radicals (ROS) → oxidative stress, inflammation**; persistence, **bioaccumulation**, food-chain entry (UPSC 2014: all three concerns correct).
[113:7:4] - **Regulation:** **no dedicated nano law**; DGFASLI (occupational), **FSSAI 2022**, **SCOMET** list (dual-use); **Guidelines for Evaluation of Nano-based Agri-input and Food Products (2020)** – **DBT, Agriculture Ministry, FSSAI**. Also cost and the "**nano-divide**".
[113:7:5] ~~ Sources: PMF S&T Part 7 p.694-695 (origin, UPSC 2022), p.704-707 (TiO2, ZnO, issues, UPSC 2014); app notes 5:113 sub 10

  [113:8:0.1] Nano DAP | Notified under the FCO on 2 March 2023; seed treatment and foliar use

[113:8:2] - Nano urea **does not fully replace** conventional urea; criticised for **rapid rollout without long-term studies** (nanotoxicity, environmental safety).

=== NOTES 5:114 | Health and Environment – Vector-borne and Water-borne Diseases, Air Pollution, Amr, One Health
## SUB 0 | Mosquito-borne Diseases – Vectors and Pathogens
[114:0:0] # Vector basics
[114:0:1] - **Vector:** an organism (mosquito, flea, sandfly, tick, mite) that carries a pathogen between hosts – insects that transmit disease are called **vectors**.
[114:0:2] - **Only female mosquitoes suck blood** (they need it for eggs) and have **bigger wings** than males; **males feed on plant juices/nectar**.
[114:0:3] - **Culex, Anopheles and Aedes** – all three genera are blood-feeders found throughout the world.
[114:0:4] # Mosquito → disease
[114:0:5] TABLE head: Mosquito | Disease (pathogen type)
  [114:0:5.0] Female Anopheles | Malaria (*Plasmodium*, protozoan)
  [114:0:5.1] Aedes aegypti | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever (all viral)
  [114:0:5.2] Aedes albopictus (Asian tiger / forest mosquito) | Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever – NOT Japanese encephalitis (most books)
  [114:0:5.3] Culex (*C. quinquefasciatus*, *C. pipiens*) | Lymphatic filariasis (nematode), Japanese encephalitis (virus)
  [114:0:5.4] Haemagogus | Forest (jungle) yellow fever
[114:0:6] - **NOT mosquito-borne:** kala-azar (sandfly), sleeping sickness (tsetse fly), Chagas (kissing bug), plague (rat flea), scrub typhus (chigger mite), KFD (ticks).
[114:0:7] - Wrong sets often asked: "Aedes – chikungunya – **bacteria**" is wrong (chikungunya is an **alphavirus**); "Tsetse – filariasis" and "bed bug – sleeping sickness" are wrong.
[114:0:8] # Disease details
[114:0:9] TABLE head: Disease | Pathogen | Key fact
  [114:0:9.0] Dengue ("breakbone fever") | Dengue virus (flavivirus), 4 serotypes | Platelets fall sharply → internal bleeding; virus suppresses platelet production in bone marrow, infects endothelial cells and binds platelets (CDS 2016: I, II, III)
  [114:0:9.1] Chikungunya | CHIKV, alphavirus | Severe joint pain
  [114:0:9.2] Zika | Zika virus (flavivirus) | Same mosquito as dengue (Aedes aegypti); also sexual and blood transmission; microcephaly risk
  [114:0:9.3] Yellow fever | Yellow fever virus | Spread by mosquito – not air, water or housefly
  [114:0:9.4] Japanese encephalitis | JEV (flavivirus), a virus | Infects the brain; pigs amplify, pigs + wild birds = reservoirs → keeping pigs away from settlements curbs JE; not water-borne
  [114:0:9.5] Lymphatic filariasis | Nematode *Wuchereria bancrofti* (thread-like roundworm) | Lymph vessels/nodes → fever early, then chronic swelling of lower limbs = elephantiasis; *Culex* is the vector, not the cause
[114:0:10] - Malaria vs dengue: common = fever, mosquito bite, human host; **different = mosquito species** (Anopheles vs Aedes) and pathogen (protozoan vs virus).
[114:0:11] - **Dengue vaccine:** **Qdenga (TAK-003, Takeda)** – live-attenuated tetravalent, age 4–60; CDSCO approval **July 2026** = India's first approved dengue vaccine.
[114:0:12] > Exam angle: vector of dengue/Zika (×8), what falls in dengue (platelets ×5), filariasis/elephantiasis organism and organ (×7), JE cause/organ/pigs (×4), "not mosquito-borne" (×5), only females suck blood (×2).
[114:0:13] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.24-26 (Sheet #15 disease table), p.28 (Sheet #16 vectors), p.31 (Sheet #18 hosts); PMF General Science Part 5 p.14-16 (Zika, dengue platelets: bone-marrow suppression, immune destruction); Rocket CA 2026 Part 02 p.111 (Qdenga, July 2026); app notes 5:114 sub 0
## SUB 1 | Malaria and Plasmodium
[114:1:0] - **Pathogen:** protozoan ***Plasmodium***; **carrier/vector = female Anopheles mosquito** (not tick, fly or louse).
[114:1:1] - Parasites multiply first in the **liver**, then destroy **red blood cells**; the **spleen** enlarges (organ affected by malaria).
[114:1:2] TABLE head: Species | Fact
  [114:1:2.0] *P. falciparum* | Malignant (cerebral) malaria – most severe
  [114:1:2.1] *P. vivax* | Relapsing malaria (dormant liver hypnozoites); old books: ~65% of India's cases (now ~40%; falciparum ~60% in 2024)
  [114:1:2.2] *P. malariae*, *P. ovale* | Milder
  [114:1:2.3] *P. knowlesi* | Zoonotic (macaques)
[114:1:3] - **Five** Plasmodium species infect humans. Vaccine is hard because malaria is caused by **several species** (with changing antigens) – UPSC 2010.
[114:1:4] - **Drugs:** **chloroquine** (prevention and treatment; *P. vivax*), quinine (from cinchona bark), **artemisinin/arteether** from the seeded plant ***Artemisia annua***; ACTs first-line for falciparum.
[114:1:5] - **Vaccines:** RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix) and R21/Matrix-M (WHO-recommended); India's **AdFalciVax** (ICMR-RMRC Bhubaneswar) at preclinical stage (2026).
[114:1:6] > Exam angle: carrier of Plasmodium (×3), malignant malaria (falciparum), 65% share (vivax), organ (spleen), drug (chloroquine, arteether), why vaccine is hard.
[114:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.25-26 (malaria: liver → RBC, spleen), p.29 (Sheet #17: falciparum malignant, vivax recurring/major share), p.33 (Sheet #20 drugs); PMF General Science Part 5 p.28 (five species, chloroquine for vivax, ACTs, vaccines); Rocket CA 2026 Part 02 p.111-112 (AdFalciVax); orfonline.org "More tests, fewer cases" (falciparum 60% of 2024 cases)
## SUB 2 | Sandfly, Tsetse Fly, Kissing Bug and Other Vectors
[114:2:0] TABLE head: Vector | Disease | Pathogen
  [114:2:0.0] Sandfly (*Phlebotomus argentipes*) | Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis) – liver, spleen, bone marrow | *Leishmania donovani* (protozoan)
  [114:2:0.1] Tsetse fly (*Glossina palpalis*) | Sleeping sickness (African trypanosomiasis) – brain in late stage | *Trypanosoma brucei* (unicellular protozoan)
  [114:2:0.2] Triatomine (kissing) bug | Chagas disease – heart, gut | *Trypanosoma cruzi*
  [114:2:0.3] Ticks (on monkeys) | Kyasanur Forest Disease = "monkey fever" – Kyasanur forest, Shivamogga, Karnataka | KFD virus
  [114:2:0.4] Rat flea | Plague (*Yersinia pestis*, bacterium) | –
  [114:2:0.5] Chigger mite | Scrub typhus (*Orientia tsutsugamushi*) | –
  [114:2:0.6] Leafhopper / whitefly | Rice tungro / okra yellow vein mosaic | Plant viruses
  [114:2:0.7] Cyclops (water flea) | Carries Guinea-worm larvae | –
  [114:2:0.8] Snail (intermediate host) | Schistosomiasis | –
[114:2:1] - Mosquito can carry yellow fever, dengue, filaria – **not kala-azar**.
[114:2:2] > Exam angle: vector of kala-azar (×2), cause of sleeping sickness (×3), Chagas vector, KFD statements.
[114:2:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.26 (kala-azar sandfly, sleeping sickness tsetse), p.28 (Sheet #16 vectors); PMF General Science Part 4 p.54 (protozoan table: Chagas – Trypanosoma cruzi, triatomine/kissing bug); app notes 5:114 sub 0, 4
## SUB 3 | Water-borne and Faeco-oral Diseases
[114:3:0] - **Faeco-oral (contaminated water/food) group:** **cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E, acute diarrhoea, dysentery, polio**; also amoebiasis, ascariasis.
[114:3:1] TABLE head: Disease | Pathogen | Fact
  [114:3:1.0] Typhoid (enteric fever) | *Salmonella Typhi* (bacterium) | Widal test; intestine
  [114:3:1.1] Cholera | *Vibrio cholerae* (bacterium) | Contaminated food/water → severe diarrhoea, dehydration; ORS
  [114:3:1.2] Dysentery | Bacillary = *Shigella* (bacterial); amoebic = *Entamoeba* (protozoan) | Blood in stool
  [114:3:1.3] Hepatitis A, E | Viruses | Inflammation of the liver → jaundice; spread by polluted water
  [114:3:1.4] Polio | Poliovirus | Enters through polluted food and water; spinal cord
  [114:3:1.5] Acute diarrhoea | Rotavirus, *E. coli*, *Shigella* | Leading child killer; acute diarrhoeal diseases caused the most water-borne deaths in India (2012-2017)
  [114:3:1.6] Food poisoning | *Salmonella* (not Anopheles, Culex, Aedes) | Contaminated food
[114:3:2] - **Unsafe water + poor sanitation** (developing countries): **malaria, acute diarrhoea, schistosomiasis**; ~**5,000 children die daily** worldwide. **Kwashiorkor** (protein deficiency) is NOT water-borne.
[114:3:3] - **Floods** spread cholera, typhoid, hepatitis, **leptospirosis**.
[114:3:4] - **Shallow hand-pump** water → cholera, typhoid, jaundice – **NOT fluorosis** (fluoride, deep groundwater).
[114:3:5] - **GI diseases:** symptoms are diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain – **kidney failure is not** a GI symptom. **Inflammatory bowel disease** = gastrointestinal tract.
[114:3:6] # Look-alikes that are NOT water-borne
[114:3:7] TABLE head: Item | Route / fact
  [114:3:7.0] Hepatitis B | Blood, sex, mother-to-child – much like HIV; has a vaccine (Hep C has none); many carriers symptomless for years; Hep B + C infections several times HIV
  [114:3:7.1] Jaundice | A symptom of liver disease (bilirubin), not a disease of one microbe – not so contagious
  [114:3:7.2] TB, pneumonia | Airborne bacterial
[114:3:8] # Chemical contaminants of water
[114:3:9] TABLE head: Contaminant | Disease
  [114:3:9.0] Arsenic | Blackfoot disease
  [114:3:9.1] Cadmium | Itai-itai
  [114:3:9.2] Mercury | Minamata
  [114:3:9.3] Nitrate | Blue-baby syndrome
  [114:3:9.4] Fluoride | Fluorosis
[114:3:10] - **MacConkey agar:** detects ***E. coli*** (lactose-fermenting coliforms – faecal contamination indicator).
[114:3:11] > Exam angle: "not water-borne" (×6), typhoid diagnosis/agent (×4), Hepatitis B "not correct" statement (UPSC 2019 ×2), hand-pump except fluorosis (×2), cholera (×3), jaundice/liver (×4).
[114:3:12] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.24-25 (polio fecal-oral, Hep B blood/sexual, cholera, typhoid), p.121 (amoebic dysentery); PMF General Science Part 5 p.13-14 (UPSC 2019 Hep B/C PYQ: Hep B has a vaccine), Part 4 p.53 (diarrhoea: shigella, entamoeba); PMF Environment Part 4 p.68 (arsenic – black foot disease; fluorosis); gktoday.in (dysentery = bacterial, SSC key); app notes 5:114 sub 2
[114:3:13] - **Leptospirosis:** spirochaete **bacterium** *Leptospira* – rat urine in floodwater.
[114:3:14] - **HBV = DNA virus** (hepadnavirus) – the only DNA virus among hepatitis viruses; A, C, D, E are RNA viruses.
## SUB 4 | Worm (Helminth) Diseases
[114:4:0] TABLE head: Disease | Worm (phylum) | Fact
  [114:4:0.0] Ascariasis | *Ascaris lumbricoides* – nematode (parasitic) | Swallowed eggs; blocks the intestine; eggs passed in faeces
  [114:4:0.1] Filariasis | *Wuchereria bancrofti* – nematode | Lymph vessels (see vectors)
  [114:4:0.2] Taeniasis | Tapeworms *Taenia solium* (pork), *T. saginata* (beef), *T. asiatica* – Platyhelminthes | Intestinal; cysts in brain = neurocysticercosis (NCC)
  [114:4:0.3] Fascioliasis | *Fasciola hepatica* = sheep liver fluke – Platyhelminthes | Liver and bile ducts; ruminants main host; raw water plants; snail host; causes obstructive jaundice in cattle
  [114:4:0.4] Schistosomiasis | Flatworm *Schistosoma* | Unsafe water; snail host
  [114:4:0.5] Guinea worm | *Dracunculus medinensis* – nematode (not annelid) | Water with infected Cyclops
[114:4:1] - **Tapeworm = hermaphrodite**; **roundworm = separate sexes**; **filaria is caused by a nematode** (UPSC 2001: 1, 2, 3 correct).
[114:4:2] > Exam angle: tapeworm/taeniasis (×3), liver fluke organ/host (×2), Ascaris (×2), phylum of Taenia/Fasciola.
[114:4:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.26 (fascioliasis, neurocysticercosis, ascariasis), p.31 (Sheet #18 parasites: Dracunculus + Cyclops, Taenia pork); app notes 5:114 sub 1
[114:4:4] - **Livestock worms:** treated by **deworming (anthelmintics)**, e.g. albendazole.
[114:4:5] - **Amphistomiasis** (rumen flukes, buffaloes/cattle): snail intermediate host → controlled by **snail control**.
## SUB 5 | Fungal Diseases, Mycotoxins and Plant Diseases
[114:5:0] TABLE head: Disease | Fungus | Fact
  [114:5:0.0] Ringworm | Dermatophytes (fungi) | The disease caused only by fungal infection; treated with griseofulvin
  [114:5:0.1] Athlete's foot | *Trichophyton, Epidermophyton, Microsporum* (fungus) | Contaminated floors, towels
  [114:5:0.2] Seborrhoeic dermatitis | *Malassezia* yeast | Fungal-linked skin disease
  [114:5:0.3] Ergotism | *Claviceps purpurea* on rye | Eating contaminated grains
  [114:5:0.4] Aflatoxin | *Aspergillus flavus, A. parasiticus* | Damages the liver
  [114:5:0.5] Mucormycosis | Mucormycetes | Nose, sinuses, eyes, brain
[114:5:1] - **Baldness** = the keyed "fungal" answer among allergy, colour blindness, AIDS (tinea capitis causes patchy hair loss); **colour blindness = genetic**, AIDS = viral, allergy = immune.
[114:5:2] - **Epidemic dropsy:** mustard oil adulterated with *Argemone mexicana* (sanguinarine).
[114:5:3] TABLE head: Plant disease | Cause
  [114:5:3.0] Spike disease of sandal | Phytoplasma = MLO (mycoplasma-like organism)
  [114:5:3.1] Rust of wheat | *Puccinia* (fungus)
  [114:5:3.2] Smut | *Ustilago*
[114:5:4] > Exam angle: fungal disease (×5), aflatoxin organ, ergotism cause, sandal spike.

## SUB 7 | Infection, Immunity and Vaccination
[114:7:0] - **Disease vs symptom:** **cholera** is a disease; fever, sneezing, headache are symptoms. Typhoid is a type of **fever** (enteric fever).
[114:7:1] - **Contagious:** **yawning** is the classic contagious reflex (not snoring, gnashing, vomiting). Infectious diseases (AIDS, chickenpox, mumps, herpes) pass from person to person; AIDS is **not spread by casual contact**.
[114:7:2] - **Measles:** infants **below six months** are protected by **maternal antibodies** (natural passive immunity); MR vaccine at 9-12 and 16-24 months.
[114:7:3] - **No vaccine** controls **diabetes**; polio, whooping cough, smallpox are vaccine-preventable. **Rickets** (vitamin D deficiency) cannot be prevented by any UIP vaccine.
[114:7:4] - **Smallpox:** WHO declared it **eradicated in 1980** (8 May); India free in **1977** – the only human disease eradicated.
[114:7:5] - **Rabies:** spread through the **saliva** of a rabid animal (bite) → nervous system, hydrophobia.
[114:7:6] - **Community transmission (COVID-19):** an infected person in the community, unaware of infection, infects others – the source cannot be traced to travel or a known contact.
[114:7:7] > Exam angle: contagious/infectious (×4), measles immunity, no vaccine (diabetes, rickets), smallpox 1980.
[114:7:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.24 (rabies saliva, measles), p.32 (Sheet #19 vaccines), p.37 (Sheet #22 terms); PMF General Science Part 5 p.5-9 (contagious diseases, HIV); app notes 5:114 sub 3; yawning contagious – general knowledge, not checked
[114:7:9] - **Pathogen:** any **disease-causing** microorganism (virus, bacterium, fungus, protozoan).
[114:7:10] - **Interferons:** proteins from virus-infected cells that protect healthy cells – **anti-viral**.
[114:7:11] - **Cirrhosis:** scarring of the liver (alcohol, chronic hepatitis) – **non-communicable**, not transmitted person to person.

## SUB 9 | Vector Control, Insecticide Resistance and Elimination
[114:9:0] - **DDT resistance** in mosquitoes = **natural selection**: resistant individuals survive and breed, so resistance spreads.
[114:9:1] TABLE head: Bio-control | Mechanism
  [114:9:1.0] *Gambusia affinis* (mosquito fish), guppy | Larvivorous fish – eat larvae
  [114:9:1.1] Bti | Bacterial bio-larvicide
  [114:9:1.2] Wolbachia | Bacterium; controls viral diseases spread by mosquitoes (dengue, chikungunya, Zika) through cytoplasmic incompatibility + pathogen blocking; no GM, no pesticide
  [114:9:1.3] Pitcher plant | Insectivorous plant – traps insects
[114:9:2] - Wolbachia: in **50-60%** of insect species; **naturally absent in Aedes aegypti and Anopheles**. Verily **'Debug'** (2 Jun 2026): Wolbachia male *Culex quinquefasciatus* released.
[114:9:3] - **NCVBDC** (ex-NVBDCP): six diseases – **malaria, JE, dengue, chikungunya, kala-azar, lymphatic filariasis** (not TB). **Elimination:** malaria, LF, kala-azar; dengue, chikungunya, JE only controlled.
[114:9:4] - **National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030):** zero indigenous cases by **2027**, malaria-free India by **2030**. **MERA India** – ICMR, 24 April 2019.
[114:9:5] - WHO malaria-free in South Asia: **Maldives (2015), Sri Lanka (2016)**. Malaria and dengue are outbreak-prone and climate-sensitive.
[114:9:6] > Exam angle: Wolbachia method (UPSC 2023), DDT – natural selection (APPSC G2 Mains 2017).

## SUB 10 | Air Pollution and Health
[114:10:0] - Main target of air pollution: **respiratory system**; also heart disease, stroke, lung cancer.
[114:10:1] - **PM2.5 raises heart disease** because these fine particles **penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the blood** (A and R true, R explains A).
[114:10:2] - Air pollution comes from **natural sources too** (volcanoes, dust, forest fires) – "only human activities" is false; **planting trees reduces** it (only Statement II true).
[114:10:3] - **WHO:** **4.2 million** premature deaths from **ambient** air pollution (**2019**). State of Global Air 2020: 116,000+ Indian infants died within a month of birth (2019).
[114:10:4] - **IQAir 2025:** India **6th** most polluted country (PM2.5 **48.9 µg/m³**); only 13 countries met the WHO annual guideline of **5 µg/m³**.
[114:10:5] - **DALY = YLL + YLD.** Noise: hearing loss, hypertension, anxiety, sleep disorders.
[114:10:6] > Exam angle: PM2.5 assertion-reason, air-pollution statements.
[114:10:7] ~~ Sources: Rocket CA 2026 Part 01 p.21-22 (World Air Quality Report: India 6th, 48.9 µg/m³, WHO guideline 5); app notes 5:114 sub 6
[114:10:8] - **Silicosis** (silica dust) and **emphysema** (COPD) are **lung** diseases.
[114:10:9] - **Occupational lung diseases:** **silicosis** (silica – pottery, ceramics, glass, mining), asbestosis, byssinosis (cotton), pneumoconiosis (coal); **emphysema** (COPD) – lungs.
[114:10:10] - **Emphysema** (COPD): alveoli of the **lungs** damaged by smoke/pollution.
[114:10:11] - **Sonic boom** effects on people: **annoyance, startle and sleep disturbance**; property damage (windows).

## SUB 12 | Antibiotics and Antimicrobial Resistance
[114:12:0] # Antibiotics
[114:12:1] - **Fleming: penicillin, 1928**; **Waksman** coined "antibiotic", found **streptomycin** (first anti-TB drug).
[114:12:2] - Most antibiotics are **natural or semi-synthetic**, mostly from bacteria (*Streptomyces*); sulfa drugs synthetic. **Prontosil** (Domagk, 1935) → sulfanilamide.
[114:12:3] - **Griseofulvin** treats ringworm; **Acetobacter** → vinegar; chloroquine = antimalarial.
[114:12:4] # How AMR builds
[114:12:5] - Causes: incorrect dose, **incomplete course** (resistant survivors left to multiply), overuse, **self-medication**, livestock use, **mutation**, horizontal gene transfer.
[114:12:6] - Severity: **MDR → XDR → TDR**.
[114:12:7] - **Biofilm:** microbes in a self-made **EPS (extracellular polymeric substance)** matrix on **implants, catheters, tissues, food surfaces**; blocks antibiotics → chronic infection; food spoilage and contamination.
[114:12:8] # Policy and new drugs
[114:12:9] TABLE head: Item | Fact
  [114:12:9.0] Nafithromycin (Miqnaf) | First indigenous macrolide; community-acquired pneumonia; Wockhardt + BIRAC (not Sun Pharma); launched 20 Nov 2024 by Dr Jitendra Singh
  [114:12:9.1] NAP-AMR | 2017, One Health based
  [114:12:9.2] Kerala KARSAP | 2018, first State AMR plan
  [114:12:9.3] Red Line campaign | 2016; red line on packs of prescription-only antibiotics (not all OTC medicines)
  [114:12:9.4] WHO Bacterial Priority Pathogens 2024 | Critical: carbapenem-resistant *Acinetobacter baumannii*, Enterobacterales, rifampicin-resistant TB
[114:12:10] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:114 sub 8
[114:12:11] - **Prontosil:** discovered **1932** (Bayer; Domagk), published 1935 – first sulpha drug, a **pro-drug** → sulfanilamide.
[114:12:12] - **Penicillin** comes from the **fungus** *Penicillium notatum*.
[114:12:13] - **WHO 2017 list (12 superbugs):** critical = *Acinetobacter baumannii*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, Enterobacteriaceae (carbapenem-resistant).
[114:12:14] - **Chloramphenicol (chloromycetin):** **broad-spectrum** antibiotic – classic **typhoid** drug.
[114:12:15] - **Sulpha drugs:** sulfanilamide, **Cibazole (sulfathiazole)**, sulfadiazine, sulphaguanidine – synthetic antibacterials.
[114:12:16] - **Antibiotics act only on bacteria** – viruses lack the cell wall and metabolic pathways they target.
[114:12:17] - **Superbug:** bacterium resistant to several antibiotics (MDR), e.g. MRSA.
[114:12:18] - **Antipyretic** = reduces **fever** (paracetamol, aspirin); analgesic = pain relief.
[114:12:19] - **Rifampicin** treats **both TB and leprosy** (leprosy MDT = rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine); PAS and isoniazid are TB-only.

=== NOTES 5:115 | Recent Trends in India's Disease Burden – Communicable and Non-communicable Diseases
## SUB 0 | Dietary Fats, Cholesterol and Heart Health
[115:0:0] # Good and bad fats
[115:0:1] - **Trans fat:** raises **LDL** and **lowers HDL** ("good cholesterol"), so it is bad for health (UPPSC 2012); excess trans fat raises cardiovascular risk.
[115:0:2] - **Bakery products** made with **hydrogenated fats** contain trans fats, and excess trans fats raise the risk of NCDs – **both statements correct** (APPSC Fisheries 2023).
[115:0:3] - **WHO REPLACE plan:** eliminate industrially produced trans fats from the global food supply **by 2023** (target date; many countries still pending). **FSSAI** caps trans fat at **2%** in fats and oils.
[115:0:4] - **Saturated fat** excess raises blood lipids and cholesterol; **HDL** removes bad cholesterol – high HDL lowers heart-disease risk.
[115:0:5] - **Triglyceride** = ester of glycerol + three fatty acids = a **fat**; the main constituent of body fat.
[115:0:6] - **Most coronary heart disease patients** have elevated **cholesterol** (LDL).
[115:0:7] # Oils and fatty acids
[115:0:8] - Cook in **oil rather than vanaspati ghee**: oils hold **unsaturated fats** (mono- and polyunsaturated) that lower cholesterol (Uttarakhand 2006).
[115:0:9] - **Sunflower oil:** suitable for **heart patients**; good-quality edible oil **because** it is rich in unsaturated fatty acids (A and R both true, R explains A); more vitamin E than other vegetable oils.
[115:0:10] - **Highest PUFA among common oils:** **safflower oil** (about 75% linoleic acid) > sunflower > soybean; **coconut oil** is mostly saturated.
[115:0:11] - **Fish** is healthier than other meat because it contains **polyunsaturated fatty acids** (omega-3) that cut LDL and heart risk.
[115:0:12] - **Eskimos (Inuit):** little heart disease despite a high meat/fat diet – food rich in **omega-3** from fish and marine mammals.
[115:0:13] - **Linseed = flaxseed:** richest source of **alpha-linolenic acid (18-carbon omega-3)**; not oats, moth or mung bean.
[115:0:14] - **Essential fatty acids** cannot be made by the body and must be in the diet; their absence causes deficiency disease – but body cells **can** make most other fatty acids.
[115:0:15] TABLE head: Fatty acid | Source
  [115:0:15.0] α-Linolenic (omega-3) | Linseed oil
  [115:0:15.1] Linoleic | Peanut oil, chicken fat, olive oil
  [115:0:15.2] Arachidonic | Liver, brain, glandular organs
  [115:0:15.3] Oleic | Olive oil, canola oil
  [115:0:15.4] Lauric | Coconut / palm-kernel oil, breast milk
  [115:0:15.5] Palmitic | Butter, palm oil, meat
  [115:0:15.6] Stearic | Meat, cocoa butter
  [115:0:15.7] Butyric | Butter
[115:0:16] - **Obesity:** excess energy intake + low physical activity → obesity and heart disease; NFHS-5 overweight/obese: **24% women, 23% men**.
[115:0:17] > 14 PYQs: the trans-fat/HDL pair, oil vs vanaspati, sunflower/safflower, omega-3 (linseed, fish, Eskimos) are the repeats.
[115:0:18] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.11, p.45, p.46; app notes 5:115 (sub 5)
## SUB 1 | Major NCDs – Heart, Diabetes, Cancer, Lungs and Brain
[115:1:0] # Heart and blood vessels
[115:1:1] - **Coronary artery disease** = result of **plaque buildup** in the arteries supplying the heart (APPSC G2 2018; not "coronary veins disease").
[115:1:2] - **Atherosclerosis** (hardening and narrowing of arteries by plaque) is a disease of the **circulatory system**.
[115:1:3] - **Blood pressure generally increases with age.**
[115:1:4] - Leading cause of death in **India = cardiovascular diseases**; world's single biggest killer (WHO) = **ischaemic heart disease**.
[115:1:5] # Diabetes
[115:1:6] - **Normal fasting blood sugar** (non-diabetic): about **70–100 mg/dL** – nearest option **60–100 mg/dL**.
[115:1:7] - **HbA1c (glycosylated haemoglobin):** average blood glucose over 2–3 months → used to manage **diabetes**.
[115:1:8] - **BGR-34:** CSIR's Ayurvedic anti-**diabetes** drug (NBRI + CIMAP, 2016).
[115:1:9] - **First State diabetes registry:** **Goa** (June 2011).
[115:1:10] TABLE head: ICMR-INDIAB (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, June 2023) | Prevalence | People
  [115:1:10.0] Diabetes | 11.4% | ~101 million
  [115:1:10.1] Prediabetes | 15.3% | ~136 million
  [115:1:10.2] Hypertension | 35.5% | ~315 million
[115:1:11] # Cancer
[115:1:12] - **Cancer** = **abnormal (uncontrolled) growth of cells**; non-contagious; can spread (metastasis).
[115:1:13] - **Oncogenes** (mutated growth genes) are associated with **cancer**; first oncogene (SRC) found 1970.
[115:1:14] - **Blood cancer = leukaemia** (abnormal WBC production in bone marrow); haemophilia is a clotting disorder.
[115:1:15] - Cases **1.41 million (2022)** → **2.46 million (2045)**; cancer is **not nationally notifiable**, **17 States** have notified it, **Telangana** latest (Jul 2026).
[115:1:16] - **Free HPV vaccination** campaign for **14-year-old girls** (cervical cancer) launched **28 Feb 2026** from Ajmer.
[115:1:17] # Lungs and brain
[115:1:18] - **COPD = Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease**; World COPD Day in November.
[115:1:19] - **Alzheimer's disease:** degenerative disorder of the **brain**, the leading cause of **dementia** (memory loss, confusion).
[115:1:20] - **PSE = Photosensitive Epileptic Seizures** – triggered by flashing lights or regular patterns.
[115:1:21] - **"Big four" NCDs:** cardiovascular diseases, cancers, chronic respiratory diseases, diabetes.
[115:1:22] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.19, p.26, p.54; NextGen Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 02 p.110; app notes 5:115 (sub 3, 6)
## SUB 2 | Dual Burden and Classification of Diseases
[115:2:0] TABLE head: Term | Meaning
  [115:2:0.0] Dual burden of disease | Rising rates of both infectious and non-communicable diseases (TB, malaria, dengue alongside diabetes, CVD)
  [115:2:0.1] Triple burden | Adds injuries (road accidents) to CDs + NCDs
  [115:2:0.2] Dual burden of malnutrition | Undernutrition + obesity
  [115:2:0.3] DALY | YLL (years of life lost) + YLD (years lived with disability) – not years gained by treatment
[115:2:1] - **Genetic disorders** (haemophilia, sickle-cell, Down syndrome) are **non-communicable**; **club foot** is a **birth defect**.
[115:2:2] - **Malaria** is communicable (Plasmodium, Anopheles) – **NOT a lifestyle disease**; typhoid and chikungunya are also communicable.
[115:2:3] - **Lifestyle risk factors:** unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, **tobacco**, alcohol.
[115:2:4] TABLE head: Disease | Vector / spread
  [115:2:4.0] Dengue, chikungunya, Zika | Aedes
  [115:2:4.1] Japanese encephalitis | Culex
  [115:2:4.2] Meningococcal meningitis | Person to person by respiratory droplets
[115:2:5] - **India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative** = **ICMR + PHFI + IHME**; part of the **Global Burden of Disease (GBD)** study.
[115:2:6] - Emerging/re-emerging: TB, dengue, Nipah, avian influenza; ICMR **MERA** (malaria elimination); **wastewater surveillance 5 → 50 cities** (2026), tracks **10 viruses**; vaccination platform **U-WIN**.
[115:2:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.26, p.28, p.34; app notes 5:115 (sub 0, 3, 4)
## SUB 3 | Road Injuries and Mental Health
[115:3:0] - **AP Road Safety Policy** was declared in **2015** (target: 15% annual cut in fatalities), not 2017; AP is **8th** in road-accident deaths; 2024 (Jan–Nov): 7,477 deaths in 16,898 accidents.
[115:3:1] - **Rural areas** had **53.8%** of India's road accidents in 2015 (MoRTH).
[115:3:2] - **MoRTH 2022:** 4,61,312 accidents, **1,68,491 deaths**; **two-wheeler users** the largest group of victims. **NCRB ADSI 2024:** road deaths **1,75,142** (~37.4% of accidental deaths).
[115:3:3] - **SDG 3:** **halve road-traffic deaths**.
[115:3:4] - **Mental disorders (GBD 2017):** **197.3 million** Indians – about **1 in 7**; most common **depressive (45.7 mn)** then anxiety disorders.
[115:3:5] - **Tele-MANAS:** 24x7 tele-mental-health support in all 36 States/UTs.
[115:3:6] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.149; NextGen Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 01 p.24; app notes 5:115 (sub 7)
## SUB 4 | Epidemiological Transition and Key Data
[115:4:0] - **Omran's stages:** 1. **Age of Pestilence and Famine** (first) → 2. Age of Receding Pandemics → 3. **Age of Degenerative and Man-Made Diseases** (last).
[115:4:1] - **"Nations within a nation"** (Lancet 2017; data 1990–2016): **4 ETL groups**; ETL = ratio of communicable DALYs to NCD + injury DALYs; **low ratio = high ETL** (more advanced).
[115:4:2] - **High ETL:** **Kerala**, Goa, Tamil Nadu, Punjab; **Karnataka** and Delhi higher-middle; NCD + injury DALYs overtook communicable DALYs for India in **2003**.
[115:4:3] TABLE head: Indicator | Fact
  [115:4:3.0] NCD share of deaths | 57% (Economic Survey 2025-26)
  [115:4:3.1] MMR since 1990 | Fallen 86%
  [115:4:3.2] Under-five mortality since 1990 | Fallen 78%
[115:4:4] - India's probability of dying from an NCD **rose** in 2001–2019 – **women over 40, men over 55** (Lancet).
[115:4:5] ~~ Sources: app notes 5:115 (sub 1, 2)
## SUB 5 | NCD Programmes and Targets
[115:5:0] TABLE head: Programme / target | Provision
  [115:5:0.0] NP-NCD (formerly NPCDCS, 2010) | NCD clinics at district hospitals and CHCs; everyone above 30 screened; funding 60:40 (90:10 NE/hilly)
  [115:5:0.1] Ayushman Arogya Mandirs | Screen hypertension, diabetes, oral/breast/cervical cancer
  [115:5:0.2] SDG 3 | Cut premature NCD deaths by one-third; mental health; halve road deaths
  [115:5:0.3] UNGA declaration on NCDs and mental health | 2030 targets; digital harms for the first time; stronger regulation of tobacco, trans fats, e-cigarettes
[115:5:1] - Rising NCDs → health system must shift from **curative care to screening and prevention**.

  [115:6:0.0] Malaria (highest) | 7,119 | —

=== NOTES 5:116 | Epidemic and Pandemic Challenges in India – Major Outbreaks, Lessons from COVID-19
## SUB 0 | COVID-19 Vaccines and Vaccine Platforms
[116:0:0] TABLE head: Vaccine | Developer | Platform
  [116:0:0.0] Covishield | Oxford-AstraZeneca; Serum Institute of India (WHO-approved) | Adenovirus viral vector – not mRNA
  [116:0:0.1] Covaxin | Bharat Biotech + ICMR-NIV | Inactivated whole virus
  [116:0:0.2] Sinovac (CoronaVac) | China | Whole inactivated virus
  [116:0:0.3] iNCOVACC | Bharat Biotech, Hyderabad (WUSL technology) | World's first intranasal COVID vaccine for the primary 2-dose schedule + heterologous booster; launched 26 Jan 2023; adenovirus vector
  [116:0:0.4] Sputnik V (Gam-COVID-Vac) | Gamaleya Institute, Russia (exported to India) | Adenovirus vector; two different vectors (Ad26, Ad5) for the two shots – heterologous boosting
  [116:0:0.5] ZyCoV-D | Zydus | World's first plasmid DNA vaccine for humans; needle-free injector
  [116:0:0.6] Gemcovac-OM | Gennova Biopharmaceuticals, Pune | India's first indigenous mRNA vaccine (EUA June 2023)
  [116:0:0.7] Corbevax | Biological E, Hyderabad | Protein subunit (RBD)
  [116:0:0.8] Moderna, Pfizer-BioNTech | Moderna (with NIAID, BARDA); Pfizer-BioNTech | mRNA
  [116:0:0.9] Novavax | — | Recombinant protein nanoparticle
[116:0:1] - **Match (TSPSC G1 2022):** Pfizer – RNA; Covaxin – inactivated; Sputnik V – adenovirus; ZyCoV-D – plasmid DNA.
[116:0:2] - **Intranasal vaccine work, 2022:** **Sapigen Biologix** (Krishna Ella group, Bhubaneswar plant) got Technology Development Board funding (Mar 2022) to develop an intranasal COVID-19 vaccine.
[116:0:3] - **ROTAVAC:** **Bharat Biotech**; live-attenuated **rotavirus (diarrhoea)** vaccine – India's first indigenous rotavirus vaccine.
[116:0:4] - **How COVID vaccines work:** introduce a **harmless piece** of SARS-CoV-2 (or instructions to make it) – not live virus or ready-made antibodies.
[116:0:5] TABLE head: Platform | Uses
  [116:0:5.0] Live attenuated | Weakened living pathogen
  [116:0:5.1] Inactivated | Killed pathogen
  [116:0:5.2] Viral vector | A modified version of a different, harmless virus carries the antigen instructions
  [116:0:5.3] mRNA / DNA | Genetic instructions for the antigen
  [116:0:5.4] Recombinant | Genetically engineered antigen protein
  [116:0:5.5] Toxoid | Inactivated bacterial toxin
[116:0:6] - **Convalescent plasma therapy:** uses **neutralising antibodies** from the blood of recovered COVID-19 patients to treat patients (passive immunity).
[116:0:7] - **Mulethi** (liquorice; glycyrrhizin) – NBRC Manesar (2021) found therapeutic potential against COVID-19 in lab studies.
[116:0:8] - Free at government centres: Covaxin, Covishield, Corbevax.
[116:0:9] > 17 PYQs: developer–platform pairs (Covishield ≠ mRNA, Covaxin = inactivated), iNCOVACC and Bharat Biotech, Sputnik V vectors.
[116:0:10] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.32, p.133, p.138; PMF Science & Technology Part 3 p.51-52; NextGen Environment APPSC 14 p.12; web: biospectrumindia.com (Sapigen-TDB, Mar 2022), indiabioscience.org (NBRC mulethi, 2021) – search results; app notes 5:116 (sub 4)
## SUB 1 | Vaccine Pioneers and Classic Vaccines
[116:1:0] TABLE head: Scientist | Associated with
  [116:1:0.0] Edward Jenner (1749–1823) | Father of immunology; smallpox vaccine 1796 – the first vaccine and first attempt at vaccination; proposed the immunisation concept
  [116:1:0.1] Jonas Salk | First successful polio vaccine (1952); Albert Sabin – oral polio vaccine
  [116:1:0.2] Louis Pasteur | Rabies vaccine, germ theory; live attenuated fowl cholera vaccine (1879-80)
  [116:1:0.3] Robert Koch | Bacteriology, TB bacterium – NOT father of immunology
  [116:1:0.4] Elie Metchnikoff | Phagocytosis, cellular immunity
[116:1:1] - **DPT** = diphtheria + pertussis + tetanus – a **combined vaccine**; MMR = measles, mumps, rubella; **BCG** – TB, just after birth.
[116:1:2] - Smallpox – **variola virus**; **rabies – a virus** (lyssavirus), spread by dog/bat bites.
[116:1:3] - **Tetanus** – bacterium *Clostridium tetani* (contaminated wounds), not *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (TB).
[116:1:4] - **Biojector:** a **painless needle-free injector** (used for ZyCoV-D).
[116:1:5] - **World Immunization Week:** **24–30 April** (last week of April).
[116:1:6] - WHO malaria vaccines: RTS,S/AS01 (Mosquirix), R21/Matrix-M; TAK-003 (Qdenga) – India's first approved dengue vaccine (CDSCO, Jul 2026).
[116:1:7] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.24, p.32, p.131, p.133-134, p.137; NextGen Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 02 p.111; app notes 5:116 (sub 4)

[116:2:0] TABLE head: Outbreak | Fact
  [116:2:0.0] Ebola | First 1976 – simultaneous outbreaks at Yambuku (Zaire/DR Congo) and Nzara (Sudan); named after the Ebola River; family Filoviridae
  [116:2:0.1] Ebola 2014–16 | West Africa: Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia; PHEIC August 2014
  [116:2:0.2] Ebola relapse, Dec 2019 | Aloya health area (Mabalako, North Kivu), DR Congo
  [116:2:0.3] SARS (2002–03) | SARS-CoV-1; first broke out in China (Guangdong); civet cats
  [116:2:0.4] MERS (2012) | MERS-CoV; dromedary camels
  [116:2:0.5] H1N1 "swine flu" | Influenza A; WHO pandemic June 2009
  [116:2:0.6] H5N1 | Avian influenza A – Robert Webster (influenza virus expert)
  [116:2:0.7] Nipah | 1998, Malaysia (Sungai Nipah)
  [116:2:0.8] Measles | DR Congo – the world's largest measles outbreak (WHO, January 2020)
[116:2:1] - **PHEICs:** H1N1 2009 → polio 2014 → Ebola 2014 and 2019 → Zika 2016 → COVID-19 (30 Jan 2020) → mpox 2022 and 2024 → **Bundibugyo Ebola (DR Congo, Uganda), May 2026** – a PHEIC, not a "pandemic emergency".

## SUB 3 | SARS-CoV-2 and COVID-19 Basics
[116:3:0] - Virus = **SARS-CoV-2**; disease = **COVID-19 ("Coronavirus Disease 2019")** – the WHO name for the disease caused by the **2019 novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV)**; it caused the COVID-19 global pause (not SARS-CoV-1 or MERS).
[116:3:1] - First identified: **Wuhan, Hubei, China, December 2019**; MoHFW screened flights for **novel coronavirus (nCoV)** illness in January 2020.
[116:3:2] - **SARS** is caused by a **coronavirus**; **MERS, SARS and COVID-19** are all coronavirus diseases.
[116:3:3] - Enters human cells via the **ACE2 receptor**; reservoir bats, **pangolin** suspected intermediate host.
[116:3:4] - **Viruses** are acellular – no cells and no metabolic enzymes of their own (unlike lichen, bacteria, algae).
[116:3:5] TABLE head: Variant | First found
  [116:3:5.0] Alpha | UK
  [116:3:5.1] Beta | South Africa
  [116:3:5.2] Delta | India
  [116:3:5.3] Omicron | Southern Africa
[116:3:6] # COVID-19 terms
[116:3:7] TABLE head: COVID term | Meaning
  [116:3:7.0] Contact tracing | Identifying and monitoring people in contact with an infected person
  [116:3:7.1] Co-morbidities | Health conditions that put a person at greater risk
  [116:3:7.2] Infection fatality rate | Deaths among all infected people in a population
  [116:3:7.3] Flattening the curve | Reducing the number of new cases day to day
[116:3:8] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.19, p.24, p.29; app notes 5:116 (sub 2)

## SUB 7 | Lessons from COVID-19
[116:7:0] - Exposed **health infrastructure and oxygen gaps**, the **migrant crisis**, dependence on imported supplies.
[116:7:1] - **IIT Bombay** converted a nitrogen generator into an oxygen generator (second wave).
[116:7:2] - Digital tools: CoWIN, U-WIN, ABDM, **eSanjeevani**; strategy test-track-treat-vaccinate with a **three-tier** facility arrangement.
[116:7:3] - TB still the top single-agent killer: **1.25 million** deaths worldwide in 2023; India's TB incidence 237 (2015) → 187 per lakh (2024).

=== NOTES 5:118 | Health Outcomes in India and Andhra Pradesh – Imr, Mmr, Tfr, Life Expectancy and Nutrition Indicators
## SUB 0 | Deficiency Diseases – Vitamins and Minerals
[118:0:0] TABLE head: Deficiency | Disease
  [118:0:0.0] Vitamin A | Night blindness (xerophthalmia)
  [118:0:0.1] Vitamin B1 (thiamine) | Beri-beri
  [118:0:0.2] Vitamin B3 (niacin) | Pellagra – not vitamin C
  [118:0:0.3] Vitamin B12 | Pernicious anaemia
  [118:0:0.4] Vitamin C | Scurvy
  [118:0:0.5] Vitamin D (+ calcium) | Rickets – weak, soft bones in the young (humans and animals)
  [118:0:0.6] Vitamin E | Sterility, muscular weakness – not night blindness
  [118:0:0.7] Vitamin K | Excessive bleeding
  [118:0:0.8] Iron | Anaemia – the main cause of anaemia (not calcium, zinc or magnesium)
  [118:0:0.9] Iodine | Goitre, cretinism; thyroid malfunction
  [118:0:0.10] Protein | Kwashiorkor; energy + protein – marasmus
[118:0:1] - **Goitre:** enlarged thyroid (thicker neck); iodine is given to goitre patients; common in **hilly areas** because the soil and food there are iodine-deficient (A and R true, R explains A).
[118:0:2] > 18 PYQs: iodine–goitre (×7) and iron–anaemia (×4) are the most repeated pairs.
[118:0:3] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Biology p.27, p.35, p.41, p.43, p.45-46; app notes 5:118 (sub 6)
## SUB 1 | Anaemia Control and Fortification
[118:1:0] - **Food fortification:** adding selected nutrients not normally present in a food (iron, folic acid, vitamin B12, iodine, vitamin A); fortified rice via PDS, ICDS, PM POSHAN.
[118:1:1] - **Iron + folic acid (IFA)** tablets prevent anaemia.
[118:1:2] - Old anaemia control programme (NNAPP): pregnant women got **100 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid daily for 100 days**; now (Anaemia Mukt Bharat) **60 mg iron + 500 mcg folic acid daily for 180 days** from the 4th month.
[118:1:3] - **Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2018), 6x6x6:** prophylactic **IFA** (not calcium) for six age groups, **deworming**, behaviour-change campaign incl. **delayed cord clamping**, testing and treatment, fortified food, **non-nutritional causes** (malaria, haemoglobinopathies, fluorosis) in endemic pockets.
[118:1:4] - AP: **180 red IFA tablets** to pregnant women; AP ranked **1st** for IFA supplementation; **Thalli Bidda Express** – free transport for high-risk and severely anaemic women.
[118:1:5] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.218-219; app notes 5:118 (sub 8)
## SUB 2 | Andhra Pradesh Nutrition Schemes
[118:2:0] TABLE head: Scheme | Target / feature
  [118:2:0.0] Anna Amrutha Hastam | Pregnant and lactating women via Anganwadis: one full meal a day + iron-folic acid tablets; aim – cut infant and maternal mortality
  [118:2:0.1] YSR Sampoorna Poshana (Sep 2020) | Pregnant women, lactating mothers, children – non-tribal mandals
  [118:2:0.2] YSR Sampoorna Poshana Plus (Sep 2020) | Same groups in the 77 tribal (Scheduled) mandals – not "all except" them
[118:2:1] - ECCE: model Anganwadi hubs supported by **ITC and Pratham**; **POSHAN Abhiyaan** was 50% funded by World Bank (IBRD)/multilateral loans at launch.
[118:2:2] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.219, p.240; app notes 5:118 (sub 9)
## SUB 3 | Mortality Indicators – IMR, MMR, U5MR
[118:3:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Definition (base) | Latest
  [118:3:0.0] IMR | Deaths under 1 year per 1,000 live births (probability of dying before age 1) | 25 (SRS 2023)
  [118:3:0.1] NMR | Deaths in the first 28 days per 1,000 live births | Fell 70% since 1990
  [118:3:0.2] U5MR | Deaths under 5 per 1,000 live births | SRS 2020: 32
  [118:3:0.3] MMR | Maternal deaths per 1,00,000 live births | 97 (2018-20) → 93 → 88 (SRS 2020-22)
[118:3:1] # IMR trend
[118:3:2] TABLE head: India IMR (National Health Profile 2018) | Value
  [118:3:2.0] 2013 | 40
  [118:3:2.1] 2014 | 39
  [118:3:2.2] 2015 | 37
  [118:3:2.3] 2016 | 34
[118:3:3] - NFHS-5 survey values: IMR 35.2, U5MR 41.9. **AP IMR (NFHS-4, 2015-16) = 35**.
[118:3:4] TABLE head: SRS 2020 | AP | India
  [118:3:4.0] IMR | 24 | 28
  [118:3:4.1] U5MR | 27 | 32
  [118:3:4.2] Crude birth rate | 15.7 | 19.5
  [118:3:4.3] Crude death rate | 6.3 | 6.0
[118:3:5] - **AP MMR 45** (SRS 2018-20) vs India 97. **Lowest IMR: Kerala**. Telangana (2026): IMR 18, MMR 43.
[118:3:6] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy P1 APPSC 01 p.62; NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 14 p.12; AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.11, p.210; app notes 5:118 (sub 0, 1)
## SUB 4 | Nutrition Indicators and Malnutrition
[118:4:0] TABLE head: Indicator | Measure
  [118:4:0.0] Stunting | Low height-for-age
  [118:4:0.1] Wasting | Low weight-for-height
  [118:4:0.2] Underweight | Low weight-for-age
[118:4:1] - **BMI** = weight in kg ÷ (height in m)².
[118:4:2] TABLE head: India | NFHS-5 | NFHS-6
  [118:4:2.0] Stunting | 35.5% | 29.3%
  [118:4:2.1] Underweight | 32.1% | 31.8%
  [118:4:2.2] Anaemia (children 6–59 months / women) | 67.1% / 57.0% | —
[118:4:3] - **AP:** stunting 31.2% (NFHS-5) → 25% (NFHS-6); NFHS-6: Madhya Pradesh high wasting; Meghalaya stunting decline.
[118:4:4] - Underweight highest among **STs (44.1%)**, then SCs. **SOFI 2025:** India's wasting **18.7%** – world's highest.
[118:4:5] - **Main cause of malnutrition in India: poor dietary habits and food insecurity**; poverty → energy-dense, nutrient-poor food; women with 10+ years of schooling 41%.
[118:4:6] - WHO "malnutrition in all its forms": undernutrition + micronutrient deficiency + overweight/obesity; triple burden (SOFI 2025) adds micronutrient deficiency/anaemia.
[118:4:7] - **Colostrum** (first milk) is rich in antibodies (IgA) – **anti-infective**.
[118:4:8] - **Calcium:** cheese and sardines with bones are very rich per 100 g; milk is the usual daily-value staple (APPSC printed key: raw cow milk).
[118:4:9] ~~ Sources: NextGen Indian Economy APPSC 14 p.12; app notes 5:118 (sub 5, 6, 7)
## SUB 5 | National Family Health Survey
[118:5:0] TABLE head: Round | Year
  [118:5:0.0] NFHS-1 | 1992-93
  [118:5:0.1] NFHS-2 | 1998-99
  [118:5:0.2] NFHS-4 | 2015-16
  [118:5:0.3] NFHS-5 | 2019-21
  [118:5:0.4] NFHS-6 | 2023-24 (results 2026)
[118:5:1] - Under **MoHFW**, nodal agency **IIPS Mumbai**; NFHS-6 also tracks NCDs, health insurance and elderly health.
[118:5:2] - NFHS-5 **included** death registration, pre-school education, **high blood pressure, diabetes**; it did **NOT include the HIV test**.
[118:5:3] - NFHS gives no single malnutrition % – stunting, wasting, underweight separately. NFHS-5 sex ratio **1020** (rural 1,037, urban 985); child sex ratio 920.
[118:5:4] ~~ Sources: NextGen Rocket Current Affairs 2026 Part 01 p.24; app notes 5:118 (sub 4)
## SUB 6 | Life Expectancy and Fertility
[118:6:0] - Life expectancy: about **32 years** at Independence; **70.3 years (2023)** (Economic Survey 2025-26).
[118:6:1] TABLE head: SRS life tables 2016-20 | Males | Females
  [118:6:1.0] India | 68.6 | 71.4
  [118:6:1.1] Andhra Pradesh | 69.1 | 72.2
[118:6:2] - **TFR** = average children a woman would bear in her reproductive years; **replacement 2.1**; India (NFHS-5) **2.2 → 2.0**.
[118:6:3] - Above 2.1 (NFHS-5): **Bihar (3.0, highest)**, Meghalaya, UP, Jharkhand, Manipur. **AP TFR 1.5** (since 2020-21).
[118:6:4] ~~ Sources: AP Socio-Economic Survey 2024-25 p.210, p.220; app notes 5:118 (sub 2, 3)
